PREFACE 

From an experience gained from more than twenty years of teaching, the author has prepared a book which will give the student a connected narrative of the struggles, reverses, and triumphs which humanity has undergone. He has kept the language, the reasoning, and the organization of the book on a plane thoroughly comprehensible to the young student of history. He has utilized political history as a main connecting link and the background upon which to build the story. 

The dependence of our modern civilization upon the classical and Christian backgrounds requires that these periods be presented as clearly as possible and that such topics as the democracy of Athens, Roman administration, and the Medieval church be described more fully than some of the dynastic or other struggles of the later centuries. The emphasis upon the 

Oriental is deliberate in the belief that world history is not merely European history. Even though to-day the Orient has borrowed much from Europe and America, still that part of the world has important contributions to make and the young student of to-day should have some knowledge of the ideas that have prevailed in the Orient and still prevail. Likewise much space has been devoted to the treatment of religion in an attempt to show as simply as possible how powerful a factor religion has been, and still is, in the life of the race. The author has endeavored to make this presentation entirely without prejudice and in such simple terms as the subject will permit. 

The modern world, in its narrower sense, can be said to have its beginnings in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. It was during these two centuries that European society became aware

vi 

PREFACE 

of the forces which were destined to end the medieval point of view. The growing power of the national states contributed to the rending of the seamless garment of the church, while the growth of capital destroyed the ecclesiastical theories of economics. The capture of Constantinople by the Turks removed 

Europe's eastern bulwark against Muslim Asia and their further occupations of territory laid the foundations for future wars of recovery and national aspiration. The discoveries of the new continents and of new sea routes disrupted the older commercial highways, replaced the older centres of trade with new ones on the Atlantic seaboard. The rising interest in the 

Greek and Latin classics reaffirmed the importance of the individual and indicated the direction of education for centuries to come. The epoch-making observations of Copernicus and 

Vesalius on the one hand deprived man of his central position in the universe and on the other revealed man to himself in a new light, while Bacon and Descartes developed a method to set science on its proper road. 

World History since that day has been dominated by the development of the European national states and their imposition of European civilization on the rest of the world. Concurrent with these changes has been the growing mastery of man over nature which has made such rapid strides during the last century and has integrated the world in such a way as earlier men had never dreamed. New discoveries and new points of view have shaken social organization to its very depths and brought new concepts to society and new values to older ones. Slowly but surely the "March of Civilization" has been directing itself toward a single channel, and a twentieth century with its airplanes, radios, and cinemas, its international organization of business and industry, its League of Nations can have no history but a World History. In a world made small by steam and electricity, humanity, in order to function at its maximum of happiness and prosperity, must unite in a common effort to

PREFACE 

vii vey solve the difficulties which these forces have engendered and must adjust itself to a peaceful solution of its problems. In the solution of these problems this book attempts to present a surof those factors which have made us what we are to-day. 

The illustrations have been selected not only with the purpose of interesting the student, but also of supplementing the text. The maps, made by experts under the author's direction, have been kept simple and as challenging as possible. In the 

 the more obvious things have been omitted for the sake of space. The bibliographies are more suggestive than complete though care has been taken to utilize only those books which are more easily accessible. 

The author wishes to express appreciation to his teachers and colleagues in the teaching of history both in college and high school and to his students, who have been the unconscious originators of many of these ideas. 

J. E. W.

CHAPTER I AN INTRODUCTION TO WORLD HISTORY 1. The Meaning of World History. World history is the story of the rise and growth of civilization. It began when man made his first appearance in the great drama of life and is still going on with its end far in the future. Its progress may be likened to a stream which, starting far back in the hills, winds along, now fast, now slowly, here turned aside by some obstruction, there joined by a new rivulet, but always growing larger until at last it becomes a mighty river. Like this stream, we shall find civilization, too, flowing peacefully and quietly until it reaches some obstacle, something corresponding to a hard stratum of rock; then it breaks into rapids and hurls itself along violently until once more it reaches the level country. 

As we read this dramatic story of the past, we shall see that, like the stream, civilization, although constantly gaining new material, still retains much of the old. Moreover, just as the growing stream continually brushes aside obstacles to its progress with increasing ease, so does civilization surmount difficulties to-day with greater ease than in former times, thanks to its accumulated wisdom. 2. 

How Can Civilization Be Defined? In America we are too ready to measure civilization in terms of material progress and frequently overlook its real nature. We forget that mighty as is our present advance in science and the applied arts, the past may show accomplishments that rival it closely.

In the jungles of Căm-bō'di-à, of Ceylon, and of Central and South America are found the remains of forgotten civilizations, with buildings so massive and carvings so superb that we stand before them in marvel. In the valley of the Nile tower pyramids which suggest engineering difficulties perhaps unequalled in modern experience. In the lower reaches of the 

Tigris and Euphrates are the ruins of an irrigation system quite unsurpassed by any to-day. In the museums at Cairo and 

Naples repose surgical instruments thousands of years old, that must have rivalled in their original delicacy those of the present. In the old astronomical observatory at Peking stand bronze instruments which date back many centuries and still almost duplicate ones now in use in the great observatories of the world.

Surely if material accomplishments are a true index of the progress of civilization, we shall be compelled to admit that society has not advanced as far as we would like to believe. 

But the real civilization of a people is determined not so much by their material development as by their ideals and motives, revealed through their daily life and relations with one another and with the rest of mankind.

If we view with sympathetic eyes the various customs and modes of life set forth in the following pages, we shall find that civilization has been a cumulative process, although a slow and difficult one. We shall see that once upon a time all mankind was divided into small, hostile family groups, somewhat like the wild tribes still found in parts of central Africa and South America. We shall observe the expansion of friendly relations among peoples until at last there are signs leading us to hope that "Peace on earth, good-will towards men" is destined to become the guiding principle of society. 

3. Why We Study World History. The purpose of our study of world history is to discover what the struggles of the past have contributed to our present civilization, and to see

INTRODUCTION TO WORLD HISTORY 

5 what lessons we may draw from these struggles to help us solve the problems which now vex society. If we will but pause to think how much of our life depends upon the past, we shall be surprised by the greatness of the influence of peoples and persons long since dead. We shall see that our only safe method of determining the good from the bad is by observing how things have worked in the past. And so it seems that world history is the record of man's great experimental laboratory, where many mighty social problems have been solved and where the experimenting is still going on while we are furnishing the elements and assisting in the reactions. This is our great responsibility. What civilization shall be in the future depends upon how well we do our part. 

4. The Sources of World History. For the study of the past we must depend upon two kinds of records-man's writings and the things he made. Both kinds are fragmentary. 

Since he began to make things long before he learned to write,

the earliest part of this story will depend largely upon articles that he lost or mislaid in the dirt of the floor of his cave home, or in the refuse heaps outside his dwelling. Sometimes, too, he buried things with his dead, and the tombs have furnished much valuable information concerning his mode of life even long after he learned to write. 

Man's written records give us more insight into his mode of thinking and ideas, but even these are frequently misleading. 

Often the earliest events in the life of a people were handed down by word of mouth for centuries before men learned to write, so naturally many mistakes crept into the record in this way. As a general rule, we find that the nearer in time the written record is to the fact itself, the more correct it is.

THE PERIOD OF BEGINNINGS Chapters II and III 

To the long period before man learned to write belong the beginnings of language, the organization of society and government, the beginnings of religion and of magic, the discovery of innumerable technical processes, the development of many of the ideas common to primitive people. All these have passed on to form the groundwork of the later civilizations. 

In this period man passed from the position of subjection to the forces of nature to the position of control of the forces of nature. The methods and impulses which led him to make these steps we can only dimly comprehend as the spade of the excavator and the researches of the scientists uncover for us more and more of the conditions under which he lived. told though it is, it is still a marvellous story. In more recent times, our ideas of the beginning of things have been much changed by the increase that has taken place in scientific knowledge. The chief point in the change has been to remove man as the centre of the universe and make him a part in it. Later, we shall have much to say as to how this came about, but for the present, we shall content ourselves by pointing out a few of the discoveries upon which the modern explanation depends. 

1. How Our World Was Made. When men began to study the actual surface of the earth, they found it made up largely of two kinds of rocks-sedimentary and igneous. The sedimentary rocks, which composed the greater part, were made by the settling of mud and sand at the bottom of bodies of water. This was a slow process, and is still going on in certain localities. 

By calculating how long it would take these sedimentary rocks to form under ordinary conditions, geologists have been able to estimate the earth's age. While this rock formation was going on, the earth was cooling and contracting, and the molten inner mass pushed up certain areas to form mountains and burst through the cracks to form igneous rocks. Even now, land is rising in some places and sinking in others. As a result of all this, the land and water surfaces have continually changed. 

2. How Plants and Animals Developed. When the mud and silt were washed down from the hills and mountains later to become rock beds, animals and plants were often carried along, and so became embedded in the strata. There

Apparently the land then was covered with swamps, filled with enormous trees. Because at this time the mass of hard material which we know as coal was formed, this period is often called the "carboniferous age. 

Later the land became dryer and some of the am-phib'i-ans, as these half-water, half-land animals are termed, learned to spend all their time on it. Then they became reptiles and many reached an enormous size. Largest of all were the di'no-saurs,

the eggs of which were recently discovered by an American exploring expedition in rock strata formed at that time in western Mon-gō'li-a. Toward the end of this period some of the reptiles developed wings and were able to glide from tree to tree. 

Later, when they had grown feathers, they became birds. 

3. What the Coming of the Mammals Meant. At the close of the age of reptiles great changes took place on the earth. It was a time of tremendous contracting and many chains of lofty mountains were pushed up—the Andes, the Alps, and the Hi-mä'la-yas. The climate too became much colder. For the first time the surface of the earth began to look much as it does to-day. It was covered with grass and with forests of the same kind of trees that we now have. 

Most striking of all the changes were the new kinds of animals which appeared. Instead of being covered with scales, they had hair or feathers to protect them from the greater cold. Some of these strange beasts developed their young within themselves and then cared for them for some time after birth by feeding them with their own milk. Because of this they are called mammals. With the mammals came the family instinct. 

4. The Coming of the Glaciers and Man. In the latter part of this age of mammals the cold increased so much that the great ice sheet came creeping down from the north. Four times the ice advanced, driving life of all kinds before it, and four times it retreated, leaving behind in the heaps of débris the story of its passage. The increased cold caused the evaporation of so much of the water of the sea that there was no Bering 

Strait and no Strait of Gibraltar. The Baltic, Adriatic, and

Red Seas were mere rivers, and Sicily was joined to Italy and 

Africa, forming a huge land bridge.

At some time during this last geologic period man appeared. 

Although he was a mammal, he differed from the others in having a larger brain capacity. Because he was weaker and slower

5. How We Know About Early Man. Our first knowl edge of man is derived from bits of stone used by him as tools, the so-called 'o-liths. We know that he must have employed for that purpose more perishable things long before he used stone, but all trace of those first tools has long since disappeared.

It is a long story from these crude fist-hatchets to our electrically-driven machinery of to-day. In fact, by the nature of tools employed scientists now classify man's cultural development. First, we have the pale-o-lith-ic or "old stone age" when tools were made of chipped stone; and then successively the ne'o-lith-ic or "new stone age" with its tools of polished stone, the "bronze age" which dates from the time when man

learned how to harden copper by mixing it with tin, the "iron age," and, finally, the "steel age" as that of to-day is known. 

6. What the Earliest Human Remains Indicate. There have been found in Java, in England, in Germany, and in Left. Batons de commandement, of carved reindeer horn, were used by the Cro-Magnon chieftains probably as symbols of authority. 

Right. The restoration of a Cro-Magnon head, after the model by J. H. McGregor from the skull found in Dordogne, France.

South Africa fragments of bone which are quite different from those of animals and still not quite like those of modern man. 

They show that the earth was once inhabited by a very primitive type of man. Far more important, however, is the skeleton which was discovered a few years ago in a cave near the German village of Neanderthal (ná-än-der-täl'), for it indicates a person much more like modern man than any of those earlier men could have been.

Since the discovery of this Neanderthal skeleton, similar

HOW THE WORLD CAME TO BE 

15 ones have been found elsewhere, sometimes accompanied with stone tools. From this skeleton we infer that by that time men had begun to live in caves, had learned how to make tools of various kinds, had commenced to kill animals for food and clothing, and to use fire. Farther than that we do not know. 

Nor do we know what became of these Neanderthal men, who apparently disappeared as suddenly as they had originally come on the scene. One explanation is that they were driven out by other men who were better able to cope with life and who had superior tools, much as the Indian was pushed out of the eastern United States by the Europeans. In any event, all of this must have happened about the time that the last ice sheet was retreating toward the north. 

7. Who Were the First Real Men? The first skeletons of men resembling at all closely those of to-day were found in the grotto of Cro-Magnon (kró-ma-nyôn) in southern France. Indeed, all through southern France and northern 

Spain are caves in which remains of this race of people have been discovered. Near some of them we still find people with forms and faces quite like those of these later paleolithic men. 

The Cro-Magnards were tall and long-headed and had large brains. They have left behind, in addition to their tools and weapons, which included bows and arrows, some wonderfully lifelike paintings and clay models of the animals that they hunted. They also painted on pebbles characters which look very much as if they might be the beginning of writing. They must have had some sort of society or government in order to live together in these caves, but whether they made love with clubs as humorous magazines of to-day would have us believe, we do not know. Surely, however, man was stronger than woman and became her protector. Although the Cro-Magnards lived largely by hunting and fishing, just as did their predecessors, there is real evidence that they ate also such wild fruits and vegetables as they could find.

8. The End of Paleolithic Man. As time went on and the earth grew warmer, the forests crept farther and farther north, and the reindeer and other animals on which paleolithic man depended for food moved northward, too. With the forests came a new kind of man. Except in the rougher parts of the country, the men of the old stone age were driven from their haunts and compelled to take refuge along the seashore. 

Here for a time they maintained themselves, eking out a livelihood from shellfish, as is evidenced by the great heaps of shells called "kitchen-middens" scattered along the coast of western Europe. In time, however, they too disappeared, and were followed by an entirely different type of man. 

9. When All These Things Happened. All these things required thousands of years to happen. Because the geologist deals with such enormously long periods, he counts time by ages rather than by years. At the best he can only estimate roughly how long ago any particular event occurred. 

He is sure, however, that the age of reptiles began not less than ten or fifteen millions of years ago, and that the age of mammals at least a third or half as far back as that. He insists that the first ice sheet began its southerly advance between two hundred fifty and five hundred thousand years ago, and according to some writers, the earliest human beings appeared at about that time. In the Mediterranean area the end of the paleolithic period could not have been later than 5000 B. C. 

10. How the "Races of Mankind" Differ. Already in this early period several distinct types of men may be distinguished. Foremost among them are the black or negroid peoples, the yellow or mon'go-loid, and the white or cau'căsian. These differ not merely in color but in the size and shape of the head and in the character of the hair. 

In a general way we can say that the black race belongs to 

Africa, the yellow to Asia, and the white to Europe. However, they are much mixed up at the present time. Because of

CHAPTER III WAYS OF LIVING AND DOING THAT HELPED MAN TO BECOME CIVILIZED 

A famous scholar once said that the greatest stretch of the human imagination took place when early man invented the bow and arrow. Let us consider the meaning of such an invention along with polished stone axes for building. What did it mean for people to learn to weave cloth and to make pottery, to cultivate plants and to domesticate animals; and to learn to use a language? How did these ways of doing multiply man's powers and give him control over nature? Somewhere ages ago these things began and they have done more to advance man along the way of civilization than all modern inventions. 

1. What Some Pre-Historic Lake Dwellings Revealed. 

In 1854, after an unusually dry year in Europe, some of the Swiss lakes dried up so much that along their shores the ends of poles began to appear out of the water. Upon investigation it was found that these poles were the remains of piles on which houses had once been built as in parts of the East Indies to-day. In the mud around these piles were discovered many articles which had fallen out of the houses. 

A study of these things showed that the Lake Dwellers belonged to a people having a culture far in advance of that of the old stone age. They polished their stone axes and consequently belonged to the neolithic age. It was the better cutting edge obtained by this polishing of their tools that made possible the building of houses and boats. But the men of the new stone age had also learned to do many other things. They 19

wove cloth, made pottery, and, most important of all, cultivated plants and domesticated animals. At last, civilization had really begun, for man had commenced to make himself partially independent of nature, or rather to control it for his own use. 

2. Where Plants Were First Cultivated. Although since the discovery of the remains of the Lake Dwellers, evidence of neolithic man has been found in almost every part of the world, it seems probable that the cultivation of plants was begun in Egypt or in western Asia, for there the earliest cultivated plants have been found in their wild state. The valleys of the Nile and the Tigris and Euphrates were especially adapted to agriculture, for the overflow of these rivers kept the soil fertile and both regions were somewhat protected from the attacks of outsiders.

How man happened to learn to cultivate plants we do not know. Perhaps some of the wild wheat or barley that he had gathered fell to the ground by accident and got trampled in the mud, or perhaps some that had been placed in graves as food for the spirits of the dead sprouted and grew. Many persons believe the latter theory because so many of the early ceremonies connected with sowing seed are also associated with laying away the dead. 

3. Why Wild Animals Were Domesticated. The do mestication of animals must have begun in localities far removed from those where the cultivation of plants started, for it needed an entirely different environment-pasture lands. 

We know that as far back as paleolithic times herds of wild horses and cattle roamed the great grassy plains that stretched across Central Europe and Central Asia. We can easily picture these herds followed by hungry huntsmen in search of food. Then, when these hunters had become more civilized, they began to capture and control the beasts. It was then easy to take the next step, to depend on animals for food. When neolithic man had turned cultivator, he, too, domesticated animals,

21 but for an entirely different purpose. He needed them to aid him in tilling the soil and for hauling his loads. 4.

But when he settled down and began to raise crops, he had a place for things, and with this came a desire to accumulate possessions. So the cultivator not only became a man of the home, but a peace-loving individual as well. When he fought, it was usually to defend himself and his property. 

The problems connected with taking care of animals were of a very different nature. Animals must have pasture and the

herdsmen must travel with them. There must be at least two pastures, one for summer, and one for winter, and often more for other seasons. This made the herdsmen a nõm'ad. The herd must be protected from animals and from man, too, for since animals could be driven away they were easy to steal. To prevent this, prompt and decisive action was necessary. One man must command, and his followers must be obedient and brave fighters. Herdsmen were a warlike crowd that looked upon stealing animals as a vicious habit in other people and a glorious pastime for themselves. They respected only other herdsmen who were also fighters, and looked with contempt upon the peaceful agriculturists whose crops they pillaged at will. 

5. The Beginning of Society. Man is a social animal. 

He almost never lives alone, but forms groups. These groups have different reasons for existing, the two most important being place and blood relationship. The place group is the community; the blood relationship group, the family. 

The family group is often expanded into the clan or gens (jěnz) by union with other families, and these in turn into the tribe. In clans, descent is traced through the mother as with the Iroquois Indians; in gens, through the father, as among the Romans. It goes without saying that the family is one of the permanent factors of history, and marriage one of the most important social institutions. Among primitive peoples it is usually not the custom to marry outside one's group, but a man frequently has more than one wife, and in some instances a woman more than one husband. 

6. What Was Woman's Position in Primitive Society? 

In many ways early woman was the equal of man; in fact, in the home she was paramount. To her fell the easier and more monotonous tasks, such as the care of the children and the preparation of food and clothing. This kept her in one place and to narrow her interests, while man was free to roam about

23 and to broaden his intellect. With more experiences to draw upon and with more leisure to devote to thinking, man was woman's superior. This relation was increased by marriage customs. The custom of buying a wife, for example, made a

7. How Slavery Came Into Being. The introduction of work which came with the domestication of plants and animals made one very important change in the treatment of persons who were captured in war. It was no longer necessary to kill them because they were extra people to feed. They could now be used to do some of the harder tasks and thus increase the production of food stuffs. They could also be compelled to perform work which was beneath the dignity of free men. 

Since slaves had no rights, they came to be considered as so

8. The Control of Society. 

In any group there must be leadership. Under normal conditions the leadership is held by those best fitted to fill it. With early man, physical strength, skill in hunting, fishing and fighting were the qualities that determined leadership. The power exercised by the leaders was largely measured by their ability in these various lines.

It was not long before some of the more clever individuals discovered that other men believed them capable of controlling this spirit world. Among the Indians such persons are called

"medicine-men." In order to mystify their followers they developed a system of curious, uncanny practices supposed to be able to hold these unseen forces and spirits in subjection. This system is called magic. The practice of magic is at the basis of every primitive religion. 

10. Language-the Basis of All Human Development. 

While we are dealing with the beginnings of civilization, we must stop to consider one of the more important factors which we have so far only implied. At the basis of all human development is language. Upon language the greater part of human progress has depended.

We do not know how language began, although there are many theories. Neither do we know whether it developed first in one place or in several places at the same time. We do know that most of the hundreds of different languages that exist today belong to a few great families. Foremost among these language families are the Indo-European or Är'yan, the Sĕ-mìtic, the Hă-mit'ic, the Tu-ra'ni-an, and the Chinese. Each of these seems to have been in existence by the end of the paleolithic period. 

11. The Great Stone Culture Is Marked by Enduring 

Monuments. Late in the neolithic age in many parts of western Europe men began to erect great stone monuments, called men'hirs (men'hérz). A group of menhirs arranged in the form of a circle as at Stonehenge (stōn'hěnj) in England is known as a cromlech (krom'lěk); or if in rows as at Cär'näc in Brittany, as an alinement. In the case of cromlechs and alinements, the menhirs are often connected at the top by huge stones weighing many tons each. 

While many menhirs are only a few feet high, five of the twenty-six at Stonehenge reach a height of over twenty feet, and France formerly boasted one nearly four times as tall. We do not know who erected these menhirs, but whoever they were, they must have been well organized to handle any such tremen-

THE PERIOD OF ANCIENT ORIENTAL CIVILIZATION Chapters IV-X The Foreword 

So long as our knowledge of the past was derived from the Bible and the Greek and Roman writers the memory of the great empires of the ancient Orient was very limited. Within a little more than a hundred years scholars and investigators have reconstructed their history for us. They have revealed the glory of Thebes with its hundred gates; of Babylon with its hanging gardens; of proud Nineveh with its mighty palaces; and what is even more amazing, they have laid bare the stories of peoples and cultures hitherto almost unknown. Not content, they are continually digging out more cities and translating more documents to throw light upon these buried civilizations whose peoples are no longer mere names. 

The four thousand years of human effort that is now revealed is not merely the story of the rise and fall of conquerors and dumb, driven masses of slaves. It is the story of the development of industry and commerce, the establishment of government, the rise of social conventions, and the evolution of religious ideas and forms of worship. If we understand this, we must realize that the contribution of the ancients was the creation of those institutions which ever since man has only refined and improved.

Let us see how religious, social, industrial and political institutions were created in Ancient Egypt and in the vast empires of Asia that were passed on to the Greeks and Romans and finally to us-refined and improved, of course, during the centuries.

CHAPTER IV THE GLORY AND SPLENDOR OF ANCIENT EGYPT 

Here is a region that has been a source of interest during all these forty centuries and more of recorded history. The glory and splendor of ancient Egypt are marked by remains and records that tell a story of achievement at which people have never ceased to marvel. So much learning of real value came out of 

Egypt, and it was the source of wisdom for so many centuries, that men have often called Egypt the "Cradle of Civilization." 

1. How Civilization Developed in Egypt. Egypt is di vided into two parts-the long, narrow valley of upper Egypt and the triangle-shaped delta of lower Egypt. Long ago a 

Greek writer named Hecatæus (hek-ǎ-te'us) truly said that this country was "the gift of the Nile," as the cultivated area was formed by the silt which had been deposited by the river during its annual overflow. This overflow is caused by the heavy tropical rains of central Africa, and begins in June and lasts until November. Since almost no rain falls in Egypt, her agriculture depends entirely upon these annual floods. 

Far back in the paleolithic age, men lived on the hills forming the sides of this great fault in the earth's surface through which the Nile flows. Apparently in that age these hills were covered with vegetation and were a good place in which to live, but when the glaciers began to retreat for the last time, this upland became the desert that it is to-day. Then the Egyptians moved down into the valley and the Nile began its great influence in the development of their country. 

During the neolithic age the Egyptians began to form little communities along the banks of the Nile and the streams of the 30

delta. They watched its overflow and discovered that the amount of land they could successfully cultivate was dependent

2. What the Coming of Copper Meant to Man. About the time of the invention of the calendar, copper was brought into Egypt. 

Apparently the original source of this metal was the Island of Cyprus, for its name in the Egyptian language was the same word. It is hard to overestimate the importance of this step in man's contest with nature. With the more effective tools which copper made possible, many new things could be accomplished. 

However, this did not happen all at once, for at first copper was scarce and costly, and many years had to pass before it came into common use. Moreover, copper is a soft metal, and it was not completely effective until man learned how to convert it into the harder bronze by mixing it with tin. from the top down, men, kheper, Rethe being of Re remains. 3. The Egyptians Invent Writing and Devise an Alpha bet. During this same period the Egyptians made another discovery which was destined to be of greater importance than any of those that had come before-the use of pictures to represent words and ideas. Such pictures are called pic'tó-graphs. At first these pictographs were representations of objects and actions only, but gradually they acquired more abstract meanings and eventually became symbolic.

At some later date—just when we do not know—the Egyptians discovered that language is made up of a limited number of sounds and hit upon the device of having a single sign repre-

sent a sound. This was an alphabet. What an important step this later discovery proved may be appreciated when we realize that the writing of many peoples never passed beyond the pictograph stage, and that even such an enlightened people as the Chinese still employ a different character for each simple idea. 

The Egyptians had only the consonants in their alphabet as did the Semites when they adopted it. This explains in part why the spelling of eastern words so often differs in western 

In the beginning the priests were the sole users of this symbolic writing and the walls of the temples were covered with it. 

As a result the Greeks later gave it the name hi-er-o-glyph'ic, meaning "sacred writing." The Egyptians developed for every day use a paper made from the pa-pyrus plant, which grows abundantly along the Nile. They also developed a simplification of the hieroglyphic characters-the so-called hi-er-at'ic writing. It was in this way that they wrote many of the manuscripts which have been found in the tombs and to which we owe much of our knowledge of ancient Egyptian history. 

Many of the hieroglyphics were pictorial; as woman; 

N ing the child (sucking a finger). By man; plac- characters for man and woman together the idea mankind was expressed, or by repeating either three times, the plural idea. Water was represented by a wavy line www; grain, by three small circles 000; wood, by a twig; rain, by water flowing out of the sky ; night or darkness, by a star suspended from the sky weeping, by water falling from an eye

Shortly after the beginning of the Christian era, the last person who could read the Egyptian characters died, and the language was forgotten. In 1798, when Napoleon invaded Egypt, one of his officers found at Rosetta in the delta a stone with inscriptions in three kinds of writing-Greek, hieroglyphic, and hieratic. Later a young French scholar named Champollion

Shän-pól-yôn') studied this "Rosetta stone" until he was able to make out the Egyptian letters and thus to decipher the language itself. To-day scholars can read Egyptian as well as any foreign language. 

4. The Organization of Ancient Egypt. With calendar, metal, and writing, Egypt advanced rapidly. During the next five centuries the separate communities of upper Egypt were slowly united into a single kingdom, and those of the delta into another. How this came about is difficult to say, but it must have been influenced by the problems attending the control of irrigation. In any event, by the end of this period another advance was made and the two kingdoms were united. Just as our capital city Washington was built on the boundary between the North and the South, so did the pharaohs (fā'rōz), or rulers of this united kingdom, establish theirs at Memphis near the boundary of the two older kingdoms. 

From this time date the earliest written records of which we have any knowledge. Among these records is a measure of the height of the overflow of the river. From pictures of that time we know that agriculture and stock raising were the principal industries, and weaving, dyeing, baking, tanning, and the making of tools, jewelry and furniture were important occupations. 

Apparently the pharaohs owned all the land and were looked upon as gods. They had officials scattered throughout the country to collect rent from the farmers and to compel them to help keep up the irrigation canals and to render whatever other service was demanded.

In the third century B. C., a Macedonian king of Egypt encouraged Man'é-tho, an Egyptian priest, to write a history of the country. Manetho divided into thirty dynasties all the kings of united Egypt from the first, whom he called Me'nes, to the coming of Alexander the Great. Since that time Egyptian chronology has been treated in this way. More recently certain of these dynasties have been placed in three groups cor-

responding with Egypt's periods of national greatness. They are as follows:

Dynasties III-VI The Old Kingdom 

2980-2475 B. C.

Dynasties XI-XII The Middle Kingdom 

Dynasties XVIII-XX The Empire

5. The "Pyramid Age." By the beginning of the Old

Kingdom, the Egyptians had discovered the process of hardening copper so that it would cut stone. Now it so happened that the pharaohs believed their bodies should be preserved for a future existence and consequently made careful arrangements for their own burial. For a long time the tombs had been merely graves dug in the earth and covered with piles of rocks, but now they began to be lined with hewn blocks of stone. 

Next the tombs became square buildings with flat tops and slop-

ing sides. Then Im-ho'tep, the architect of King Zō'ser, erected smaller stories on top of the lower ones, thus making a "step pyramid.” And finally, Khufu (kōō'fōō), or Cheops (kē´õps), as the Greeks called him, built the Great Pyramid, one of the “seven wonders" of the ancient world. Although for hundreds of years succeeding pharaohs followed his example, they were never quite able to equal the effort of the great Cheops. 

6. The Significance of the Pyramids. Because of their size and of the skill of their builders, these imperishable specimens of man's handiwork deeply impress all who see them today. Massive stone blocks cut from the hardest granite and fitted together so closely that a knife blade cannot be inserted between the blocks testify to the ability and ingenuity of the builders. What is even more important, the pyramids show how powerful and well-organized must have been the kingdom, in order that its pharaohs could devote so much energy and wealth to the construction of mere burial places for themselves. Indeed, when we remember that everything was done by hand, the amount of this effort is almost beyond human comprehension. 

Herodotus said that it took a hundred thousand men twenty years to build the Great Pyramid. 

7. Troubles from Within Bring the Old Kingdom to an End.

Still Khufu and his successors did not devote all their time to building pyramids. From the inscriptions that have been preserved, we learn that they kept watch of the Nile and recorded its rise. In the west they fought with the Lib'yans who were always trying to push their way into the delta, and in the north with the Asiatics who kept interfering with the copper mines in Sinai (si'ni). They sent expeditions to the coast of Syria for cedar with which to build ships, and to the shores of the Red Sea for aromatic gums and incense and other tropical luxuries, and up the Nile into Nu'bia for gold dust, ivory, ostrich feathers, and negro dwarfs to serve as palace attendants.

8. The Middle Kingdom and What Was Achieved in 

Building and in Writing. Between the fall of the Old Kingdom and the beginning of the Middle Kingdom, the rulers of the different provinces became quite independent. At last the

one at Thebes (thebz), a city far up the Nile, with the assistance of the priest of the sun-god Rä, was able to assert his supremacy over the other rulers. Because the pharaohs of the 

Middle Kingdom were never able to exercise the same autocratic power as their predecessors, this period is termed Egypt's "Feudal Age."

Although deprived of much of their power, the pharaohs of

the Middle Kingdom wrestled with some of the same problems as those of the Old Kingdom. Yet in spite of fighting much of the time with the peoples on their frontiers, they found time to make many public improvements. One of the pharaohs, to improve communication with Sinai, built a canal from the Nile to the Red Sea, a distance of about eighty miles. A great dam was also built across a depression west of the Nile to store water for irrigation.

The massive temples whose ruins are still admired were begun-evidence of the increasing importance of religion and the priesthood. To adorn these temples the pharaohs caused enormous statues of themselves to be erected, some of which still remain, such as the "Co-los'si of Měm'non." 

So much writing was done during the Middle Kingdom that the language was then more fully developed than at any other time. For this reason the period is often called Egypt's "classical age." Although much of this literature has perished, we still have a few stories to indicate the literary taste of the times. One of these is of a shipwrecked sailor who was cast away on an island in the Indian Ocean and finally sent home loaded with gifts by the great snake which ruled the place. 

Another tells of a page at the palace who was forced to flee and took refuge with one of the tribes in the desert of northern 

Arabia. Like Sinbad the Sailor in the Arabian Nights, when they returned home, they had marvellous stories of their adventures.

Science, too, had its beginning during the classical age. We still have a long papyrus dealing with the medical knowledge of the day, and another about mathematics. Both show that the 

Egyptians had already learned many important scientific facts, and had developed a scientific point-of-view, even though they had not yet fully organized their knowledge. 

9. The Book of the Dead. One of the things that interested the Egyptians most was the future life. They believed

that when they came to die their souls would be brought before O-si'ris to be judged. He would then weigh their good and bad deeds and determine whether the future should be spent in comfort or in misery. Even if they were successful in pass-

Because this examination before Osiris was so difficult, it was believed that instructions as to how to answer the questions were essential. These instructions were prepared by the priests for placing in the coffin and were known as The Book of the Dead. This book must have been very costly for only a few complete sets have been found in all the tombs that have been opened.

Conquest. The power of the great feudal kings of Thebes was overthrown by an invasion from the north. The Hyk'sōs

or "shepherd kings" seem to have been the leaders of a body of Asiatics who poured down into Egypt and occupied the delta and a part of the valley. We know very little about them except that they were much less civilized than the Egyptians. 2+AG:MAAE

They were able to defeat the latter because they possessed horses and probably iron weapons.

Again it was a ruler of Thebes who restored the power of Egypt. We have scattered hints of the long fight needed to drive out the Hyksos and then of the long period of foreign conquest that followed. In the end the pharaohs extended their control as far as the Euphrates, and even hunted elephants on its eastern bank. From this story we get our first information about organized warfare. Thoth'mes III, who year after year led his armies into Asia, has left enough of his exploits written on the walls of the temples to convince us that he was the world's first great general. 

11. The Splendor of the Empire. The wealth brought back by Thothmes and his successors from these conquests raised the Empire to the height of its splendor. Great royal

4I fleets loaded with all sorts of luxuries plowed the Red Sea. 

The most famous of these was sent out by the first queen of history, Hat-shěp'sut. Now that the constant warfare necessitated the organization of a standing army, the farmers could stay at home to look after their crops, and production became so great that for a long time Egypt was the granary of the Mediterranean world. With all this prosperity more and great temples were built. The Great Temple of Ä'mon at Kar‍nak was finished to stand to this day as one of the most magnificent edifices ever put together by man.

TUTANKHAMON'S CORONATION CHAIR 

This chair of gold and many colored glass was found in his tomb. The scene on the back shows his wife standing before him. was supported by 134 columns arranged in 16 rows. Those of the two central rows are 78 feet high and 33 feet in circumference-all brilliantly painted and sculptured. In one of the inner courts were a colossal statue of Osiris, and two obelisks 97 feet in height, much like the one now standing in Central Park, New York. Leading to it was an avenue lined with Sphinxes.

While they covered the walls of the temples and the faces of the obelisks with accounts of their power, the chief object of these pharaohs still seemed to be to provide for themselves a secure final resting place. Pyramids had long since been given up because so often they were opened and plundered. 

Now they had their tombs excavated in the hills on the west bank of the Nile.

Although the entrance to the tomb was carefully hidden, after the body of the pharaoh had been placed within it, most of the tombs have long since been plundered. Only recently an 

American archæologist stumbled upon the first one and found it just as it had been left more than three thousand years ago. 

Even though Tutankhamon (toot'änk-ä-mon) was not a great nor a wealthy ruler, his tomb proved to be almost unbelievably rich in its contents. Gold-adorned furniture, elaborate models of boats, jewelry, and many articles of every-day use were crowded around the golden mummy case. 

12. The Problems of the Empire. The Asiatic conquests of the pharaohs brought them in direct contact with other powers and compelled them to be ever on their guard. The control of their new possessions was difficult and the best that could be done was to establish garrisons in strategic places and to bring the sons of the native princes to the Egyptian court to be educated. For the first time a pharaoh took a wife from outside his own people.

At home there were also difficulties. More and more land had to be set aside for the maintenance of the temples. No doubt this was partly responsible for an extraordinary attempt on the part of one of the pharaohs to establish the worship of a single god. 

13. The Coming of the Hittites and the Beginning of the Iron Age in Egypt. From the archives we learn that the Hittites, a people of Asia Minor, gradually wrested from Egypt her Asiatic possessions. Răm'é-sēs II attempted to re-

conquer these territories. He fought a great battle with the 

Hittites at Ka'desh in which he claimed to have won a victory; and a few years later he made a treaty with them on a basis of equality.

This treaty was recorded on the walls of one of the temples at Thebes. Not long ago a copy was found in the ruins of 

Ptě'ri-a, the capital city of the Hittites. This is the first treaty of which we have the text, and it carries phrases that are still in use in modern diplomacy. It is a treaty of peace and friendship, and a defensive alliance, and provides for the extradition of political criminals.

After this the relations between the two powers were peaceful and the Egyptian pharaohs sent to their Hittite brothers for iron, thus inaugurating the iron age in Egypt. 

14. The Decay of the Empire. The great struggle with the Hittites and the increasing cost of keeping up the temples sapped the strength of the country. Besides, in the thirteenth century B. C. there were great stirrings among the peoples of the eastern Mediterranean region. Large armies marched down the Syrian coast and attacked the outposts of the Empire. The pharaohs fought them off as they did the Libyans from the west, but were gradually forced to yield all their territories outside of Egypt. As the curtain falls, we have the pathetic report of an Egyptian official who was sent to Tyre for timber. The ruler of Tyre shows him where former officials on similar missions had been executed and then leaves him to escape as best he can. During the centuries that followed, the Egyptians occasionally interfered in Asiatic affairs, but their help usually was more of a hindrance than a benefit.

CHAPTER V  AND THE WONDERS ACHIEVED IN ANCIENT BABYLONIA 

The valley of the Tigris and the Euphrates has been known by various names. The lower part of it was often called Bab'ylō-ni-a; the middle part Mes-ō-pō-ta'mi-a, meaning “between the rivers." We shall speak of it as the "Land of the Two 

Rivers." Both rivers have shorter courses and swifter currents than the Nile and their valley differs from that of the Nile, in that the fertile lower part is short and broad. The presence of two rivers instead of one and a considerable rainfall make the irrigation problem simpler than in Egypt. Consequently the unity of the country was not necessary for its development.

Nor is it so well protected as is Egypt. On the northwest a belt of fertile land extends all the way to the Mediterranean. 

The valley of the two rivers, together with this fertile belt and the narrow coastal plains as far south as the Isthmus of Suez, form the so-called "Fertile Crescent." This serves as a green fringe to what is now known as the Arabian Desert, which contains many oases and has always been a great reservoir of nomad Semites. North and northeast of this Fertile Crescent there are lofty mountain ranges pierced by a few easy passes. 

This is the setting for our next adventure among early Oriental civilizations. We shall see how the people in this region were making their contributions to civilized ways of living, how they were setting their records down in cuneiform writing; how one great conqueror tried to unify the country as far as the Mediterranean Sea and another great ruler set down a great code of laws for men to live by. 46

Apparently the Sumerians migrated into this region from the north and settled down as farmers in the lower part of the 3/

The Semites appear to have come from Arabia and are still found there. They were nomads and often wandered great distances during the year with their flocks and herds and were a constant source of danger to the little agricultural communities on the edge of the desert. 2. The Use of Clay for Building. Because there was no stone convenient for use in the lower part of the Land of the Two Rivers, the Sumerians built their houses of clay bricks which they baked in the sun, like the a-do'be of the southwestern part of the United States and Mexico. Stone was

used only for door sockets and for articles where baked clay would not serve. This use of clay spread over the Near East. 

These sun-baked bricks would not withstand much water, consequently buildings constructed of them were always liable to be destroyed by heavy rains. After such an accident, it Hittites

MESOPOTAMIA IN ANCIENT TIMES 

Gulf was easier to level off the ground and build new houses than to repair the old ones. And so as the centuries passed and villages were destroyed and rebuilt, the level gradually rose until to-day the Land of the Two Rivers is dotted with mounds. representing ancient towns and cities. The modern excavator finds these mounds arranged in layers, each layer containing the remains of the life of a particular period. 

3. The Sumerians Were the First to Divide the Day into Hours, Minutes and Seconds. We do not know so much about the early history of the Land of the Two Rivers as about that of Egypt. We do know that as early as 4000 B. C

there were already a number of little cities scattered through the land, each with its own god and temple. The temple together with the city and country round about belonged to the god, and the priest was the ruler.

Even in these early times, the Sumerians had learned to count-not by tens as we do, but by twelves and by sixties- 

WRITING WITH A STYLUS 

and divided the day into hours, minutes, and seconds. Thus we have twelve hours in our day, twelve in the night, sixty minutes in an hour, and sixty seconds in a minute. We have also inherited from them our earliest weights and measures. 

4. Cuneiform Writing and How Men 

Learned to Read It. Like the Egyptians, the Sumerians began to write with pictographs; but unfortunately, they had no papyrus for paper.

They used pieces of wet clay shaped like a cake of soap. On these they drew their characters with a three-cornered stylus, an instrument resembling a modern awl. Since it is difficult to make curved lines on wet clay, the Sumerians devised a system of writing which employed only straight lines. Because the stylus gave these lines a wedge shape, this system is called cúnet-form. Unlike the Egyptians, they never used signs for single sounds, but employed them for syllables, consequently their writing is somewhat more complicated than the Egyptian. 

All knowledge of this ancient language was lost at about the same time as that of the Egyptians, and the numerous cuneiform inscriptions found in the Land of the Two Rivers remained a secret until the middle of the nineteenth century. 

Then, while some of the leading scholars of Europe were trying to decipher the characters, Sir Henry Rawlinson began to study the great inscription which had been cut in three languages on the face of a cliff at Behistun (bā-his-tōon') in Persia. By a series of fortunate guesses Rawlinson succeeded

in reading a few words. From that simple beginning the old cuneiform characters were entirely deciphered. 

5. Sargon, the World's First Great Conqueror. Al though we have some information about many of the early cities and rulers of the Land of the Two Rivers, the first man of whom we know much was Sär'gon. He lived about 2800 

B. C.; that is, about the time that the pyramids were being built in Egypt. He was a Semite and tried to gain control over the whole Land of the Two Rivers. It seems probable that he actually did extend his power as far to the west as the Mediterranean, for during the following centuries cuneiform writing spread over all of western Asia. Apparently Sargon had little genius for organization, for shortly after his death the empire began to break up. 

6. The Rivalry of the City States. After Sargon's day some cities attempted to assert supremacy over their neighbors, and sometimes this control would last for a generation or two. 

Each priestly ruler endeavored to favor his particular god by increasing the size of its temple, and to enlarge his income by clearing out and extending the canals. The temples were important centres of business since all the public accounts were kept in them. Attached to them were schools to train the clerks who were needed to look after the god's property. 

About 2200 B. C. the city of Babylon with its god Marduk (Mär'dook) began to extend its authority over the other states. 

The line of kings at Babylon was more successful than many of its predecessors had been, so the power of Babylon grew steadily. 

7. Hammurabi, the Great King, and His Gift to the 

World. One of the greatest kings of this Babylonian line was 

Hammurabi (hàm-oo-rä'bé). Hammurabi was a prodigious letter writer. Some years ago the royal archives of his reign were found in the ruins of Babylon and thousands of tablets containing copies of letters which he had written to his officials

were brought to light. Although his conquests extended to the 

Mediterranean, his fame rests upon a code of laws which was found a few years ago in the ruins of Susa, whither it had been 

ONE OF HAMMURABI'S BRICKS

How does this differ from modern bricks? carried by the Elăm-ītes after their overthrow of the Babylonian Empire. In this code we can get a picture of Babylonian society such as is not possible for any other early state. It gives us much information about the different classes of society, the organization of the family, the occupations of the people, and the business and social life of Hammurabi's day. 

8. In Social and Economic Life the Babylonians Seem 

Almost Modern. Beside the king and his family, society

consisted of the nobility, the freemen, and the slaves. The nobility included the officials and the priests. It enjoyed special privileges but was compelled to pay more for medical attention. 

The artisans and the farmers together with the merchants constituted the freemen. Their position in society was similar to that of freemen of later times. The slaves were looked upon very much as animals, and regarded as property. 

Normally Babylonians married only one wife, but they might have assistant wives or concubines. Marriage was strictly a contract. The woman brought with her a dowry. 

Women as well as men could obtain divorce. The children belonged to the father and were under his control.

Although women could hold property in their own right and could carry on business, in general they occupied a subordinate position.

9. The Religion of Babylonia. The great god of Baby lon was Marduk. Not only at home, but wherever the Babylonians exercised control, Marduk was all-powerful. How-

ever, there were other gods who had special powers under certain conditions; such as Sin, the moongod, Ea (a'ä), the earthgod, and Ish'tar, the goddess of love. These latter gods had

10. Some Ancient Babylonian Legends. The Babylonian priests had many legends concerning the beginning of things, some of which bear a close resemblance to stories found in the Old Testament. One of these stories was about a monster which bothered the gods so much that they held a meeting to decide what should be done. After considerable discussion they voted to send Marduk to fight the monster. Marduk took with him a gale of wind which he blew into the monster's mouth. When she was inflated, he split her into two parts, and made half of her the sky and the other half the earth. 

Another of these legends was about a man who was told by the gods that there was to be a flood. Like Noah, he built

himself a boat, took on board his family, and floated on the water until everybody else was drowned. When the flood subsided, he landed and by sacrifices appeased the god who had caused the flood. 

11. In Face of Defeat Babylon Remained a Centre of 

Culture. After Hammurabi's death came a period of unrest for Babylon, marked by an invasion of eastern nomads somewhat resembling the Hyksos in Egyptian history. Not long after these foreigners were uprooted, Babylon fell before the onslaughts of a strong warlike people—the Elamites, whose home was in the mountains of what is to-day Persia. 

For a number of centuries there was no strong government in the Land of the Two Rivers, and it became the prey of Egyptians and Asiatics alike. In spite of conquest or pillage, Babylon still retained its position for more than 1,500 years as chief city of the Land of the Two Rivers.

CHAPTER VI THE EARLY ÆGEANS, CARRIERS OF ARTS AND CULTURE TO LATER PEOPLES 

Since the days of the ancient Greeks, Homer's story of the Trojan War had been accepted as a historical fact. Early in the nineteenth century some doubted the story and even denied that Homer was a real person. In Holland a poor grocer's clerk, Henry Schlie'mann, was so much interested in the Homeric tales that he vowed should he ever become rich, he would try to find the ruins of Troy. The young man finally made a fortune and true to his vow went to the banks of the Där då-nĕlles and began digging in what was thought to be the site of that city. Success crowned his efforts, and after bringing to light the remains of several later cities, down under these he at last came upon one that he took to be the Homeric Troy. 

When a quarrel with the Sultan of Turkey compelled him to abandon his work, he returned to Greece and began to dig on the site of old Mycena (mi-se'ne). Here he found a number of graves containing what he thought were bones of Agà-mem'non and his heroes. We know now that what he discovered was not the remains of the early Greeks but an entirely different civilization which had been wholly forgotten. 

From the old Greek legends and traditions, a scholar, Arthur Evans, believed that more of this civilization might be found at Cnossus (nos'us) on the island of Crete. He began to dig there, and soon uncovered the ruins of a great palace which has been identified as that of the "sea-kings" of Crete. This palace dates back to the days of the Egyptian Empire, but there had been a civilization here as early as the Pyramids. Unfortunately the men who were responsible for this civilization 58

The most impressive work of the

It was built in several stories and contained scores of rooms. The latter are grouped around courtyards and show that the palace was divided into two main parts-one for men and the other for women. Centuries later the Greeks had a tradition of the sea power of a certain Minos, King of Crete. That they must have controlled the sea is borne out by the total lack of fortifications around their palaces. We feel sure that they were interested in sports, for pictures have survived that show bull fights in which girls as well as boys were taking part.

Their dress was strikingly modern. A statuette of ivory depicts a woman in a gown consisting of a low-cut bodice and flounced skirt. 

Since she holds in her hands a snake, some think that this is a likeness of one of their goddesses. However, the chief divinity of the Ægeans was the "Great Mother," or nature goddess, whose shrine was in a cave on Mount Ida.

5. The Philistines Gave the Name Palestine to an Im portant Region. After one of these unsuccessful attempts, a group of the invaders called the Pulstu (pool-stoo) settled down near the southeastern corner of the Mediterranean not far from the Isthmus of Suez, and became known to history as 

Philistines. The Philistines founded five cities, which were

united into a loose confederacy. Incidentally they gave their name to the whole country which is still known as "Palestine." 

6. The Phoenicians of Ægean Descent Fell Heir to

Their Sea Power. Shortly after the destruction of the Ægean power, a number of cities, especially Tyre and Sidon, farther north on the eastern shore of the Mediterranean rose to prominence with a people known as the Phænicians (fé-nish´anz). 

They were descended from the Ægeans. At first, no doubt, they were merely pirates and slave-raiders, but by 1000 B. C. they had begun making trading voyages over the whole Mediterranean Sea and their cities had become great commercial centres with outposts. 

Navigation in those days was perilous. The ships were small and were propelled largely by oarsmen. With no compass to guide them, masters were forced to hug the shore closely and could navigate only by day and in fair weather. At night and when the atmosphere was hazy, the boats were dragged up on the shore, much as rowboats are to-day, for anchors were unknown.

The chief Phoenician trading posts were at Carthage, where Africa juts out toward Sicily, at Măs-sĭlĭ-a, near the mouth of the Rhone, and Gä'dēs, near the southwestern corner of Spain. 

Thither they carried the manufactured articles which they had learned how to make, and brought back raw materials of all sorts, gold and silver in particular. 

7. How the Phoenicians Made Important Contributions to Civilization. The chief trade secret of the Phoenicians was a beautiful purple dye known as "Tyrian Purple,” which was made from a little shell fish. This dye was so difficult to obtain and the Phoenicians kept the secret so well that in later times it came to be used only by kings.

Their commercial instincts made them the great borrowers of antiquity. They carried so much knowledge to the Greeks and Romans that they are supposed to have invented many

of the things which they had obtained from others. Chief among these was the alphabet which they simplified from the Egyptian, apparently to use in keeping their accounts. From both Egypt and the Land of the Two Rivers they obtained the knowledge of many technical processes they passed on to the Greeks.

CHAPTER VII INDO-EUROPEANS, OR ARYANS, ESTABLISH THEIR LAN- GUAGE AND NEW SEATS OF CULTURE FROM THE ISLES OF THE ÆGEAN SEA TO INDIA 

We have seen that the check to civilization in the Land of the Two Rivers and the destruction of the Egean power were due to invasions from the north. Who were these invaders and what is the significance of their conquests? From the Carpā'thi-an Mountains eastward stretches a great grassy plainan ideal place for nomad peoples. Somewhere in this area in remote times there seems to have arisen a group of peoples of great energy. They were tall, long-headed, light-haired, and blue-eyed, and, like the Kirghiz (kir-gēz') who to-day roam over much of the same region, they were nomads. Whatever may have been their origin, they developed a language which is thought to have been the original Indo-European or Ar'yan tongue that comes down to us. 

1. Indo-European Invasions Can Be Traced by the 

Language Remains. As early as 2500 B. C. waves of Indo 

Europeans must have begun to move southward and eastward, for at that time we find faint traces of them in the valleys of the Tigris and Euphrates. By 2000 B. C. they had begun to press down into the Balkan peninsula and were crossing over into Asia Minor. Five hundred years later another wave pushed southward into the Ægean area, and still another swept down through the mountain passes into India. We can trace all these movements through the aid of language, for even when the invaders were so few their language has remained.

These Indo-Europeans believed that the forces of nature were gods. Among these gods they accorded first place to Zeus (zus), the "lord of the heavens." They also believed in spirits and in immortality, and on the day we call Hallowe'en they thought that the souls of the dead returned to earth for a visit.

They made offerings and sacrifices to their gods and worshipped them with songs and dances, and sometimes with revelry ending in intoxication. Unlike the Egyptians and Babylonians, they did not build temples for their gods, but dedicated to them

3. The Aryans in India Established a Rigid Caste System and Borrowed an Alphabet. The Aryans or Indo 

Europeans who pushed into India about 1500 B. C., within two centuries had established their control over all the peninsula north of the Narbada (nur-buď'ä) River. Protected

69 by the Himalayas on the north and east, they founded a series of little states. Although originally a fighting, drinking, meateating people, under the influence of the climate and of the native population, they began to change and to break up into social classes. Originally there were three of these the religious teachers, or Bräh'mans, the warriors, and the farmers and merchants. From this developed the rigid caste system which is so striking a feature of Indian society to-day, and to which may be traced very largely the lack of any practical nationalist spirit in that country.

According to the scheme each class was forbidden to have social relations with the others. Below these three classes were two others, the Sudras (soo'dras) and the Päri-ahs. The Sudras, who were the Press.

These Indian Aryans or Hindus, as we shall call them, learned to write from the Phoenicians, developing an alphabet of their own-the Săn'skrit-in which appeared the first Indo- European literature, the Rig Veda (va'da), a series of hymns which had long been handed down by word of mouth. Later they composed three other Vedas and two long epic poems dealing with their conquest of the country.

4. In Addition to Their Religion the Brahmans Gave the World the Decimal System. It was not long before the 

Brahmans, as the religious teachers were called, gained supremacy over the other castes. They created a new god, Brahma, whose soul is supposed to pervade the universe. There are

AN UNTOUCHABLE From Mayo's Mother India. 

souls in everything, in plants and animals-and even in stones-and these souls pass from one thing to another toward the great soul of Brahma of which they are a part. This is known as the transmigration of souls. 

When a good man dies, his soul passes through a heaven to enter the body of a saint; but when a bad man dies, his soul passes through hell into a woman or even into a plant or an animal. 

A soul must continue being reborn until it becomes pure enough to return to Brahma.

The Brahmans invented the decimal system of notation and made considerable progress in mathematics. 

5. Another Aryan Migration Formed the Greece of Homer's Famous Epics. About 1300 B. C. another wave of these Indo-European peoples began to sweep down into the Balkan peninsula and to overrun the land which later became known as Greece. This invasion originally consisted of three distinct movements, and the Greeks had a tradition that their people had been divided into three tribes-the Eolians (e'ō-lians), the Achæans (a-ke'ans), and the I-o'ni-ans. Later came another invasion, that of the Do-ri'ans. These Indo-Euro-

71 peans, whom we shall call Homeric Greeks or Hellenes (hěllēnz), subdued the Egeans already settled in Greece, and occupied their cities. They were not civilized enough to appreciate the culture they found, and generally left destruction behind them, as in the case of Cnossus. 

One of their barbaric exploits has become famous through Homer's great epics-the

Iliad and the Odys sey. According to these stories, a large body of these Hellenes made an expedition against the city of Troy.

Odysseus (ó-dis'ús), another of their chieftains, who was especially renowned for his craftiness, had the misfortune to anger Pó-sei'don, the god of the sea. Our interest in these stories lies in the picture which they give of this early Indo- European society, out of which arose that of the Greeks. 

6. Agriculture was the Basis of Society in the Homeric 

Age. During the "Homeric Age" the leaders of the people were called kings; but some of these kings seem to have been

little more than well-to-do farmers. Below the kings was an extensive group of free warriors whose opinion had to be consulted on any question concerning the state; below these, in turn, were the slaves.

Agriculture, stock-raising, and fighting were the chief occupations. There were few artisans and almost no merchants. 

So infested with pirates was the eastern Mediterranean in those days that if any one did start out with a shipload of goods, he was likely to lose it. 

7. The Homeric Greeks Humanized Their Gods and 

Were Very Intimate with Them. According to the Homeric

Greeks, the gods differed from men only in their immortality, their super-human strength, and their ability to move from place to place with extraordinary rapidity. Their home was supposed to be on snow-capped Mount O-lỹm'pus, where they spent their time drinking nectar and eating ambrosia. They quarrelled and fought, loved and hated like ordinary persons. 

Zeus controlled the lightning and the storms. He was married to He'ra, the jealous queen of the sky. Below them came 

Poseidon, who acted as god of the sea; A-põľlo, the sun-god, whose special care was wisdom, poetry, and medicine; Ā'rēs, the god of war; and Hephæstus (hé-fes'tus), the god of fire. 

Hēr'mēs, the messenger of the gods, was the god of the wind, and at the same time the god of cunning, commerce, and of thieves. Athena, or "Pallas Athena" as she was often called, was the goddess of wisdom; Ar'té-mis, the goddess of the moon as well as of hunting; and Aph-ro-di'te, the goddess of love. The control of plants and growing things belonged to 

Dé-me'ter, the earth-goddess, while Hěs'ti-a, the goddess of the hearth-fire, was the goddess of the home. 

Men tried as far as possible to keep on the good side of the gods. They made sacrifices to these divinities lest the latter should become angry and cause trouble. In extreme cases they even resorted to human sacrifices to appease them. As a rule

each head of the family dealt directly with the gods, and priests were necessary only to help interpret the omens by which men. were advised concerning future happenings.

CHAPTER VIII MIGHTY ORIENTAL EMPIRES RISE AND FALL TILL THE EMPIRE OF THE MEDES AND PERSIANS COVERS THE WHOLE OF WESTERN ASIA AND EGYPT 

We shall now see how the great military empires of the Assyrians, the Chaldeans, the Medes and the Persians were formed in the centuries which followed the Aryan invasions; how powerful rulers tried to build more luxurious palaces and to conquer more territory than their predecessors; how as borrowers of culture their civilization had no enduring qualities aside from the military organization of the Assyrian Empire. 

This became the model for the Persians and we shall see how years later, when Alexander the Great with his little band of Greeks conquered Persia along with the rest of the known world, he took over the political organization and put his own trusted lieutenants in the places of the Persian officials. 

1. The Rise of Assyria. The first great power to develop after the Indo-European invasion was Assyria. Centuries before the Semites had founded the city of Assur (ăsh'ŭr) on the Tigris about two hundred miles north of Babylon. Later much of the upper valley of that river was dotted with the cities of the As-syrians, the name by which these people are known to history.

The land of the Assyrians consisted of a triangular-shaped district lying across the "Fertile Crescent" on both banks of the Tigris. It was not a large country, particularly fertile, although, near the river, on rolling plains, in spite of their stony soil, crops grew with the aid of irrigation, and farther away hills furnished pasturage for flocks and herds.

On the south, Assyria was separated from the Land of the 74

ASSYRIANS, MEDES, AND PERSIANS 

75 Two Rivers by a belt of arid country; and on the north, was bordered by a wall of lofty mountains; but even so, it was open to attack on all sides. This made it necessary for the 

Assyrians to cling to their primitive fighting instincts long after they had settled down. During their entire history they suffered from invasions and were compelled to keep watch on the mountain tribes who lay just beyond the northern frontier. www.d

2. Assyria Becomes a Mighty Empire. While, at the height of their power, the Babylonians seem to have conquered the Assyrians, this domination was short-lived, for about 1100 B. C. the Assyrians under the leadership of King Tig'lath 

Pi-le'ser I brought Babylonia under their control. Quite likely this was possible because the Assyrian use of horses and chariots in fighting gave them a decided advantage over their neighbors. Very wisely they kept their capital in Assyria instead of moving it to the more ease-loving Babylon. The Assyrians adopted the scheme of naming each year after a particular official, and we are fortunate in having an almost unbroken list of these officials from 893 B. C. onward.

In 884 B. C. Ashur-nasir-pal (a'shoor-nä-zér-päl'), one of the greatest of Assyrian kings, came to the throne. From the

story of his deeds written on clay tablets, it is possible to follow his campaigns in detail. Although he was continually fighting enemies on all sides, he devoted his efforts especially to raids along the "Fertile Crescent." 

3. How the Assyrians Controlled Their Empire. These numerous conquests bear witness to the skill of the Assyrians

They were equally able in political administration. They organized their conquered territories into provinces and placed over them Assyrian governors. In order to keep in touch with these provinces they inaugurated a postal system and, like the Egyptians, they took a census of the people.
