4. The Assyrians Were Borrowers of Culture. The As syrian kings were great builders. Nearly every important ruler during the last three centuries of the nation's history felt that he must build himself a new palace, and the capital was thus moved from place to place. Although they had stone in abundance, the Assyrians seem to have preferred to use brick, but they wainscoted their walls with slabs of alabaster, on which were carved marvellous winged lions, pictorial reviews of their

kings' campaigns, and sometimes long accounts of their reigns. 

They were too busy with fighting and with the administration of their conquests to devote much time to culture. 

What they accomplished in this direction was to study such omens as the livers of freshly slaughtered beasts to ascertain the proper time for various undertakings. The culture they did possess was copied for the most part from the older civilization of Babylon. 

5. The Fall of the Assyrian Empire. While Ashur-banipal was busying himself with historical studies, trouble was brewing in the northeast. The nomad Medes poured down out of the mountains and overran much of the empire. Babylon again regained her independence and made an alliance with the Medes for a joint attack upon her ancient rival. In a final effort the Assyrian king allied himself with the restored Egyptian kingdom, but in vain. For three years the armies of Babylon and hordes of Medes besieged Nineveh. With its fall in 

612 B. C., the Assyrian Empire passed into history—in fact, so completely was the city destroyed that two hundred years later its ruins had lost their identity. 

6. The Chaldean Empire and the City of Babylon are 

Destroyed. When the Babylonians finally rid themselves of 

Assyrian overlordship, they organized a "New Babylonia," the so-called Chaldean (kăl-dē'an) Empire. With the fall of Nineveh this empire became heir to the southern half of the Assyrian domain, and thus came into conflict with the Egyptians and Hebrews. Nebuchadrezzar (něb-ú-kăd-rěz'ȧr), the Chaldean king, planned to conquer Egypt, but all that he accomplished was the destruction of the Kingdom of Judah and the deportation of her leading citizens to Babylon in 586 B. C. 

The Chaldean Empire was not destined to last, for already the Persians were beginning to threaten its northern borders. 

In 539 B. C. one of the generals of Cyrus of Än'shan, sometimes known as "Cyrus the Great," turned aside a stream that

8. The Organization of the 

Persian Empire was Highly

Efficient. The control of so large an empire demanded a very complete organization. This was the work of Darius the 

Great (521-486 B. C.). Darius divided the empire into twenty provinces, placing over each a Persian governor assisted by a secretary and a commander of the garrisons. To keep in touch with all these provinces he provided inspectors, called the "eyes and ears" of the king, who travelled throughout the empire, reporting to their royal master what they saw and heard. 

Along the more important caravan routes, as from Susa (soo'sȧ) to Sardis, and from Susa to Memphis, Darius established stations where royal messengers might obtain horses or camels to carry them on their journeys. This was a continuation of the Assyrian postal system. 

9. The Persian Empire Was the First Great Cosmo politan State. The Persians developed little real culture of their own. They were content for their boys to learn to ride horseback, to shoot with bows and arrows, and to speak the truth. However, unlike some of their kinsmen, they appreciated culture, and when they came in contact with the higher civilizations of Babylon and Egypt, they borrowed much from them. From the Lydians the Persians adopted the system of coining money and the "Dăric" with its figure of an archer became the first internationally known coin.

At the court of the "great king," as Darius and his successors were called, strangers were made welcome. Hither came 

Greek adventurers in great numbers to pursue their philosophical investigations. It may be said that the Persian Empire was the first great cosmopolitan state and from it the world learned its first lesson in political tolerance. It was this disposition to practise tolerance which so undermined the empire that finally its overthrow became easy.

CHAPTER IX THE RISE OF THE HEBREW AND OTHER ORIENTAL RELIGIONS 

Although the ancient civilizations of Egypt and the Land of the Two Rivers made many contributions to society, it is to the little hill country of Palestine that we owe one which outweighs in importance all the others. This is the religion of the 

Hebrews. Who were these Hebrews to whom we are so indebted? 

1. The "Children of Israel" Escape from Bondage and

Found Homes in Palestine. Palestine had early come into contact with the Land of the Two Rivers, for its inhabitants used cuneiform writing in their letters to the pharaoh. Long afterward, the Hebrews had a tradition of the coming of the patriarch Abraham from “Ur of the Chaldees." According to the same tradition, his grandson, Jacob, who was also called "Israel," moved his family to Egypt to escape a famine. On the eastern side of the delta they grew and flourished until the pharaohs made their lot "bitter with hard bondage in mortar and brick and in all manner of service in the field." Under the leadership of the prophet Moses they fled and, after long wandering, reached the banks of the Jordan. The children of 

Israel, as they now called themselves, crossed the river and found homes in the unoccupied parts of Palestine. The twelve tribes into which they were divided soon lost their unity, but they never lost their memory of their escape from bondage. 85

2. The Rise of the Hebrew Kingdom to Power under 

David. These disunited peoples were tormented by their neighbors, and the Philistines for a time held the ark, or chest, in which the Israelites carried the memorials of their tribal God, Yäh'wěh, or "Je-ho'vah." This constant oppression led the 

Israelites to demand a more efficient leader than the "judges," and they decided to have a king. The warrior Saul was raised to this position and he was anointed by the prophet Samuel. 

Under Saul's leadership they fought valiantly until the Philistines killed him and hung his body on the walls of the Beth'she'an. Saul was succeeded by David, an abler fighter and a better organizer. David seized the strong city of Jerusalem for his capital and then proceeded to conquer the other cities of the land. He became the real founder of the Kingdom of the Hebrews. 

3. The Kingdom of Israel at the Peak of Greatness in the Reign of Solomon (ca. 950 B. C.). Under David's son,

Solomon, the kingdom reached the peak of its glory. With the aid of architects hired from Hiram, King of Tyre, Solomon built himself a great palace, and a famous Temple for Yahweh. 

He also joined with Hiram in commercial expeditions on the Red Sea and on the Mediterranean. The heavy taxes necessitated by all this bore heavily on the people and alienated some of the outlying tribes, with the result that the Children of Israel were divided into two hostile groups. 

Still Solomon left behind himself such a reputation for wisdom that many clever sayings were later attributed to him; and even to-day the Muslims relate stories of his ability to converse with birds and animals. With the death of Solomon ends the brief story of Hebrew greatness, for shortly afterward the ten northern tribes broke away from Jerusalem and formed a separate Kingdom of Israel with its capital city at Sa-ma'ria. The two tribes which remained loyal to him became known as the 

Kingdom of Judah.

For three centuries the two kingdoms quarrelled and fought with each other. While Israel engaged more in industry and commerce, Judah remained a purely agricultural and stockraising country. Both lay in the "Fertile Crescent" and in the line of Assyrian advance, and both were used by Egypt to protect herself against that power. As early as the ninth century, Israel was fighting the Assyrians, and in 738 she saved herself only by paying a tribute of a "thousand talents of silver." We have already seen her destruction in 722 B. C., and how Judah fell a victim to Nebuchadrezzar. 

5. How the Hebrew Religion Developed. The early be liefs of the Hebrews were expressed in the Ten Commandments which were revealed to Moses on Mount Sinai after the escape from Egypt. "I am Yahweh, thy God, who brought thee out of the land of

Egypt, out of the house of bondage.

Thou shalt have no other gods before Me. 

Thou shalt not make unto thee a graven image. 

Thou shalt not take the name of Yahweh thy God in vain. 

Remember the Sabbath Day, to keep it holy.

Thou shalt not kill. 

Thou shalt not commit adultery. 

Thou shalt not steal. 

Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbor. 

Thou shalt not covet thy neighbor's house."

When the Children of Israel settled in Palestine, they came into contact with many other gods and began a struggle that lasted almost to the end of their kingdom. They did not believe in a future life. At first Yahweh dwelt in an ark and was worshipped in various places, but when Solomon built the Temple at Jerusalem, this became Yahweh's home. After that the history of the Hebrews centred around the efforts made by the priests to confine his worship to this temple. To accomplish this, they developed an elaborate series of sacrifices and ceremonies. 

6. The Prophets Teach a Religion Based on Justice and Righteousness, Instead of Ritual. While the priests were developing a religion based on ritual, other leaders were devoting their time to the fundamental lessons of ethics which underlie all religion. These were the prophets—men who maintained that Yahweh had called them to be his mouthpiece. Their influence must have been tremendous, for they frequently rebuked kings as well as common people. 

One of the first prophets was Elijah, the man who fought the priests of Ba'al, as related in I Kings, 18. But a more important one was Amos, the herdsman of Té-kō'à. According to this reformer, the prayers and sacrifices of the priests meant nothing to Yahweh. What the God really demanded was justice and righteousness in one's personal conduct. Amos lived at the time when the Assyrians were attacking Israel.

C.? a great aid to the prophets, for no longer able to worship according to the ritual prescribed by the priests, the people turned more and more to the priests for their spiritual guidance. During this time there appeared in Babylon the greatest of all the prophets, whose teachings are recorded in the second half of the Book of Isaiah (i-za'yȧ). His name is lost, but scholars call him the "Second Isaiah." He taught that Yahweh was a universal god-not exclusively a Hebrew god as had been claimed previously-and that the Hebrews were only instruments for bringing other peoples to his worship. He also proclaimed the coming of a great leader or "Měs-si'ah" who would bring the Hebrews back to Palestine to rebuild the Temple as a sanctuary for all the peoples of the earth. Thus was born the idea of one God for all people.

8. An Age of Religious Reformers in Other Parts of the World. The century that gave to the Hebrews the "Second Isaiah" saw also the rise of great religious reformers among many other peoples. The Persian Zo-ro-as'ter, the 

Hindu Gautama (go'ta-ma), and the Chinese Lao-tzu (lä'ótsu) and Confucius (kon-fu'shi-us) developed systems of ethical belief that were destined to be of great benefit for genera-

From Maspero's Passing of the Empire. tions to come. And at about the same time the Greek philosophers were devoting themselves to the same task. 

9. Zoroaster the Persian. Zoroaster was a Persian scholar who taught that there were two, and only two gods-the god of light, and the god of darkness. From the god of light came all the good in the world, and from the god of darkness all the evil, and between them there was constant conflict. Each was assisted by a horde of lesser beings-angels and devils-and through their services man's whole life was an incessant struggle.

Since fire was sacred and the earth must be kept pure, the dead could be neither burned nor buried. The followers of

Zoroaster adopted the custom of exposing the bodies in socalled "Towers of Silence" to be fed upon by birds. Among them, too, agriculture was regarded as almost a sacred occupation; and honesty and uprightness of conduct were demanded.

Zoroaster's teachings proved very popular and secured a strong hold on the Persians and some of their Indo-European kinsmen, but to-day their adherents are only a small group of people-the Par'sees of India. This idea of two gods, one good, the other evil, has had a powerful influence on many peoples. 

10. Gautama the Hindu. Form and ceremony developed in the worship of the Aryans in India much as it did among the Hebrews. The Brahmans insisted on all sorts of practices as a means of acquiring perfection. This often led to extraordinary attempts to do without food or clothing in an effort to rid the body of earthly desires.

Gautama, a young Brahman prince, whose father had kept him shielded from all the troubles and sorrows of the world, accidentally found out about disease and death. This preyed upon his mind so much that finally he left home and young wife, and gave the remainder of his life to seeking a way for man to escape all this misery.

Gautama tried all the practices of the Brahmans without avail, until one day while seated under a fig tree by the side of a river, he had a vision. He saw that the sorrows and difficulties of this world arise from man's selfishness, and that the solution lay in enlightenment, or, as he expressed it, in Nirvana (nér-vä'na). His mission then became to impart to his fellow men the wisdom he had acquired. Gathering about himself a few disciples, he established a school. Because the Hindus had a tradition that Wisdom revealed herself to man from time to time, through some specially chosen person, whom they called a "Buddha" (bood'a), Gautama soon came to be regarded as such, and his teachings were known as Buddhism. 

11. The Teachings of Buddhism. Gautama called his philosophy of life the "Aryan Way" or "Eight Fold Path." It consisted of right views, right aspirations, right speech, right conduct, right occupation, right effort, right mindfulness, and

right rapture. To follow this meant Nirvana or peace of mind, and the doing away of all selfishness. The three obstacles in the way were sensuality, ill-will, and stupidity.

While he paid no attention to the worship of gods, he insisted on reverence for one's ancestors. He regarded knowledge as the basis of all virtue and he undertook to gather together the wisdom of the ancients into five books, which are known as the "Five Classics." These form a body of sacred literature which bears the same relationship to the Chinese that the Old Testament does to the Hebrews, or the New Testament to the Christians. It may be said that no other man has ever influenced so many people as Confucius with his "Five Classics."

It was the philosophy of Confucius which caused the Chinese to be content with their laborious system of writing handed down by their ancestors. For ordinary purposes one had to know at least twenty-five hundred different characters; the scholar had need of two or three times as many. Until quite recent times the only entrance to the civil service of China was through a knowledge of these sacred writings.

CHAPTER X THE SIGNIFICANCE OF THE ANCIENT ORIENTAL WORLD 

1. Society's Inheritance from the Ancient Oriental 

Peoples. We have now brought to a close an important chapter in the story of the march of civilization. We have seen man in the Valley of the Nile, in the Land of the Two Rivers, in India, and in China, lift himself to a state of unquestioned civilization. We have seen the civilizations both of Babylon and Egypt tested under the assault of the Northern Barbarians, but rising again to the grandeur of the first great Indo-European empire of history. As we follow this changing story, we shall find roots of that later development to which we give the name Modern Civilization reaching back to the dim origins in the past. 

2. Social Contributions. One of the great debts of society to the ancient oriental world was the disposition of its peoples to make the family the centre of the state. That a man had more than one wife was not allowed to interfere with the sacredness of the home.

From this ancient world, society received first ideas of social distinction, based upon wealth or occupation. To this time may be traced the curse of human slavery. Last, we found the priesthood becoming established in its monopoly of divine worship, and thinking members of society already in revolt against its ritualism and arrogance. 

3. Economic Contributions. In agriculture the ancient world had advanced far. Not only had it fully mastered the process of tilling the soil, but it had learned how to improve seed by selection and how to adapt plants to new conditions. It had also solved the problem of feeding the growing crops by systems of irrigation. In mining it had tapped most of the 98

SIGNIFICANCE OF ORIENTAL WORLD 

99 great ore fields in its area and had quarried blocks of stone unsurpassed in size.

In industry it had acquired many technical processes, in the manufacture of textiles, pottery, and metals, and it had obtained a fineness of design and execution that has never been surpassed. Money had been invented and a system of banking like that of to-day had been evolved. Over the same routes to-day traversed by the railway and the automobile plodded slow-moving caravans serving effectively as their more expeditious successors. Its shipping still crept along the shore but it had breasted the stormy Atlantic, and there is a tradition of the circumnavigation of Africa.

With the exception of the inven- Courtesy of the Macmillan Company. tion of steel and the compass, no further material progress in the economic field was to be made for over two thousand years.

4. Political Contributions. In the realm of politics, not only had the ancient oriental world developed the idea of the city-state, but also that of monarchy and empire. To it may be traced the theory that kings ruled by virtue of their own divinity or by the authority of the gods. This theory has prevailed throughout much of the world until recent times. With the idea of sovereignty there was the corresponding idea of responsibility. Even in Egypt, where the pharaoh was supposed to be a god, justice to his people was held to be an essential quality of a good ruler.

5. Religious Contribu tions. In no field did the ancient world make greater advances than in religion. 

Starting with the lowest type of animism, it progressed to the idea of a single god.

More important still was the change in its idea of the divinity. At first this was wholly without any moral or ethical basis, at last it became with the Hebrews a spiritual conception of the highest order. 

Hand in hand with the ad- vance in the conception of the divinity was the matter of worship Beginning with the crudest kind of sacrifices-sometimes even of human beings-it finally attained the position that self-denial was regarded as the only true sacrifice. 

6. Intellectual Contributions. As a result of all these advancessocial, economic, political, and religious-knowledge grew among the ancient oriental peoples. 

In Egypt and Babylon the temples became beehives of intellectual activity where the priesthood devoted its leisure time to all sorts of observations,

Throughout the world there developed a growing desire for knowledge. This had its beginning with the old Egyptian who advised his son to obtain an education so as to avoid hard, manual labor, and reached its climax in the teachings of Gautama and Confucius, both of whom insisted that knowledge was essential to life and that ignorance and stupidity were sins.

THE PERIOD OF GRECO-ROMAN CIVILIZATION Chapters XI-XX 

The Foreword

Seven or eight centuries before the birth of Christ there arose in the Mediterranean basin a civilization to which is usually given the name Græco-Roman. It originated in the cultural gifts which the empires of the East gave to the Greeks. These 

Greeks were a simple folk, so when they took over this culture of the Orient, they organized and developed a system of thought and art free from mental and moral complexities. 

For the political ideals of kingship, autocracy, and religious monarchy of the Orient, the Greeks substituted the ideas of democracy, freedom, and individuality. In the fields of art and literature they neither dreaded the future nor bowed in reverence to the past; instead they sought to inject into earthly life the beauty, moderation, and justice with which they were wont to endow their gods.

This Greek civilization expanded eastward and westward. 

In the Orient it finally found its highest expression in Christianity; and to the Roman world a culture such as the Romans alone could never have had. In this culture were found the eiements out of which they builded their magnificent system of law, and the incentive for those great engineering works that gave an indelible stamp to Roman civilization. 

And because this culture of the Greeks has been a model and an inspiration to the poets, painters, and sculptors of later times, the world owes to the Græco-Roman civilization a debt far beyond its ability to express. 102

CHAPTER XI  STAND FOR DEMOC- RACY, FREEDOM, AND INDIVIDUALITY FOR ALL CITIZENS 

We left the Hellenes established in Greece and on the islands and eastern shores of the Egean. We know little of their early history except for such brief glimpses as are afforded by the poems of Homer and He'si-od. Their primitive tendency to live in little groups was fostered by the small islands and the isolated plains and valleys of the mainland. Out of this situation arose the polis, or "city-state," the distinguishing feature of Hellenic life. How these little city-states became centres of culture and learning will always be of interest o us. 

1. What Was a City-State? The centre of the city-state was some easily fortified place-usually a lofty hill. Within this fortress or à-crop'ó-lis was an open market place, around which stood the temples of the gods and the other public buildings. Outside the walls of the acropolis were huddled 103

most of the shops and houses, and beyond these stretched the farm lands belonging to the community. The area of a citystate usually was no greater than that of a modern township. 

Athens and Sparta were exceptions. By uniting several kindred communities, they had become as large as our present-day counties.

Most of the city-states were small in population; even Athens probably never exceeded 250,000 inhabitants, and Sparta, although mistress of the entire region. south of the Gulf of Corinth, the so-called Pěl-ó-pon-ne'sus, could not count 50,000 persons. And yet, the most insignificant of the city-states possessed the rights of independent nations-they could declare war, enter into alliances, and conclude treaties. 

Citizenship was characterized by its exclusiveness. It was a privilege conferred by birth alone. Citizens of a particular city-state were supposed to be descended from a common ancestor and consequently were under the protection of the same patron god. Whenever a person moved away from his native city-state he lost his citizenship and became a "man without a country" without legal rights. 

2. The Early Government of the City-States. The Ho meric poems picture the city-states ruled by kings. Because land and flocks were the chief sources of wealth, the position of these kings in society was not much superior to that of the other large land-owners.

In northern Hĕl'lås we find a few, such as Ætolia and Ê-pi’rus, which retained their tribal chieftains and never reached the status of city-states at all, but remained little agricultural and stock-raising communities to the very end of Greek history. 

Sparta, partly because of her isolated position, which cut her off from direct communication with the other city-states, remained a kingdom. 

3. Sparta Develops the First Responsible Representa tive Government in History.

Sparta was located in the south-

ern part of the Peloponnesus in the narrow valley of the Eurotas (ū-rō'tas). The Spartans traced their ancestry to the 

Dorian migration. They found the country already inhabited, and were compelled to overpower the earlier settlers in order to secure homes for themselves. Because these people were more numerous- -at least ten to one-the Spartans found it necessary to develop a military organization for their own protection. 

All able-bodied 

Spartans were di

There was a double sovereignty consisting of two joint kings of equal power. Their real authority was gradually lessened, for not only were they assisted by twenty-eight men at least sixty years of age, but later they were guided in their actions by five officials, elected annually from the several regiments by the entire body of citizens. This was the first responsible representative government in history, and that it was successful is shown by the fact that it lasted for five centuries without serious constitutional violence. As the control of Sparta rested in the hands of a few people, it was known as an ŏl'i-gär-chy. 

4. The Spartan Military Autocracy and Its Conse quences. To maintain the efficiency of this military autocracy the Spartans gave remarkable attention to their children. At

ΙΟΥ 

birth each child was inspected by a committee, and if it had any blemishes or appeared to be a weakling, it was carried away to the hills and exposed to wild animals. Until they were seven years old, boys and girls grew up together, but at that age the boys were gathered into groups and placed under the control of tutors. They were taught to be brave and to bear hardships, and were fed frugally in order that they might learn how to forage for a living. They were also taught to be brief in speech whence comes our word “la-con'ic," for the Spartans called their land “La-cō'ni-a.”

At the age of eighteen boys began their military life by being enrolled in the secret police. As members of this organization they had the right to kill helots whenever they thought it necessary for the safety of the state. At twenty they were enrolled in the army and might marry, but they could not live with their wives until they were thirty, when they became full citizens. Until the age of sixty, except when on military expeditions, Spartans took their meals in the barracks, each man contributing a specified amount of provisions as his share of the mess. The immediate result of this military system was to make the Spartans extremely aggressive neighbors. Owing to the narrowness of their training, the Spartans always had an arrogant military attitude, and never were able to meet the other Greeks on a basis of equality. In spite of this, the others had great admiration for Sparta's prowess and simplicity, and her oligarchic government became the ideal of the aristocrats of all Hellas. 

5. The Greeks Colonize the Islands and Shore Lines in the Eastern Mediterranean Area. So limited were the lands belonging to the city-states that soon the younger sons of many land-owners found themselves landless. They turned their attention to the sea and discovered many new places where Greeks could find comfortable homes.

Minor Coast were the first to plant colonies for the purpose of trade. They had many flourishing colonies scattered along the 

Sea of Mär'mó-ra and the Black Sea. So rapidly did the idea spread among the city-states that soon Greek colonies dotted the unoccupied shores of the Mediterranean area from Massilia at the mouth of the Rhone to Nau'crȧ-tis in the delta of the Nile, and they were threatening the commercial supremacy of the Phoenicians.

Although each of these colonies was wholly independent of the mother city-state, its citizens continued to look upon that place as "home," as the present-day English settlers in Australia and Canada think of England. They were usually ready to assist the mother state when she found herself in trouble. 

6. How Colonization Affected the Landowners at 

Home. The immediate effect of all this colonization was a great demand for the things which the colonists had had at home. To pay for them the colonists sent thither all sorts of raw materials, especially foodstuffs. The result was that grain from abroad became so cheap that farmers found themselves unable to raise it in competition. Eventually many gave up and moved into the cities to swell the ever-increasing number of artisans. Those who lacked the initiative to do this remained on their farms and soon found themselves little better off than day laborers, or even slaves. 

7. The Rise of the Tyrants. Such conditions were bound to cause trouble. In many city-states the small arrogant class of large landowners which controlled the government was opposed by the rich merchants and artisans, who felt that they were without the political rights to which their importance entitled them. Out of this situation arose a new kind of ruler called a tyrant.

In those days the word "tyrant" did not mean a person of

evil intentions, but merely a usurper of political power. Usually the tyrants were ambitious, wealthy men who saw an opportunity to obtain control of the government. Sometimes, however, they were real reformers who were anxious to relieve the condition of their people. 

8. Solon Gives a Democratic Tinge to His Reforms at

Athens. At Athens because of the size of Ăt'ti-ca participation in the colonization movement had not been necessary. The landowning nobles had long before taken over the power of the king and administered the state through a board of nine annually elected archons (är'kons). At the end of their year of office, these archons became members of the "Council of the Är-é-op'ȧ-gus" which controlled the government and tried certain criminals. Although Athens did not send out colonies she could not escape the influence of the movement and some of her farmers were enslaved for debt. In 594 B. C. to remedy this situation, Sō'lon, a prominent noble and merchant, was empowered to make reforms.

Solon reduced indebtedness by changing the currency and forbade the selling of a citizen into slavery for debt. He limited the amount of land a man could own and forbade the exportation of certain crops. He established a new constitution with four classes of citizens based on wealth. Only the two upper classes might hold office or sit in the "Council of the 400" which directed public business. The others could only vote in the assembly of the citizens and serve on juries. As an official could be summoned before a jury, this right has led to Solon's being called the "Father of Democracy." 

9. The Tyranny of Pisistratus. The reforms of Solon did not prevent Athens from falling victim to a tyranny. 

Pi-sis'trà-tus, a young man from the hills, gained the privilege of a bodyguard from the Council on the plea that his life was in danger. He soon employed this guard to overthrow the government and, although he was twice driven out,

IIO 

he controlled Athens forty years. Pisistratus favored the merchant class and to protect the trade in grain and salt fish with the Black Sea he seized the fort at the entrance to the Hěl'lèspont. He began the erection of a new temple to Athena, the patron goddess of Athens, and subsidized the preparation of a new edition of the Homeric poems. 

10. Cleisthenes Makes Drastic Reforms in Effort to 

Guard the Public Welfare. After Pisistratus Athens summoned another expert, Cleisthenes (klis'the-nez), to reform her government. First of all he abolished the organization based on the four original tribes and established ten new tribes, composed of citizens selected in such a way that in no single tribe would farmers, drovers, or artisans have a majority. For 

Solon's Council, he substituted a council consisting of fifty men chosen by lot from the two upper classes of each tribe. To supervise the army and the public finances, he provided boards composed of ten citizens, one from each of the tribes. The generals who commanded the army were elected by ballot. 

To insure that no one might become too powerful in the state, Cleisthenes provided that once each year the whole body of citizens should be called together to vote on the question of whether any of their number should be exiled. If any person received a majority of the votes cast, he was Ŏs'trȧ-cīzed, that is, he was banished from the city-state for ten years. 

11. The Rise of Hellenic Consciousness of Superiority. 

Because of the expansion of their world, the Greeks began to feel a strong national pride. They regarded themselves as superior to other peoples, whom they termed "barbarians," because they did not use Greek but seemed to say "bar-bar-bar" when they talked. Out of this consciousness and their common traditions eventually developed certain interstate institutions, especially the great Greek shrines and the Hellenic games.

Among the City-States.

13. What the Hellenic Games Meant to the Greeks. 

The Greeks were an athletic people and as early as 776 B. C. they began holding contests every four years at Olympia in the western part of the Peloponnesus. Other contests were held at Delphi, Ne'mé-a and Corinth. Those at Olympia were dedicated to Zeus. They were open to all Hellenes, but in order to enter them a person had to bear an unblemished reputation as to his everyday conduct and his performance of religious duties.

These contests consisted of horse races and various kinds of track events, such as running, the broad jump, hurling the discus and javelin, and wrestling, and the prize was a crown of wild olive. They also afforded an opportunity to poets to recite their poetry and to authors to read their works to the assembled multitude, and thus they became most effective means of disseminating the literary productions of the Hellenic world. 

Since printing had not yet been invented, these gatherings served the people very much as our press and libraries now do. 

14. The Beginnings of Greek Civilization. Although the 

Indo-European invaders destroyed the earlier Ægean civilization, they must have retained many of its features. As the 

Hellenes advanced in civilization, they borrowed extensively from many different quarters. From the Phoenician traders they obtained the alphabet, to which they added the vowels. 

From the Egyptians, they acquired mathematics; from the 

Babylonians weights and measures, methods of computing time, and a knowledge of the heavenly bodies. 

The way in which the Hellenes used these acquisitions was unique. Among oriental nations the priests had been the only persons who had the leisure and opportunity for study and investigation. In Greece, there were no great priesthoods, so knowledge could develop independently of religion. The Greeks

15. The Advance in

Material Things. In material things the early 

Greeks also made rapid progress. Although the statues of their sculptors still remained rather stiff and had faces with a curious grin, unlike those of their oriental tutors, they stood erect without any back support. Their temples, which originally had been made of wood, they now began to build of stone. For the tree trunks which had served to hold up the floor they substituted columns, and often decorated the exterior with flutings and carved capitals.

From the various kinds of columns used by the 

Greeks have come their three orders of architecture, Doric, Ionic, and Corin'thi-an. In the Doric order columns had twenty

flutings and rested directly on the floor. The capitals were square blocks with round bases. On the capitals rested stone beams or the är'chi-trave, above which were tri'glyphs and mět'ó-pès. In the Ionic order the columns had twenty-four flutings and rested on a base. 

Their capitals were decorated with vólute. There were no tri'glyphs or měť'ópes above the architrave. The Corinthian was like the

Ionic except that the capitals had decorations in the form of à-can'thus leaves.

A GREEK TRIREME

The Doric with its shorter and thicker column gave the impression of solidity and strength, the Ionic that of slenderness and grace and the Corinthian of richness and ornamentation. 

Shipping developed from small open boats to great tri'rêmes with three banks of oarsmen, and some of the tyrants seem to have possessed considerable navies. The manufacture of pottery appears to have appealed to the early Greeks more than ter testing a vase taken from did any other industry, and the trail of their traders can be traced by the potsherds. Some of these vases already showed the remarkable form and lines which were to make Greek art unexcelled throughout the ages.

CHAPTER XII HOW WARS WITH PERSIA AWAKEN THE GREEKS TO A SENSE OF POWER 1. The Athenians Win a Great Victory at Marathon. 

When the Greek cities along the Asia Minor coast rose against their Persian Master, they called on the city-states of the mainland for aid. Sparta refused, but Athens and the little town of Ě-ret'ri-a together sent twenty-five ships. The Persians were successful and Darius ordered the punishment of those upstarts who had presumed to interfere in the affairs of the great Persian Empire.

In 490 B. C. the Persians sailed across the Ægean and after burning Eretria landed on the little plain of Măr'a-thon, barely twenty miles from Athens. The terrified Athenians dispatched a runner to Sparta for aid. This man ran the hundred and fifty miles in thirty-six hours, only to find the Spartans unable to start because they were in the midst of a religious festival. 

Meanwhile, from a position on the hillside back of the plain, the Athenians under command of Mil-ti'a-dēs gave battle to the Persian host, and were so successful that the Persians fled to their ships and sailed back to Asia.

Darius was so angered by this defeat that he was more determined to humble the Athenians, but his death postponed this for ten years. 

2. Athens Sets Her House in Order. The Athenian vic tory had two far-reaching effects. First, the Athenians adopted the use of lot for the election of archons who still retained much power. Then, under the leadership of their great statesman, Thé-mis'tó-cles, they decided to rely upon a fleet for their defense. 118

WARS WITH PERSIA AWAKEN THE GREEKS

DARIUS PLANNING WAR ON THE GREEKS 

Part of the vase painting showing Darius on his throne consulting his advisers, while below, the treasurer is collecting the war taxes. 

Themistocles realized that it was hopeless for the Athenians to muster an army large enough to overcome the Persians, but he believed that a fleet might so harass them that land attack would prove useless. Just at this time a new vein of silver was discovered in the state mines at Lau'rï-um and there was a great sum of money to be distributed among the citizens. Themistocles prevailed upon the people to use this money to build and equip a fleet of triremes. The other city-states were asked to join in the defense of Hellas, but even in the face of danger 

Greece could not unite. 

3. The Persians Again Invade Greece and Destroy 

Athens. In the autumn of 481 B. C. it was announced that 

Xerxes (zûrk'sēz), the new "Great King," was assembling the greatest army and navy the world had yet seen. Already he had sent envoys to the Greek city-states, demanding earth and

water as a symbol of submission. Athens and the states in southern Greece refused, but some of those in the north yielded. 

The great problem for southern Greece was to find some means of acting together. The tyrant of the Greek city of Syracuse in 

Sicily offered to join forces with them if they would intrust to him the supreme command. Fortunately for him this was refused, for soon afterward he had troubles of his own, since the Persians stirred up the Carthaginians to attack the Greek colonies in Sicily. In the end the Spartans were given command of all the forces, sea as well as land, but the total number was pitifully small compared with the great host which Xerxes led into Greece.

Crossing the Hellespont by a bridge of boats, the Persians advanced along the north shore of the Ægean, meeting with no opposition until they reached Ther-mop'y-læ, a narrow pass between the sea and mountains filled with hot springs, its name meaning "hot gates." Here the Spartans under Lé-ŏn'ì-dàs made a brave but futile attempt to hold back the enemy, since a traitor showed the Persians a badly guarded trail over the mountain. Leonidas sent away his other troops, but he and his Spartans with some Thebans and Thespians died fighting. 

4. The Greeks, Thoroughly Aroused, Defeat the Persians on Both Land and Sea. As nothing could now save 

Athens, the army withdrew to the Isthmus of Corinth, the only practical place where they could make a stand, leaving the city to its fate. Meanwhile, the Greek navy lay in the bay of Săl'a-mis, and here the wily Themistocles by strategy induced the Persians to make an attack. The battle which followed became one of the most famous in history. The Greeks won a complete victory. Xerxes, fearing a loss of his bridge, hastened back to Asia, leaving under a trusted general an army for the subjugation of Greece.

The Greeks now roused themselves for a final effort. The next spring, near Pla-tæ'à, they defeated the Persians on land.

121 On the same day, the Persian fleet sustained a terrible defeat off Myc'a-le on the Asia Minor coast. Salamis and Mycale gave the Greeks control of the sea and drove the Persians from the Egean, although not till thirty years later was a treaty concluded acknowledging Greek rule over the Ægean sea and binding the Persians not to maintain an army within three days' march of its shores. 

5. The Rise of a New Athens. When the Athenians returned to Athens, they found their homes burned and their temples and other public buildings destroyed. Out of the ruins, however, soon arose a larger and far more beautiful city. They wished to surround the place with a wall, but the Spartans opposed the idea, insisting that the Persians might capture Athens again, and if so, this wall would enable them to enslave the Greeks. 

Once more Themistocles resorted to a trick and gained time to build a part of the wall before the Spartans knew what was happening. 

Evidence of this haste may still be seen in the old buildings which are found in its ruins. 

ATHENIAN GRAVE STONE 

Themistocles also developed Athens' new fortified port, the Pi-ra'us, five miles distant from the city proper. Later this port was joined to Athens by two long walls so that the city should never be cut off from the sea. 

Athenian foreign commerce now increased rapidly and the city began to enjoy a time of unheard-of prosperity. The "good times" were not shared by all, for while the profits of the traders and manufacturers were large, wages were low and the cost of living was high.

6. The "Delian League" Grows Into an Athenian Em pire. Out of their conflict with the Persians, the Greeks inherited two live questions. First, how should Greece be defended against a Persian "come back"; and secondly, should the Greeks of Asia Minor be included in their defensive plans.

Among other requirements each member of this league (eventually there were two hundred or more) had to contribute annually either ships and men or an amount of money for the common defense. The amount of the assessment was said to have been set by År-is-ti'dēs, the Athenian, and so fair was it that he was called "the just." Because the treasure belonging to the league was to be kept in the Temple of Apollo on the Island of Delos, the confederacy became known to his tory as the Delian League. 

7. Athens Becomes a Democratic State. After the Persian wars there were two parties in Athenian politics-the Conservatives and the Democrats. The Conservatives were landowners and wealthy aristocrats, who wished to keep the control

WARS WITH PERSIA AWAKEN THE GREEKS 123 

of the state in their own hands and to maintain a close friendship with Sparta. The Democrats were members of the lower classes. They did not care much for Sparta and were eager to increase the power of Athens in the League, partly because the building and manning of its ships offered them employment.

In 461 B. C., while Cimon (si'mon), the leader of the Conservatives, was away, the Democrats enacted a law which weakened the power of the Council of the Areopagus, the stronghold of the Conservative party. After that, the government of Athens passed into the hands of the De'mos or lower classes, whence our word "democratic." In order that the Demos might be able to afford to serve as jurors in the law courts, their new leader, Pericles, arranged for the state to pay a small fee for their service. It is interesting to observe that Pericles ΠΕΡΙΚΛΗΣ 

ZANBINDY ΑΘΗΝΑΙΟΣ PERICLES 

He is said to have worn the helmet because of the peculiar shape of his head. The inscription reads, "Pericles, Son of Xanthipcos, Athenian." and most of the Democratic leaders gained control of the state through the army, since the generals were now the only officials elected by ballot. 

8. Athenian Imperialism Leads to Downfall of Athens.

The Democratic system of Athens was intensely disliked by the oligarchic Spartans, and when Pericles made a series of alliances with the Greek states on the mainland, war broke out, and Athens had to give up these connections. The Athenians then turned their attention to the trade with the west which brought them into conflict with Corinth, an important member of the Peloponnesian League. About the same time they ex-

cluded another member, Megara, from the Athenian markets because she was competing with Athenian gardeners. Such actions led to the great Peloponnesian War (431–404 B. C.) and brought about the downfall of Athens. 

Sparta had an army and Athens had a fleet. The Athenians gathered within their walls and the Spartans ravaged Attica. A plague broke out and killed a third of the Athenians and soon afterward Pericles died. The control of Athens then passed into the hands of the politicians. The war dragged on for a few years with little accomplished until the death of two vainglorious leaders, the Spartan Brä'si-das and the Athenian Cleon (klā'on), permitted a peace. Falling under the spell of Alcibiades (ǎl-si-bi'à-dēz), a brilliant young schemer, the Athenians soon started hostilities again with an expedition against Syracuse, but their whole force was destroyed. 

When Athens' allies began to revolt, Sparta surrendered the Asiatic Greeks to Persia in return for money to equip a navy. 

Even with this advantage the war lasted eight years more until treachery permitted the destruction of the last Athenian fleet. 

Athens had to surrender her navy, tear down her long walls, and give up the League. 

9. The Greek States Exhaust Their Resources and Dis union Triumphs. The example of Athens in attempting to control the Greeks was followed by the Spartans. Sparta established oligarchies in many of the city-states, and protected them with garrisons, but she soon fell out with Persia. She was forced to turn to Persia again, and asked the great king to intervene. In 387 B. C. he sent down the famous decree ordering the Greeks to keep the peace.

Under E-păm-i-non'dăs, who was able to defeat the Spartan army by new tactics in battle-the use of the phalanx,―Thebes now hoped to take the place of Sparta but the early death of her leader at the battle of Mantinea (măn-tế-në'yȧ) in 362 soon ended her hopes. In these struggles the Greek states exhausted

their resources and wore themselves out. They had often held interstate congresses to reach a basis for peace, but the ambition of leaders and the influence of Persian gold and their own adherence to the city-state kept them from forming a union.

CHAPTER XIII ATHENS HAS HER GOLDEN AGE DURING THE DAYS OF PERICLES 

The period during which Pericles controlled the destinies of 

Athens is known as her "golden age." Athenians then enjoyed a freedom of life such as has been seldom seen before or since. In no other country or time have people been allowed to talk so freely or to ridicule so many things-even their officials and gods-as Athenians during the golden age. They enjoyed this license only because Athens believed in her own institutions and was confident of her strength. The golden age was also a period of great æsthetic advancement for Athens. 

Pericles adorned the city in ways that have never since been equalled, and Athenians wrote some of the finest literature that has ever been produced. 

1. Society During the "Golden Age." Athenian society was divided into three classes-citizens. foreigners, or měť'ics, and slaves. Although citizens alone enjoyed full political rights and privileges, the gulf between them and the other two classes was not so great as might be imagined. Slaves and freemen worked side by side on the public buildings at the same rate of pay; in fact, one Athenian insisted that one could not tell the difference between a freeman and a slave either by dress or conduct. The position of foreigners could not have been very embarrassing, for they made up a large part of the population. 

2. Women Led Restricted Lives in Athens. The life of an Athenian woman was much restricted. She was completely under the control of her husband or other male relatives. She 126

ATHENS HAS HER GOLDEN AGE 

127 was supposed to stay at home and busy herself with domestic duties, where, if married, she had certain authority. In the simpler homes, she did the cooking, made the clothes, and looked after all the other affairs of the establishment; where there were slaves to do this work, she had full charge of them. She was not supposed to go about the streets, nor to be seen in public places except at the

A vase painting. special festivals for women, unless accompanied by her husband. 

3. How Children Were Educated. Education was strictly

ATHENIAN SCHOOL 

This vase painting shows the pupil before his teacher who is holding a book. The man with the staff is the boy's pedagogue, or tutor. On the wall hang a counting device, a lyre, and a wine cup. a private affair. If his father could afford it, at the age of seven the 

Athenian boy was led off to school by his "pedagogue" or "boy leader." 

The cheapest of these schools were conducted in the streets and marketplaces; the better schools, in the residences of the masters. For the girls, meagre educational opportunities only were available, on the theory that women did not need an education beyond what they received at home.

The curriculum consisted largely of reading, writing, and arithmetic-together with singing and reciting poetry, especially the Iliad and the Odyssey, and oftentimes playing the

lyre. Much attention was given to athletics-running, jumping, wrestling, boxing, and discus throwing-on the principle that a sound body meant a sound mind. 

As the boys became older, they spent a considerable part of their afternoons at the gymnasium, which was the meeting place of the most brilliant minds of the community. At the age of eighteen, they were given shields and spears for their two years of military training required of young citizens. At this time they took the famous oath of citizenship: 

I will not disgrace the sacred arms, nor will I abandon the man next to me, whoever he may be. I will bring aid to the ritual of the state and to the holy duties, both alone and in company with many. 

Moreover, my native commonwealth I will not transmit lessened, but larger and better than I have received it. I will obey those who from time to time are judging; and the established statutes I will obey, and whatever other regulations the people shall enact unanimously. If any one shall attempt to destroy the statutes, I will not permit it, but will repel (such a person) both alone and with all. 

Furthermore, I will honor the ancestral religion. 

4. Public Service Was Required of All Citizens. The average Athenian's life required that he should have a certain amount of leisure to devote to politics. If he had to work for a living, he planned that this would not prevent him from finding time for public service. This explains why Pericles arranged for the payment of a small fee for service on the jury, so that even the poorer citizens might be able to spend some time in public service.

Even if he were not serving in the army or navy, or on the jury, or in one of the many state offices, the Assembly demanded his presence thirty times a year. Besides, there were several public festivals that lasted from one to three days, in which he was supposed to take part. All of this service was rendered cheerfully, for the average Athenian was not animated

ATHENS HAS HER GOLDEN AGE 

129 by a desire to amass a fortune. Moreover, most of the taxes were paid by the rich, while most of the work was done by the slaves. 

5. Various Ways a Citizen Could Serve the State. The public life of a citizen began with his attendance upon the Assembly. Here he voted upon all laws that were proposed by the committees of the Council of the Five Hundred, looked into the conduct of the magistrates, and decided whether there should be war or peace.

As he became older, he might become a member of this Council. Then he would help to supervise the administration of the state, as well as to prepare the laws to be laid before the Assembly and to determine what persons might hold office.

In old age he would give a part of his time to serving on the  juries.

But these were not all the ways in which a citizen might

Lysicrates, whose chorus won the prize, set this up in 344 B. C. serve the state. Many able-bodied men were needed for garrison duty or as marines for the navy. Hundreds of other men were required for the choruses of the plays which were an important part of the annual festivals, and this practically amounted to a public service, even though it was paid for by private individuals. A mason or a stonecutter or a painter could work on the public buildings. One branch of the public service was closed to them-the police force-for Athenians resented being arrested by their equals.

STANDARD WEIGHT OF ATHENS 7. How Business Was Conducted in Athens. The busi ness of Athens was centred around the market-place and the Place of Commerce. In small permanent shops and temporary stalls the buying and selling of goods were carried on. The farmers brought their vegetables and animals, and fishermen their fish, much as they do to a modern market. The Place of Commerce dealt in big business. Here were received the cargoes of grain, salt fish, wine, and the other things which were brought to Athens from all parts of the Mediterranean to be exchanged for her pottery, olive oil, and cosmetics. The word demo(s)—“people." shops and factories were small. As far as possible business was carried on only in the morning, to leave the afternoon free for gossiping and exercise. 

8. Athens Becomes the Centre of Hellenic Culture. 

The Athens of Pericles inherited from the Ionian cities of Asia Minor their pre-eminence in learning, after the latter had been ruined by the Persians. The desire of Pericles to make 

Athens the most beautiful city of the Hellenic world, and the enthusiasm of his fellow citizens for learning attracted the foremost artists, men of letters, and teachers of the day. 

This four pound weight carries the stamp of the metronomos- regulator of measures in the centre.

The large letters form the While the artists busied themselves decorating the new public buildings and the men of letters competed for the prizes which were awarded at the state festivals, a group of popular teachers, the Soph'ists, were instructing the man in the street in those things needed for a political career.

The Sophists devoted themselves to the problems of society.

A CORNER OF THE PARTHENON 

Above the capital of the Doric column are the abacus, the architrave, the triglyphs and metopes, the gutte, or drops, the cornice, the cymatium, and the antefixes at the eaves.

The basis of their teaching was common sense and they endeavored to approach every problem from the standpoint of logic. Crude as was their teaching, they were really the first teachers of political science and sociology.

CHAPTER XIV THE GREEKS DEVELOP GENIUS AND TALENT SUCH AS THE WORLD HAD NEVER KNOWN 1. How Greek Life Changed. The three generations fol lowing the Persian Wars saw some important changes in Greek life. First, there was a marked increase in individuality, resulting in a number of outstanding characters. Next, there was a violent conflict between different types of government, particularly oligarchy and democracy, and this conflict gave rise to much political thinking and discussion.

Although democracy passed through some terrible struggles during the Peloponnesian War and after Logg

De votion to the state was no longer sufficient to induce public service. Henceforth the citizen expected to be paid, not only for holding office, but even for attending the Assembly, and, strange as it may seem, for his presence at the theatre. 2. How the Drama Developed in Greece. The wine god 

Dionysius had long been publicly worshipped at Athens with songs and choruses, in which the singers were dressed in goat skins, hence the name tragedy or "goat song." After the Persian Wars Eschylus (es'ki-lus) introduced a speaker in addition to the chorus leader and real drama began. Later Soph'ocles added a third actor. Twice each year competitions were held at which twelve of the best plays were selected for presentation. Most of these plays have disappeared but we still have a few from Eschylus, Sophocles, and Euripides (ū-rip'iděz).

Comedy arose in the same manner from the "village songs" of exuberant revellers. Contests in the writing of comedies were also held each year but we have now only those of Ăris-tŏph'a-nēs. He lived during the Peloponnesian Wars and his works are full of witty reference to the political and social life of the time. 

3. The Beginning of History Writing. Prose literature had its beginning among the Ionians of Asia Minor during the sixth century B. C., but history proper did not make its appearance until the "golden age" when Herodotus, a native of Hǎl-i-cär-năs´sus, wrote a history of the struggle with Persia. 

In such high regard was this work held that three centuries later Herodotus was declared by the Roman orator Ci-ce-ro to have been the "father of history." Almost of the same date as

Herodotus was Thú-cydi-dēs, who wrote a history of the Peloponnesian War. Herodotus travelled far and wide to collect his materials and filled his pages with interesting and valuable information, Thucydides dealt with a smaller field and probed deep into the passions and motives of men. Herodotus attributed many events to the will of the gods, while Thucydides sought his explanations in the passions and wills of men. 

4. Oratory Was of Great Importance in Greek Life, 

Among the ancients, owing to the lack of books, oral speech was much more important than with us. 

In Hellas, every citizen was required to be his own lawyer, and much opportunity for public speaking was afforded by the assemblies. At an early date there appears to have developed an art of speech with definite rules, to which was given the name rhetoric. 

This was first taught at Syracuse, but was brought to Athens in 427 B. C. by a Sophist. Under the tutelage of these teachers men learned how to make the weaker cause seem the stronger by subtle argument and by clever grouping of facts. Ï-soc'rà-tēs had much influence in freeing oratory from many of these defects. The greatest of Greek orators was Dë-mos' thế-nēs, who

137 fought for the ideals of the "golden age" but a century too late. 

5. Socrates, the Great Teacher and Foremost of Early 

Philosophers. Of all the gifts to posterity by the Greeks, the desire which they aroused in man to seek an explanation of the origin, nature, and relationship of things, that is, to philosophize, still ranks high. An important change in philosophical 

SOCRATES, PLATO, AND ARISTOTLE 

The busts of these three philosophers give one a good idea of how an intellectual Greek looked. thinking was brought about by Socrates. While the Athenians. were fighting Sparta for control of Greece, this interesting man was standing in the market-place searching for truth but he did not teach for money.

Socrates' teaching consisted primarily of asking questions. 

These questions were meant not so much to acquire information as to set the person to thinking. According to Socrates, much of the thinking was poor because persons did not understand exactly what was meant by the words and terms they

used. He sought, therefore, to make his hearers grasp what such terms as "truth" and "justice" really meant.

Socrates was interested in questions of ethics and he tried to associate belief in the gods with ethical ideas. Because he believed in the immortality of the soul, he was finally charged by the father of one of his disciples with corruption of the youth, and was found guilty and put to death by being made to drink a cup of hemlock juice. 

6. Plato Had One of the Greatest Minds the World 

Has Known. The most illustrious of Socrates' disciples was 

Plato, upon whose Dialogues or imaginary conversations between Socrates and his disciples we depend for most of our knowledge of the master's teachings, since Socrates himself wrote nothing. Following the work of Socrates, Plato proceeded to investigate things in general, and developed the theory of a spiritual world outside the material. To him this spiritual world formed a part of every person. This emphasis upon the spiritual side of things has made Plato's influence of great importance in the history of human thought. 

Plato loved the beautiful and orderly, and pondered much over the social and political discontent which pervaded Hellas during the period following the "golden age." From his thinking came his Republic and Laws in which he attempted to solve some of the important political problems in an idealistic way. 

This was the first of a long series of attempts that have been made by philosophers and others to describe an ideal state. 

7. Aristotle's Writings Become Almost the Sole Text- Books for Over a Thousand Years. To the school estab lished by Plato in the Academy at Athens came one day Ăr'istot-le of Stagira (sta-jï'rà). It is doubtful whether any age ever produced another such mind as Aristotle possessed. He differed from both Socrates and Plato. He would have nothing to do with the imagination, and confined his reasoning to facts.

With aid from Alexander of Măc'é-don, whose tutor he had been, Aristotle was able to collect from far and near much that was known on many subjects, and to publish the first treatises which dealt with science, literature, and politics in a scientific way. For a thousand years or more these were almost the only text-books of Europe. 

Aristotle had no confidence in democracy. From a study of the constitutions of more than a hundred states, he became a firm believer in monarchy as the only government capable of insuring order and stability. Because slavery and the subjection of women apparently had proved successful, he approved both.

CHAPTER XV  IN ALEXANDER OF MACEDON WHO CONQUERS AND HELLENIZES ASIA MINOR AND EGYPT 

While Athens and Sparta and Thebes were wasting the strength of all Greece with their struggles for supremacy, a new power was rising on their north-the Măc-e-do'nì-ans. 

The Macedonians were descendants of one of the later Indo- European races which swept down into the Balkan Peninsula. 

They were closely related to the Greeks. They had been slow in their development.

During the days of the Theban supremacy one of their princes, Philip by name, had served as a hostage at Thebes, and while there had learned the art of warfare at the hands of her great general, Epaminondas. There, too, Philip seems to have had the idea that, if all the Greek city-states could be brought together, the Persian power could be overthrown. We shall see how Philip put his idea into effect, and how his son Alexander with a genius for leadership such as the world had never known unified the world of the Greeks and Persians. 

1. Philip of Macedon. Soon after Philip returned to 

Macedon, he usurped the kingship, overpowered the nobility, and compelled all to recognize his leadership. He at once seized the gold mines on Mount Pån-gæ'us and used their wealth to make the Macedonian army the most perfect fighting machine the world had seen. He improved the "Theban Phalanx" by making its ranks deeper and he used catapults to hurl stones. 

Philip extended the power of Macedon far to the north and along the Thracian shores to the Hellespont. Apparently Athenian Demosthenes was the only Greek who saw the danger 140

threatening the city-states. So indifferent were the Athenians that they failed to heed Demosthenes' denunciation of Philip, even after he had begun the conquest of the Thracian allies. 

2. Philip Organizes a New League of the City-States. 

Philip soon found an excuse for interfering in Greek affairs. 

The Phocians (fō'shăns) had seized the Delphic shrine. Philip was asked to help drive out the Phocians and as a reward he was selected to preside over the games. 

At last Athens organized a combination of city-states against him, only to be defeated in 338 B. C. Shortly afterward Philip called a council of states at Corinth to which all except Sparta sent representatives. A new League between the city-states provided for the independence of each, for peace between them, and for the freedom of the sea. There was to be an alliance with Philip, and both were to wage war on the Persians under his command. Early in 336 B. C. Philip sent an army across the Hellespont, but was assassinated before he could follow. 

3. Alexander Becomes King of Macedon. Philip's son, Alexander, the pupil of Aristotle, was hardly twenty when he came to the throne. Both the kingdom and the league rose in revolt only to find a master. He was elected to his father's office as head of the expedition against Persia and in 334 began to free the Greeks of Asia Minor. The lack of a navy forced him to occupy Phoenicia, but before he reached it, the "Great King," Darius IV, had slipped in behind him. Darius was defeated at Is'sus in a narrow place between the mountains and the sea. On reaching Egypt, Alexander was welcomed by the 

Egyptians as a deliverer from Persian tyranny. To protect himself from being attacked in the rear by the peoples of northern Africa, he founded the city of Alexandria near the westernmost mouth of the Nile. In order that he might be looked upon as a legitimate pharaoh, he caused himself to be recognized by the priesthood of Amon, whom the Greeks identified with their god Zeus.

Alexander then felt at liberty to invade Persia and in 330 B. C. he started along the Fertile Crescent. Near Är-be'lä 

Darius made his last stand, but the heavy-armed cavalry and the phalanx proved superior to the scythed-chariots and mounted archers. The "Great King" fled and was later hunted down like a wild animal. Alexander and his army occupied Babylon and seized the treasures of Susa and of Persepolis and burned the palace of Xerxes to avenge the Persian destruction of 

Greek cities. Alexander himself became the "Great King." 

4. Alexander Becomes the "Great King" Over Almost

All the Known World. Alexander was no longer king of little Macedon, but ruler of "the East and the West," and conceived the idea of unifying the Greek and Persian worlds. As the first step he married a Persian princess, and ordered his officers to take Persian wives. Next he established colonies of 

Greeks in many places, and thus extended Hellenic culture throughout the East. He adopted the Persian system of political organization and in some cases even left Persians in control of provinces. And finally, in place of the simplicity which had marked the Macedonian court, he surrounded himself with all the pomp of the Persians. So vast was the treasure which he distributed that even in distant Rome prices began to rise on account of the increased amount of money put into circulation.

The next seven years were spent by Alexander in a conquest of the strange half-civilized peoples toward the north and east, leaving behind a line of Greek settlements. At last, on the banks of the Indus his soldiers mutinied, and he was compelled to abandon his conquests. On his way back he marched a part of his troops straight across the desert to Babylon, and embarked the remainder upon ships which finally reached the head. of the Persian Gulf.

While Alexander was in Babylon planning the conquest of Arabia and the west, he contracted a fever, and died before his

thirty-third birthday. No other man had ever conquered so much territory in so short a space of time, and few have ever conceived of organizing human affairs on so grand a scale as Alexander. 

5. Alexander's Empire Is Divided Among Three of His 

Generals. Alexander had devoted too much time to conquest

One after another of his generals tried in vain to seize the royal power, until at last three were content to become rulers of only such parts as they could hold. Ptol'é-my took Egypt, Palestine, and the

The memory of Alexander's success and their own conflicting claims kept these dynasties in continual conflict. All the rulers were absolute and most of them considered themselves divine. 

Ptolemy located his capital at Alexandria and made this place the greatest city of the age. In order to aid mariners in finding its harbor, he caused to be built a great lighthouse, the Pharos, towering 325 feet above the sea. His son, Ptolemy II, founded the famous Alexandrian Museum and Library and endowed them with funds that scholars might live and study there as guests of the state.

Although the Seleucids (sé-lu'sīds) originally ruled over a kingdom far greater than that of the Ptolemies, they were at war much of the time with the Ptolemies, seeking control of Palestine and Asia Minor. As a result of dynastic troubles, their territories dwindled away.

The Antigonids soon lost Thrace. Although they tried to exercise control over Greece through garrisons at Corinth, Chalcis, and Dē-mē'tri-us, they met continual opposition from the new leagues and from the Ptolemies. 

6. Colonists to the New Kingdoms Weaken the Old 

City-States. The opportunities for colonization afforded by the Hellenistic kingdoms in the East drained the population of the city-states, and the strength of the kingdoms put an end to their importance. Rhōdes alone retained its prestige because it lay at the crossroads between Hellas and the new kingdoms in the East. In vain had Dē-mē'tri-us, the son of Antigonus, laid siege to it, and when he realized it could not be taken, he turned over to the Rhodians all of his siege material. Out of the proceeds from the sale the Rhodians erected the great "Colossus," one of the "seven wonders" of the ancient world.

Athens remained the intellectual centre, but Sparta struggled

along with a steadily decreasing number of citizens, a mere shadow of her former greatness. In their struggle with the 

Antigonids, the city-states were again forced into union, and formed two leagues instead of one. Those states south of the Sinope 2 MACEDONIA

These leagues were federal states. Each had a central assembly and a central executive. This executive had power to raise taxes, to levy armies, to make war and peace, and to settle disputes between the component city-states. 

7. The Changes Wrought by Alexander Turn the 

Greeks to Trade and Manufacturing. We have seen how

Alexander's conquest of Persia let loose a flood of gold and silver upon the world and threw open half a continent to Greek commerce. When the rise of the great Hellenistic kingdom pushed the city-states into the background, the pursuit of politics lost much of its interest. More and more the Greeks turned

to trade and manufacturing, and developed that skill in business which still makes them an important part of the commercial life of the Near East. This brought about marked improvements in the standards of living. The rugs and fabrics and furniture of the East, its cosmetics and perfumes, and its fruits and sweets were soon in high demand.

Greek commerce increased rapidly, and Greek vessels became familiar sights not only on the Red Sea and in the Persian

Gulf but even on the Indian Ocean. Greek manufactures were carried eastward in constantly increasing quantities to supply the needs of Greek colonists and to be exchanged for the jewels and spices of India, and the aromatic gums and tropical products of Arabia and Central Africa. Alexandria, Antioch (ăn'ti-ok), and Rhodes became the leading markets of the eastern Mediterranean.

Due to their association with the serfdom that existed in Egypt and in the Kingdom of the Seleucids, the Greeks came to look upon slavery as a proper condition for those who worked the soil. Slavery, too, became an important part of society, but seems to have been largely confined to the cities. 

However, the worst feature of this society was the enormous number of free men who were little better off than slaves. 

8. Hellenistc Culture Spreads Far Into Asia. There was another side to the picture. Greek culture was spread over great sections of the East where with the culture of the older civilizations it produced the development now known as Hěl-lenistic. In the process the Greeks themselves developed a common language. Syria, the coast of Palestine, and parts of the interior of Asia Minor became Hellenized, while India and Central Asia gained a new cultural impulse from the Hellenic contact. A Greek kingdom survived in Central Asia for over two hundred years.

The new Greek cities of Asia, to which this cultural development was so largely due, were strangely like modern cities.

They were laid out in rectangular blocks and adorned with colonnades and statues. They had paved streets, a water supply, policing and lighting arrangements, and theatres, gymnasiums, THE NIKE OF SAMOTHRACE 

This beautiful statue, set up in honor of a naval victory, is a winged figure of Nike, or Victory, poised on the prow of a warship. It is one of the finest examples of Hellenistic art. and parks. Most of them enjoyed independence in local affairs, but all paid the taxes and accepted the authority of the kings. 

9. How the Alexandrian Museum Gave a Priceless Service to the World. The Ptolemies, as we have seen, founded the great Museum at Alexandria. This was the first real university in history, and it was unequalled until modern times. 

In this institution were found lecture halls, botanical and zoological gardens, an astronomical observatory, and a great li-

brary. For this library funds were provided to collect copies of all the books that could be found. In the process of doing this scholars compared closely the various editions and thus developed the science of phi-lŏl'ó-gy. To these Alexandrian scholars we owe the division of literary works into separate books or chapters, so that the text might be more conveniently found on the rolls.

The Library at Alexandria served also as a sort of great publishing house, for an army of editors and copyists was continually employed revising and duplicating its parchments. To some of these copies which eventually reached Europe we owe much of our knowledge of the wisdom of the Greeks. Here, too, was made the first translation of the Old Testament into Greek, the so-called Sep'tú-a-gint, because it was said to have been done by seventy scholars. 

10. Many Wonderful Discoveries in Science Were

Made at the Museum. To the Museum came many of the most renowned scientists of the times. Foremost among them was the mathematician Euclid (u'klid), whose geometry was used as a text-book until the nineteenth century. Another was 

Ēr-à-tõs'thé-nēs who set up sun-dials at Alexandria and Sỹe'nē, and by measuring the angle of the sun, computed the circumference of the earth, making it only one-seventh larger than it really is. Hither came Ăr-is-tär'chus of Sã'mos insisting that the sun was much larger than the earth and that the earth revolved around the sun. Unfortunately this theory was not accepted, but an older theory, later known as the Ptolemaic System, which taught that the planets revolved in spheres about the earth, prevailed. A visitor to the Museum was Är-chimēdēs, of Syracuse, who discovered the principles of the levers, of the screw, and of specific gravity. It was he who kept the besieging Romans in terror by the machines which he devised to tip over their ships and to pick up men from the ground outside the walls of Syracuse.

11. New Philosophies Devised to Meet the New Con ditions of Life. Such great political and social changes as accompanied the expansion of Hellenism had their effect upon 

Greek thinking. The older philosophies of Plato and Aristotle which rested on the idea of the city-state were no longer valid. 

To meet the new conditions various novel systems were devised. Foremost among them stand out Stoicism (stō'ĭ-sĭzm) and Ép-i-ct-rể ănism. 

Stoicism taught that there was one supreme god who manifested himself in nature. Since man was a part of this nature, it was his duty to conform to the natural laws by which this supreme being expressed itself. This, of course, implied the brotherhood of man. It also meant that whatever happened was a part of the divine scheme and should be accepted calmly without joy or sorrow, hence our word "stoical."

Epicureanism insisted that pleasure was the main aim of man's existence. But Epicurus, its founder, did not mean merely sensuous pleasure; but rather pleasure that should be lasting or permanent. Because of the wrong application of the doctrine made by many of his disciples, the word “Epicurean" has come to have a meaning of "care-free."
