CHAPTER XVI HOW ROME RISES TO POWER IN THE WESTERN MEDITERRANEAN WORLD 

We have dealt with the contributions of the Greeks to Græco- Roman Civilization. We are now ready to consider the contributions of the Romans. Considering the marvellous gifts of the Greeks which Rome absorbed as part of her culture, we may wonder what worthwhile things Rome could give to the world. Fortunately, genius lay in the very fields in which

Greece showed deplorable, weakness-the fields of law, order, and organization of government. By means of this Rome established a supremacy which she was able to maintain for over a thousand years.

Let us see how Roman leaders stood by their ideals in defense of the Republic; how the splendor of Empire displaced it, and how as master of the whole Mediterranean World Rome carried her ways of living to the barbarians of northern Europe as far as Britain; how in the years of declining power her institutions stood, while her citizenship declined in character and in manpower until the barbarians from the North overran the Empire of the West and led the way to a new order of things in western Europe. 

1. Early Peoples in the Western Mediterranean Basin. 

The Italian peninsula and the island of Sicily almost divide the Mediterranean into two seas. The western of these saw no great early civilization rise along its shores, although it had been inhabited since paleolithic times. Its civilizations, when they did develop, were the result of invasions of peoples and cultures from the primitive North and the more advanced East. 151

The earlier of these peoples brought with them a knowledge of primitive agriculture, and eventually of the working of iron. 

At some time before 1000 B. C. a group of Indo-European peoples, who may roughly be called Italians (i-tǎl'yans), poured through the passes in the Austrian Alps and overran the greater part of the Italian peninsula, settling in many little groups. 

One of these, the Latins, established themselves along the

Families played an important part in the history of Rome. They were grouped into gěn'tēs, and every Roman bore the name of his family and of his gens. At the head of the family was the oldest father, who enjoyed almost absolute authority over it. In every 

Roman home, the busts of forefathers occupied a prominent place. 

5. Rome Becomes a Republic.

In 509 B. C. the rule of the Etruscan kings became so unbearable that Tär-quin'i-us Su-per bus, the last of the traditional seven, was expelled. The patricians now established a new form of government, headed by two con'suls, to be elected annually by the army voting as centuries. Both of these consuls exercised the same power as the kings and acted as a check on each other. In time of emergency they could appoint in their place a single official, known as a dic'ta-tor, who might hold office for not more than six months. All law-making was still controlled by the Senate, which continued to be a strictly patri-

HOW ROME RISES TO POWER 

155 cian body. Although this government was called a Republic, the control by the patricians really made it an oligarchy. 

6. The Plebeians Revolt and Better Their Condition. 

Naturally the plebeians were dissatisfied with their condition, and waited for an opportunity to better it. From the beginning the new state had to fight its neighbors. As both plebeians and patricians were enrolled in the army, the more numerous plebeians made up a large part of it. On the eve of a campaign they mutinied and demanded to have officials of their own to represent them in judicial affairs. This was permitted, and they elected two trib'unes, the number later being increased to ten. These tribunes were given only negative powers-the right of veto-and their persons were made sacred, but by their veto they might stop judicial or legislative action, or even elections.

This victory of the plebeians was soon followed by a demand for written laws. After much delay a commission was despatched to Athens to study the laws of Solon. On its return the commission drafted a code, to which was given the name the "Twelve Tables," because the code was engraved on twelve bronze tablets set up in the Fo'rum, or public square. These 

Twelve Tables became the text-book used by Roman schoolboys and probably was the cause of much of the legal skill which the Romans later developed. 

7. The Plebeians Win Full Political Rights. The next demand of the plebeians-the right to intermarry with the patricians was quickly granted, but the latter immediately established a new official, the censor (sensor), to keep a roll of the citizens. Then began another struggle-this time for the right of a plebeian to hold the consulship. By various devices the patricians fought it off for a long time. For ten years the tribunes forbade the election of consuls. At last the patricians yielded and permitted the election of a plebeian consul (367 

B. C.).

8. To Protect Herself Rome Conquers Italy. Starting in an alliance with the Latin towns to the south, the power of Rome slowly expanded during the first two centuries of the Republic. It was no desire for conquest but the necessity of protecting herself against her enemies that led Rome

forward. The neighboring Etruscan cities wished to control her resources and the hill tribes to the east and south looked longingly at her fertile plains. She first hesitated to add to her territory, preferring, wherever possible, to make allies of her neighbors.

Shortly before this, a revolt of Rome's allies had led to the establishment of a new plan of representation. Some of the nearest cities were given full citizenship and added to the Roman tribes, others were given all the rights of citizens except those of voting, and others were kept as allies. As allies they furnished troops for the Roman army and enjoyed the right of trade with her, but not with each other. To safeguard her interests, Rome established co-lo'ni-a, settlements of Roman citizens, at strategic points. This new system functioned for nearly two hundred years.

10. The Aftermath of the War. The years immediately following the First Punic War were filled with serious troubles for both sides. While the Carthaginian government

wrangled with its returned soldiers, Côr'si-ca and Sär-din'î-a revolted, quite likely with Rome's connivance, and soon both islands were annexed by her. The Gauls took advantage of 

Rome's plight to spread south of the Arno. This ended with the establishment of two Roman colonies north of the Apennines. To meet the situation, she adopted the Carthaginian government and organized the region into a province, thus inaugurating the plan of government which she employed in all her later conquests.

In order to obtain suitable men for the governorship of the provinces, Rome extended the powers of certain officials for a year with the understanding that they would spend this much time in that service. Their official names were changed by the addition of "pro,” as “prō-con'sŭl." For a time the provincials seem to have been treated fairly. Their taxes were high but they were allowed to pay them in produce. 

11. Hannibal Proves Himself a Great General, but 

Carthage Is Again Defeated in the Second Punic War.

Hatred was the cause of the Second Punic War. Hamilcar, smarting under his defeat, had himself appointed governor of Spain so that he might obtain revenge. In spite of the fact that 

Rome sought to limit him to the country south of the E'brō, he built up a strong army, and extended the influence of Carthage. He compelled his son Hăn'ni-bal to swear eternal hatred of the Romans. After Hamilcar's death, Hannibal clashed with 

Rome because she undertook to interfere in affairs within Carthaginian territory. Hannibal proved himself to be one of the world's greatest generals by leading his forces up the Mediterranean coast, and through the snow-covered passes of the Alps down into Italy. Here he held out against one Roman army after another for fifteen long years, winning every battle. He had little help from Carthage, but had to rely on obtaining such aid as he could from the Gauls, and on stirring up revolt among 

Rome's allies.

61 Despairing of beating Hannibal in Italy, the Romans undertook the conquest of Spain in order to destroy his base of supplies. The Romans succeeded in overwhelming the army of 

Hasdribal, brother of Hannibal. Finally, one of the commanders, Scipio (sip'i-o), who had learned the art of warfare through long service in Spain, persuaded the Romans to strike at Carthage.

When Scipio landed in Africa and began detaching their allies, the Carthaginians became panic-stricken and sued for peace. In the midst of this situation Hannibal, realizing the futility of pursuing his Italian plans any longer, returned to Carthage, and persuaded the Carthaginians to put up a fight. 

At Za'mȧ, not far from Carthage, he fought his last battle with the Romans, and met his only real defeat. Capitulation was now inevitable. Carthage must retire from Spain; give up all but ten of her war-vessels; pay a heavy indemnity; and finally, agree not to make war without securing Rome's consent. The surrender of Hannibal was also demanded. Carthage was saved from having to meet this humiliating condition, for Hannibal fled to Asia, where he later committed suicide. At last Rome was mistress of the western Mediterranean.

CHAPTER XVII ROME BECOMES A WORLD POWER 1. Rome Frees Greece from Macedonian Control. The 

First Punic War produced one result which was destined to have a profound influence on history. The Il-lyr'i-ans, who lived along the Adriatic, north of Epirus, were kinsmen of the Greeks and much given to piracy. After Rome had assumed responsibility for policing the Adriatic, she soon came into conflict with these Illyrians. In suppressing them she formed alliances with some cities on its eastern shore and earned the thanks of the Greek Leagues. This contact with Greece was encouraged by Romans who were interested in Greek culture. 

During the war with Hannibal, his alliance with Philip V, King of Macedon, had caused the Romans to send an army to Greece to aid the Leagues in fighting Philip. The Romans had been compelled to withdraw on account of affairs in Italy, but as soon as peace was signed with Carthage, they again crossed the Adriatic at the request of the Greeks and quickly freed Hellas of all Macedonian control. Rome took no territory for herself, and announced to the astonished Greeks that their cities were to be free and independent. This act betrays the high regard which the Romans had for Greek culture. 

2. Rome Interferes in Asia. Although the Ætolian

League had taken sides with Rome in this war, the several states of the League were dissatisfied with the results. They wished to dominate Hellas and they doubted the sincerity of the Roman promises. They appealed for aid to Ăn-tiô-chus the 

Great, one of the Seleucids.

When Antiochus arrived in Hellas, the Romans drove him out of the country, crossed over to Asia Minor and, in 190 163

B. C., defeated him in the great battle of Magnesia (măg-nēzhi-a). According to the terms of the treaty which followed, Antiochus was compelled to pay 10,000 talents, to withdraw beyond the Taurus Mountains, and to cease from all political interference in Greece and the islands of the Ægean. 

3. Rome Establishes Her Control. The Romans hesi tated for several years to make Macedonia a province. As the advantages of imperialism became more apparent, however, they sought to cripple their possible rivals. To restrict the commercial strength of Rhodes they made the island of Delos a free port and it soon became the great slave market of the Mediterranean. A revolt in Carthage furnished the opportunity for Cato's demand that it be destroyed. In the same year, 146 

B. C., a revolt in Greece brought the same fate to Corinth. 

Henceforth Rome's will was law in the Mediterranean world. 

4. The Decline of Agriculture and Other Economic 

Changes. The whole fabric of Roman life and government was changed by these conquests. Most important of all were the economic changes. At the beginning of the Punic Wars, Rome was an agricultural state and her citizens had been able to carry on their farms in spite of the frequent calls to arms. 

Now that she was continually engaged in war outside of Italy, this was no longer possible, as the legions were often kept in the field for years. Much of the land passed into the hands of great landlords, and Italy instead of being a country of small homesteads became one of great estates. Because enormous supplies of grain came as tribute from Sicily and elsewhere, the price became so low that the grain could not be raised with profit. What had once been fertile fields supporting a contented peasantry was given over to vineyards or to flocks and herds.

6. Roman Literature Was Written or Inspired Largely by the Greeks. It is hard to overstate what Roman literature owed to the Greeks. In fact, it was a Greek slave that first began to write what can really be called Latin literature. This man was a teacher and used his writings as textbooks. 

With the production at Rome, in 240 B. C., of a drama by 

Liv'i-us An-dró-ni'cus, Roman literature passed almost wholly under Hellenic influence. Foremost among the literary remains of this period are the comedies of Plau'tus and Terence. 

Prose literature did not make its appearance in Rome until after the Second Punic War, but at once it made a strong appeal to the Romans on account of its usefulness. Just as in 

Greece, it was first employed in the compilation of annals.

Because many of these old annals were written by Greeks who tried to make them fit into the history of their own country, much of the early story of Rome is in doubt. 

7. Dependence of Rome on Greek Culture and Teach ers Made Her a Hellenistic Power. That Roman literature should imitate so closely that of the Greeks is not surprising, when we remember that during the last two centuries of the Roman Republic Greek slaves were almost the only teachers in the land. Greek became a fashionable study. In fact, Romans often finished their education in some Greek city. Greek philosophic ideas spread across the Adriatic and aroused considerable interest among the educated classes, though these ideas were too speculative to make any strong appeal to the practicalminded Romans as a whole. This dependence of the Romans upon Greek culture justifies us in saying that with Rome's occupation of Greece and her control of the Eastern Mediterranean, she became an Hellenistic power. 

8. Cato, the Censor, Fights for the Old Roman Culture. 

In protest against things Greek, one man stands out in bold relief-blunt old Ca'tō, a well-to-do farmer of the patrician class. 

Cato divided time between demanding the destruction of Carthage and trying to prevent the introduction of any modern ideas. He was so enthusiastic about farming that he wrote the first Latin book on agriculture. In order to enable his boy to grow up untouched by any of the Hellenism which he himself detested, he wrote text-books on all sorts of subjects from the Roman view-point. He was also the author of a history of 

Rome which brought out the virtues of the ancient Roman people.

Cato had himself elected to the office of censor, and then used his power to strike from the senate-roll some of those who were too much given to the new ideas. He also drew up regulations against the excessive use of jewelry by women and too luxurious banquets. In order to keep alive hatred of Carthage,

ROME BECOMES A WORLD POWER 

169 he is said to have ended every speech in the Senate with the sentence, "Carthage must be destroyed." 

9. Causes for Decline in Political Morality. The growing complexity of the Roman government as well as its numerous crises overturned the political system which had developed. The Senate, a wieldy and efficient body, gradually regained its powers. One of the boasts of early Rome had been 

PROW OF A ROMAN GALLEY 

Notice the arm of the catapult. 

From a bas-relief. the integrity, if not the efficiency, of its officials. These officials. served without pay and only for the honor of the office. Many of them were far from being rich men. With the increased cost of living which now prevailed, there was a corresponding increase in the expenses attached to holding public office. 

Only the wealthy now could afford to hold office and even they sought recompense. Because these offices could be obtained more easily in the provinces where large gifts were often given the officials for special favors, many Romans ended their careers either as provincial officials, or as "publicans" or taxgatherers.

The most serious political consequence of the expansion of

Rome was the citizens' escape from bearing any part of the financial responsibility of the state. By 169 B. C. so great had become the income of the Republic from indemnities imposed on conquered peoples and from tribute levied on the provinces that it was no longer necessary to collect any taxes at home.

CHAPTER XVIII  IN THE TASK OF GOVERNING AN EXTENSIVE EMPIRE 1. Reasons Why the Republic Begins to Decline. The 

Roman Republic had no sooner extended its sway over the Mediterranean world than it began to have serious difficulties. 

For this there were two important reasons. In the first place, there were, as we have seen, many citizens who had lost their property and had drifted to Rome. There they formed a mob which could be easily swayed by popular orators, and at the same time they ceased to be available for military service. Another element were the allies, who had received little advantage from the assistance they had rendered Rome in her conquests. 

A second and far more important reason, however, was this. 

The Romans were trying to administer a great empire with the machinery of a city-state. What was needed was a reorganization of the government. There were men who saw these difficulties clearly and tried to remedy them. The task, however, was so great and the obstacles so hard to overcome that the 

Republic itself was overthrown. 

2. Tiberius Gracchus Is Mobbed Because of His Re forms. The first attempt to reform the situation was made by 

Ti-bē'ri-us Gracchus (grăk'us) in 133 B. C. Tiberius was a young man of the upper classes who had served in Spain. On his way back to Rome he had seen that large sections of Italy had only a scanty population while the city itself was crowded with landless men. It was his ambition to get these men back to the farm. He had himself elected tribune and introduced a bill limiting the amount of land that any citizen might hold. He created such ill-feeling that the younger and 171

more hot-headed senators broke up the furniture of the Senate house and mobbed him. Tiberius lost his life but his law remained. We do not know exactly how it worked out, but we do know that the census showed a great increase in the number of Roman citizens during the next few years.

3. Caius Gracchus Tries to Continue the Work of Re form. Rome was not yet done with the Gracchi, for ten years later Caius (ka'yus), a brother, came forward to continue the work of reform. Caius proceeded to attack the land problem from a new angle. Instead of getting the poorer citizens back to the farms individually, he wanted to send them out in large groups. Another of his measures was designed to lighten some of the more pressing distress among the proletarii by allowing the government to sell grain to them at a reduced price.

While Caius was effecting these reforms, a number of the allies in Italy began to demand full Roman citizenship. Caius was charged by his enemies with favoring the idea. As a result, he and his followers were attacked by a mob and at least three thousand lost their lives, while Caius committed suicide.

4. The Jugurthine War Brings About a Change in Character of the Army. With the death of Caius Gracchus the reaction against reform began in earnest. The reformers were hunted down and put to death, and the land laws were repealed. One of the most disgraceful affairs was the trouble with Jugurtha (joo-gûr'tha). Jugurtha was a nephew of the king of Numidia who had assisted the Romans against Carthage. When his uncle died, Jugurtha prepared to get rid of his two cousins. In response to the appeal of one of them, Rome intervened, but Jugurtha was able to buy off commissioners, senators, and generals alike. Finally war was begun but the citizens rose and elected to the consulship an honest soldier, Mari-us by name. Marius immediately enacted a law which permitted any one, Roman or Italian, to volunteer for service, whether he had property or not. This afforded an opportunity for many poor men to obtain employment and changed the character of the army completely. Jugurtha was soon brought to Rome in chains to grace the triumphal procession in honor of 

Marius and his legions. 

5. Marius Is Proclaimed "Savior of the Republic" but 

Is Forced to Retire. While the Jugurthine War was going on, the Germans who lived across the Rhine attacked the Roman frontier and actually destroyed several Roman armies. The terror-stricken Romans, as soon as Marius returned from

Africa, re-elected him consul, something without precedent in Roman history. Marius took the field, and won such decisive victories that he was proclaimed "the savior of the Republic."

Although no politician, Marius became the hero of the popular party, which tried to use him to advance the reform movement. The old general was soon forced into a position where he had to turn from his supporters. The reforms were stopped, and Marius was soon so much out of favor that he had to retire to Asia to escape the popular fury.

6. Two Years of Civil War Follow. The conservatives were in control once more. In 96 B. C., an honest governor of the province of Asia was actually convicted in the courts because he had tried to protect the people of his province from 

THE TESTUDO 

Roman soldiers advancing under shields joined together to form a larger area of protection.

From the Trajan Column. 

illegal demands. The more thoughtful Romans deplored the situation but they were at the mercy of the politicians who were kept in office by the votes of the lower classes.

The allies still hoped to obtain justice, but when Drusus (droo'sus), a newly elected tribune, was assassinated because he had proposed to extend citizenship to all the people of Italy, they revolted. The whole peninsula blazed with civil war. The startled Roman government surrendered and granted citizenship to those who would lay down their arms, but the war dragged on for nearly two years.

In the midst of this conflict another blow fell. Mith-ri-datēs, king of Pon'tus, had long planned to drive the Romans out of Asia, and scized this opportunity to cause the murder of the Romans and Italians in that province. Marius became consul to get command of the army against Mithridates, but Sul'la who had just ended the war with the allies, marched to Rome and Marius fled. Sulla's act was illegal but it demonstrated the change in the army which Marius himself had caused. After Sulla had gone to the East, Marius returned and

put to death some friends of his rival. He sent another Roman army against Sulla, but he died before he could accomplish his purpose. 

7. Sulla Attempts to Restore Senatorial Government. 

Sulla finally made a treaty with Mithridates and returned to

Rome with his army, prepared to avenge the death of his friends. He took the office of dictator and ordered the execution of a large number of the popular party. He was a conservative and believed that the Senate should control the government. The new constitution which he established wiped away all the changes made since the days of the Gracchi. The lower classes and the equites lost all their privileges, although the selling of grain at a reduced price was allowed to continue. 

In a few years the popular party again rose and supported for the consulship Cnaeus Pompey (ne'oo pom'pi). Pompey's election was the signal for another era of reform, marked by

an almost complete disregard of the constitution. In order to suppress the pirates now so bold that they attacked the corn ships bringing tribute to Rome, there was enacted in 67 B. C. the so-called Ga-bìn'î-an Law. This provided Pompey, now only a private citizen, with a fleet and an army. It took Pompey only a few months to clean up the pirates, and as a result he was given command of the whole East. 

8. Catiline Conspires to Overthrow the Government. 

While Pompey was fighting in the East, a group of dissatisfied citizens formed a conspiracy to overthrow the government. 

One of the leaders was Căt'i-līne, a dissolute young man, who had been defeated for the consulship by the orator Märcus Tulli-us Cicero, a strong believer in the Republic. This conspiracy was far-reaching and involved some important people. 

Cicero found out about it, and proceeded to impeach Catiline in a series of famous speeches before the Senate. Eventually a part of the conspirators were put to death without trial, but Catiline escaped to Etruria (é-troo'ri-ȧ), where he was killed and his followers dispersed. 

9. A Triumvirate Composed of Pompey, Cæsar, and Crassus Take Matters in Hand. When Pompey returned from the East, he disbanded his army and called on the Senate to confer on the soldiers the rewards which he had promised them. But the Senate refused, and Pompey found himself in an uncomfortable position. At this moment there appeared on the scene a man who knew how to take advantage of the situation-Caius Julius Cæsar. His early career had been rather wild and he was reputed to be heavily in debt. His chief adviser and creditor was Marcus Li-cin'i-us Crassus, another politician and rich adventurer.

These three men formed a "ring" known as the First Triumvirate. Cæsar, who was elected consul, turned to the Assembly to put through the bills that the three desired. He obtained for himself the governorship of the province of Cisalpine

Gaul for a period of five years. He was aware of certain events which would lead to military intervention in Farther Gaul and he hoped to win this territory for Rome and military glory for himself. Events occurred as he had planned and he plunged into the task which has made him famous. To justify his actions, he wrote a careful account of his wars in such good Latin that high-school students still study it to perfect their knowledge of that language. 

10. Cæsar Becomes Master of Rome. Trouble soon broke out between Pompey and Cæsar. Pompey had the support of the Senate and Cæsar had the support of the people. When the time drew near for the return of Cæsar to Rome, Pompey caused the

Senate to require Cæsar to leave his province and return to Rome. Realizing that this would be fatal, Cæsar marched his legions across the Ru'bicon, the boundary of his province. This was an act of rebellion.

JULIUS CAESAR 

This statue of Cæsar in armor was set up in Rome in the days of Augustus and is now in the Capitoline Museum there. 

Pompey, who had been granted an army by the Senate, fled eastward. Cæsar, after he had taken charge at Rome, followed him and defeated his army. Pompey soon after committed suicide but it took Cæsar nearly three years to bring peace to the state.

On his return to Rome, Cæsar was appointed dictator, first for ten years and then for life, with powers of tribune and also censor. In the meantime, he devoted himself to reforming the government. He laid out plans for a large number of internal improvements, such as the building of a great port for Rome and the reconstruction of the Forum. To cope with unemployment he placed his veterans in groups on farms in both Italy and the provinces. His act of greatest interest to later times was the introduction of the Egyptian calendar as corrected by the Greeks. His name was bestowed on the fifth 

Roman month, hence our word July. 

Like Alexander the Great, Cæsar then began to dream of conquering the East. He was encouraged by Clē-ó-pa'tra, the beautiful queen of Hellenized Egypt, with whom he had become greatly enamored while he was pursuing Pompey. There is evidence that he was planning to become a ruler like the Hellenistic Kings and to move the capital of his empire from Rome to Alexandria. His conduct finally became so intolerable to some of his associates that in 44 B. C., just before his expedition was ready to start, he was stabbed to death in the Senate House, and by the irony of fate died at the foot of the statue of Pompey. When his will was read, it was found that Cæsar had left to each Roman citizen a sum which would be about fifteen dollars in our money, and had named his nephew and adopted son, Ŏc-ta'vi-an, as his heir. 

11. Octavian Triumphs Over Mark Anthony in the 

Struggle for Control. The Republic was dead and the monarchy was not yet established. Cæsar's death was followed by thirteen years of turmoil, with the Senate hardly more than an insignificant onlooker. The chief actors in this struggle for supremacy were Octavian and Mark Antony, one of Cæsar's stanchest friends. A compromise was effected between them. 

Octavian took command of the army in Italy and the West; 

Antony, of the army in the East, and from his headquarters

in Alexandria planned to carry out Cæsar's dream of oriental conquests. But for this he lacked the energy. While Octavian worked hard solidifying his control, Antony wasted his time in making love to Cleopatra. 

Courtesy of the American Numismatic Society.

In 32 B. C., in response to Octavian's demand, the subservient Senate deposed Antony. In the civil war which followed, Octavian defeated his rival in a great naval battle off Actium (ǎk'shi-um), a little town on the western coast of Greece. Shortly afterward Antony committed suicide.

Failing to ensnare Octavian with her charms, and fearful lest she would be forced to march in his triumphal procession in Rome, Cleopatra committed suicide. With her death Octavian took control of Egypt and treated it as though it were his personal property. 

ROMAN GOLD COIN 

On one side is the head of Augustus and on the other a quadriga, or fourhorse chariot, and the letters which stand for "Senatus Populusque Ro manorum"-The Roman Senate and People. 

12. As First "Princeps" Octavian Becomes an Absolute

Monarch in Powers. On his return to Rome, Octavian went through the formality of surrendering all his powers to the Senate. It was decreed that he should add to his name the honorary title Augustus, meaning "majestic," and that he should be considered princeps or "first" citizen. Even though the Senate and Assembly and other outward forms of republicanism were continued, a monarchy had really been established, for it was within the power of the princeps to name his own successor and to appoint the senators. 

Although in theory the princeps was only the first citizen. of the state, because he spoke first in the Senate, Augustus easily became the leader of that body. He was also granted the right to command the army and this gave him the power to decide on peace or war. By virtue of his power as a tribune, he became the representative of the people as opposed to the

Senate, and thus acquired the right to initiate legislation and to veto any undertaking of the government. He had the right to coin money, and he had a treasury of his own called the fis'cus. His wealth was far greater than that of any other 

Roman. As pŏn'tì-fèx măx'i-mus, he was intrusted with the supervision of all religious measures. It was he who decided all questions of sacred law and regulated the calendar, and settled the time for festivals, legal transactions, and meetings of the Assembly. Finally, he was proclaimed the "divine Augustus" and altars were erected to him as the personification of the state. 

13. Under Augustus Rome Enjoys a Golden Age. The government of Augustus lasted for over forty years. This was Rome's "golden age." During that period the city was largely rebuilt, much more splendidly than before, and the Forum which had been begun by Cæsar was greatly enlarged. 

Marble was used in the construction of public buildings and temples in place of the earlier bricks and tufa (too'fȧ). Indeed, with truth did the poet write: "I found a Rome of clay," imperial Cæsar cried, "I left a Rome of marble, no other Rome beside."

While the Senate continued to govern the Republic much the same as formerly, Augustus put a stop to some of the most glaring abuses. In the provinces he appointed to office men whom he could trust and he kept them there as long as they were efficient. In this way he built up a body of trained administrators who served the state far better than the Senate's appointees in the provinces nearer home. 

14. Roman Culture During the Last Century of the 

Republic. In spite of all the turmoil and disturbance after the days of the Gracchi, this period brought forth many of the greatest writers and thinkers. Some were men of action like

Cæsar and Cicero, but others, such as Livius and Lucretius (lú-krē'shi-us), were men of leisure who devoted their lives to literary undertakings.

The most striking characteristic of all the literature and learning of this period was its dependence upon the Greeks. In fact, it was from the Greeks that Cicero learned the art of making polished sentences, and Ver'gil acquired the form and even the content of his famous epic, the E-ne'id. We have already seen how Cæsar turned to the Greeks for help when he sought to reform the Roman calendar; likewise also most of the other learned men of the day depended upon Greek materials.

15. The Literary Trio of the "Golden Age." To the writings of Cicero, Vergil, and Livy the Republic in its last years owed much of its literary greatness. The charm of their work and the purity of language of these three men were the greatest influence in keeping alive the study of the Latin language.

Cicero won his place as an orator and a pleader in the Roman courts by an attack on the misgovernment of Ver'rēs in Sicily. 

However, the most famous of his orations were those against the conspiracy of Catiline. Cicero was also the author of a number of philosophical essays and treatises on oratory. Besides, he left behind a collection of letters to which we owe much of the information we possess concerning the life of well-to-do Romans.

The writings of Vergil and of Livy express a belief in the fore-ordained greatness and glory of Rome, which stirred so many Romans after the establishment of peace throughout the Roman world. Livy wrote a history of the Republic in one hundred forty-four books, to glorify the Republic and to show to his fellow citizens why and how Rome had become so great. It was said no Roman could read the story without a patriotic thrill. The poet, Ver-gil'i-us Märō, better known as Vergil, sang of the beginnings of Rome, tracing the story of E-ne'ăs, its legendary founder, from his flight after the fall of Troy to his landing in Latium (la'shi'um). This poem, too, stirred the pride of the Romans, by showing the relationship of their forefathers to the early Hellenes. 

16. The Moral Decline of the Republic. The last cen tury of the Republic was marked by a rapid decline in morals. 

Rome seems to have gone money mad. There are sordid tales connected with Sulla's proscriptions and Cæsar's tyranny in which wealth was often the cause of a person's death warrant. 

During this period, divorce became common. The birth-rate decreased so much that finally Augustus decreed that any man

with three children should be exempt from taxation. The shows and games for the benefit of the lower classes became more coarse and more bloody. The treatment of the gladiators was so cruel that, in 73 B. C., they revolted under the leadership of

Spär'tà-cus, a Thessalian. In the end the 

Romans appear to have been most inhuman, for we read of 

6,000 slaves being crucified along the great highway which led south from Rome.

However, not all the laxity which marked the last years of the Republic should be regarded as evidence of a moral decline. Rome was no longer a little country town, but rather the metropolis of a world empire. People came to her from every quarter, bringing new ideas and new ways of looking at things. What was really happening was that Romans were trying to adjust themselves to these new conditions and were finding the task difficult.

CHAPTER XIX THREE CENTURIES OF EMPIRE BRING COMPARATIVE PEACE AND EFFICIENT GOVERNMENT 1. The Vast Extent of the Roman Empire. The Empire at the time of the elevation of Octavian to the rank of princeps extended a thousand miles north and south, and more than two thousand east and west. However, much of this vast area was the Mediterranean Sea. On the south its natural boundary was the Desert of Sahara; on the west, the Atlantic 

Ocean; and on the north, the Rhine and Danube Rivers. On the east it had no natural boundary, and there was constant friction between the Romans and the Pär'thi-ans. There were times, too, when the Empire extended far beyond these bounds. 

For example, for nearly four hundred years it included a large part of the island of Britain, and for half that time the province of Dacia (da'shi-a), which comprised the region now known as Roumania.

The Empire was divided into provinces and these provinces in turn into municipalities. The central government appointed the provincial officials, but the municipalities elected their own councils, judges, and police officers.

Three distinct types of civilization were included within the Empire. The western part was Latin-speaking, and as time went on, became quite Roman in its culture. Southern Italy, Sicily, and the Balkan peninsula, together with the shores of the Ægean, were so strongly Hellenic that the Latin tongue was never able to replace the Greek. In Asia and Egypt, the thin Hellenistic veneer could not conceal the fact that the population was really oriental. To bind together these incongruous 185

elements there were two bonds-a common system of political administration and a common geographical centre in the 

Mediterranean basin. 

2. The Neighbors of the Empire. On the south, Rome had for neighbors only a few desert tribes. In this direction 

ROMAN LIGHTHOUSE 

As it still stands at Dover, England. she was open to attack only through the valley of the Nile, and no power of any importance ever developed in that area. 

Her neighbors on the north were semi-nomadic tribes of forest-dwellers, who for a time were held in check by means of frontier garrisons.

Later a wall was built between the headwaters of the Danube and the Rhine, and a similar wall was built across the island of 

Britain. So long as these artificial frontiers were properly maintained with trustworthy troops, there was no danger in that quarter.

The only real power with which Rome had to deal was the Parthian Empire. This oriental state considered itself to be the successor of the Persian Empire and had established its capital at Ctesi-phon in the valley of the Tigris. There was no well-defined natural frontier between the Parthians and the Ro-

PEACE AND EFFICIENT GOVERNMENT 

187 mans, but a series of small buffer states served as a frontier line which the two powers tried to control. 

3. The Problem of Succession Was Most Troublesome. 

The biggest problem for the Roman Empire was the question 

THE CLAUDIAN AQUEDUCT 

One of the nine aqueducts of Rome. It was built in 38 A. D. and is about forty miles long. of succession. At first, succession was a matter of heredity, and for fifty years after the death of Augustus the princeps was chosen from his family. In theory the power of the princeps was the Senate, in practice, it was really the army. When the last princeps of the Augustan line died, one of the armies along the frontier succeeded in placing its general, Vespasian (věs-pā'zhi-ăn), on the throne. The attempts of this man's son, Domitian (dó-mishi-ăn), to deprive the Senate of its political power led to his own assassination. After that the senators chose one of their own number, Ner'va, to be princeps.

Nerva realized that the state needed a good administrator, and adopted as his son and heir an experienced man. So successful did this plan prove that it lasted for the next seventyfive years. In this way the principle of heredity was maintained, and at the same time the Empire was assured of a good administrator. After the death of Marcus Au-rē'li-us in 180 

A. D., the principle of blood-relationship was established and there followed a series of poor rulers. The army had once more undue influence in the selection of the princeps and for a hundred years the Empire suffered from almost constant conflict over the succession. This importance of the army led to the use of the title Im-pe-ra'tor or "commander-in-chief" when referring to the princeps. 

4. Prosperity Comes to the Empire. The two centuries following the death of Augustus were a period of comparative peace. Aside from frontier wars and the disturbances which marked the death of Ne'ro, there were only a few petty revolts to disturb the Roman peace, Păx Rō-mä'na, which now became almost a proverb. One of the most brilliant emperors of this period was Trajan. His triumphal column is still at 

Rome. It was during Trajan's reign that the Empire reached its greatest extent by annexing the province of Dacia, as well as Armenia, old Assyria, and Mesopotamia as far as the Persian Gulf. Trajan's successor, the more cautious Ha'dri-an, abandoned the land recently added east of the Euphrates and in northern Britain, and set his legions to building walls to keep back the land-hungry barbarians. 

This was a period of prosperity in most parts of the Empire. 

Especially did the commerce of the Greeks and other orientals thrive, for the magnificent roads reaching to the most distant provinces made travel easy. Thanks to the luxurious habits of life acquired by the wealthier Romans, trade with India increased rapidly. This was greatly assisted by the discovery. that the monsoon winds.might be a help in sailing across the

THEN IGNEMOIS THE ARCH OF CONSTANTINE IN ROME

Indian Ocean. The only drawback to this trade was the fact that large quantities of gold and silver had to be drawn from the Empire and sent eastward to pay for the goods coming to Rome in increasing volume, and for which she had few products of her own to offer in exchange. 

5. Trouble Appears on the Horizon. During the second century the Empire was swept by a terrible plague from the East. This continued for a generation, until many sections of the country were all but depopulated. The situation was so serious that Marcus Aurelius moved a whole tribe of Germans across the Danube and settled them in the Empire. 

The agricultural situation also became threatening. The use of slaves and large-scale farming had reduced the fertility of the soil, and great areas had been withdrawn from cultivation altogether because of lack of labor. To make matters worse, land was being overtaxed, for the basis of the Roman system of taxation was a land tax assessed against all except citizens. 

When Căr-à-cal'là, in 212 A. D., granted citizenship to all the provincials, he did not free them from these burdensome land taxes, and soon the older citizens as well found themselves taxed in this way. Socially the situation was somewhat improved, because the slaves were being changed into co-lo'nī, serfs who were bound to the soil but who paid a rent in services and products.

Last, but not least, there had begun an extensive invasion of new ideas which were changing all previous notions and traditions. When the orientals began to move westward after the annexation of the eastern provinces, they brought with them their various religions and cults. From Egypt came the worship of I'sis, from Syria and Mesopotamia the worship of Mith'răs, from Asia Minor that of the "Mother of the Gods," and from Palestine, Christianity. These oriental beliefs substituted a new feeling of sin for the old matter-of-fact relationship that had existed between the Roman and his gods.

PEACE AND EFFICIENT GOVERNMENT 

191 These religions turned out to be short-lived except Christianity. 

6. The Remains of the Culture of Imperial Rome. 

Wherever the Roman went, he carried the Roman idea of roads and public buildings. From the Sahara to the Rhine, and from the Atlantic to the Euphrates even to-day stand the 

WOMEN CARRYING GIFTS TO ISIS 

From a bas-relief in the Vatican. ruins of Roman towns of the Imperial Age, each with its forum, baths, theatre, and villas. Of these the best preserved is Pompeii (pom-pa'yē), which was buried beneath a layer of ashes during an eruption of Vé-su'vi-us in 69 A. D. The work of the modern excavator has made it possible to-day to walk down its streets rutted with the chariot wheels of long ago, and to see the shops where the people purchased the necessaries of life. On the walls of the houses the frescoes painted after the Greek fashion are as fresh to-day as they were eighteen hundred and fifty years ago. And by studying the furniture, tools, utensils, and clothing in the museum at Naples, we may realize how modern these old Romans were after all. 

In the large cities of the Empire, the government appointed

professors of Greek and Latin grammar and rhetoric, and yet the general standard of education declined. Except in the public service there were few opportunities for educated men.

There was one notable exception to this-the law. This study always appealed to Romans, and two lawyers of the second century, Gaius (ga'yus) and Pa-pin'i-ăn, actually laid the foundations for the later codification of the law. 

From the days of the "Twelve Tables," the Romans had been adding to their laws, and Roman law became so complex that lawyers had begun to specialize in its different phases. 

Under the early Empire the opinions of these lawyers came to have the same force as law, much as judicial decisions do with us. Eventually the vast mass of law was codified by the order

7. The Literature of This Period Shows Signs of a 

Decline. During the imperial period the Empire produced no great writers to compare with those of the last century of the Republic. Sen'é-ca, the tutor of Nero, wrote some tragedies in imitation of the Greeks. Tac'i-tus, an imperial official, made a detailed study of the history of the first century, giving us our earliest extended account of the Germans. 

Two writers, however, still have an interest for us, and both of them wrote in Greek-Jō-sephus and Plutarch. The words of Josephus furnish us our almost only account of the history of the Jews in the first century written at the time. Plutarch, in addition to his famous Parallel Lives, wrote essays which help us to know what people were thinking about in his day. 

The greatest essayist of the imperial period, however, was Lucian (lu'shan), whose pungent satires upon the ideas and customs of the times are still enjoyable reading. The Romans never contributed much original thought in philosophy, but 

Marcus Aurelius in his Meditations expressed the highest ideals of pagan Rome under the influence of Stoicism.

CHAPTER XX THE SIGNIFICANCE OF THE GRECO-ROMAN WORLD 1. The Living Græco-Roman World. Whenever we at tempt to estimate society's debt to the Græco-Roman World, we are startled by the wide variety of the interests of these old Greeks and Romans and by the extraordinary flexibility of their minds. The more we read their literature and study their history, the more we are impressed by the range of their experiments. It matters not whether we turn to the world of mind or matter, we are confronted by evidences of their presence, and in the field of art, their sculpture and cé-răm'ic painting still remain the standard by which we measure our own. 

2. The Greek and Latin Languages. Foremost among the contributions of the Græco-Roman world to society was that of language. The large number of words of Greek origin in everyday use betrays the work done by the Greeks in laying the foundations of much of our science and philosophy, while those of Latin origin demonstrate how firm a hold the Roman Empire had upon western Europe. Although the English language comes from the northern barbarians, the Greek and Latin words in English are proof of the civilization which our ancestors derived from the world they helped to destroy. The 

Romans themselves turned to the Greeks for many words and language forms, and then passed them on to later peoples. 

Latin became the language of culture, which it remained until modern times. Even now through its descendants-Italian, French, Spanish, Portuguese, and Roumanian-it is a living force. 

3. Political Contributions. Our very word "politics" comes from the name which the Greeks gave to their citystates, and rightly so, for the first political parties developed 195

there. Out of the struggles between these parties arose various types of government, and the ancient record presents a series of experiments unrivalled in the world's laboratory of political science. Democracy was achieved by a long and painful process. Although the problem of interstate relationships was never completely worked out, an effort was made in connection with the governments evolved for the federal leagues. The oriental idea of a divine monarchy, however, became the law of the Hellenistic world, and was bequeathed to the Roman Empire.

Each of the various types of government has had its imitators in succeeding ages. The Church inherited the Roman autocracy as well as its administrative machinery; the Italian princes of the Renaissance (ren-e-säns') took as their models. the tyrants of ancient Greece; and even the founders of our own Republic studied the framework of the Ætolian and Achæan Leagues. 

4. Social and Economic Contributions. Without slavery there would have been no "golden age" in Athens, and little disgrace was attached to being a slave. Rome's wars vastly increased the number of slaves, and the lot of the slaves became correspondingly hard. During the Pax Romana there was a steady growth of humanitarianism and slavery all but disappeared. In place of bondage to a master, the law substituted attachment to the soil, an idea which the Romans passed on in the foundation of the system of serfdom which continued in parts of Europe until quite recently. 

The Græco-Roman World had extremes of wealth relatively as great as those to-day, and the great areas under a single political control raised the standard of living so much that the villas of Imperial Rome became the models of the country estates of later times. From the Romans, too, we have obtained our first treatises on scientific and applied agriculture, although the Romans had got them from the Carthaginians. Even the

THE GRÆCO-ROMAN WORLD 

197 guilds of the Middle Ages may be traced back to the colleges of workmen at Rome.

For centuries the roads and bridges built by Roman engineers remained the only routes of communication throughout much of Europe and western Asia. Even to-day some of them are in use. This Græco-Roman World also discovered the direct sea route to India and opened up communications with China. The sea law of Rhodes furnished the basis for modern "maritime laws.” 

5. Scientific Contribu tions. 

Science owes its beginning to the Greek mind.

In mathematics the Greeks discovered the properties of numbers, perfected geometry, and made the beginnings of algebra. Although their system of numbering was clumsy, the Greeks used it for the most complicated computa-

These old Greek scientists had made their biological observations so carefully that some of their work was not improved upon until the invention of the microscope in the seventeenth century. In medicine they understood that diseases followed natural causes, and the medical works of Hip-poc'rȧ-tēs and Ga'len became the text-books of Europe for more than a thou-

6. Literary Contributions. To the Græco-Roman World we owe the models of all our types of literature, except the short story and the body of literature we call "classic." We can

We can scarcely read a book or magazine without finding allusions to classical things, to say nothing of the plots borrowed from the Greeks and Romans which have become famous in their modern forms. And finally, the Græco-Roman World first studied literature for literature's sake, and as a part of education. 

7. Artistic Contributions. In art the Greeks took the oriental sculpture and painting and related it to nature. Thanks to their athletic exercises they knew and expressed the human form with a success that has never been surpassed. The loss of

THE GRECO-ROMAN WORLD 

199 their painting deprived the world of much it might have learned in this field. So beautiful are their vases that they serve even to-day as models for modern potters.

The orders of Greek architecture have influenced exterior 

THE ROMAN THEATRE AT NIMES IN FRANCE 

design, while the Roman arch and use of cement made buildings of extreme usefulness as well as buildings of beauty. Even to-day the Parthenon stands as the world's perfect building, and nearly every state capital in our country recalls the Roman Păn-the'on. Many modern universities are reproducing the stadium of the Greeks, while no city is lacking in theatres and music halls. 

8. Classic Ideals. The "classic ideals" came from the 

Græco-Roman World. The ancient Greeks and Romans had only a shadowy idea of immortality. The all-important thing to them was this life, and each man strove to get from life the greatest fulfilment in his own way.

The Greek, in his inquisitiveness and in his love of change, idealized a life of dignified moderation-one without poverty so that he might have leisure for politics and discussion, but without wealth so great as to excite the envy of mortals or gods. The Roman was more practical-minded and devoted himself to the material things of life. His ambition was to make a fortune and to own a great estate. 

On both Greeks and Romans the bonds of family and state bore heavily, but the Romans had an abiding faith, and bequeathed this to the ages in the Roman concept of an “Eternal Rome." So from the Græco-Roman World society obtained its concept of beauty and the embodiment of justice in law. 

These were the "classic ideals."

THE PERIOD OF THE NEW ORIENTAL CIVILIZATION Chapters XXI-XXVII 

With the triumph of Christianity, Oriental influence became supreme in the Græco-Roman World. Although the West was despoiled of its culture by economic exhaustion and barbarian invasion, the Church lived on. Later the Oriental ideal expressed by Islam in "submission to God," and based upon the old Græco-Roman culture and the older culture of the East, was carried by Muslim arms westward to the Atlantic and eastward to the heart of Asia. At the same time, over eastern Asia and the Spice Islands there was a revival of Buddhism. 

During this period Muslim and Buddhist lands reached their greatest glory. While Christian Europe was struggling to find itself under a weary load of ignorance and barbarism, Muslim scholars were delving into the knowledge of the Greeks, and Hindu and Muslim traders were exploring far distant lands and were establishing contacts with peoples of whom the western world had no knowledge.

The mission of these three great religions-Christianity, Islam, and Buddhism-was the same, namely to unite men in a common brotherhood, but years of bloodshed had to pass before this could be even partially realized. 20J

CHAPTER XXI 

WITH THE TRIUMPH OF CHRISTIANITY, ORIENTAL INFLUENCE BECOMES SUPREME IN THE GRECO-ROMAN WORLD 

Rome cared little about the religion of her subjects. Even if she had, it is doubtful if she would have heard of the religious excitement in Palestine near the little town of Ca-pernå-um toward the close of the reign of Ti-be'ri-us. A strange teacher, Jesus by name, had arisen among the Jews and was wandering around the country, preaching a new doctrine, that God was a universal, loving, and forgiving father. We shall see how this teaching became a great new force in the world; how Christianity undermined the authority of the Roman Emperors by teaching that man's first allegiance is to God, and finally how it came to be the religion of both emperors and people. 

1. Christianity Arises from the Life and Teachings of 

Jesus. The Jews had had hard struggle with Greek civilization. In 165 B. C. they had rebelled against their masters and had kept their independence until they were brought into the Roman domain by Pompey a hundred years later. During this hundred years the high priests had exerted a tremendous influence on the government and had dominated the religious thought of the people. Observance of Mosaic law had become so important that, on two occasions, the people had allowed Jerusalem to be taken rather than to rise to its defense on the Sabbath.

The coming of the Romans had been a severe check to aspirations of the Jews, yet many of them still looked forward with confidence to the arrival of The Messiah who would re- 202

ORIENTAL INFLUENCE 

203 store the "Kingdom of the Jews." These Jews looked upon

Jesus with all his talk about a "Kingdom of Heaven" as a pretender. Their minds refused to accept such an intangible thing as a spiritual kingdom. The insistence of Jesus that man was more important than the law, and that love for God and for JONAH An early Christian painting of his adventure, from the catacombs at Rome. one's neighbor was the last and greatest commandment soon brought him into conflict with the Jews.

In the thirty-third year of his life, when Jesus and his disciples had come to Jerusalem for the celebration of the "Feast of the Passover," the Pharisees, led by the high priest Cai'àphas, accused him of sedition. He was arrested, tried, and convicted. Pontius (pon'shi-us) Pi'láte, the Roman governor, had doubts of the guilt of Jesus, but he confirmed the sentence of death, in order to keep peace among the Jews. Jesus was then led away and crucified, according to the Roman custom. 

If the Jews expected that the death of Jesus would put an end to his teachings, they little understood the hold which those promises had on his followers. Their loss of faith in their leader occasioned by the death of Jesus was followed by a period of intense devotion and tremendous proselyting. Within twenty years after the death of Jesus, Christianity, from the Greek word Chris'tus meaning "the Messiah," had been car-

ried throughout Palestine and Syria, and into the more distant provinces, and even beyond the confines of the empire. SCS PE TR VS VN

2. The Apostle 

Paul Systematizes 

Christianity. At 

Jesus' death Christianity was simply a collection of religious teachings. It accepted the Old Testament, the sacred writings of the Jews. Soon, however, it had a sacred literature of its own, the New Testament, consisting chiefly of the four lives of Jesus -the Gospels-and the writings of the 

Apostle Paul and of other leaders. 

Paul was a Roman subject of Greek speech and Greek training, and a religious teacher. In early life he had persecuted the followers of Jesus, and while doing this had become convinced that the latter was really the Son of God. It was Paul who organized 

Jesus' teachings into a system, and who explained the crucifixion as a human sacrifice through which mankind was to be saved. Paul not only gave to Christians their creed, but he organized them into churches-at Athens, Corinth, Eph'e-sus, Rome, and elsewhere.

3. Christianity Comes Into Conflict with the Roman 

Government. At first the Romans ignored the Christians, as they had ignored the Jews. The Christians refused to show their loyalty by burning incense to the emperor. Being men of peace, they would not serve in the Roman armies. 

They held secret meetings in violation. of Roman law. Such acts naturally brought them into conflict with the authorities, especially when it was found that they were making many converts among the poor and dissatisfied members of society.

These early Christians were regarded with suspicion by the rabble and the learned alike, and were accused of all sorts of crimes, even such as eating the flesh of their children in religious feasts. When Nero was accused of having set fire to 

Rome, he found it easy to say that it was the Christians, and many of them were executed. 

4. The Christians Are Subjected to Terrible Persecu tions. Marcus Aurelius, a sincere believer in the ancient religion, saw in the ravages of the plague and the attacks of the northern barbarians evidence of the anger of the gods. And so it came about that he, the most pious of all the Roman emperors, was the first to proclaim persecution of Christians who boasted that their God was the only God and that all other Gods were false. Persecution reached a climax during the reign of

Diocletian. It began with the tearing down by Christians of the edict at Nicomedia in 303 A. D. and continued for eight

years. Copies of the Gospels and of the Acts of the Apostles were seized; churches were demolished; bishops and priests 

CHRISTIAN MARTYRS 

This is a painting by J. L. Gérôme of the Colosseum at Rome with Christians praying before the lions attack them. Other Christians are crucified, and some are set on fire. In the background is the Capitoline Hill. were imprisoned; and thousands were tortured, crucified or burned to death. 

5. The Beginnings of the Church. The Christians at first had been organized only as separate communities with presbyters and deacons. The presbyters looked after the spiritual side of the community and helped to keep alive Christian ideals; the deacons collected money to be used in caring for the poor. These early Christians seem to have had only two important ceremonies-baptism and the Lord's Supper. 

Before long the separate communities within the municipalities began to organize into bishoprics, presided over by a bishop, while the churches were served by a single presbyter, or priest. 

As long as the faith was not recognized by the state, this organization could not go much further. But Christian thinkers were beginning to dream of a united church with a single head.

207 Different bishops, too, were setting up claims-the one at Jerusalem because his church was the earliest; the one at Antioch because his was the first to be founded by Peter; the one at Alexandria because that city was the centre of Christian thought; the one at Rome since his church was the last founded by Peter. There is an early tradition that Peter was the first bishop of Rome.

6. Christianity Becomes the State Religion Under the Emperor Constantine. The persecutions themselves showed that the number of Christians in the Empire was so great that it seemed hopeless to destroy them. Realizing this, Ga-lē'ni-us, the Emperor in the East, in 311 granted them freedom of religion. The next year Con'stăn-tine placed on his banners. the Christian monogram. Attributing his victory at the Mil'vi-an Bridge to the aid of the God of his Christian soldiers, he humbly renounced the divine pretensions of the Cæsars, and in 324 declared Christianity to be the religion of the state. 

7. Orthodoxy Is Established in the Church. Among the unorganized churches of the first three centuries there was abundant opportunity for difference of opinion. As a result, the rise of the new faith was marked by quarrels from the very beginning. When the church became a state religion, these differences of belief or heré-sies became of vital importance. A serious difference of opinion started by A'ri-us, a priest of Alexandria, led the Emperor Constantine to arrange for a church Council to determine the true doctrine. This met at 

Nicea and drew up the first Creed, or set of Beliefs, for the church. A person must believe this in order to be orthodox. 

Shortly after this St. Jerome translated the Bible into Latin and this new version, called the Vulgate, became the official text for the church in the West.

8. Constantine Unites the Empire Under a Single Head for a Time. Constantine united the empire once more under a single head and established a new capital at Byzantium (bizăn'shi-um), which henceforth was known as Constantinople. 

However, in 395, at the death of Theodosius the Spaniard, the

This division indicated clearly the growing weakness of the whole machine, which was slowly breaking down under the weight of internal difficulties and external pressure. 

The transfer of wealth to the church and the exemption of the church from taxation and the freeing of church officials from all public burdens threw. greater responsibilities on the rest of the people. The chief burden of taxation fell on the land. When a farmer was unable to pay his taxes, they were collected from his neighbors. This often forced small landowners to abandon their farms or to turn them over to the wealthy, and then poor farmers drifted into the same conditions as coloni. The situation became so bad that the emperor decreed that the children of farmers should follow the same occupation as their fathers in order to make sure that there would be enough of the necessities of life.

During the next forty years, they wandered at will throughout Greece and Italy, even sacking Rome on the way. They finally settled in southern Gaul and Spain. Meantime, other German tribes forced their way across the frontier and invaded much of the European portion of the Empire, and crossed into Africa and Britain. 

10. The Year 476 A. D. Marks the "Fall of the Empire" 

in the West. The authority of the Empire in the west declined rapidly. In 406, Roman officials ceased going to Britain. 

The control of the western emperors passed into the hands of the barbarian commanders of the imperial guard. These men elevated and deposed emperors at will for twenty years until O-do-a'cer in 476 dethroned the last of the line, by the irony of fate named Rom'ū-lus Au-gus-tū'lus, and despatched the crown, the purple boots, and other imperial insignia to Constantinople. Henceforth there was to be a single emperor, but his control over the western part of the Empire was gone. 

11. Justinian Attempts to Restore the Empire. Egypt and the Asiatic part of the Empire and Constantinople remained unravaged, consequently the eastern emperor suffered comparatively little from barbarian interference. True, the Parthians attempted what the barbarians had done, but their hour had not yet come. In 527, Justinian, a man of great energy and ambi-

During Justinian's reign closer connection between Europe and China was established. Monks brought back cocoons of the silkworms hidden in a bamboo cane. With these, the silk industry in the eastern Mediterranean was started, and all the silkworms of Europe are said to be descended from them. 

Justinian also devoted himself quite as much to religious matters as to secular. He believed that the emperor was head of the church as well as of the state, and by imperial decrees, settled theological disputes. In this way he alienated a considerable part of the eastern portion of his empire, whose inhabitants had never fully accepted the Greek ideas of doctrine. At the same time, he was responsible for the sending of missionaries to Ab-ys-sin'î-a, and made it a Christian land. The great church of Sanc'ta Só-phi'à with its magnificent dome, stands as a monument to Justinian's faith and energy.

CHAPTER XXII ISLAM, KNOWN AS MUHAMMADANISM, COMES OUT OF ARABIA IN THE SEVENTH CENTURY 

In the next two chapters we shall find how a religion founded by Muhammad and known to its followers as Islam, built up a following in the vast territory extending from India to Spain south and east of the Mediterranean Sea. Islam had many points in common with Christianity, but Muhammad denied the divinity of Jesus. He said that Jesus was only a great prophet like himself. His followers believed they were called by God to overthrow all other governments. This brought them into constant conflict with the Christian Nations in Asia Minor and Europe. How near they came to the realization of their plans will be evident. We shall find how Muslim scholars kept alive the learning of the Greeks and made contributions in mathematics and science to mankind while European countries were struggling up from barbarism. 

1. The East Reasserts Itself. The one great rival of the Romans was the Parthian Empire which arose about 250 B. C. and lasted about nine hundred years. On account of a change of dynasty it was called the Sassanid Empire during the last four hundred. It received cultural influences from 

India and protected the heretical Nestorian Christians. Early in the sixth century A. D. it overran Roman Asia but was driven out and seriously weakened by the Romans. At the same time the Roman East was much torn by religious difficulties and resented Roman control. Such was the preparation for a new power to control the eastern end of the Mediterranean. 213

2. Arabia at the Dawn of the Seventh Century. At the beginning of the seventh century the great peninsula of Arabia was the home of many Bedouin (běd'oo-in) tribes that wandered over its sandy wastes seeking pasturage for their flocks. 

Here and there were oases where towns of considerable size had developed, especially Mec'ca along the main caravan road lead-

The only business of any importance was the carrying trade. In the towns, as well as in the country, the people were divided into tribes, and there was almost always warfare. 

However, a month's truce each year permitted the tribes to meet for trade.

The sacred city of the Arabs was Mecca. This city had grown up around some hot springs in the desert and owed its

3. The Early Life of Muhammad. At Mecca in 570, called "the year of the elephant" because the king of Abyssinia 

MECCA DURING THE PILGRIMAGE 

This photograph shows the crowd around the Kaaba with its black covering which is renewed each year. In the centre is the pulpit. brought an elephant to help in his attack on the city, was born Muhammad (moo-häm'måt), or, as he is incorrectly called, Mohammed. Little is known of Muhammad's early life except that he was of humble parents and worked as an ordinary shepherd boy and later as a servant to a wealthy widow. He must have been a man of some attractions, for he married his employer. He withdrew each year to the desert for a period of thinking. During one of these periods, the angel Gab'ri-el appeared to him and commanded him to read, a thing which he did not know how to do. Apparently he had no more visions

for a number of years, when suddenly the angel again appeared and revealed to him a new religion. 

4. The Doctrines of Muhammad the Prophet Are Not 

Accepted at First. Muhammad insisted that this religion was that of Abraham, and his first utterances resembled closely those of the old Hebrew prophets. He looked upon Jesus as a prophet. At first, he limited his teaching to his friends and relatives, but later he preached a joyful future life for all who would acknowledge Al'läh as the one and only true God. This teaching and his hatred of idols brought down upon him the enmity of his fellow townsmen, who foresaw a sure destruction of the income of the city of Mecca. The citizens brought pressure upon Muhammad and his followers. Some of them fled to Abyssinia, while Muhammad himself was protected by his uncle.

Muhammad was deep in despair. The Jews and the Arabs of the neighboring city of Yathrib came to Mecca to invite Muhammad to come and be their governor. The Meccans decided to kill him. To prevent this, on July 16, 622, Muhammad secretly left the city. From the date of this flight, or Hěj'i-ra, the whole Muslim world reckons its time. 

5. Muhammad Becomes Governor and Makes Mecca the Sacred City. Muhammad, the Governor, found himself in a very different position from that of Muhammad, the Prophet. 

The Jews, who at first had been interested in his teachings, discovered how little Muhammad knew of their sacred literature and began to laugh at him. Muhammad retaliated by driving them out of Yathrib, or as it now began to be called, Medina (mé-de'nä), meaning "city" of the prophet.

Muhammad's greatest problem as governor was brought upon him by his followers who had come with him from Mecca. They had been compelled to leave behind all their property, and so they felt justified in seizing the property of any Meccans they met. The result was a war between the two cities.

217 While this was going on, Muhammad sent missionaries to the other Arab tribes, and one by one won them over to his side. 

6. The Faith of Islam. The religion founded by Muham mad was called Islam, meaning "submission," and its followers 

THE ANGEL GABRIEL APPEARING TO MUHAMMAD 

This thirteenth-century Persian miniature indicates the changed ideas of art among the later Muslims. 

From F. R. Martin's Miniature Painting. were called Muslims. The practice of Islam rested on five pillars. First of these was the confession of faith, "There is no god but Allah, and Muhammad is his prophet." The others were commands which every good Muslim must obey. The faithful must pray five times a day, carefully purifying themselves before each prayer; they must give alms to the extent of one-tenth of their income; they must fast during the day-time for one month each year; and they must make a pilgrimage each year to Mecca. This last command was afterward changed to make one pilgrimage in a lifetime sufficient.

Islam was a personal religion. It demanded that each individual should deal directly with Allah. It was a religion of right conduct which demanded that its followers should "do unto others as ye would that they should do unto you," although in time the "others" were limited to the faithful. CHAPTER XXIII WITHIN A CENTURY THE EMPIRE OF THE MUSLIMS EXTENDED FROM INDIA TO SPAIN 

1. The Muslim Empire Grows Rapidly. After Islam had swept over Arabia, Muhammad sent letters to the emperor at Constantinople and to the Sassanid king, demanding that they should embrace the new faith. Their refusal led him to set out to win Syria in the Bedouin manner-with the sword-but death overtook him before he had accomplished his purpose. 

His friend, Abu-Bakr (ä'boo-běk'r), was then elected to succeed him with the title of Caliph. 

For a time the new Caliph had to cope with a revolt in Arabia, but he did not give up the Syrian expedition. The war was declared to be a holy war and any one who was killed became a martyr and went directly to heaven. With this promise and the hope of plunder the armies became irresistible. The forces of the empire were beaten in 634 and Syria and Palestine were occupied, and shortly afterward Egypt as well. A short time later the weakened Sassanid power went down in defeat and the Muslims found themselves in possession of wealth of which they had no previous conception. And so it went on, until within barely a century of Muhammad's death the banner of Islam floated from the Indian Ocean to the 

Taurus Mountains and from the Indus River to the "Pillars of

Hercules." Such was the effect of a great unifying idea upon hostile and disunited peoples. 

2. How the Muslim Empire Was Organized. Abu-Bakr was succeeded by O'mar. Omar organized the Muslim conquests into a great political state in which the power of the caliph was absolute. Not only were all Muslims free and equal, but they were entitled to receive pensions from the government. 220

THE EMPIRE OF THE MUSLIMS 

221 Muhammad had insisted that all conquered peoples should be given their choice of embracing Islam, paying tribute, or being put to death. Muslim law prevailed for Muslims, but outside the peninsula the Arabs interfered very little with the liberties of their subjects, provided the tribute was paid properly. Not only was the government left much as it had been before the conquest, but Arabs were even forbidden to settle

3. In the Face of Schism in the Muslim World the 

Muslims Extend Their Empire. Although Mecca and Medina continued to be the sacred cities of Islam, Damascus became its political capital. The effect of this was a further attempt to extend Muslim control westward. In 668 and again. in 717, the Arabs actually attacked Constantinople. Meanwhile there was constant warfare along the whole frontier because there could never be peace between Islam and the rest of the world. In 712 the Muslim hosts crossed the Strait of Gibraltar and invaded the Spanish Peninsula.

4. Social Life Among the Muslims. Social life in the 

Muslim Empire bore a close resemblance to that prevailing today in the same regions. The centre of every village was the mosque (mosk), or meeting-house, where the faithful gathered for prayer, and for a long sermon on Friday, the Muslim Sabbath. The mosque was always bare except for a carpet and a pulpit. On the side toward Mecca there was a little niche to indicate the direction one must face in his praying. On the outside of the mosque stood a tall tower, or min'-à-ret, from the top of which five times a day an official, known as a muzzein (mú-ězʼzin), called the faithful to prayer.

In every Muslim community there was a teacher who taught the boys to read and write. The schools were usually connected with the mosques and consisted of colonnaded courtyards surrounded with rooms in which teacher and pupils sat on the floor cross-legged and spent the day reciting the Koran. 

By the time of the Abbassides, public libraries were also found in many places; for among them the building and endowing of schools and libraries were looked upon as pious acts. 

There developed the practice of women veiling their faces whenever exposed to the gaze of men, and with this came the idea of segregation, a custom which had long been observed among the Greeks. While this resulted in the exclusion of women from society generally, it became such a powerful influence that even to-day no woman is safer than a veiled one on the streets of a Muslim city. It was due to this segregation that every Muslim house had one thing in common-one part was reserved for men and another, the harem, for women. 

The teachings of Muhammad forbade the killing of female children although it was a common practice in many parts of the oriental world. Muslim law, however, did permit a man to have as many as four wives, provided each was given a separate establishment and all were treated on an equality. The most serious charge against Islam was the ease with which divorces

THE EMPIRE OF THE MUSLIMS 

223 could be secured. All that a man had to do to get rid of a wife was to say to her, "I divorce you" and then to return the dowry she had brought him. A woman, too, might secure a divorce under certain conditions. 

5. Muslim Literature and Art. Liter ature among the Muslims took the form largely of scientific, philosophical, and religious works. Still there were some very charming poems produced, even though Muhammad cared little for poets. Their most famous single literary contribution is the collection of stories known as known the 

Thousand - and - One- 

Nights, or as more commonly named The 

Arabian Nights' Entertainments.
