6. Muslim Contri butions in Mathematics and Science Are Very Important. Our debt to Muslim scholars in mathematics and science is large. To them we owe the Hindu system of decimal notation, including the zero character. Just what this has meant for us may be appreciated by attempting to make the simplest arithmetical computations by means of the older systems. Their own greatest mathematical contribution was algebra, in which the Greeks had only made a start. As a result Muslim scholars

Striking effects were obtained by using stones of different colors, elaborate carving, and these peculiar arches. 领​野

were able to carry on the astronomical investigations of the Greeks, and to become the teachers of medieval Europe in both of these subjects. What chemistry owes to the Muslims is shown by such Arabic words as alcohol and alkali, as well as by the name of the science itself. 

Although Muslim physicians were hindered in their study of zoology and physiology by the refusal of Islam to allow the dissection of corpses, they carried on extensive researches in medicine, and substituted drugs and chemicals for the prayers and religious rites of the Christians. Apparently, too, their surgeons were the first to employ anæsthetics for the deadening of pain. In fact, until well into the eighteenth century Muslim text-books in medicine, adapted from the Greek, were the standard for the civilized world.

In applied arts the Muslims also attained high rank. Their knowledge of metals was extensive throughout the western world for centuries, and even to-day a "Damascus blade" is synonymous for beauty of design and perfection of workmanship. They were scientific farmers, understanding well the art of irrigation, rotation of crops, use of fertilizers, the adaptation of crops to soil, the grafting of trees, and plant breeding. 

7. What the World Owes to Islam. The spread of Is lam was a social as well as a religious revolution. Often it found society staggering under selfish, unsympathetic governments without confidence in either the ability or the sincerity of its rulers. Seldom did it meet with any popular resistance, but instead it was regarded as a deliverer, with promise of a rule founded upon justice and mercy.

So long as the caliphs were men of the humility and righteousness of Abu-Bekr and Omar, Islam was a powerful force for the uplifting of mankind. Although in the opinion of many persons it has seemed to fail, we must remember that to-day 270,000,000 persons find the Koran their sole guide to human conduct. For them it is a code of civil and criminal law as well

as a system of theology. Nor must we forget that it was through the great Arab universities which grew up around the mosques at Baghdad, Cairo, and Cordoba that much of the wisdom of the Greeks was kept alive during those centuries of confusion and insecurity which followed the breakdown of the 

Roman Empire.

CHAPTER XXIV THE BYZANTINE EMPIRE AND WHAT EUROPE AND THE MODERN WORLD OWE TO IT 

After the Muslim conquest of Palestine, Syria, and Egypt, Greek was the only language spoken in the lands controlled by the emperor at Constantinople. Although Latin continued to be the official language of the government for a few years longer, at last it was supplanted by Greek. This official Greek was very different from the Greek employed at Athens in the days of Pericles, while the spoken language resembled closely that of the Greeks to-day. This change of language in what was left of the old Roman Empire is recognized by historians through the use of the term By-zăn'tine. Henceforth, we shall speak of that empire as the Byzantine Empire. How it stood for centuries as the guardian of Christianity and as a bulwark between the ambitions of Islam and disorganized western Europe will be made clear in this chapter. 

1. The Difficulties That Beset the Byzantine Emperors. 

The Byzantine emperors were beset by difficulties from within their realm, as well as from without. From the political chaos and social demoralization that had followed the overthrow of the emperor in the West, the Eastern Empire had inherited many administrative problems. For a time all Italy acknowledged the rule of Constantinople, but soon an imperial edict was little recognized outside of Rome, Rä-věn'nä, the southern end of the peninsula, and Sicily.

The greatest task of the emperors was to hold the frontiers. against the pressure of the Muslims in the East and of the barbarians in the North. In fact, the capital was saved from cap- 228

He divided his fifteen thousand prisoners into companies of one hundred and then put out the eyes of all except one man in each company who was spared in order to lead his comrades back home. Basil was ever afterward known as the "Bulgar-slayer." 

2. Why the Christian Church Divided Into the Roman 

Catholic and the Greek Catholic. There was the same close connection between church and state in the Byzantine Empire as in the old Roman Empire, for the emperor claimed supremacy over both the patriarch of Constantinople and the bishop of Rome. However, as Constantinople lost her control over

Italy, the bishop of Rome became more and more independent

THE BYZANTINE EMPIRE 

231 of imperial authority, until in 726 an open break occurred. 

The emperor, Leo III, stung by the taunts of the Muslims that the images and pictures in the churches were evidences of idolatry, had ordered their removal. The bishop of Rome refused to obey the decree. At home this Image Controversy finally was compromised by allowing the use of pictures as sacred memorials. 

As a result of the Image Controversy and of other differences of practice, the church split into two organizations-a Latin church in the West and a Greek church in the East. It was due to this eastern church that the contact of the Byzantine Empire with its neighbors was not wholly a military one. In the ninth century two of its missionaries, Cyril and Měthō'di-us, began the conversion of the Slavs, and in the following century these missionary efforts were extended to what is now Russia. For this reason eastern Europe remains to this day Greek Catholic. To Cyril is ascribed the adaptation of the Greek letters to the needs of the Slavic tongue, and the alphabet now used in Russia and elsewhere is called the Cy-ril'lic.

3. Reasons for the Decline of the Byzantine Empire.

Constant pressure from without and dynastic difficulties from within gradually exhausted the strength of the Byzantine Empire. One evidence of this was a decline in the power of its navy, and this in turn was followed by a lessening of its rich Mediterranean trade and a corresponding loss of imperial revenue. Toward the middle of the eleventh century the throne was occupied by a number of inefficient emperors, and soon after a vicious attack by the Seljuk (sěl-jook') Turks, fierce Muslim fanatics from Central Asia, cost the empire almost the

whole of Asia Minor. This attack was followed by another from the north, and then came the crusades, and the rise of the commercial cities of Venice and Gen'ó-a with their eyes turned on the Byzantine capital.

Constantinople became a great centre to which were brought the raw materials of the West to be exchanged for the products of its work shops, and for the furs that reached it by way of the great trade route along the valley of the Dnieper (ne'pir) to the shores of the Baltic. Lured by the rumors of its wealth and splendor, so many warriors flocked thither from the rocky fiords of Scăn-di-na'vi-a and the forested shores of the North Sea that they gave the name Va-răn' gi-ans to the famous body-guard of the Byzantine emperors. Life in Constantinople retained. many of those luxurious features which had characterized the Roman Empire in its palmiest days. The streets of the city were paved with blocks of stone and were lined with magnificent churches and elaborate homes. Here and there were squares adorned with statues brought from every part of the Hellenic world. The Prince's 

Islands and the shores of the Bosphorus were dotted with the summer homes of wealthy Byzantines. The royal palaces, in which the apartments for men and women were separate, were decorated with beautiful marbles and cared for by thousands of slaves. The emperor was looked upon as sacred and the

approach to his presence was guarded by an elaborate ceremonial. 

6. The Significance of the Empire. As we close this important era in world history, let us consider for a moment just what society owes to, the Byzantine Empire. First of all, it carried on the Roman tradition for a thousand years. 

It kept alive Roman ideas of government and served as a model

CHAPTER XXV THE CHURCH, THE PAPACY, AND MONASTICISM CARRY FORWARD MUCH OF THE OLD GRÆCO-ROMAN CIVILIZATION 

The Church came to be the most permanent institution which the Roman Empire left behind in western Europe. This was due to the fact that after Christianity became the state religion, it was greatly strengthened by the granting of favors. It could hold property. Its clergy were freed from all public duties. 

It was allowed to have church courts which were wholly independent of the imperial courts. Because it had developed a highly organized set of principles, the so-called "church doctrine," and a well-established code of rules and precedents, it could carry on when the regular government of the Roman Empire ceased. How the Christian Church carried many treasures of the past over into a new age and formed the bridge by which civilization was carried to the new nations of western Europe will be realized by reading this chapter. 

1. The Bishop Becomes the Outstanding Person in the 

Community. The bishop, whose origin we have seen, was a most important official with both spiritual and temporal duties. 

As the spiritual head of his church, he admitted persons to communion and he ordained the clergy. As its temporal administrator, he had charge of all church property and looked after the relations with the civil authorities. He was head of the local church court, in which cases involving the clergy were tried. He had also a school for the training of those who wished to become priests. These duties necessarily made him a busy person and left him little time for spiritual leadership. When 238

THE CHURCH AND CIVILIZATION 

239 the empire withdrew from the West, the bishop remained the outstanding person in the community, and he often assumed the duties of the civil officers. 

2. How the Primacy of the Bishop of Rome Was Estab lished. The bishop of Rome was the most important of all the bishops in the West. His church, in addition to being in the imperial city, was the only western church that had been founded by an apostle. So it was insisted by many of the western Christians that the bishop of Rome would have the best knowledge of church teaching, and therefore arose the practice of referring to him doctrinal questions for settlement. Bishop Leo I prevailed upon the emperor, Văl-en-tin'i-an III, to decree that the bishop of Rome took precedence over all the other bishops. 

Papa, the Greek word for priest, at first used for all bishops and priests, came to

3. How the Monks Began. The sixth, seventh, and eighth centuries were a period of social reorganization throughout western Europe. The church, through its various agencies, was doing a great service in keeping society from complete break-

ing up. Not the least of these religious agencies was the institution of monasticism (mó-năs′ti-sizm), which we have already seen in our study of Buddhism. It seems to have grown from that love for self-torture which has always compelled men to seek spiritual solace in lives of solitude and penance. 

The movement seems to have begun in Egypt as early as the third century; and the word "hermit" comes from the name 

Ěr'é-mites or "desert dwellers."

These early Christians deprived themselves of food, eating barely enough to keep alive, and they clothed themselves in hair-cloth shirts, wore belts studded with spikes, and scourged themselves. One very famous man, St. Sim'é-on, took up his abode on the top of a pillar where he remained day and night for forty years, his food being brought to him by an attendant. 

He gained such a reputation that people made long journeys to have him heal their diseases. 

4. St. Benedict Brings Orderliness to Monasticism in

Western Europe. Instead of living singly, the monks began to gather together in mon'ăs-tĕr-ies, or community houses, where each had a cell of his own for prayer and meditation. 

Monasticism was introduced into western Europe by Athanasius and soon spread as far as the British Isles. Two names stood out most prominently in its history-St. Bĕn'é-dict, who established a monastery on Monte Cassino (mon'tá käs-sẽ nó), midway between Rome and Naples, and Căs-sì-ó-dō'rus, who founded a monastery in southern Italy. 

St. Benedict was a Roman of a well-to-do family, who had received a good education, and had held a number of important offices. In middle life he withdrew to a cave to become a hermit and in a few years attracted a large number of followers. For their government he drew up a set of regulations, the Benedictine Rule, which later was adopted by most of the monasteries of western Europe.

The Benedictine Rule provided for a period of training during which the novices (novi-ses) should become acquainted

241 with monastic life. After this training they became monks by taking the vow of poverty, chastity, and obedience. Their lives had to be lived strictly according to the Rule. Eight times each day they gathered in the chapel for prayer. Which buildings were used for the monks themselves and which for other purposes? bound to obey. To distinguish them from the secular clergy who lived out in the world, the monks were known as the regular clergy, from the Latin word "regula" meaning "Rule." 

5. What the Monastery Did for Civilization. The mon astery was the one place where spirituality found a refuge during the turmoil of the "Dark Ages," as the period of tran-

sition in Europe is often called. There practically all the later movements for the betterment of the church had their origin. 

It was due to the monks that manual work, which had been lost through slavery and serfdom, once more assumed a new dignity. The monasteries kept alive the ancient arts and crafts and the monks spread the knowledge abroad when they went out as missionaries. Also through their schools for the training of novices the little learning which had survived was kept from perishing at a time when hardly one priest in ten could read the service that he recited. To their painstaking copyists we owe no small part of our knowledge of the literature of the ancients. And, too, the monasteries served as inns and asylums when nowhere else in the western world did such places exist. 

6. The Expansion of Christianity Into Britain, Ireland, and Germany. We have already seen how the church in the 

Byzantine Empire Christianized eastern Europe. The Latin church did the same in the West. Under the leadership of the 

Pope, it converted the Germanic barbarians and their cousins, the peoples of Scandinavia. In Britain, missionaries from 

Rome came into conflict with Christians from Ireland. 

These Irish Christians were descendants of the earlier converts to Christianity before the barbarian invasions. They had lost contact with other Christians and had slightly different practices. They went out as missionaries to Britain and to the continent and founded the monasteries of St. Gall and Bob'bi-ō, which became famous as centres of learning. 

The Roman missionaries were victorious and Christian England soon furnished missionaries in turn for Germany. The most famous of these, St. Boni-face, founded the great monastery of Fulda (fool'dä) and established the influence of the 

Pope north of the Alps. 

7. How Christian Ideas Changed. As ignorance pre vailed in the West, the Church had to rely more and more upon forms and symbols to express its teachings. This fact

CHAPTER XXVI THE BARBARIANS UNDER CHARLEMAGNE BUILD A GREAT EMPIRE IN WESTERN EUROPE 

We left the barbarians wandering over Europe and northern Africa. They moved as tribes under the leadership of chieftain-kings and then carried their possessions with them. When they settled they established tribal kingdoms. The power of the kings depended upon their fighting ability, and consequently they devoted themselves to military matters. What little civil government there was seems to have been left to minor leaders known as counts and dukes, whose chief duty was to command their fellow tribesmen in war. The right to bear arms was an evidence of freedom and one's only public duty was to perform his share of military service whenever summoned by his chieftain. 

1. The Disruption Caused by the Barbarians. The ravages of the barbarians before they established these tribal kingdoms troubled society very generally. The structure of society which had been built up under the Romans collapsed, wealth disappeared, and the rich and powerful were reduced to the level of the masses. 

Just how great was the actual destruction of property cannot be estimated, but it must have been very great, for Rome alone was sacked twice-in 410 by Alaric and his Visigoths, and again in 455 by the Vandals. Indeed, the very word vandal has come to mean destroyer. However, we cannot prove that the barbarians, when once in peaceful possession of the land, showed any disposition for wanton destruction, but they had little inclination to repair or to stop natural decay. Because they preferred life in the open places to that of the town and 246

city, the barbarians could not appreciate the civilization they inherited. Towns fell into ruins and roads into decay, and agriculture and industries became all but lost arts. 

2. The Barbarians Had a Primitive Idea of Law and 

Justice.

How primitive were the barbarians can be seen from 

A GERMAN COUNCIL 

This scene of the early Germans is carved on the column Marcus Aurelius erected in honor of his victories. their ideas of law and justice. Every man was to be judged by the law of his tribe, but the administration of the law was a personal matter. In case of an injury there was no official to bring the wrong-doer to justice. Instead, the wrong-doer was accused by the injured man, or by his relatives and friends, and then was tried either by ordeal or by compurgation (kompur-ga'shun).

There were various ordeals, such as fire, hot or cold water, and combat. In the ordeal by fire the accused person was required to walk on live coals or other hot objects. After that his feet were wrapped, and he was declared innocent, if at the end of three days his feet healed properly; otherwise, guilty. In the ordeal of cold water the hands and feet of the

accused were tied and he was thrown into a pond. If he sank, he was innocent; if he floated, guilty. In the ordeal by combat, he proved his innocence by fighting the accuser or some person who represented his accuser. If he won, he was adjudged innocent.

In compurgation, or purifying by oath, the accused swore that he was innocent, and then had a number of other persons swear that he was a truthful man. Here, as well as in trial by ordeal, no attempt was made to ascertain the facts, but the determination of the guilt or innocence of the accused was supposed to be left to God. 

3. The Barbarians and the Romans. The number of barbarians invading the Roman provinces was small compared with the number of the Romans. With the exception of the 

Franks, they died out rapidly on account of their continual fighting and the change of climate. That the Franks were an exception was due to the fact that they never forsook their homeland which lay just beyond the Rhine. 

The barbarians were able to hold the land which they won by their conquests because of the disappearance of the rich and powerful class. At first there was little intermarriage between the barbarians and the Romans, because, except the Franks, they were Arian heretics. Because they believed that law and government were personal matters, they retained Roman law and taxation alongside of their own. To this there was one notable exception-in Italy. When the Ŏs'tró-goths under Thé-ŏďó-ric occupied that country, they continued largely the Roman practices, as their king had spent much time at Constantinople in a high official position. 

4. The Franks Build Up a Kingdom in Gaul. Most of the barbarian kingdoms disappeared within three centuries except those of the West Saxons in Britain and of the Franks on the continent. The Franks differed from the others, in that they did not abandon their homeland. They embraced Chris-

tianity after one of their chieftains won a battle in which the victory was attributed to the assistance of the Christian God. Although their Christianity was only a veneer, the fact that they were orthodox linked them closely with Rome. This also gave them an excuse for warring against their neighbors, the Visigoths and Burgundians. When Clo'vis, the founder of their kingdom, died, they controlled all northern Gaul and the valley of the Rhine.

In good Teutonic fashion Clovis divided his kingdom among his sons and let loose a storm which continued as long as any of his descendants ruled. In the wars that followed, each king tried to gain control of the entire domain, and such confusion prevailed that the counts and dukes and wealthy land-owners became more and more independent of royal authority. 

5. The Mayors of the Palace Come Into Power and 

One Is Crowned by the Pope. The Frankish kings acquired more of the vices of the peoples whom they conquered than they did of the virtues. They fought with each other and committed horrible crimes.

The government of the country gradually passed into the hands of the counts and dukes, and the little authority which remained to the kings was exercised by servants. Since his position brought him closest to the king, the major dō'mō, or mayor of the palace, became the most powerful person in the kingdom. By the seventh century the mayor of Austrasia (aus-trā'shi-a), as one of the Frankish kingdoms was called, became so strong that he was able to usurp the kingship. He was assassinated by the other nobles, but the power of the mayors of the palace continued. They did, however, proceed more slowly, until Pěp'in of Heristal (ha'ris-tal) was able to establish control not only over Austrasia, but also over some of the other kingdoms. Pepin was followed by an illegitimate son, Charles.

Charles turned out to be an able ruler. He re-established the authority of the king over counts and dukes, and re-organized the church. It was Charles, too, who defeated the Muslim hosts at Tours (toor), and won for himself the name

From a silver group in the Monza Treasury. of Mär-tel', "the hammer." In organizing his army to meet the 

Muslims, Charles siezed the lands of the church and turned them over to certain Franks.

Even so powerful an individual as Charles Martel did not dare to dethrone the "do-nothing" kings. It remained for his son Pepin to take that step. Pepin wrote to the Pope and asked whether the man who had the power without the title, or the man who had the title without the power ought to be king. 

The Pope decided in favor of the man who had the power. 

His envoys hastened to Frankland to anoint the new ruler, thus establishing the principle that kings ruled by divine right,

25I instead of the older tradition that their power rested upon the will of the tribe and upon military prowess. 

6. The Franks Under Pepin Defeat the Lombards and 

Make the Pope a Temporal Ruler. The Pope had another reason for wanting to crown Pepin. Since his break with the

Byzantine Emperor in 726, he had been the ranking authority at Rome. This independence had its dangers, for the king of the Lombards from his capital at Milan was casting greedy eyes upon the fertile lands to the south. The Pope hoped to find in the Franks allies who would help to keep the Lombards at a distance.

Pepin listened to the papal entreaties and marched against the Lombards. After defeating them, he presented to the Pope the lands in the peninsula which formerly belonged to the Eastern Empire. Thus the Pope became a temporal ruler and in the minds of the later occupants of the throne of St. Peter, the spiritual leadership of Christendom and the temporal control of territory have often been confused. 

7. Charles Becomes King of the Franks. Pepin left his kingdom to his two sons, Charles and Kär'lo-man. Inasmuch as Karloman preferred the life of a monk, Charles became sole ruler.

Charles was a large and powerful man and much better educated than any of his predecessors, even though he could not write his name. His boundless energy inspired him to undertake to bring the Germanic peoples on the continent under one rule. Although he had difficulty with the Lombards who objected to Frankish interference in the affairs of Italy, this difficulty was slight when compared with the difficulty which he had with the Saxons on the northern frontier. In an effort to subdue them, Charles led expedition after expedition into their country, but with little success. At last he sent missionaries among them to establish monasteries with the hope of civilizing them and inducing them to settle down. The situa-

tion was not solved until he forbade all pagan practices on pain of death. The trouble with the Lombards was settled by 

Charles placing their "Iron Crown" on his head.

Charles also had trouble with the Muslims in the southwest. 

CHARLEMAGNE'S IMPERIAL CROWN 

A fine piece of gold work from the ninth century. 

To put a stop to this, he crossed the Pyrenees and occupied the northeastern corner of Spain. During this invasion his rear guard was attacked by mountaineers and one of his captains,

Roland (ró-län'), was killed. 

In later years this incident inspired the first piece of French literature, the Song of Roland. 

8. Charles Inaugurates More Efficient Government. To govern successfully so large a territory as Charles now ruled it was necessary to have a careful organization. The old counts and dukes were retained, but their powers were clearly defined, and inspectors, called missi (me'sē), were sent about the country to keep watch over them. These inspectors travelled in pairs—a clergyman and a layman-to serve as a check upon each other. Along the frontiers Charles organized a special type of province, called the "County of the Mark." The märgrāves, as the governors were called, had powers; for example, they could call out troops to repel attacks without waiting to obtain royal permission.

Charles also recognized that military service had become a

serious burden now that the kingdom was extensive, so he arranged that four poor men might join and equip one of their number for the army. Since there was no system of taxation, except military service, and the king had to depend for his income on his personal property, Charles made arrangements for the management of his own farms or villas. In doing so he set an example for his subjects. 

9. Charles Is 

Crowned Emperor by the Pope. In 800 the Pope had trouble with some of his subjects. They mistreated him so shamefully that he appealed to Charles for aid. Charles went to Rome to settle the affair. 10. Charles's Interest in Education and His Famous

School. Charles was tremendously interested in education. 

He welcomed scholars to his court from every quarter, and organized the "Palace School," bringing from England Alcuin (ǎl'kwin), the greatest scholar of the day, to preside over its

From Vétault's Charlemagne. activities. In order that there should be no embarrassment due to a difference of rank, both students and teachers assumed names taken from the 

Bible or from the classics, Charles being known as "David" and Alcuin as "Horace." When Alcuin tired of his duties, he withdrew to Tours, and founded a school which spread learning over much of western Europe. 

Charles's interest in education did not stop with this "Pal- ace School," for he insisted that the clergy should be educated sufficiently to read correctly, and also that the schools in the monasteries should be open to any who wished to attend. During his reign, too, a new system of writing was developed in which the characters were so distinct that centuries later they served as models for the movable type made necessary by the invention of printing.

That Charles had an artistic soul is shown by the many beautiful buildings of a Byzantine type which his Italian architects erected for him at his capital Aachen (ä'ken). They serve as testimony to his liberality, for in that moneyless age no such beautiful buildings could have arisen without imperial aid. 

11. The Significance of Charles's Reign. Charles had a perfect right to be called Charlemagne or "Charles the Great."

Not only did he build up a great realm, but he governed it well. 

Only a man with extraordinary energy and strength could have carried on so many campaigns and undertaken so many reforms. As an emperor crowned by the Pope, he symbolized Britons ENGLAND

THE DIVISIONS OF CHARLEMAGNE'S EMPIRE IN 888 A. D. 

Where is the present northern and eastern boundary line of France? RAISL what is said to have been the task of the "Middle Ages." When the greatest of the barbarian leaders received from the hands of the head of the Church the highest office in the Græco-Roman world, the unification of these three elements into a new civilization may be said to have begun. 

12. The Break-up of Charles's Empire. Charles's empire went to pieces not long after his death. It was so large and so

lacking in unity that in 843 the three sons of Louis the Pious voluntarily divided it up. Charles the Bald took the western part; Louis the German, the eastern; and Lothaire (ló-thâr′), with the title of Emperor, took Italy and a narrow strip in the north which included the imperial capital Aachen. 

How great was the difference between the east and the west even in those days may be seen in taking the so-called "Strǎss'bûrg oaths" which sealed the treaty between Louis and Charles.

Charles took the oath in the German language so that the soldiers of Louis might understand him; and Louis took the oath in a corruption of the Latin language that eventually became known as "French," so that he might be understood by the soldiers of Charles.

In 870 another division took place and the emperor was left with only Italy. These divisions are important because they serve as mileposts in the struggles among the kings of the parts of his empire which later became France, Italy, and Germany. 

In order to secure the support of the nobles, the kings handed out property on all sides and even freed the nobles from the supervision of the royal inspectors by granting immunities.

The result was the kings were so weakened that they found themselves powerless to meet the attacks of the new hordes of invaders who harassed the western world.

CHAPTER XXVII EUROPE IS MENACED BY NEW INVASIONS 

While Charlemagne's empire was being weakened from within, new dangers were threatening it from without. In the north, the inhabitants of the Scandinavian peninsula were becoming restless and were beginning to ravage the coasts and river-valleys of western Europe. In the south, Muslim pirates were overrunning the Mediterranean and raiding the adjacent mainland. In the northeast, the Slavs were beginning to push their way into the lands of the Germans, thus starting the long struggle which has continued even to this day. In central Asia, the Mongol peoples were again overflowing toward the west and crowding out of their homes bands of Magyars (modyors) and their kinsmen, the Turks. How great was the unrest may be appreciated when we realize that only Egypt of the Muslim lands and Constantinople of the Christian were able to save themselves from these new invasions. 

1. The Northmen Are Especially Aggressive. The in habitants of the Scandinavian peninsula were closely akin to the 

Teutons. These Northmen, or Vi'kings or "fiord (fyôrd) men," as they were sometimes called, were a fierce, uncivilized people accustomed to a wild free life with plenty of fighting. 

Before the death of Charlemagne their warriors had begun to come in long, open boats to raid the shores of western Europe, partly to avenge the Emperor's fire and sword method of substituting the worship of Christ for the worship of Odin. 

After the introduction of Christianity into Scandinavia in the ninth century, some Northmen desired peace and quiet.

They supported a king who placed a limit on private warfare with the result that the more turbulent part of the people turned 258

2. The Later Conquests of the Northmen Carry Them to Greenland, Russia, and Sicily. The Northmen were the first Europeans to put out to sea in defiance of all the myths about the sea. By 900 there were Norse settlements in Iceland. and, if the old Sagas are to be believed, by 1000 there were settlements in Greenland, and Northmen had visited the American coast, perhaps as far as Rhode Island. 

Meanwhile, other Northmen sailed eastward through the

Baltic to the shores of Finland and under the name of Rus (rooz) pushed their way southward, partly afoot and partly by boat, until at last they reached the Caspian and Black

Seas. At Novgorod (nôv'gó-rót) their leader Rurik (roo'rik) established a settlement which grew into a great trading centre. 

From there Rurik's successor, Duke O'leg, set out to capture Kiev (ke'ef) and laid the foundation of the Russian Empire. 

To complete this story of the Northmen we must turn to southern Italy. Early in the eleventh century some Normans from Normandy returning from a pilgrimage to the Holy Land were invited to take a hand in a little war which was going on there. Within a few years they succeeded in taking the southern end of the peninsula, and Sicily from the Muslims. 

3. The Magyars Invade Europe and Finally Settle in 

Hungary. After the overflow of the Teutons and Slavs, central Asia seems to have enjoyed a period of comparative quiet. 

By the ninth century the Mongols were in commotion again. 

Waves of Mongolian Magyars and Aryan-Avars (ä'värs) pushed westward and were soon raiding the fertile plains of southwestern Europe. The Magyars drove a wedge straight through the Slavs, who after Charlemagne's death had pushed westward almost to the Elbe. 

4. The Real "Dark Ages" Follow These Invasions.

These invasions brought upon western Europe a new series of misfortunes. The slight gain in civilization during Charlemagne's reign was practically wiped out. Thousands of persons were killed or carried off, and much property was destroyed. Worse than everything else was the failure of the governments to furnish protection.

Because the kings and emperors were too weak to cope with the invaders, the local authorities afforded such protection to the people as they could. The bonds that should have held a people together were broken and each community developed the habit of standing alone. If we may give the name "Dark Ages" to any part of history, it is to the period from 850 to 1050. 

5. The Decay of the Caliphate Sets in at This Time.

While Charlemagne's Empire was breaking up in the West, the

empire of the caliphs was doing the same in the East. Powerful governors of the provinces became independent, and rival caliphates were established in Spain and North Africa. Dissension among the Arabs and between them and the Muslim converts from other races, together with the differences of Sunnite and Shiite rent the Muslim world from end to end. 

THE SIEGE OF ANTIOCH 

A medieval conception of the Christian attack. 

From a miniature in the Livre des Merveilles. 

As early as the ninth century, Egypt and northern Africa were lost never to be regained, while soon afterward the East also broke up into small states. 

6. The Turks Become Muslims and Seize Asia Minor for a Time. In the Muslim world the Turks played much the same part as the Normans did in Europe. These nomads of central Asia ravaged the Muslim frontiers until the weakness of the Caliphate permitted them to enter. They embraced Islam and in the tenth century founded a strong state in Af-ghǎn'î-

stän and began the conquest of India. Another group, the 

Seljuks (sel-jooks), took control of the Caliph himself and conquered Asia Minor from the Eastern Empire. Although their ruler gathered around himself able men, like the astronomer and poet Omar Khayyam, they attempted to control too much territory and their empire broke up. It left the Muslim world more disturbed than ever and their harsh treatment of Christian pilgrims at Jerusalem was one of the causes of the attack of western Europe against Islam.

THE PERIOD OF MEDIEVAL CIVILIZATION Chapters XXVIII-XXXVII The Foreword 

To modern people the Middle Ages seem a time of superstition and ignorance. The reason for this is because the real meaning of the Middle Ages is concealed by the tradition which surrounds every event of the time. In reality, however, there were steady growth and progress which, in spite of a thousand difficulties, was carried on through the whole period. 

The Christian church, which kept the light of culture burning through the storms of the invasions, became the centre around which all the life of the time revolved. Its ideas dominated men's actions and led them to feel that this world was manifestation of the work of the Creator and moved according to his will.

Its organization, derived from the Roman Empire, sought to control society for the glory of God. It stamped out opposition to its ideals and labored to improve and to develop its teaching to explain the Christian world. It accepted the inequality of men in the social scale but it permitted the lowest to rise by his virtues to the throne of St. Peter and to rule over kings and emperors.

At the same time the system of feudalism taught the ideas of personal honor and furnished the code of chivalry and a foundation for law. Meanwhile the slow development of commerce and industry caused the rise of towns and cities and established a new class in society, which was destined to lead the march of civilization into the modern age.

CHAPTER XXVIII THE MEDIEVAL SYSTEM OF AGRICULTURE PROVIDED ONLY THE BARE MEANS OF SUBSISTENCE 

We have seen how commerce and industry declined during the later Roman Empire, and how it disappeared, except in southern Europe under the barbarians. This was because the wants of society became fewer and fewer. Except for those articles needed in the church service and for the weapons and some of the finer clothing of the upper classes, everything that was required could be produced in the separate community. 

Under the later Roman Empire each estate had tried to become self-supporting by reducing the number of things to be obtained from abroad.

Under the barbarian kings there was no system of taxation other than military service. All the officials from the kings down to the poorest subjects depended on the agricultural lands. Even so great a ruler as Charlemagne found it necessary to move continually from one estate to another in order to feed his court and their servants and animals. 

1. Medieval Estates Were Known as Manors. These estates, many of them the villas of wealthy Romans, were known as manors (măn'ers). Each estate consisted of a tract of cultivated land surrounded by pastures and woodlands. Each had a house for the owner or his representative, sheds for the live stock, and huts for the peasants, who were known as serfs or villeins (vilins). There was usually a grist mill owned by the lord, and often a church which was also controlled by him. 

In many instances the manor house was fortified to serve as a refuge in case of attack. 265

Common Pasture 

Mill 

2. The System of Cultivation Was Very Crude. The cultivated lands of the manor were usually divided into three main fields. These fields were divided into strips one or two rods wide and often a quarter of a mile long and separated by low ridges of unplowed turf. The reason for this division into three fields was a lack of knowledge of artificial fertilizers, and the difficulties of cultivation.

It was customary to sow on one of the fields one year a winter crop of wheat or barley; on another, a summer crop of oats; the third was

All of the fields lay fallow once in three years. Since there were no cultivated grasses as on modern farms, whether there was any coarse hay for fodder depended on the presence of some swampy ground.

The land was worked with a very heavy plow, of which the only metal part was the point. All further cultivation was carried on by hand. As might be expected with such a poorly prepared seed bed, crop yields were small; in fact, a fourfold return for wheat was considered good. There was little seed

A SIXTEENTH-CENTURY MANOR FARMYARD

From a miniature in a Flemish fifteenth-century edition of Vergil's Georgics.

improvement and little practice of diversification of crops. 

Very few vegetables were raised except beans and turnips.

Owing to the scarcity of fodder, the number of draft animals was limited. Horses were seldom used because they could not be eaten when they died. Sheep were raised principally for their wool. Pigs furnished a large part of the meat supply because they were easily fattened on acorns and could be wintered with little difficulty. 

3. The Serf or Villein Did the Work and Was Attached to the Land. The work on the manor was done by the serfs or villeins. Three days of each week they worked for their lord except at sowing and harvest time when they frequently had to put in so many extra days that they neglected their own crops. 

In addition they had to grind their grain at the lord's mill for a fee, and to pay him a "due" whenever they sold any of their produce. Besides, they were expected to make him presents now and then, eggs, poultry, a shote or calf, honey, etc. If they got into a fight or had any difficulties with their neighbors, the matter had to be settled in the lord's court, and the lord received a fee. To the lord, too, went the fees which the serfs were required to pay for the support of the church. 

Moreover, the work of the manor house was done by their wives and daughters, who helped in the spinning of the wool and the weaving of the cloth.

In return for all this, they were allotted about thirty acres of land which they could cultivate for themselves, but which were usually so widely separated that the results were quite unsatisfactory. The serfs were attached to the soil and could not leave the manor, nor even marry, without the lord's permission. Under such restrictions, it is not strange that they were never satisfactory farmers. 

4. The System Had Many Disadvantages. With such a system of cultivation the margin between living and starving was relatively narrow. A drought or storm might completely

ruin the crops and lack of communication of means of exchange would prevent the importation of food from any distance. As in India to-day, there were famine and pestilence in some part of western Europe nearly every year. 

About the only thing which may be said in favor of this system is that it kept agriculture alive. Certainly its influence on the character of the peasants was bad, for it developed lazy habits. There was no incentive to one person to improve his strips or to keep down the weeds, when the attempt could be defeated by the carelessness of his neighbor. Since the serfs could not move about, they had no means of learning that there were better ways of doing things.

CHAPTER XXIX WITH THE DECLINE OF CENTRAL AUTHORITY FEU- DALISM AFFORDED A WAY OF UNITING PEOPLE INTO LOCAL UNITS 

We have seen how the idea of tribal unity which had held the barbarians together when they settled down and began to form kingdoms of their own was weakened later by the idea of empire. Likewise we have seen how the strength of the central authority was undermined by the struggles which went on among the successors of Charlemagne, by the granting of immunities, and by the invasion of hostile peoples. With society in such a disorganized condition, it was essential that some new means of uniting people should be found, and feudalism seemed to offer the remedy. 

1. The Origin and Sources of Feudalism. Feudalism had its beginning when the local authorities undertook to protect their communities against the violence of the "Dark Ages." 

Some of these authorities were counts, some dukes, others bishops, archbishops, and even abbots. The task of all was to find a new kind of relationship by which men might be bound to obey them, while they themselves in turn would be bound to obey others. They understood well the relationship between master and slave and knew that this would not succeed, for the whole undertaking depended on a willingness to fight. A good fighter is always a free man. They understood the old relationship between the Teutonic chieftains and their followers, to which the Romans had given the name of com-i-ta'tus. The young men were supplied with weapons and food by their 270

leaders, and they realized that there was nothing degrading in this relationship and it lasted as long as the chieftain furnished plenty of fighting and showed no signs of cowardice. 

2. The Institution of Feudalism Rested upon the Relationship between Lord and Vassal. Feudalism rested on three things: the lord, the vassal, and the fief (fēf). It grew up at a time when protection was the great need of society, and any one with the power and strength to get other persons to obey him could become a lord. Under such conditions the ablest fighter naturally won the highest position. 

If the territory controlled by a lord was more than he could administer personally, he would turn over a part of it to some other person, who would become his vassal and would hold the property as a fief. As time passed, any kind of property capable of furnishing an income might be given as a fief. 

Moreover, the lord might be forced to become the vassal of some other lord more powerful than himself, and to receive from him his own property as a fief. 

3. The Complexity of the Feudal Relationship. Since feudalism was devised for the purpose of fighting, warfare became the normal condition of society. Lords were continually quarrelling with one another and trying to steal each other's fiefs, and vassals frequently rebelled against their lords. 

One of the chief causes of all this strife was the complex feudal relationship which developed. Many ambitious men became vassals of more than one lord. There were plenty of instances, too, where a vassal was his own lord's lord of another fief which he had granted to his lord as a vassal. Attempts were made to get rid of some of these difficulties by stipulating in the oath of fealty that if two lords who had the same vassal got to fighting, this vassal would not have to serve on both sides. However, this did not prevent him from taking the side opposed to that which his oath called for, if he saw that he might gain any advantage by so doing.

4. The Vassal and His Duties to His Lord. The vassal, who got his name from the Latin word väs'sus meaning a slave, became vassal by going through elaborate ceremonies. First, he did homage by kneeling before the lord and placing his hands in the lord's, thus becoming the lord's homo, or man.

Next, he rose and took the oath of fealty, by placing his hand on sacred relics. These two acts constituted the feudal bond. After the oath, the lord invested the vassal with the fief by giving him a piece of sod taken from the fief. IGILL RAI

VASSAL RECEIVING HIS FIEF 

The seal of Raymond de Mondragon showing him pledging faith to the Archbishop of Arles.

In the National Archives of France. 

A vassal's first duty was to serve his lord as a fighting man for forty days each year.

Such fighting men were called knights and the size of the fief determined how many knights would be at the lord's command. In case the lord was besieged in his castle, it was the vassal's duty to aid in the defense. 

He also was bound to attend the lord's court to assist with his advice in settling disputes between other vassals. And finally, he was expected to entertain his lord for a specified time each year, and to pay to him sums of money known as aids. There were three of these aids, one to help pay the cost of knighting the lord's eldest son, another to help make up the dowry for the marriage of his eldest daughter, and a third to aid in securing his ransom in case of capture by an enemy. Other money payments, known as reliefs, were required when either the lord or the vassal died and he was succeeded by his son. 

It must be remembered that this list of duties was not universal

because feudalism was subject to many local variations.

5. The Knight and the Practices and Ideals of Chivalry. 

In feudalism the term knight meant a fighting man on horseback. When this horseman began to wear armor and so had 8000

LALPLAY THE OATH OF KNIGHTHOOD 

A modern painting by Edwin A. Abbey in the Boston Public Library indicating the religious element in the ceremony. to have a squire to assist him, it included the latter as well. 

Before feudalism ended, the art of fighting became so complicated that a knight's service meant actually the mounted man with six attendants. That the art of fighting became so complicated was largely due to the development in the manufacture of weapons and armor. In order to be able to use these effectively the knight had to undergo a long period of training, consequently only he who had sufficient wealth to pay for this

and to buy a horse and accoutrements could expect to be a knight. Thus, a knight enjoyed a privileged position in society, which resulted in a set of practices and ideals which came to be known as chivalry.

The result was that a man eligible for knighthood must have completed the necessary technical training, and besides he must show himself possessed of the high ideals which characterized chivalry. Although in exceptional cases, he might be dubbed a knight on the battlefield as a reward for some deed of unusual valor, as a rule it followed a long period of training and many tests. Then it was a very formal ceremony, accompanied by fasting and prayer, and finally by a bath. 

6. The Castle Was the Centre of Feudal Life. At first the castle was often only a wooden building in some inaccessible place, such as a hill or crag, a swamp, or an island, and surrounded by a palisade or hedge. Later it was built of stone, and it was protected by high walls and a moat or ditch, which was filled with water and was crossed by a bridge that could be hoisted in time of danger. Within the walls was a courtyard, surrounded by living quarters for the knights and servants, stables for the animals, and storehouses for supplies and weapons. In one corner was the donjon (dun'jun), a strongly fortified tower, on the fourth floor of which the lord and his family usually had their apartments. 

Many of these castles were so strong that they were practically impregnable until the invention of gunpowder changed warfare and brought feudalism to an end. Feudal warfare often degenerated into long-drawn-out sieges in which there was great suffering on the part of the peasants. 

7. Feudal Life at Its Best Was Crude. Taken as a whole, feudal life was rough and uncomfortable. Even the apartment of the lord's family had few of the conveniences we enjoy to-day. The walls, although frequently hung with exquisite tapestries, were badly chinked, and the windows were so

seldom of glass that the rooms were swept by the wintry blasts. 

The only heating arrangement was an open fireplace. Often the floor was covered with rushes to protect the feet from the cold and to hide the dirt. 

The centre of the life of the castle was the great hall. Here the household feasted, and the lord dispersed justice and received the homage of his vassals. At one end of the room

The lady holds a falcon. Compare the room and its furnishings with a modern bedroom. stood a small table on a raised platform for the iord and his guests. Below this were long tables at which were seated the knights and men-at-arms, and members of the household, each according to his rank. Dinner as a rule was served at noon and consisted of several meat courses with plenty of wine. 

Forks were unknown and spoons were used only for eating broth. Each person cut with his own knife what he wished from the great roasts, and dished out with his hands generous portions of the meat pies. The hands were dried by crumbling within them pieces of bread.

The chief amusements of feudal life were fighting, hunting, and gambling. In order that there should be plenty of game, JOUSTING Notice the blunted lances, the heralds, and the spectators in the background on this ivory panel.

all the wild animals in the forest roundabout the castle were reserved for the lord, and it was an offense punishable with death for any serf or villein to be caught poaching. Nearly every castle had its jester or professional clown, whose antics

were frequently supplemented by wandering minstrels and jugglers. On great occasions, like the knighting of the lord's sons or the marriage of his daughters, there were elaborate entertainments, consisting of tournaments in which the knights fought with blunted spears. As the victor had the right to the horse and armor of his adversary, these contests were spirited affairs in which men sometimes lost their lives. 

8. The Life of the Feudal 

Women. Although, as a rule, the women of the feudal age were not fighters, still they played an important part in the society of that day. They were almost as rough and uncouth as the men. They supervised the life of the castle during the absence of their husbands, and they dressed wounds and cared for any simple ailments. 

Because they might become heiresses to fiefs, their marriage was usually arranged while they were mere children. Since

A GAME OF CHESS 

there was no question of love in these marriages, knights were prone to pay court to other men's wives. Not only did they frequently fight for the women, but they performed deeds of valor merely for their smiles. 

9. Feudalism Had a Corrupting Influence on the

Church. Feudalism had very serious effects upon the church. 

The clergy often appeared both as lords and vassals, and many of them took a greater interest in their temporal oppor-

tunities than in their spiritual duties. This sometimes led to simon-y, or the buying of church offices, by men ill-fitted to hold them. Worse still was the control by laymen over the church offices. This led to the practice of lay investiture, in which the laymen assigned the newly elected bishop the fief and also the spiritual prerogatives of his office. A third abuse threatened the whole economic position of the church. Although marriage of the clergy had long been forbidden by the Latin church, it still persisted and received a new life by development of feudalism. Even the Pope could not escape the general breakdown of society. The Donation of Pepin had made him a temporal ruler and this position seemed to overshadow his headship of the Church. 

10. Enforcement of the Truce of God Eliminates Some of the Fighting. Out of the monastery came the influence which was destined to bring about a reform, and eventually to lead an attack upon the worst evils of the feudal system. Early in the tenth century a new monastery founded at Cluny (klü-ne') in Bur'gun-dy started a great reform which had an influence on all Central Europe. To the Church we owe the first attempt to limit feudal warfare. In the eleventh century 

Church councils decreed and attempted to enforce the Truce of God by which fighting was to cease from Wednesday evening until Monday morning. Although the barons bitterly resented this interference of the Church, the terrors of excommunication had a profound influence in improving conditions. 

11. The Significance of Feudalism. Feudalism was an attempt to solve a great political problem. From it started a new line of political thought which can be traced down to the present day. Because fiefs could not be successfully divided, there arose the custom of pri-mo-ġěn'i-túre, or inheritance by the eldest son, to take the place of the old Teutonic equal division among all the sons. This custom developed a code of morals and ideals by which many of the people of Europe are

still influenced. To it we trace that exaggerated sense of personal honor which was responsible for the system of duelling..

DUATE FAR OLDVO ADVVILGELMVM NORMANNORVM: DVCEM CHAPTER XXX HOW FEUDALISM WAS PRACTISED IN ENGLAND AND FRANCE 1. The Prevalence of Feudalism. Feudal ideas and prac tices did not develop everywhere at the same time, nor did they always develop in the same way. Their earliest appearance was in France and from France they were carried by the Normans to England. In Germany they were strongly modified by the old tribal customs, while in Italy they never obtained the same hold which they had in other parts of western Europe. 

Feudalism was also present in the Byzantine Empire and among the Muslims, but in different form. In the East, too, it enjoyed a longer life than in the West; .n fact, as recently as the nineteenth century it was being practised in Japan. 

Since time will not permit us to discuss all its different forms under the influence of national traditions and customs, we shall content ourselves with showing how it worked in medieval 

England and France. 

2. How Feudalism Was Established in England. In 

1066, William, the powerful Duke of Normandy, invaded England, insisting that the throne had been promised to him by the former king, Edward the Confessor. He defeated Harold at 

Hastings and on Christmas day was crowned King of England.

William carried with him to England the feudal organization. He was fully aware of the difficulties of a feudal lord in holding his vassals in control, and in order to prevent the Norman barons who had crossed over with him from becom- 280

FEUDALISM IN ENGLAND 

281 ing too powerful, he allotted them fiefs so distributed that no one might become strong enough to defy the royal authority. 

In doing this, he was careful not to despoil completely the old English nobility. As an additional measure of protection, he built castles in strategic places and manned them with garrisons, wholly under his control. 

As a feudal lord had control over his own vassals only, William compelled all who held fiefs in England to swear allegiance to him, at a great meeting on Salisbury (Sôlz'ber-i) Plain. In order that he might know how strong each of the barons was, he compiled a census, known as the Domesday (dōmz'dā) Book, in which all the taxable resources of the land were shown. In this manner William adapted the feudal system to the necessities of a strong kingdom. 

3. William's System Failed for Lack of Strong Successors. The system worked well in the hands of a powerful man like William, but not all of his successors were strong rulers. They held at the same time the position of kings of 

England and dukes of Normandy. This led to constant friction, for one or the other group of vassals was always ready to take advantage of their absence. And besides, the interests of the two positions were often quite opposed, for as Duke of Normandy the King of England was a vassal of his rival, the King of France.

When William's direct male line gave out, the Crown of England and the duchy of Normandy passed to another family, the Plăn-tåg én-ěts, who were counts of Anjou (än-zhoo'). 

Henry II, the first Plantagenet, married the Duchess of Aquitaine (ǎk-wi-tān'), and thus increased his continental possessions so that he held almost half the kingdom of France. 

4. Henry II Reorganizes the Judicial System. When 

Henry II ascended the throne, his English vassals had become nearly as independent as if the regulations of William had never existed. It was Henry's work to put a stop to this feudal

anarchy. This he did by reorganizing the entire judicial system of the country.

In controlling the courts of justice, a feudal lord not only exercised authority but also obtained money, for he received the fees and a part of the fines of the court. To offset this, Henry developed courts of his own and caused judges to travel through the kingdom on definite "circuits" to hear any cases that might be brought before them. These judges established such a reputation for integrity and justice that the people soon began to prefer to settle their disputes in the royal courts. In fact, their decisions became so famous that they were actually accepted as law, thus giving rise to what is to-day known as the "Common Law."

This development of royal courts was also accompanied by an enlargement of the old English jury system. Henceforth there were two kinds of juries, the grand jury and the petit (pěti) jury. The grand jury was composed of twenty-four men who were to ascertain what crimes had been committed and to make accusations against the wrongdoers. When a man was accused by a grand jury, a petit or "small" jury, consisting of twelve men, was summoned to try him. The men composing this jury had to be of the same rank as was the person to be tried, hence the expression, "a jury of one's peers." 

Both of these juries are still a part of our own judicial system. In connection with this fact, it is interesting to note that their names are French words, and when the sheriff opens court, he still cries out, “Ō'yěz! Oyez!” the French word for "Hear ye!" From such things as these we learn to appreciate the real significance of the Norman invasion. It brought to England the French tongue, which served for several centuries as the official language of the country. In the end the old Saxon language supplanted the speech of the conquerors, but the influence of the Norman invasion is still to be seen in the French words that are to-day a part of the English language.

6. Why the Magna Charta Is So Important in English 

History. The Magna Charta contained almost nothing new, but it was a written statement of the things an English king could not do. How great this triumph of feudalism was may be appreciated when we realize that the Magna Charta authorized rebellion against a king who violated its provisions. 

According to the terms of the Magna Charta, towns were not to be oppressed; merchants were not to be deprived of their property for trivial offenses; taxes were not to be imposed without the consent of the Great Council, an old Saxon advisory body continued by the Normans after the Conquest. 

Henceforth this council was to include all the. prelates and nobles, not just those who happened to be the king's vassals. 

The more important were to be summoned by individual command, and the lesser by a general summons to be read in open court, by the sheriffs of the several counties. 

The Magna Charta also declared that every man accused of crime should be accorded a speedy trial at the hands of his peers. This provision did not apply to villeins or serfs, who were regarded as so much live stock. It did ordain, however, that they should not be dispossessed of their oxen or plows. 

7. Feudalism in France Followed Different Lines. The history of feudalism in France ran along different lines. In the first place, the west Frankish kingdom which came to be known as France, because its lords were the Dukes of Francia, developed its own great feudal lords. Besides, the Duke of 

Normandy, the Count of Flăn'ders, the Count of Champagne (shăm-pan'), the Count of Toulouse (too-looz'), and the Duke of Aquitaine were as wealthy and powerful as the king himself. As a result, for more than one hundred years after 

Hugh Capět, in 987, was elected to succeed the last of the line of Charles the Great, the French rulers made no effort to exercise royal authority outside their own feudal possessions. 

It was Louis VI, sometimes known as "the Fat," who began

285 the task of strengthening the royal power by compelling his own vassals to recognize its authority. 

8. How the King of France Increased His Power. The 

Capetians were more fortunate than the family of William of Normandy, because for nearly three centuries a son was not lacking to succeed to his father's power. 

By warfare, by marriage, or by court procedure they brought the great fiefs, one after another, under their control.

Indeed, his long merciful reign (1226-1270) was devoted so successfully to consolidating the realm that his grandson, when he came to the throne, was the most autocratic sovereign of Christendom.

In a country the size of 

France, the problem facing the king was a difficult one, for his vassals could hardly be expected to come to his court very often. Moreover, so large a territory, distributed among so many vassals, made necessary a vast amount of court work. To handle the situation, Saint 

Louis divided his court into three groups: one group was to serve as advisers to the king, another was to look after the finances of the kingdom, and a third, the parlement (pär-lá-môn'), was to act as a court of justice. In this way persons who were especially gifted along a certain line began to serve in that capacity. It was no longer necessary to call together all of the vassals in order to transact business, although the "Estates," as the entire body of the vassals and higher clergy was called, were still summoned on important occasions.

10. The Significance of French Feudalism. While the power of the king in England was weakened by his feudal vassals, the power of the king in France grew gradually stronger. 

This was largely due to the lack of union among the great French vassals themselves, who held to feudal ideals long after the English vassals had become interested in other things. 

The French king, however, found himself in difficulties during the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries and his progress toward absolutism was long delayed.

CHAPTER XXXI 

OTTO THE GREAT OF GERMANY REVIVES THE TITLE OF EMPEROR AND ESTABLISHES THE HOLY ROMAN EMPIRE 

1. Otto Becomes King of Germany. As we have seen, feudalism in the East Frankish kingdom was considerably modified by the old Teutonic tribal customs. This was due to the fact that in that part of Charlemagne's empire, Roman influence was never strong; consequently, German customs were kept alive long after they had disappeared farther west. 

The country was in the hands of a number of powerful lords, foremost of whom were the dukes of Saxony, Franconia,

Bavaria, Swa'bi-a and Lorraine (ló-rān'), and the archbishops of Mainz (mints), Köln (kûln), and Trier (trer). It was to their votes that Henry the Fowler owed his election to the throne of Germany after the line of Charles.

Henry was content to be king in name only, but far different was his son, Otto I. In order to strengthen the royal authority, Otto had a number of his relations made dukes when the thrones of certain duchies became vacant. When he found that this scheme did not work, as these men proved to be as unmanageable as their predecessors, Otto turned his attention to the bishoprics. In this he was more successful. After he pushed the Slavs back beyond the Elbe, he had the opportunity to establish a number of new bishoprics. One of the more important was Brandenburg (brän'den-boork), which later developed into the Kingdom of Prussia.

Two other important European states can trace their roots to the reign of Otto. After his defeat of the Magyars at Lechfeld (lěk felt), we saw them form the Kingdom of Hungary. As protection against them he re-established the old "East Mark" which in time became the Archduchy of Austria. 288

2. The Empire Becomes Known as the Holy Roman 

Empire of the German Nation. The successors of Charlemagne kept the title of emperor, but after the days of Louis the Pious it was little more than a name. The widow of one of these so-called emperors got into difficulty with the Pope and appealed to Otto for aid. The outcome was that he married her and was crowned emperor. Although this act brought back the imperial power to Germany, it greatly weakened the authority of the king over the powerful German barons. Not only was it impossible to bring Germans and Italians under the same control, but actual communication between the two countries was difficult because of the Alps. However, in the next century this latter difficulty was partially overcome by the acquisition of the Kingdom of Burgundy.

Otto had to face the same problem of forcing recognition for himself as did Charlemagne. When he sent to Constantinople for a bride for his son, Otto II, the Byzantine court sent him a princess who was not of the imperial family. Even so, the union served to introduce eastern civilization into Germany, and to stir up in the minds of her kings a desire to re-establish the Roman Empire. Because the imperial sceptre was now held by Germans, the empire was henceforth known as the 

Holy Roman Empire of the German Nation. 

3. The Emperor of the Holy Roman Empire Takes a 

Hand in Selecting a Pope. The emperor was crowned by the 

Pope, so he was interested in the choice of the new occupant of the Holy See. In 1046, a curious situation arose. Three different persons claimed the papal throne and the Emperor, Henry III, went to Rome to settle the matter. Over the protests of a large part of the clergy, he installed the German bishop Bruno as Pope Clement II, and by that act laid the foundation for much trouble between the emperors and the popes.

Among those who had opposed most violently the appoint-

OTTO THE GREAT OF GERMANY 

291 ment of Bruno was a young Italian, Hil'dé-brand by name. Besides serving as secretary to Gregory VI, this young monk had spent considerable time in the reformed monastery at Cluny. 

He returned to Rome with a new German pope, Leo IX, imbued with ideas of re- form and the dignity of the papacy. 

4. Hildebrand Sets About to Reform the 

Church. As a servant of the popes, Hildebrand assisted in the first step in church reform. In 

1059, a papal decree created a college of cardinals to elect future popes and thus excluded laymen from control of the elections. Other decrees against simony and marriage of the clergy followed, but the real reform did not get started until Hildebrand himself

5. The Church Wins in the Quarrel over Lay Investi ture. The Pope saw clearly that no real reform of the church could take place until the practice of lay investiture was ended. 

Already it had aroused friction with the emperor but, in 1076, Gregory issued the decree forbidding it.

When Henry IV, the young emperor, refused to accept this decree, the Pope excommunicated him and released his vassals

from their oath of allegiance. The German barons allowed 

Henry a year in which to make peace with the Pope. Meanwhile the Pope got ready to proceed to Germany to take a hand in the election of Henry's successor. To forestall the Pope, Henry hastened to Italy and at Cä-nos'sà compelled him to remove the excommunication.

Henry was soon in conflict with the Pope again. This time his vassals took his side so he was able to march to Rome and to drive Gregory into exile. Although the latter died before this exile was ended, the Emperor had started a great movement. The struggle went on until 1122 when it was settled by a compromise, known as the Con-côr'dat of Worms (vōrms), in which it was agreed that the prince should bestow the sceptre, symbol of the bishop's temporal authority, and the church would bestow the crosier and ring, emblems of his spiritual power. Later popes frequently refused to be bound by this Concordat, claiming that it was only a private agreement between Henry V and the Pope. Consequently the struggle was often renewed, even as late as the nineteenth century. 

6. The Emperor Fails to Establish Old Imperial Rights in the Italian Cities. While the struggle between the emperors and the popes was going on, the emperors often found it difficult to maintain their authority in Italy, and sometimes even in Germany. The large and powerful cities developing in northern Italy added to the difficulty by assuming all sorts of rights. In the middle of the twelfth century they came into conflict with Frederick Bär-ba-ros'sȧ who claimed imperial rights over the mines, fisheries, and other natural resources in Italy.

In this struggle the Pope aided the cities against the Emperor, who had to be content with only a formal recognition of his claim. Frederick then married his son to the heiress of the Norman Kingdom of Sicily to strengthen his position in Italy and to deprive the Pope of any asylum in that direction.

OTTO THE GREAT OF GERMANY 

293 The death of Henry VI in 1196 upset all these plans, for the heir to the combined thrones was an infant child. Before this boy could grow up, there appeared several rival claimants for

So bitter was the contest, in which the Pope himself took part, that the royal authority was completely shattered. 

7. Frederick II, "the First of the Moderns." With the aid of the Pope, Frederick II became emperor, thus combining in one person the three thrones, as had been the wish of

his illustrious grand father. His long reign was marked by a terrific struggle with the Holy See, in which the Popes issued bulls of excommunication and the Emperor retaliated with open letters to the princes of Christendom, in which they denounced the papal pretensions and actually went so far as to capture and imprison the members of a church council and to propose a general confiscation of the wealth of the Church. 

Frederick II may be called "the First of the Moderns," for he had a mind, which insisted upon thinking for itself, even if it ran counter to the teachings of the church. He challenged the right of the church to control the scholarship of Christendom, and he welcomed to his court the learned men of the day, whether they were Christian, Jew, or

Muslim. He even wrote a book on the falcon in which he discussed its habits and training in a strictly modern manner. On one occasion he used stamped leather like our modern currency. 

THE IMPERIAL ORB 

The symbol of the authority of the Holy Roman Empire. 

8. The Significance of the Holy Roman Empire. The 

Holy Roman Empire was built on the idea of a united Christendom, a medieval "League of Nations." It could be a success only so long as that idea was generally accepted by rulers. By the middle of the thirteenth century other ideas had begun to take root which were destined to break up western Europe into a number of strongly nationalistic states. While the term "Holy Roman Empire" continued to exist for over five hundred years, it was little more than a name.

The most serious effect of the Holy Roman Empire on civilization was its influence on the royal power in Germany. In try-

ing to maintain his imperial authority, the German king practically lost all his rights as a king in Germany. So great was the demoralization within the realm after the death of Frederick II that there were actually twenty years of "fist law," after which Germany became a land of many semi-independent principalities-counties, duchies, marks, and "free cities." So it remained until the nineteenth century.

CHAPTER XXXII HOW THE CRUSADES AND THE RISE OF TOWNS GAVE NEW LIFE INTERESTS, AND DIRECTION TO HISTORY 

We shall find in the Crusades and in the rise of towns two events that were to have a great influence on medieval, and also on modern life. There could scarcely have been a more perfect expression for the ideals of chivalry than the glorious endeavor to rescue the birthplace of Christ from the hands. of unbelievers. Here was a way to serve God that appealed greatly to the people of that time. The Crusaders failed miserably and Christian leaders quarrelled over the spoils of war but they helped to bring an end to the stagnation in life in Europe. New wants came from contact with the older centres of civilization and a new class of people devoted to industry and commerce built towns, organized guilds and leagues, secured charters from kings to protect them from feudal lords, and led directly into the Modern Age. 

1. The Causes of the Crusades. The isolation which had marked the early part of the Middle Ages was broken by the Crusades, the name given to those great efforts to rescue Jerusalem from the hands of the Turks. Since the days of Constantine religious persons had made pilgrimages to Palestine to visit the Holy Sepulchre. When the Turks captured Palestine in the eleventh century, they imposed many hardships on these pilgrims, and often refused to allow them to enter Jerusalem.

Pope Urban II felt the time suitable for delivering the Holy Sepulchre from the "infidel Turks," hoping no doubt to increase the prestige of the papacy. In 1095, he preached a great 296

2. Enthusiasm for the Crusade Was Without Bounds.

The idea was received with the greatest enthusiasm. The crowd broke out with shouts of "God wills it" and men were sent out to spread the news throughout western 

Europe. One of them, Peter the Hermit, rode through 

France and Germany on an ass, bearing aloft a huge cross. He aroused the people by his thrilling story of how the Turks, after the capture of Jerusalem in 

1073, had destroyed the 

Holy Sepulchre, and of the cruel treatment of the Christian pilgrims. Never before had there been such a universal response to a human appeal. Every one wished 

THE HOLY SEPULCHRE

So great was the enthusiasm that even before the chosen leaders were ready, a mob of men, women, and children-possibly as many as 50,000-under the leadership of Peter and the poor knight, Walter Lackland, was working its way down the valley of the Danube toward Constantinople. When their supplies gave out, they stole food, and by the time they reached Constantinople had become so careless that they even robbed churches. To protect his capital the Emperor hastened to ship them across into Asia. There the Turks made an end of the whole undertaking in a terrible massacre at Nicæa (1096).
