3. The First Crusade Reached Its Goal. The next year the real crusade, consisting, it is said, of 600,000, set out from 

France, Germany, Italy, and Sicily, and travelling overland because of lack of boats, came to Constantinople. After being cordially received by the eastern emperor, they crossed the Bosphorus and took Nicæa for him, and then pushed on to Antioch, which they captured after a memorable siege. Then a part of the crusaders, led by Godefroy de Bouillon (gód-frwä dě boo'yôn), marched south to Jerusalem, which surrendered to them on July 15, 1099.

No sooner was Jerusalem in their hands than the Crusaders began to quarrel with the Greek Christians and to attempt to take away from them the guardianship of the Holy Places and to give it to the Pope. Disregarding the rights of the eastern emperor, Godefroy was elected King of Jerusalem, and rival Latin principalities were established at Antioch, E-děs´sa, and

Trip'ó-li. To all this the Byzantine emperor appears to have made little objection, being content to recover Nicæa and the rich Ăn-a-to'lĭan country nearer home, together with Rhodes and Chios and others of the ancient Greek islands. 

4. The Other Crusades Fail and Jerusalem Is Lost. 

The Crusaders had been successful because the Muslims were not united. When the Muslims began to combine against the "Christian dogs," the Christians found themselves in difficulties. In 1144 the Muslims recaptured Edessa and Saint Ber'nard preached the Second Crusade, which was a failure in spite of the fact that the kings of both France and Germany took part. Not long after this Săl'à-dîn, the Kurd (koord), united all the Muslims bordering on the Christian state, and, in 1187, won back Jerusalem. This called for a third crusade under the personal leadership of Richard of England, Philip 

Augustus of France, and the Emperor Frederick Barbarossa.

Of all the crusades this was the most romantic, but like the second, it ended in failure, for after the death of Frederick trouble arose between Richard and Philip and nothing was accomplished.

During the next fifty years there were four other crusades, but they failed to hold the Muslims in check. Bit by bit the 

Crusaders lost their possessions in Asia, and after 1291 western Europe had only the island of Cyprus to show for all the sacrifices it had made. 

5. The Crusaders in Europe Are More Successful. Al though the Second Crusade had been a dismal failure, it was responsible for two issues of great importance. For centuries a struggle had been going on in the Spanish peninsula between the Muslims and the Christians. During the Second Crusade the Christian cause was prosecuted with such vigor that Lisbon was captured and the foundation of a Christian kingdom was laid in what is to-day Portugal. Then in 1212, the Muslim power was so shattered that it was no longer a serious menace,

although the Moorish Kingdom of Granada lasted for nearly three more centuries.

At the time of the Second Crusade, too, the pagan Slavs east of the Elbe were subjugated. Later, when the Crusaders had lost their foothold in Asia and were looking for other fields to conquer, the Germans turned their attention to the heathen who dwelt along the shores of the Baltic Sea. In the fourteenth century a party of them, known as the Order of Teutonic Knights, crossed the Vis'tu-la and established themselves in Prussia. 

After conquering the Slavic population, they proceeded to introduce Christianity and to plant German civilization, advancing the German frontier against the Slavs. 

6. The Military Orders of Knights and What They 

Did. The first result of the Crusades was to establish a new kind of monasticism, consisting of orders of monk-knights. 

Besides the Teutonic Knights, many of these orders were established in Spain, but the earliest and most famous were the Knights of the Temple and the Knights of the Hospital. 

Both of these orders were formed to assist and protect pilgrims to the Holy Land. Later, when they had become rich and powerful, they became the main defense of the Christian lands in the East.

Not only did they establish houses in the West, but the Knights of the Temple developed a system of looking after the pilgrims and of taking care of their money, much as the American Express Company serves travellers to-day. In the fourteenth century this order was suppressed because of its great wealth, but the Hospitalers continued to wage war against the Muslims until Malta, their last stronghold, was seized by Napoleon in 1798. 

7. The Italian Cities Profit by the Crusades and Crusaders and Venetians Even Attack Constantinople. The 

Italian cities contributed to the First Crusade seamen, who soon gained control of the carrying trade of the Mediterranean.

They supplied the Crusaders with the things they were accustomed to have back home, and they carried to Europe the products which they found in the East. Consequently they became immensely rich and by the time of the Third Crusade their fleets had so increased in size that they were able to transport the greater part of those who took part in that undertaking. 

The interests of the traders and of the Crusaders were often opposed. For example, in their eagerness to make money the traders not only dealt with the Muslims, but they even supplied the Muslims with slaves and arms, until at last the Pope put a stop to the practice. This difference of aims finally reached its climax in 1204 in connection with the Fourth Crusade proclaimed by Innocent III. Arrangements had been made with the Venetians to furnish transportation to the Crusaders, but the Crusade proved so unpopular that the few Crusaders who reached Venice were unable to raise the passage money. The matter was settled by their agreeing to assist the 

Venetians in the capture of the Greek city of Zä'rä; although in defiance of the papal commands. .

Later the expedition sailed on to Constantinople. The city was looted of property valued at nearly $24,000,000 and the Empire was divided among the Crusaders and the Venetians. 

This undertaking did much to terminate the rivalry which had long existed between Genoa and Venice by making the latter place supreme, but in the end it brought ruin to the Venetians by destroying the power that had served Europe as a bulwark against Islam. 

8. Results of the Crusades and the Rise of Towns. The 

Crusades brought to an end the stagnation from which the people of western Europe had suffered ever since the invasion of the barbarians. Once more people began to move around and to become acquainted with new things. Whenever they stopped at the manors and villas which served as inns along the main routes of travel, they bought the wares of the in-

Although the duties of a serf or villein interfered with his becoming a merchant, at first the lords did not object to the change of occupation, because of the increased income which they hoped to derive. Very soon, however, the merchants discovered that they must be freemen in order to carry on their business successfully, so they combined into associations or guilds and sought to purchase from the lords freedom and the right to govern themselves. Some of the lords agreed quite willingly or were driven to it by their financial difficulties, while others resisted stubbornly. In some parts of Europe, the kings even took the side of the townsmen in their struggles with the feudal lords. 

9. Life in a Medieval Town Was Far from Ideal. As soon as a town secured its freedom, usually the townsmen built a wall around it and erected a watch tower for its protection. Within the wall was a maze of crooked, unpaved

streets, often barely wide enough for three persons to walk abreast. In front of the principal church there was an open square in which the market was held, usually on Sundays. To this came farmers from the adjoining country and merchants from other towns.

The various industries of the town were grouped so that each had its own street. The shopkeepers were also manufacturers, for in the little workrooms behind their shops they made the different articles they offered for sale.

As a rule they and their families lived in rooms above the 

There were practically no street lights, no system of water supply except cisterns 

THE BUTCHERS' GUILD HALL IN HEREFORD, ENGLAND 

and public pumps, no sewers and drains, and no street-cleaning department to dispose of the garbage and refuse which were thrown into the streets. In fact, it was the pollution of the cisterns by this filth and by cess-pools that caused the virulence of the pestilences which swept over western Europe so frequently during the Middle Ages. 

10. The Craft Guilds Had Very Definite Regulations. 

The industrial life of a medieval town was quite different from that of a modern city. All the trades were organized into separate guilds-the shoemakers in one, the silversmiths in another, and so on. The guild had a patron saint and served as a mutual benefit society. Each guild regulated the number of persons who should work at its trade, the materials which should go into its products, and the prices to be charged for the

latter. Every workman began as an apprentice to some master guildsman and served an apprenticeship lasting from three to seven years, during which time he was furnished by his mas- 

A SHOEMAKER'S SHOP 

The apprentices are working while the master is making a sale. 

From a contemporary woodcut. ter with food, clothing, and lodging. After his apprenticeship he became a day worker or journeyman and worked for wages for two years, moving from town to town so as to broaden his experience in the secrets of his trade. Then if he could obtain entrance to a guild and had the necessary money to open a shop he might become a master guildsman himself. 

11. Medieval Trade and 

Commerce Were Slow in 

Growth and Difficult to 

Carry on. The trade and commerce of the Middle Ages were regulated by the towns. 

Merchants outside the towns had to pay tolls as in Oriental cities to-day. All trading in raw materials had to be done in the market to prevent forestalling or monopolizing the product. An attempt was also made to establish a just price for articles. This price was based on the cost of the materials and on the wages of the labor and these wages were determined by the necessities of an average guildsman's standard of living. As the church forbade the taking of interest and the just price eliminated private profit, business developed only slowly. 

An even greater hindrance to the development of trade was the condition of the roads. The roads were only tracks; bridges

A MEDIEVAL FAIR 

The innkeeper has moved his tables to the open air. Various games are in progress. 

From a contemporary woodcut. were often lacking and robbers numerous. Local lords, no better than robbers, frequently charged toll for no reason except that they could collect it. In some places, particularly in 

Champagne, great fairs were held every year to which merchants came from all over Europe. The weights in use at one of them, Troyes (trwä-ya'), are still in use as our Troy weights. The pirates and the laws concerning shipwreck, by which people who owned the shore could claim everything washed upon it, made sea trade as hazardous as land trade.

In spite of these difficulties commerce increased and individuals and families slowly became rich. 

12. How the Hanseatic League Controlled and Pro tected Trade. Merchants often grouped themselves together in a town and formed a hănse. This association led to a uniting of the towns for the purpose of advancing their commercial interests. In the thirteenth century the merchants of the 

Flemish cities formed a hanse at London which controlled for more than a century the trade of England with the continent.

Other leagues of towns were formed in the valley of the Rhine and in southern Germany. The most famous was the Hăn-séătic League, which grew out of a hanse of German merchants

The strength of the Hanseatic League lay in its control of the trade with Russia and England, and of the herring fisheries in The Sound, the narrow strait leading into the Baltic. It gathered raw materials through its great trading factories at Novgorod, Bergen, and London, and exchanged them at

CHAPTER XXXIII THE CHURCH IN THE MIDDLE AGES WAS IN ORGANI- ZATION A PAPAL MONARCHY 

In the Middle Ages the Church played a far greater part than it does to-day. Every one belonged to it in much the same way that to-day every one is a citizen of some state. When a child was born, he was baptized by the Church and was given a name. When this child became older, he was confirmed by the 

Church and became a regular member. When he married, the 

Church performed the ceremony, and when he came to die, the Church gave him extreme unction to prepare him for heaven. 

How important was this latter service may be appreciated when we realize that without it he could only be buried like an animal and not in sacred ground.

Education and the care of the sick, indeed all charitable work, were in control of the Church. Moreover, the Church had full direction of legal matters pertaining to family affairs, such as the probating of wills, the administration of estates, and the guardianship of orphans. And lastly, besides owning at least one-third of all property, its clergy were exempt from any control by the secular courts. 

1. How the Church Obtained Its Power. The Church was so powerful chiefly because it controlled the means of salvation through the "Seven Sacraments." We have mentioned four of these sacraments-baptism, confirmation, marriage, and extreme unction. There were three others, penance, the mass, and ordination. The Church could withhold these sacraments from an individual by excommunication, and from a whole community by interdict. 310

THE CHURCH IN THE MIDDLE AGES 

311 Penance consisted in the confession of a sin to a priest and the priest imposing a penalty on the sinner. The mass, most important of all the sacraments, was the commemoration of the last supper of Jesus before his crucifixion. In the mass the substance of the bread and wine was supposed to be changed in a miraculous way into flesh and blood, although the outward appearance remained the same. This miracle was called transsubstantiation and could be performed only by the clergy. The power to do this was conferred by ordination setting the priests apart from laymen and gave them an "indelible character." 

2. The Power of the Papacy Expanded Until It Was 

Thought All Authority Rested with the Church. We have seen how the Pope became the head of the Church, and how Gregory VII extended the papal power. The Holy Father considered himself to be God's vicegerent upon earth and therefore responsible to Him for the salvation of the souls of mankind. This belief led Gregory and his successors to struggle so hard with both emperors and kings to free the Church from all interference by laymen. It was responsible for the insistence on the supremacy of the Pope over the other bishops, and even over the councils of the Church. To their belief may be traced the claim that the Pope had the sole right to interpret for Christendom the Bible and church doctrine. We can easily understand the Pope's position, if we remember that in those days all knowledge was thought to rest with the Church, and that its organization had been derived from the autocracy of the 

Roman Empire. 

3. Under Innocent III the Papacy Reached the Summit of Its Power. Under the leadership of Pope Innocent III 

(1198-1216) the papacy realized its claims for the control of society. He re-established control over the papal states in Italy and then undertook to enforce his political influence over all Europe. He interfered in the affairs of the empire, and compelled King John of England to become his vassal. The Kings

of År'a-gon, Hungary, Bohemia, Poland, and Denmark officially recognized his authority over them. Stirred by the heresies in southern France, he summoned the Fourth Lateran

Council in 1215, to which came representatives from all Europe and the East. The heresies were condemned and many reforms were begun, especially the one which abolished trial by ordeal. At the death of Innocent in the following year, the papacy had reached the summit of its power. 

4. How the Vast Wealth of the Church Stood in Its 

Way. The greatest obstacle to the spiritual development of the medieval church was its vast wealth. We have already seen how this wealth drew it with disastrous results into feudalism. No sooner had Pope Calixtus won his fight over the question of lay investiture, than the Church was threatened by another question, which was directly traceable to wealth. The 

Popes stubbornly resisted the proposition to tax church property for the support of the state. Since medieval clergymen were human, it is not surprising that they often relied more upon the power of the purse than upon that of the spirit, and neglected their religious duties. 

5. St. Francis of Assisi Turns Attention of the Church to Its Supreme Mission. It remained for a young Italian, afterward known as St. Francis of Assisi (äs-se'zē), to turn the attention of the Church once more back to its supreme mission. At the close of a serious illness, he had become a monk, but instead of shutting himself from the rest of the world, St. 

Francis went about helping the poor and the sick, and rendering many kinds of service to the unfortunate. So great was his enthusiasm that he was joined by many followers and as a result founded the order which still bears his name. Such was its popularity that it was not long until every city in western Europe had a Franciscan monastery. 

6. The Black Friars Become the Agents of the Inquisition. While St. Francis was developing his orders, St. Dom'-

THE CHURCH IN THE MIDDLE AGES 

313 i-nic, a Spanish monk, organized the "Black Friars" or Dominicans, which also developed two attendant orders. The 

Dominicans were such an aid to the Church, that they were made the official agents of the Inquisition, the name given to the machinery set up for the suppression of heresy.

7. The Supremacy of the Church and the Political Interests of the State in Conflict. We have seen how the papacy won its struggle with the emperors. So complete appeared this victory that in the year 1300 a great jubilee was held at Rome, which was proclaimed by Pope Boniface VIII to celebrate the fact that the supremacy of the Church had at last been acknowledged by the whole Catholic world. However, there had been growing up in France and England strong po-

litical states, which were destined to offer violent opposition to the claims of the papacy. Indeed, by the close of the thirteenth

CHAPTER XXXIV THE  FINDS EXPRES- SION IN THE UNIVERSITIES FOUNDED AND IN THE BUILDING OF THE CATHEDRALS 1. A Revival of Interest in Study Begins. After the dis appearance of the Roman Empire in western Europe, the only schools were those attached to the cathedrals and monasteries. 

From the Romans they inherited their course of study, the socalled "seven liberal arts." Although there were subjects for those interested in the study of law, medicine, or theology, the meagreness of the curriculum may be appreciated from the fact that one text-book of barely two hundred pages sufficed for all the liberal arts. However, in those days little learning was needed outside the Church, and even in the Church there were few who knew more than how to read and write. 

And yet at the beginning of the Middle Ages there were occasional students who showed a considerable amount of learning. Is'i-dōre of Seville compiled a great encyclopedia, and the Venerable Bede and Alcuin won places among the foremost students and teachers of the time. By the tenth century the 

Christians of Spain with the help of the Jews had become acquainted with the knowledge of the Muslims. Pope Syl-věs ter 

II learned to compute the height of a tower by comparing the length of its shadow with that of a stick, and incidentally he earned the reputation of having had dealings with the devil. 

The twelfth century, however, witnessed the real revival of interest in learning. Not only did the pilgrimages and the crusades make people familiar with many new things, but the investiture quarrel gave them something to think about. As a result, there was tremendous enthusiasm for learning and students began to flock in constantly increasing numbers to the more famous teachers. 316

2. Abelard Attempts to Use Reason As a Guide to 

Truth. About 1100, a young Breton by the name of Ab'ě-lärd arrived in Paris to attend the lectures of a famous teacher in the cathedral school. He soon surpassed his teacher in argument and began to teach for himself. To make his pupils work he prepared a text-book, Sic et Non, meaning "so and not so." 

This book was composed of opposite statements taken from the 

PARIS IN THE FOURTEENTH CENTURY 

Saint Germaine des Prés in the foreground, the Louvre across the Seine, and the hill of Montmartre at the rear. fathers of the Church about matters of belief. He attracted large crowds of students, and when he began lecturing on theology he was tried for heresy. He was forced to retire for a time but returned to teaching with the same success. Again he was charged with heresy, this time by the famous St. Bernard.

Abelard died while on his way to Rome to appeal his case. 

His long and stormy career had done much to attract students to Paris, which henceforth became a great educational centre. 

Abelard's chief contributions to the advancement of knowledge

were his use of argument as a method of teaching, and a new reliance upon reason as a guide to truth. 

3. The Beginning of the Universities. The universities of the Middle Ages were not founded in the way that modern universities are founded, they just grew. For example, the 

University of Paris, one of the oldest, developed from a body of students and teachers. The teachers organized into a guild, and the students grouped themselves according to the nations from which they came.

In the British Museum.

The students soon secured such a privileged position in society that they were not subject to the same regulations as people from outside

UNIVERSITY LECTURE 

the town. About 

1200, those in Paris got into a fight with the townspeople and threatened to leave the city unless they were allowed to have their misdemeanors passed upon by the guild of teachers. Because the students were a source of income to the town, their threat brought the authorities to terms. Later, some did withdraw and started a new university at Oxford, England. 

4. How Students Studied and What Degrees Were 

Granted. These medieval universities had no buildings; each teacher hired a lecture room and received all students who would pay the required fees to study under his guidance. The teachers lectured three or four hours a day, and since the stu-

dents had no text-books, the lecture consisted largely of readings from some book and comments on what the author said. 

By writing down these lectures, the more diligent students at the end of the course possessed copies of the text-books. 

There were no examinations until the entire seven liberal arts had been completed, for which four years were usually required. After passing these examinations, the student became known as a bachelor of arts, and then by studying two years longer and passing more examinations, he became a master of arts. After that he might take up teaching, or perhaps go to one of the three professional schools for further study. In the latter case he might

From the original in the Bibliothèque nationale de Paris, Cab. des Estampes. hope to become a Doctor of Law, or of Medicine, or of Theology, in from four to seven years. 

5. The Students Enjoy Many Privileges. The life of a medieval student was very attractive. A person could become a student as soon as he had learned to read. There was nothing to prevent him from remaining a student all his life. Students had the same legal rights as the clergy and could not be held responsible for the debts of their fellow townsmen. Rich students frequently brought servants to the universities so that they might be waited upon, while poor ones found it easy to beg their way. The less serious-minded ones attended classes during the winter months only, and then spent their summers wandering about the country. 

In more ways than one these medieval students were like

those of to-day, as can be seen in the letters they wrote home asking for money. In this particular connection the students of the University of Bologna (bó-lō'nyä) enjoyed a peculiar advantage, for the city was obliged to lend money to any needy student attending that school. Students, it may be truthfully said, were among the first persons to enjoy life during the 

Middle Ages. 

6. Medieval Intellectual Interests Centred in Religion.

The centre of all medieval intellectual interest was the Christian religion. Educated persons generally devoted themselves to the study of the Bible and of Christian doctrine and of theology. So well done was some of the work that modern 

Biblical students have not been able to improve upon it, while the canon law developed then is still in use in the Catholic Church. And this intense interest of these medieval students in religion naturally affected their attitude toward other forms of learning. Although sometimes their scientific ideas cause us to smile, we must remember that they were quite as sincere as ourselves, and that so far as their knowledge went, possibly quite as scientific.

Second only to the study of the Bible was the study of Aristotle, a part of whose works medieval students had inherited through Latin or Arabic translations. How great was their veneration for this old Greek philosopher is evidenced by the fact that they gave him the title of "Master of Those Who Know." 

7. How Theology and Canon Law Took the Form 

They Were to Keep in the Catholic Church. The medieval scholar turned first of all to religion as a field of investigation and upon the beliefs and practices of the church he lavished unstinted effort. Gra'tian made an attempt to gather the decrees of popes and councils into a body of law. His successors developed the study of canon law into a great code, the final edition of which in 1317 remains to-day the law of the Catho- 20000

lic Church. In theology and philosophy St. Thomas Aquinas (a-kwi'nas) formulated in his Sum'ma the theories and dogmas which still form the basis of the beliefs of the Church. Finally in his great poem, the Divine Comedy, Dăn'té expressed the hopes and aspirations of the medieval world, and in his treatise on government he defended the medieval empire as the ideal type of 

Christian state. 

8. Medieval Science Did Not Ask Why or How Things Hap pened. The medieval scientist was not at all interested in the things which interest a modern scientist. It did not occur to him that it was necessary to explain. why or how it rained or snowed, because that was under the control of God. Nor was he

Medieval Literature Takes a Wide Range. Since the scholars of the Middle Ages were primarily interested in religion, much of the literature of this period had a religious meaning. As the worship of saints increased, a great collection of stories developed which were associated with their lives, and particularly with the miracles which they performed. 

For the nobility there developed a special kind of literature, the chanson de geste (shäN-sôn' de zhěst'), which consisted of long poems picturing the battles and other deeds of the knights.

Later, groups of these tales centred around certain characters, the best known of them being the legend of King Arthur and his Knights of the Round Table, immortalized by Tennyson in the Idylls of the King, and the Nibelungenlied (në’bẽ-loong-ĕnlēt) by Wagner (väg'ner) in his famous operas. There were also the sä'gås of the Norsemen which recounted in heroic style the deeds of the Vikings, and one charming love story, Aucassin (ō-ka-san') and Nicolette (nē-kō-lěť′). 

One of the most interesting literary forms of the Middle 

Ages were the Fabliaux (fàblé-ó)—a type of stories originated by the townspeople for the purpose of making fun of the faults of the clergy. Some of these consisted of humorous tales in verse; others were allegories, such as the tales of 

Reynard the Fox, in which Reynard represented the Merchants, the Wolf the Clergy, and the Lion the feudal Lords. 1 

10. The Highest Artistic Expression of the Middle Ages 

Is the Cathedral. Although during the centuries immediately following the invasion of the barbarians, art like every other form of culture was all but completely crushed in most of western Europe, no one who has ever seen a medieval cathedral will admit that the Middle Ages were really "dark" ages. Never before, nor since, has man been able to translate so effectively into brick and stone his reverence for God and his aspirations for a heavenly home. Indeed, in his art even more than in his literature, medieval man found opportunities to express his tremendous interest in religion. And so, while in castles and houses utility was the chief concern of the architects of the Middle Ages, in the cathedrals and churches and monasteries they allowed their feelings full sway. Little by little, they developed a new style of architecture known as the Rō-mănesque' because of its resemblance to that of the Romans. 

11. The Characteristics of Romanesque Architecture. 

Since the Christian church was a place of meeting as well as a place of worship, the architects of the Middle Ages had to meet

a very different problem from that of the builders of pagan temples. They adopted from the Romans the ba-sil'i-cà, a long building with a roof supported by two rows of columns, with an apse or semi-circular projection at one end. To the space between the rows of columns they gave the name nave; and to the space between the columns and the walls, the name aisles. 

The altar was placed in the apse, facing the main entrance at 

THE CATHEDRAL AT PISA 

A Romanesque church built about 1100. the opposite end of the edifice. The building was roofed with semi-circular Roman or "barrel" vaulting. To have more room near the altar, wings were added in front of the apse, forming the Transept and making the ground floor of the church look like a huge cross. In some cases, a dome was used to roof the great space over the crossing between the nave and the transept. 

Because of the weight of these Romanesque roofs, the walls were thick and the ceilings comparatively low, otherwise the buildings would have "spread out." As a result, little space could be given to windows, consequently the lighting was bad. 

While churches with few windows might be built in the south

of Europe where there was much sunlight, they would not do in the cloudy north. At first an attempt was made to get more light by raising the roof of the nave higher than the aisles

12. The Characteristics of Gothic Architecture. Some time in the twelfth century, the architects of the Isle of France

found a new way of supporting the roofs. From each pillar they built stone ribs, extending from pillar to pillar and from pillar to wall in such a way that each would counteract the 

CLOTH HALL, YPRES, BELGIUM 

"push" of the others. In order that the walls should not bulge out because of the weight of the ribs, props called flying buttresses were built on the outside. The roof rested on the diagonal arches formed by the ribs, and under them was abundant space for windows. The diagonal arches gave a pointed effect to the roof of the nave and that made the pointed arch a feature of this type of architecture. And finally, to make the building more impressive two graceful spires were added. The more conservative Italian architects contemptuously gave the name Gothic to this new type of architecture, intimating that its creators were still barbarians and consequently were unable to appreciate beauty, although to-day some specimens, notably the Rheims (rēmz) Cathedral, are looked upon as "religious aspirations in stone."

14. Medieval Secular Art Achieved Excellent Results. 

The rise of towns and the increase of wealth of guilds were followed by great rivalry in the building of halls. In these we find expressed the same daring and the same love of the beautiful that characterized the church architecture of the period. Perhaps the most famous of these medieval halls was the Hall of the Clothmakers at Ypres (epr"). It was built in the 

Gothic style and was adorned with fine paintings and tap-

estry. Tapestries were much used in the houses of wealthy merchants and nobles, not only for ornamentation but to keep the rooms warm. Often they consisted of pictures or of elaborate designs. The best-known tapestry is now preserved at Bayeux (ba-yû), the so-called "Queen 

Matilda's Towel," which pictures the history of the conquest of England by the Normans. 

15. Medieval

Art Was Highly 

Conventional. Soon after the beginning of the Crusades, heraldry was introduced, with the result that

FIGURES OF APOSTLES AND SAINTS FROM every knight had a de- THE CATHEDRAL AT CHARTRES 

sign upon his shield.

However, these heraldic designs never became really artistic, because they were too formal and conventionalized. In fact, except in the field of architecture, medieval art always suffered much from its tendency to be conventional. Not only did the artists in their paintings and sculptures follow closely those who came before them, but in their formal work they did not even attempt to copy nature. So it came about that if the artists were depicting a group of apostles, they made them all the same except for some distinguishing mark, such as a bunch of keys for Peter, a lion for Mark, and a lamb for John. Even in the use of colors they were restricted because each was supposed to be symbolical, and so was protected by the same idea of convention.

CHAPTER XXXV THE DECLINE OF THE MEDIEVAL IDEAL AND THE WANING OF THE MIDDLE AGES 

The advance in government, trade, and learning during the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries led to great changes in medieval ideals. We have seen how the struggle between the emperors and the papacy eventually reduced the Empire to a mere name. The increased power of the kings and the development of a national feeling among the masses, together with the new type of warfare caused by the introduction of gunpowder, led to the destruction of feudalism. The rise of towns and the growth of trade undermined the old medieval system of agriculture and gave rise to a new class in society, whose interests were bound up with the king. These several movements were spread over a long period of time and were accompanied by numerous events which either aided or retarded them. We shall now see what these events were that marked the decline of the 

Middle Ages. 331

1. How the Royal Power Expanded by Recognition of the Commons. We have already learned that Louis IX of 

France found it necessary to divide the duties of his vassals, and that Philip IV got into conflict with Pope Boniface by attempting to tax the clergy. In the struggle which followed, Philip called into council representatives of the towns, as well as of the estates, and by this act officially recognized the new relationship between the kings and the towns. These new representatives were known as the "Third Estate."

In England the first official recognition of the towns came when Simon de Mont'fort invited each shire to send two knights and each borough or large town to send two citizens, the socalled burgess-es, to sit with the Great Council of the realm. 

In 1295 Edward I summoned knights and burgesses, who were called Commons, to sit with the Council in its deliberations at Westminster Hall. This he was able to do as he was popular with the people on account of his military successes. He had conquered the Welsh, who had long harassed England on the west, but later he won their affection by creating the title "Prince of Wales," which has ever since been held by the heir to the English throne.

Why Edward was so anxious to see the towns represented in the Great Council becomes perfectly simple when we recall that they had suffered from the tyranny of the barons and had more than once appealed to the kings for redress of their grievances. 

For this reason he believed that he could count on their representatives in any quarrel with Parliament. 

2. The Hundred Years' War Is Europe's First Great 

Commercial Struggle. In 1327 the Capetian line of kings. came to an end from lack of a direct heir to the throne. Among the claimants to the throne was Edward III of England, a grandson of Philip IV. Causes for friction between France and England were not lacking. Not only had the French helped the Scotch in their wars with England, just as the Eng-

lish had helped the Flemish, as the inhabitants of what is to-day Belgium were called, in their struggles with France, but England still held Găs'có-ny, much to the chagrin of the French. 

Moreover, with the development of royal power in western Europe, the kings determined to place burdensome taxes upon all foreign trade. So it came about that France because of her geographical position became a serious obstacle to British merchants wishing to sell wool to the Flemish weavers, or to buy wines from the Bordeaux (bôr-dō') vintners. Consequently, the war which finally broke out in 1337 and continued at intervals for more than a hundred years may be looked upon as Europe's first great commercial struggle. 

3. The Last War Fought According to Feudal Tradi tions. The Hundred Years' War is especially noteworthy for the long series of victories of the English armies, and also because it was the last great war fought according to feudal traditions. Because it seemed to offer a solution to England's economic troubles, Parliament granted the aids asked by the crown. To this fact was due much of the success that attended the armies of England. In 1346 the English administered a defeat to the French near Crecy (krā-sé′), in spite of the fact that their own forces were largely made up of light-armed archers while the enemy consisted mainly of mail-clad knights. 

The same things happened at Poitiers (pwa-tya') in 1356, and at Agincourt (ȧ-zhăn-kōor') in 1412. It was at the battle of 

Crecy that the English are said to have introduced gunpowder by employing some "bombards" to hurl little balls of iron into the ranks of the French knights.

During the war the English ravaged a great portion of France, and at one time actually controlled almost half of the country. At the darkest moment, a French peasant girl, Joan (jōn) of Arc, restored the courage of the French and led an army to the relief of Orleans (ôr-lä-äN'), claiming that she had been commanded by divine voices to free France from

the hated English. She inspired among her countrymen such fervent loyalty to their king that not only was Orleans saved, but twenty-two years later all that was left to the English crown of its one-time vast continental possessions was the town of Calais (kǎl'a) just across the Strait of Dover. 4. Reasons for the Decline of Feudalism and the Power of the Knight. In the battles of the Hundred Years' War there developed a new kind of fighting which did much to complete the uprooting of feudalism. The medieval knight, who was accustomed to fight in single combat, was now much hampered in his movements by the weight of his armor. Besides, he was entirely dependent upon his horse and once over-

When cannon came to be used to batter down the walls of castles, feudalism and the feudal knight became obsolete. 

5. The Black Death Brings 

Discontent against the Whole

Social Order. While the English, and French armies were fighting on the plains of France, the Black 

Death, the worst pestilence of history, was spreading westward from the shores of the Black Sea. It entered Europe by way of a Genoese ship returning from the Cri-me'a, and crossed over to England in

In addition to the loss of life, the Black Death had a profound effect on the social and economic conditions of western Europe. Even before its appearance, the growth of trade and the rise of towns had so undermined the old medieval agricultural system that many landowners were finding it more profitable to lease their manors for a money rent than to farm themselves. Now, they found it difficult to secure farm labor of any kind, and the wages were extremely high. 

6. The Babylonish Captivity and Loss of Respect for the Papacy. We have seen how Clement V removed the papal capital to Avignon. Here it remained for about seventy years, the period of Church history known as the "Babylonish Captivity" (1309-1377). Life at the papal court became so luxurious and pretentious that the papacy lost the respect of many sincere persons. To meet the expenses caused by this extravagance the popes had to increase the fees charged for the services of the Church, and to anticipate some of their income by irregular procedure. The popes began to appoint new bishops in advance of vacancies, on condition that the appointees, who were known as provisors (pró-vi'zers), would make certain payments.

These new methods which the Holy See adopted for raising money and its very intimate relations with their enemy, the French king, caused such bitter feeling among the English that laws were enacted forbidding the appointment of any bishops in England in advance of vacancies, or the sending of money to Avignon before the bishopric became vacant. The Germans, too, felt a strong feeling of resentment, while the Italians actually threatened to seize the entire papal domain in the peninsula. 

7. John Wyclif Questions the Power of the French

Popes. This English opposition to the demands of the papacy

came to a head in the preaching of a priest, John Wyclif by name. While a teacher in Oxford University, this man began to question the power of these French popes, and made bold to attack some of the church doctrines. He helped translate the 

Bible into English and organized a body of "Poor Preachers" ​

The movement spread rapidly and gave rise to a sect known as Lol'lards. Although Wyclif escaped prosecution for heresy because of his friendship with a powerful nobleman, and because of English hatred for everything French, after the papacy had returned to Rome his bones were dug up and burned as those of a heretic. Meanwhile, the movement spread to Bohemia. 

8. The Great Conflict in the Church Shakes Men's Faith and Leads to Demands for Reform.

Shortly after the pa-

pacy returned to Rome, a new Italian pope, because of his narrow-mindedness and tyranny, became so obnoxious to the French cardinals that they declared the election void and proceeded to elect another pope. This second pope returned to 

Avignon, and the Catholic world found itself with two popes, and with no way to determine which was the lawful one. 

Italy, England, and Germany supported the first elected pope, while France, Spain, Portugal, and Scotland recognized the second. For a time there seemed to be no way out of the situation, but at last the professors at the University of Paris claimed that the voice of God could be heard through a general council of the whole Church. 

After long negotiations, both popes were persuaded to sanction the calling of a council. This council met at Pisa (pē´sä) in 1409 with neither of the popes present, and proceeded to depose both of them. Thereupon the council elected a pope of its own, but as neither of the deposed popes would step down, nothing was accomplished. 

A new council was called to meet in Constance in 1415. Not since the Fourth Lateran Council had there been such a gathering of prelates and princes, and of clergy and laity of Europe. They had assembled not only to re-unite the Church, but to stamp out the heresy in Bohemia and at the same time to effect reforms which this heresy showed the Church needed. 

Through the efforts of the Emperor Sig'is-mund the kings of France and Spain agreed to give up their pope, and a new pope was elected. 

9. The Decay of the Manorial System and the Beginnings of Free Tenantry. By the end of the twelfth century the manorial system was beginning to change. The growth of towns and the rising standard of living began to furnish the landowners a market for their surplus products, while the increasing use of money caused the landowners to seek means of obtaining more of it. The easiest way to do this was to change

from the payments made by the serfs from personal service to rent in the form. of money or a share of the crops. Little by little the landowners adopted this new method although they still retained most of their other rights. Not only did free tenantry begin with the leasing of land to freemen, but also with the plan of working it with hired labor. 

In England and France this development was checked by the Black Death which so reduced the number of laborers that the survivors were able to demand increased wages. An attempt of the landowners to stop this by law, making it an offense for a laborer to ask any increase, led to revolts which were put down only after much bloodshed. In spite of all this, wages continued to rise, and living conditions among the country people grew slowly better. Under the changed conditions the manorial system broke down as a means of production, although its social and other features lingered on for many centuries. 

10. The End of the Middle Ages Has No Absolute

Date. We have followed the history of western Europe during the two centuries beginning with 1300, and we have noticed the great changes in medieval institutions and ideas. Although many of these were in existence at the close of this period, and continued to exist for centuries, the conditions under which they operated were completely changed. 

Because of this persistence of institutions and ideas on the one hand, and of the changed conditions on the other, it is impossible to set any absolute date for the close of the Middle Ages and the beginning of Modern Times. To understand the difference between these two periods, it will be necessary to study the rise of the new conditions. This we shall do forthwith, but meanwhile we shall take a brief glance at Asia where great changes were also taking place. The rise of a great empire opened a way from Europe to the Far East and permitted the first extension of its knowledge to the West.

CHAPTER XXXVI ASIA DURING THE MIDDLE AGES DESTROYED MUCH AND GAVE LITTLE IN RETURN 

We learned about the advances in culture made by Asiatic peoples when western Europe was still in a state of barbarism. 

We shall now find how during the Middle Ages the Muslim Empire declined in power and culture, how the Mongol tribes from central Asia ravaged eastern Europe, subjugated China, and overran and destroyed the civilizations of Persia and Syria. 

We shall see how a small tribe of Ottoman Turks was pushed into Christian territory and how this tribe increased and absorbed Christian lands in Asia Minor, crossed over to the Balkans, and in 1453 conquered Constantinople. 

1. The Muslim Empire Is Disrupted. We ended our study of the Muslim world with the decline of the Abbassides at Baghdad. We saw that this momentous event in Asiatic history was brought about by the invasion of the Turks just at the time when western Europe was beginning to revive from its centuries of lethargy. Although the Turks did leave behind in Asia Minor one strong Muslim state, their influence combined with that of the Crusades disrupted the entire world of Islam. The great Saladin united for a short time Egypt, Syria, and Mesopotamia, but his work soon disappeared. The economic disruption of the Turkish conquest was followed by the 

Christian seizure of the Mediterranean trade, and western Asia lost its chief means of recovery. 

2. The Mongols of Central Asia Go Out for Conquest under Chingiz Khan. The central plateau of Asia has been a breeding ground of nomad peoples. Under some great leader 341

they would break forth in a spectacular orgy of conquest. One of these we have alreaay met in the rise of the Huns under Attila, but an even greater occurred near the close of the twelfth century under the leadership of Temujin (těm-oo-jé'), better known by his title, Chin'giz or Genghis (jen'giz) Khän, "Invincible Emperor."

The father of Chingiz Khan was the leader of a small group of tribes in central Mongolia. He died while Chingiz was still a boy, and the lad's mother succeeded in holding the leadership for her son until the boy was old enough to fight for his rights. 

Chingiz had a strong personality, great physical strength, and extraordinary courage. No sooner had he established his leadership than he began the conquest of the neighboring tribes, and made the Mongols into the greatest fighting machine Asia has ever known. In a few years, not only did he gain control of all the Mongol tribes, but he forced the surrender of the Tartars of the Kirghiz steppes and the Tarim Basin, and looked about for other fields to conquer. 

3. The Empire Founded by Chingiz Khan Grew into the Largest the World Had Ever Known. In 1212 letters came to Chingiz from the emperor of the "Middle Kingdom," as China was then known, commanding that they be read on bended knee. Chingiz had no use for such nonsense, so his answer was the Mongol army. It ravaged northern China and even captured Peking. Meanwhile, Chingiz despatched another army westward across the lofty Pä-mïrs' and soon brought all Turkestan, with Samarkand, its capital, under his control. Onward swept the victorious Mongols to Là-hōre' in northern India and to the Caspian Sea in the west. 

North of the Caspian Sea the Mongols defeated the Grand

Duke of Kiev. They pushed on to the northern shore of the 

Black Sea where they spread consternation among the Latin conquerors of Constantinople. Then Chingiz Khan died, while on his second expedition to China (1227), but he had built an

4. Christian Europe Misses a Chance A silver coin of a to Convert the Mongols. After they had ravaged Poland and Hungary, the Mongol army retired but left behind bands which continued to harass these countries for fifty years. In Russia, however, they remained in control. The terror which they had inspired in western Europe was relieved when they turned their attention to the Muslims. They were looked upon as allies by the Crusaders, and missionaries were despatched to convert them to Christianity. Although the Mongols were pagans, they welcomed these missionaries, and one of the khans sent word to the Pope that he would receive a hundred of them. The latter was unable to heed this request, and the Church lost its one great opportunity to convert Asia to Christianity. Instead 

Islam stepped in and reaped the harvest. Even so, Louis IX did not hesitate to ask the Great Khan to co-operate with the Christians in making further attacks on the Muslims.

ASIA DURING THE MIDDLE AGES 

347 8. The Significance of the Mongols to History. Although the conquests of the Mongols afforded Europeans an opportunity to learn about the Orient and to acquire from it such important things as gunpowder, the mariner's compass, and the art of printing, their influence upon southwestern Asia was far from beneficial. The death of fully three-quarters of the inhabitants of that part of the continent was largely due either to them or the Black Death. Muslim civilization largely disappeared. 

9. The Ottoman Turks Come into Asia Minor. Even with all the destruction caused by Mongol warfare, a new power arose in Asia Minor near the end of the Middle Ages. 

When the Mongols began to press westward, they sent scurrying before them a small wave of Turks. In time one hundred and forty-four families of these people reached Asia Minor and settled on the frontier between the Muslim and Christian lands. 

Because their chieftain was named Uthman (ooth'man), they were called Uthmanli or Ottoman Turks. 

10. The Beginnings of the Balkan States. During the 

Middle Ages, there arose in southwestern Europe several new states. The old Kingdom of the Bulgars, which in the eleventh century had fallen under the control of the Byzantines, was revived, and its Tsär or king was crowned by a legate of Pope 

Innocent III. 

By this time, too, farther to the west, the Serbians united to form a kingdom of their own and their first king was actually crowned by Gregory VII. Under the leadership of Ste'făn 

Nē-män'yä and of his brother St. Sävä, a beginning was made in Slavic literature and art, and a Serbian church was founded. 

Serbia's control gradually extended through the Balkan peninsula until in the fourteenth century her king, Stefan Du-shan, assumed the title of emperor. Although he organized the kingdom and established a new code of laws borrowed from the Byzantines, at his death the empire broke into two parts.

North of the Danube the close of the thirteenth century saw the rise of two principalities-Wallachia (wō-lā'kĭ-ȧ) and Molda'vi-ȧ. Both were inhabited by people of obscure origin, who spoke a language derived from the Latin and later called Roumanian (roo-mani-ặn). 

11. How the Ottoman Turks Become a Power in Eu rope As Well As in Asia Minor. The Ottoman Turks were often hired by the Eastern Emperors to help in their petty wars. 

In 1354 one of the Emperors refused to pay his Turkish mercenaries, and they seized the fort on the European side of the Där'dȧ-nelles. With this foothold, they began their advance into the peninsula, aided alike by the weak government at Constantinople and by the dissensions among the Bulgars and Serbs. 

In 1361 they moved their capital to Adrianople. Shortly afterward they forced the Bulgarians to accept their control and broke the power of the Serbs at Kôs'ó-vō, "The Field of the Blackbirds," in 1389. In the meantime Moldavia and Wallachia began to pay tribute to the new Turkish power. 

The Christians of the East appealed to those of the West for help, but in vain. Even the Italian cities, in spite of their trade relations with Constantinople, entered into treaties with the Ottomans, while the Pope was more interested in effecting a union of the Greek and Roman Churches than in defending the former from them. The chief defense of Europe was the king of Hungary who almost alone carried on a constant struggle. When Tamerlane for a time broke the Ottoman power, western Christendom failed to take advantage of the situation.

Finally, in 1453, to satisfy a long-felt ambition, the Ottoman Muhammad II attacked Constantinople, and with the aid of the newly invented cannon battered down its walls. On the walls the last Christian emperor died fighting. Muhammad rode his horse into the great church of St. Sophia and proclaimed it to be the Muslim mosque and so it has remained to this day.

CHAPTER XXXVII THE SIGNIFICANCE OF THE MIDDLE AGES 

1. The Medieval Ideal. Back of the great movements of the Middle Ages stood the powerful influence of Christianity. 

In season and out of season, the Church through its two great institutions, the papacy and monasticism, endeavored to mould society into a unified Christian world. To this the employment of Latin as a common language contributed, for it made those who were born on the most remote frontiers feel at home wherever they might happen to be.

To the humblest the opportunities of a saintly life opened chances of fame and influence that might lead even to the throne of Saint Peter. No disciple of the Lowly Nazarene ever followed more closely in the Master's footsteps than the happy St. Francis of Assisi, who welcomed poverty with a song and gave himself with joy to the service of leper and pauper. That his example had a wide-spread appeal is proved by the popularity of his order and of its auxiliaries, together with the multitude of others with similar ideals in the thirteenth century. Even though this earth as compared with the heavenly home was of little moment, saint and sinner alike believed it to be the pathway thither and saw in its pitfalls and obstructions only the necessary trials to purify one's faith. 

2. The Middle Ages in Politics. In the Middle Ages a single state, which came down from the Roman Empire, held equal importance with a single church. Emperor and pope ruled on earth just as the sun and moon in the heavens. With the increase in papal authority came an inevitable conflict for supremacy. In the end the Pope won, only to find his prize turn to dust in his hands, when other forces loosened by medieval developments arrayed against him the newly strength- 350

SAINT FRANCIS AND THE BIRDS 

This is Giotto's famous picture of Saint Francis preaching to the birds.

ened kings. However, this papal power, so foreign to our modern ideas, served a useful purpose in a rough and turbulent age, serving as a bulwark between the downtrodden masses and the arbitrary whims of warlike feudal nobles and tyrannical kings.

In these same Middle Ages the foundations of modern nationality were laid in the struggles between those great feudal lords who had won for themselves crowns during the age of transition and who had learned to restrict their ambitions to areas where there was practically the same language. In England, France, Spain, and the Scandinavian countries, this condition prevailed, but in central and eastern Europe imperial ambition or foreign conquest still clogged the wheels of progress. The Middle Ages, too, saw in its struggles between kings and feudal lords numerous attempts to restrain the rapidly expanding royal power, but the curb on papal interference did not come in its fulness until the free burghers got more power. 

3. The Middle Ages in Business and Industry. Starting with agriculture as almost the only means for the production of wealth, the Middle Ages introduced into western Europe many technical processes from the East, together with the rise of industry, and the development of trade, and of commerce both by land and sea. Although the civil rulers and local lords paid little attention to this commerce and even placed obstacles in its way, the towns formed combinations to protect and foster it. Thus came the end of the isolation which had kept western Europe in ignorance since the barbarians had wrecked the old civilization of the Roman Empire. 

All these new forms of economic life were grouped by towns rather than by nations and their organization was based on the individual and the guild. By its opposition to monopoly and by its regulation of quality and price the guild placed the emphasis upon workmanship. This helped to protect the consumer against overcharging in the interests of private profit. The

SIGNIFICANCE OF MIDDLE AGES 

353 church was opposed to the taking of interest, but the people evaded this and laid the foundations of financial capital through the development of great family fortunes which became available for loans to the state and for the furtherance of trade. 

An astounding feature of medieval life was the difference that existed in the division of wealth. More than one-third of the land, in some cases one-half, belonged to the church and was controlled by the clergy, and of the remainder the greater part belonged to the ruling aristocracy. The laborers received a bare living and often hardly that. Even with the rise of the towns, only a favored few engaged in the privileges of trade and industry, although the mass of workers by association did gain an incentive for demanding better things. 

4. The Middle Ages and Society. In medieval society the classes were sharply defined. Only in a most exceptional case could serfs pass the great gulf which separated them from the feudal aristocracy. When the free townsmen arose, here came a new class bound by none of the older ties. It drew its recruits from the lower classes and passed on to the upper class wealth, wives, and even members, thus giving to industry and trade a dignity which it had long lacked. Slavery played little part since the line between it and serfdom was so fine. 

The church and the monastery, the manor, the guild, and the town made these local groups something like the clubs of today. This importance of the group was further fostered by the medieval attitude toward the individual, an attitude which had grown out of Christian theology. Among the feudal aristocracy arose a code of conduct upon which the church set its seal and impressed its ideal of the Christian gentleman, and that may be taken as an expression to-day of true nobility even though in practice that ideal was seldom attained. 

5. Medieval Religious Ideals. To the religious life, especially in monasticism, the medieval man and woman were particularly devoted. They saw in it man's duty in life and

realized they lavished their physical and their mental efforts upon it and upon the study and interpretation of the faith. By their piety they won such esteem that they came to be the advisers of kings and the leaders of people. By their intellectual labors they interpreted the Scriptures and the teachings of the fathers of the Church, and erected a theological system which has no equal.

Lacking the modern scientific attitude toward the works of nature, they saw miracles in everything and displayed a sublime faith in the power of bits of bone, cloth, wood, or even less sanitary things, to effect cures or even raise the dead. They recognized in the saints the power to divert the processes of nature even as the clergy performed the daily miracle of the mass. 

With all this simplicity, there abode a sublime faith in the essentials of the Christian life-love, humility, charity and service-which expressed itself in their veneration of the Virgin Mary or "Our Lady" as they called her. In her name they did great deeds and they took their troubles to her as to an understanding mother. Such was the magic of her name that it was finally believed to have the power to stop demons and even the devil himself, as nothing else could.

Because of its wealth, the Church became proud and haughty, but it served as the great binding power of society and stood opposed to the more outrageous acts of the secular rulers. Its failings have caused so much comment that the great and lasting things which it did are often forgotten. At its side stood monasticism which has also suffered so much from a parade of its shortcomings, that its real contribution, as the spiritual reservoir out of which came the inspiration for the great reforms, has been quite often overlooked.

II MODERN WORLD 

1453-1931

THE PERIOD OF CIVILIZATION IN READJUSTMENT Chapters XXXVIII-L The Foreword 

After the fall of Constantinople the economic and intellectual outlook of the people of western Europe changed rapidly. The new discoveries in the field of science, the circumnavigation of the globe, and the invention of the telescope, each played an important part in revolutionizing earlier conceptions of the universe.

The printing press made possible the rapid spread of the new and radical ideas of Luther, Zwingli, and Calvin, while the rising power of the new monarchs and the employment of gunpowder in warfare did much to break down feudal ideas and imperial conditions in Europe. The later religious wars, in which religion was complicated with nationalism, may be called a dying expression of medieval ways of thinking. 

While Columbus and those other intrepid discoverers and explorers who followed in his footsteps carried both royal and religious banners, traders and priests were soon bringing old world thoughts and ideas into the newly discovered lands beyond the seas. And so it came about that the medieval world died hard, and devils and witches still continued to occupy the thoughts of many long after a new system of ideas had brought in a new age.

CHAPTER XXXVIII THE RENAISSANCE MARKS THE  

Modern History begins the movement known as the Renaissance (ren-ě-sans'). The word "renaissance" means re-birth, or to be more exact, the re-birth of classical knowledge. Scholars began to study anew the old Latin classics of Virgil and Cicero. Greek scholars came to Italy as teachers bringing the works of Plato, Aristotle, Homer, and the Greek dramatists. 

These opened up the almost forgotten world of the ancient Greeks and Romans, and produced a new learning full of the spirit of free inquiry that was antagonistic to the authority which the Church had held over education. But that was only one phase of the movement, and by no means the most important. The Renaissance included also the development of a keen curiosity concerning everything in the world, and the discovery of many new technical processes. It was marked by a disposition to invent things, and by the beginning of a new point of view toward individuals and society, and toward life itself. 

1. The Renaissance Begins in Italy in the Fourteenth 

Century. The first stirrings of this new movement occurred in Italy in the fourteenth century. The reason for this seems to be found in the character of Italian life at that time. In northern and central Italy, where the cities enjoyed a greater development than anywhere else in Europe, the fall of the medieval empire during the preceding century, and the removal of the papacy to Avignon, had left them free from all outside interference. As a result of the increased commerce which followed the Crusades and of the development of medieval 357

trade, many of their citizens had amassed great fortunes which gave them leisure to think and to evolve new ideas. 

2. How the Italian Cities Were Governed. Each of the 

Italian cities attempted to gain control of as much as possible of the territory surrounding it. In this Venice, Florence, and 

Milan were especially successful. The government of each was much influenced by their material interests. In Venice, the commercial aristocracy obtained control and kept the government wholly in its own hands; at Florence, under the influence of the guilds, the government tended toward a democracy; at 

Milan, the diversity of interests enabled the commander of the city troops to establish a military autocracy. 

Since most of the citizens were more interested in trade and commerce than in fighting, they hired their soldiers. As they found it more convenient to engage these mercenaries en masse, certain energetic persons made themselves leaders of strong fighting organizations which sold their services to the highest bidder. These leaders, bound by no ties save those of money, often betrayed their employers or used their position to usurp the government. Out of this corruption developed the new political theory that government was an institution for the benefit of the governor rather than for the governed. This was ably expressed by the deposed Florentine secretary, Nic'co-lō Machiavelli (mä-kyä-věl′lē), in The Prince, a book which has had a profound influence on history. 

3. The Beginnings of Capitalism. When the merchants of the Italian cities began to accumulate wealth, they soon discovered that it was easiest to handle in the form of money. At first they tried to use it themselves by extending their trading operations to all parts of western Europe, but when this proved inadequate they began to lend the money at home and abroad. 

A memory of this is still retained in Lombard Street, the banking centre of London, where the Italian bankers had their offices.

The Italian bankers counted among their clients both kings and princes, and often these royal borrowers failed to pay their

4. Francesco Petrarch, the "First Modern Scholar and

Man of Letters." In its narrower sense the Renaissance is generally said to have begun with Francesco Petrarch (frånchěs’kō pē’trärk), aptly called the "First Modern Scholar and Man of Letters." Francesco's father, who was papal secretary at the time of the removal of the Holy See to Avignon, planned to make his son a lawyer, but the young man was more interested in poetry than in law. When the father discovered this, he compelled the boy to destroy all his pagan books, but on the death of his father, Francesco was left free to study what he wished. Francesco had always been interested in the sonorous language and elegant style of Cicero. Now he turned enthusiastically to a study of his works. He travelled around collecting and comparing manuscripts, and thus laid the foundations of the modern study of Latin. 

Petrarch devoted much of his life to combating the narrowness of the scholastics, insisting that the universities were mere "nests of ignorance." His appeal for a revival of the culture of the ancients found a response in the minds of the rich and leisure classes of the Italian cities. Students in all northern

Italy became enthusiastic over the work of those whom they called the ancestors of the Italian people, and sent their own compositions to Petrarch for correction. Men searched far and wide for copies of the writings of the old Roman authors. 

Not only did Petrarch himself become famous as a writer of classical Latin, but in his old age he began the study of Greek because he realized that Greek literature had been the basis of much of the Roman learning. He was proud of his own accomplishments and left to posterity a letter to insure that what he had done might not be forgotten. 

5. How the Greek and Latin Classics Became the Basis of a Liberal Education. Petrarch's enthusiasm for Greek

aroused so much interest in the language that by the close of the fourteenth century the teaching of it had begun at Florence. 

Byzantine scholars who were beginning to feel Turkish oppression were encouraged to cross over the Adriatic with their manuscripts. When Con- 

stantinople fell in 1453, the study of Greek was established in western

Europe. Thus the literature and learning of the 

Greeks were saved for society. 

Although scholars found in the Greek and 

Latin classics new material in all the great fields of knowledge, and literary forms worthy of close imitation, the greatest effect of this revival was in education. It is significant that at this time, when the education of the laity was just beginning, the study of Greek and Latin should become a fundamental part of a liberal

6. The Art and the Versatility of the Artists of the 

Renaissance. The struggles of the cities and of the great banking families to outdo one another in the magnificence of their buildings gave a great impetus to architecture. Here the classic past extended a helping hand. In spite of all the sieges

it had passed through, Rome still contained many ancient buildings and statues, and to them the architects and artists of the Renaissance turned for inspiration. In fact, they were so influenced by classical remains that it was only in painting where there was little to imitate that they showed greatest originality. 

To-day we are accustomed to think of artists as either painters, sculptors, or architects, but the great artists of the Renais- 

SAINT PETER'S AS IT IS TO-DAY 

On the right you may see the Vatican, which is the home of the Pope. sance did not limit themselves to any one of these phases of art. Men like Michelangelo Buonarroti (mē-kěl-än'já-lo bwô-närrô'tě) and Leonardo da Vinci (lá-on-ar'dô dä vēn'che) were noteworthy for their versatility, actually attaining as great success in painting as in sculpture or architecture. Not only that, but Michelangelo wrote poetry, and Leonardo put on amateur theatricals and made investigations in mathematics, science, and philosophy. We know that they must have been practical business men and engineers, because they usually superintended the construction of their buildings. It was this all-round character that marked them as men of the Renaissance, for that was an age of developing individuality which gave men courage to undertake anything.

8. Great Names Connected with the Rise of Painting. 

The painters of the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries had no classical models to guide them, and so in trying to obtain satisfactory effects they had to do much original studying and experimenting. Not only did they learn many technical facts of great importance in connection with the mixing of colors and the preparation of canvas, but what was more important, they

discovered the use of perspective and some of the other principles that govern artistic painting. Last but not least, they became convinced that living models were necessary to give reality to a picture. 

Giotto (jôt'to), who decorated the great Church of St. Francis at Assisi, is considered the first painter of the Renaissance. His work was carried on by Fra Angelico (frä än-jěl'é-kō) and Botticelli (bot-té-chěl'lē) and reached a climax in da Vinci, Răph'á-ěl, and Michelangelo. Since much of the painting of these men. was in the decoration of churches, it was necessarily religious in character; still, the adornment of villas and palaces, and a demand for portraits led all the painters into secular work.

While the earlier of these palaces, such as those of the Pitti (pēt'tē) and Uffizi (oof-fe'tse) at Florence were massive, forbidding structures, which had been built for defense, the later palaces were supplied with larger windows and were adorned with sculpture and statuary. New styles of clothing and new kinds of textiles came into general use among the upper classes, to be imitated in time by the lower classes. A new emphasis was placed upon cookery with the result that many novel recipes were invented. Along with this went a corresponding develop- ment of table manners, which included the introduction of the fork. Perhaps because so many of the rulers of the Italian cities had risen from the lower strata of society, the rulers placed a high valuation upon manners and etiquette. 

The little court of Urbino (oor-be'nō) became so noted for its refinement that one of the courtiers, Baldassare Castiglione (bäldäs-sär'a cäs-tēl'lyô- nē), embodied its

ideals and practices in the first great modern book on etiquette entitled The Book of the Courtier. 

In Italy the Renaissance was a fun-loving age. Not only were medieval religious amusements multiplied, but many new secular ones were introduced. The palio (päl'yō), or horse race, was greatly enjoyed at Siena (syếnä), but the most famous amusement was the carnival of the Florentines. With its procession of grotesque figures, and its extraordinary gaiety and license, it resembled closely the Mardi Gras (mär’dé grä') held each year at New Orleans. 

10. Leading Ideals of the Renaissance Were Individual 

Freedom and a Zest for Life. Italy expressed itself in the 

Renaissance somewhat differently from the rest of Europe. 

The new individuality assumed arrogance which frequently became offensive. It led to an independence of spirit that brooked no authority or master. Scholars squabbled over intellectual questions and called each other names that smacked of the gutter rather than of halls of learning. Not only did they ignore church and clergy but they found in pagan literature a reflection of their own enjoyments of this life, and flung themselves into the joy of living with an utter abandon. 

In this period of new moral values, crimes of violence became frequent. Princes and prelates alike often did not hesitate to remove their enemies by poison or by assassination. But the picture was not all dark and sordid, for on the other side. can be placed the search for truth and beauty. It left to society such a mass of painting, sculpture, and architecture that Italy ever since has attracted lovers of the beautiful in art. And last but not least, these new artistic impulses spread beyond the Alps and helped to mould and direct similar impulses in the rest of western Europe.
