CHAPTER XXXIX THE NEW CONCEPT OF MONARCHY AND THE NEW MONARCHIES 

We have seen how feudalism and the kingship developed in 

France and England. The Hundred Years' War showed how weak the French King became owing to his dependence on vassals for his military strength. This war had also convinced the kings that some scheme of taxation was necessary to supply the funds needed to maintain their thrones. There had been growing a conviction that feudalism would have to be supplanted by some new arrangement better fitted to meet the new conditions. As early as the thirteenth century, the French kings had begun to undermine the powers of the feudal nobles, only to have their work largely undone by the Hundred Years' War. 

In England the triumph of the barons over King John had been only partially overcome even by such a powerful king as Edward III, and their position had been strengthened again during the long period of foreign wars. We shall now see how kings asserted their powers and broke the power of the nobles. 

1. How the Wars of the Roses Break the Power of the

Nobles. The power of the English nobles was seriously crippled after the close of the Hundred Years' War. A struggle broke out between the rival houses of Lancaster and York, whose badges were red and white roses respectively. In these 

Wars of the Roses, as they were called, the Yorkists had the support of the clergy and the London merchants, while the Lancastrians enrolled beneath their banners the remnants of the old feudal aristocracy, especially those in the north of England. Frequent plots and conspiracies, and a number of bloody battles caused the death of a large part of the nobility. They 369

came to an end with a victory for the Lancastrians, whose leader, Henry Tudor, became king in 1485 and in the following year married Elizabeth of York, thus healing the breach.

The death of so many of the nobles and the expulsion of others made it possible for Henry VII to appoint new peers who proved less independent than their predecessors had been. 

Henry also set up a new court, called the Star Chamber, composed of judges appointed by the king. Not only could the Star 

Chamber summon before it those accused of crime and try them without the aid of a jury, but through it Henry was able to enforce a law which forbade the nobility, for their own use, to keep retainers, or fighting men. So effective were these two methods that by the end of his reign Henry broke the power of the nobility. 

2. How Louis XI of France Consolidated the Royal 

Power. Shortly before the end of the Hundred Years' War the Estates General, as the French parliament was called, passed a law permitting the king to levy a tax on property, known as taille (tä'y'). Although this tax was authorized for only one year, the king continued it and obtained revenue with which he could hire soldiers independently of the feudal nobles, who had themselves lost the right to coin money and to hire soldiers. 

Since the thirteenth century, however, the French kings had raised up some powerful opponents by granting provinces to their own younger sons. By this time the houses of Orleans, Anjou, Bourbon (boor'bun), and Burgundy had become almost as strong as the royal family itself.

When Louis XI came to the throne in 1461, he undertook to bring all of these opponents under his control. For this undertaking he was eminently fitted, for he was so shrewd and successful at intrigue that he became known as the "universal spider." His chief opponent was Charles the Bold of Burgundy, whose ancestors gathered under their control a large part of what is to-day eastern France. The death of Charles

NEW CONCEPT OF MONARCHY 

371 in 1477 gave Louis an opportunity to make himself master of Burgundy. Later, with the aid of his lawyers and of diplomatic intriguing, not only did he weaken the power of the other great houses, but he prepared the way for the acquisition of Brittany which had long been independent in everything except name. With the death of 

Louis XI, the task of consolidating the royal power in France was well under way. 

Alongside of this development of the royal power, there began to appear sure signs of nationalism in the making. 

Where the spirit of Joan of Arc had contented itself with restoring the morale of the French knights, this new spirit took in the lower class of society. Although we can hardly picture these lower classes as having a part in the control of the kingdom, still they were beginning to be conscious that they, too, were Frenchmen, and as such a part of the state.

3. Spain Unified Becomes the Leading Nation in Western Europe. In the Spanish peninsula also there was springing up a feeling of nationalism, although it was showing itself in a somewhat different way. Ever since the Muslim conquest of the eighth century the Spanish Christians had been struggling to get rid of the Muslims. For two centuries they made little progress, and even since that time they had been ham-

pered because the peninsula was cut up into a number of little kingdoms-Leon (lä-ōn'), Castile (kǎs-tēl'), Är'a-gon, and 

Nå-värre, and later Portugal.

During the Middle Ages, Castile and Leon had been united. 

In 1469 Aragon was joined with them through the marriage of its king, Ferdinand, to Isabella, Queen of Castile. Now that the greater part of the peninsula was under a single rule, it was possible to prosecute the assault against Granada, the last stronghold of the Moors, with such vigor that the place fell in 1492. Twenty-four years later control of all Spain passed into the hands of a single monarch and the country became the leading nation of western Europe. 

4. The Rise of Dynasties Was an Outgrowth of Feu dalism. One of the significant reminders that the new kingships were an outgrowth of feudalism was the importance of family. 

Under the older system it had been customary for the feudal lords to gather many fiefs under their control and to pass them on to their eldest sons. Likewise the kings frequently obtained the crown of more than one kingdom, and added to this a generous number of counties, duchies, and margravates. Thus 

Charles I of Aragon became king of Castile and Leon, and of Naples and Sicily, Duke of Căt-à-lo'ni-a and the possessor of nearly fifty other titles. Even to-day the King of England is still Duke of Normandy, and by that title rules the little islands of Jersey, Guernsey (gûrn'zi), and Alderney (ôl'der-ni) in the English Channel. Out of this practice arose a number of powerful families, like the Habsburgs of Austria, and later the Bourbons of France, all of whom played an important part in the history of their respective countries.

6. What Were the Ideals of the New Monarchs? In

Henry VII of England, Louis XI of France, and Charles I of 

Spain are to be found exemplified the ideals of the new type of kingship. All of these monarchs desired an increase of royal power and the centralization in the hands of the monarch. They were eager to extend their territory and were often able to fire the ambitions of their subjects so that the latter would aid

them in realizing these aims. They were not always scrupulous in their methods, and their eyes were centred as much upon the aggrandizement of themselves and their own families as upon the betterment of their kingdoms. In fact, in these men appeared more pronounced than ever before the evidences of an individuality, which, as we have seen, was one of the outstanding features of the whole Renaissance movement. From their rivalries and ambitions arose the new troubles which were destined to throw Europe into turmoil.

THE WORLD KNOWN TO EUROPEANS IN 1490

CHAPTER XL  ACROSS THE SEAS 

The spirit of curiosity, which expressed itself in Italy in art and literature, expressed itself in Portugal and in the other countries of western Europe in geographical discovery. Fired by a desire to attack the Moors of northern Morocco with whom his father was waging war and to bring about the rapid conversion of Africa to Christianity, Prince Henry, later known as "the Navigator," began sending ships along the western coast of Africa. To assist his captains in their voyages, he set up an observatory at Sa'gres and collected there the best map makers of the day. Although the sailors often were greatly terrified by the real or fancied dangers they faced-contrary winds, boiling seas, and mythical monsters-each year the Prince's little ships crept a trifle farther down the African coast, with the result that by the time of his death they reached Cape Verde (vûrd) and the adjacent Guinea (gin'i) coast. 

Meanwhile Portugal had annexed the Ä-zōres' and the Madeiras (ma-de'ras), and farther south, the Cape Verde Islands, all of which she holds to this day. How Portugal might have 375

had the honor of sending Columbus across the Atlantic is one of the ironies of history. How the rulers of Spain finally agreed to finance the expedition for Columbus and how his discovery stirred the imagination of the people of western Europe and made world-wide Empire for Spain before England and France is an example of how an incident directs the course of history. 

1. The Portuguese Find a Water Route for Oriental 

Trade. The most profitable foreign trade of the Middle Ages had been in spices. Control of this trade had gradually passed into the hands of the Venetians and they had become so rich and prosperous as a result that they were the envy of other Europeans. These spices reached Europe by three main routes -through the Red Sea and Egypt, up the Persian Gulf and across the Syrian Desert, and by way of Constantinople. Gradually men began to ask whether some other route to India might be found by which this monopoly of the Venetians could be broken and the Muslims deprived of the profits. By the last quarter of the fifteenth century the new discoveries in Africa had begun to be valuable and the possibility of reaching India by sea began to seem feasible. 

In 1486 Bär-thŏl'ó-mew Diaz (de'äs) rounded the Cape of Good Hope and eleven years later, with the aid of an Arab pilot picked up at Zän'zi-bär, Väs'cō dä Gä'mä found his way across the Indian Ocean to Căl'i-cut, the centre of the spice trade. On his return to Lisbon, the voyage showed a total profit of 6,000 per cent and gave Portugal control of this valuable trade. Other Portuguese navigators made extensive explorations along the eastern coast of Africa, the Persian Gulf and the shores of India, and the peninsulas and islands beyond. 

They attacked Aden and seized the island of Or'muz, and tried to stop trade westward through the Red Sea and the Persian

Gulf. Under the leadership of the great Af-fon'sō de Albuquerque (dä-äl-boo-ker'kě), a capital was established at Gō'a and a great empire based on trade established in the East. 

2. Christopher Columbus Becomes the Hero of One of the Greatest Human Achievements. While Ferdinand and 

Isabella were still in camp at 

Santa Fé (fa) after the conquest of Granada, the queen agreed to finance the expedition of Christopher Columbus, a former Genoese clerk, to the Indies in the hope of gaining for Spain the control of the Oriental trade and of "spreading the knowledge of 

God and the light of the faith to many nations." In August, 1492, Columbus set sail from Pä'lōs and in the following May returned with the news of his discovery of the islands which then received their name of the 

West Indies.

From a photograph 

Brown Brothers.

THE SANTA MARIA 

From a full-sized reconstruction of 

Columbus' flagship. 

The "Brave Admiral," as he was now known, made three other trips across the Atlantic in his search for a "southwest passage," and although he touched the mainland of both Central and South America at many points, he died without knowing that he had really found a new continent. By an irony of fate, the new world which he discovered for Europe was not named after him, but for another traveller of less importance, Amerigo Vespucci (a-mér'ē-gó věs-poot'chē). 

3. The Effects of Columbus' Discovery. Though the work of Columbus affected the popular conception of a flat

earth, it took some time for these ideas to take effect. Of more immediate importance was the Spaniards' invasion of Portugal's monopoly of exploration. The Spanish sovereigns at once took measures to secure their rights to the discoveries of Columbus. 

Since the Pope had already given the East to the Portuguese, Infula hyspana

Portugal protested, and in 

1494 a treaty between the two powers established the line three hundred and sixty leagues west of the Cape 

Verde Islands, giving Portugal a basis for her future claims to Brazil. 

Meanwhile the Spanish sea captains were trying to find the passage around America.

In 1513 Bäl-bo'ä crossed the 

Isthmus of Panama and saw a new ocean which he called the "South Sea." Six years later, Ferdinand Mă-gel'lăn with a fleet of five ships and two hundred eighty men sailed along the coast of South America to Păt-à-gō'nĭ-a, where he spent the winter. In the spring he threaded the strait which bears his name, and sailed into the South Sea, which he named the Pacific Sea because it was more calm than the Atlantic.

After ninety-eight days of further sailing, he and his halfstarved crews reached the islands, later called the Philippines in honor of Philip II of Spain. Magellan was here killed in a

local war, but in 1522 his one remaining ship, the Vit-to'ri-à, with thirty-one survivors, crept into the harbor of Seville. 

4. The Portuguese Build a Colonial Empire. Both the 

Portuguese and Spaniards made haste to follow up their dis-

coveries with colonies. At first the colonists consisted almost wholly of soldiers and traders, but later planters became an important part of the population. In this colonization the Portuguese were outstripped by the Spanish, for the reason that much of their own field of action was already so thickly settled it would not permit of colonization on a large scale, even if there had been the necessary surplus population back home. So vast were the new dominions that most of their energy was used up in administering them and in protecting their trade. 

In Brazil alone did the Portuguese colonize on a large scale, and this land eventually became Portugal's most valuable col-

ony and the main source of her riches until its separation from the mother country in the nineteenth century. To-day all that is left of the vast Portuguese colonial empire in the East are a few scattered ports on the southern coast of Asia and a number of large tracts of unhealthy coast lands near the mouth of the Congo river and along the southeastern shore of Africa. 

5. Spain Rises to Wealth and Power through Conquest. In the West Indies and the two Americas there was more room for settlers, consequently large numbers of Spanish grandees, eager for wealth and excitement now that the wars with the Moors were ended, came to settle. 

All those regions were peopled by widely dispersed tribes of red-skinned natives, whose ancestors are supposed by many to have crossed over in remote times either by the old land bridge which connected Asia with Alaska, or, in their canoes by way of the islands of the South Pacific. In any event, when the 

Spaniards first met the red men or Indians, the latter were still for the most part living in the neolithic age. To this there were three exceptions-the Aztecs, of southern Mexico, the Mä'yäs of Yucatan (yoo-kä-tän'), and the Peruvians, whose In'cä or "First Son of the Sun," ruled a gigantic commonwealth comprising what is now Ecuador (ěk'wa-dôr), Peru, northern Chile, the Brazilian province of the Amazon, and Bolivia.

A great impetus was given to this Spanish colonization movement by the conquest of Mexico by Cortez (kór-tās') in 1517. Although Ponce (pons) de Leon found no fountain of youth in Florida, Cortez did find a fountain of gold and silver in the mountains of Anahuac (ä-nä'wäk). In addition he found an advanced civilization with a well-organized government and a considerable literature, but all of this was swept away by the Spaniards' greed for gold and by their zeal to extend Christianity. Montezuma (mon-té-zoo'mȧ), the Aztec king, and the whole royal line were put to death, and the capital

city was destroyed. On its ruins Cortez built a new city to serve as the seat of government for New Spain. In 1528 

Cortez returned to Spain with gold worth $900,000 and 12,- 

000 ounces of silver.

With little difficulty he made himself master of Cuzco (koos'kō), their capital city, and then, as Cortez had done farther north, he put to death the whole royal line. After the Peruvians were despoiled of their wealth-temples, palaces, and tombs were looted, and their treasures of gold, silver, and precious stones were sent back to Spain. Philip II the most powerful monarch of Christendom. 

6. How the Spaniards Treated the Native Americans. 

Few of the natives took kindly to being required to labor in 

THE CATHEDRAL AT LIMA, PERU 

It was built in the sixteenth century. mines and on plantations. Many are the tales of Spanish cruelty which have come down to us, especially from the great feudal estates in the rich valley of the Lä Plä'ta, where the Spaniards developed one of their later and stronger colonies. 

To the credit of the Catholic Church it must be said that Pope and clergy were violently opposed to the enslavement of the natives. The great Dominican de Läs Cä'säs crossed the Atlantic fourteen times in behalf of the downtrodden people of what is to-day Paraguay (păr'à-gwā). The victory was finally won, but not until negro slaves from the coast of Guinea furnished a more satisfactory supply of labor. 

Farther north among the Incas, Mayas, and Aztecs the rec-

ord of the Church is not so good, for in their zeal to make converts to Christianity the missionaries tried to wipe out traces of the early native culture, and so completely did they succeed that little of its literature has survived. Only recently we have begun to see how far these people had advanced toward civilization. With the conversion of the natives to Christianity, intermarriage with the Spaniards became possible, and as a result the people south of the United States are still largely a mixture of Spanish and Indian blood. 

7. The Conquest of the Philippines by Spain Was More 

Humane. When Magellan discovered the Philippines, he found them rather thinly inhabited by many different tribes of Malaysian peoples mixed with a certain amount of Chinese blood, and possibly with that of the more primitive Negritos (né-grē’tōz). These tribes were ruled by independent chiefs and were engaged in frequent inter-tribal wars. Because the Philippines seemed to yield neither gold nor spices, the Spanish leaders opposed any outlay for their conquest, consequently no serious effort to colonize them was made until the time of Philip II. 

Philip was so eager to extend the "true faith" that he declared that he would spend the wealth of the Indies to save a single soul, and ordered the viceroy of New Spain to fit out an expedition to establish a post in the Philippines. As a result, in 

1564 a fleet of four căr-'à-věls sailed from Acapulco (ä-käpool'kō) under command of Legaspi (lá-gäz’pē), and seven years later, after extensive explorations among the islands of the archipelago, the Spaniards founded Ma-nila.

The occupation of the Philippines escaped much of the oppression that had prevailed in the Americas, for the conquest of the Philippines was made more by friars-Augustinians, Franciscans, Dominicans, and Jesuits-than by soldiers. Churches were established so widely that within two centuries all the Filipinos were Christianized except the Muslims in the south, who to this day are known as Mo'rōs, and the Negritos and other

pagans whose homes were back in the mountains. Here too the literary traces of the native civilizations were destroyed. 

8. Why Were Other European Powers Indifferent to 

Colonization for So Long? Why were the Spanish and

Portuguese allowed by the other European powers to enjoy such a monopoly of early colonization? To begin with, we must remember that the kings of England and France were both interested in other things at the time, England in her internal problems and France in her attempts to control Italy. 

John Cabot, an Italian of Bristol, interested the king in an expedition to seek Cipango and in 1497 reached the coast of North America and furnished the basis of England's claim to part of that continent. Cabot noticed the presence of "certayne bigge fysses like unto tunnies that sometymes stayed the shyppes," and the fishermen of England and Brittany soon began to frequent the banks of Newfoundland. The rising interests of trade to the Baltic and the Mediterranean drew the attention of English merchants away from the new lands. 

The French showed their first interest in exploration in 1524 when, aroused by the tales of wealth the Spanish were obtaining, Francis I commissioned the Italian sea captain Ver-ra-za'no, especially to look for a northwest passage to the Pacific. 

Verrazano cruised along the coasts of North America from Georgia to Nova Scotia. Ten years later Cartier (kartia') reached the Gulf of St. Lawrence and sailed up the river on the same quest. The name of the La Chine (la-shēn') rapids bears witness to the search for the route to China. 

That the Dutch showed so little interest in the New World was due to the fact that Charles I of Spain was their sovereign prince, and it was hardly to be expected that he would allow them to share in the wealth that was pouring into his coffers from the rich monopoly enjoyed by the crown of Castile. Indeed, so exclusive were the Spanish colonies, expecially Mexico and Peru, that no strangers were permitted to enter them with-

out permission from Madrid. Down to 1778 only registered 

Spanish vessels could land in the harbors of Vera Cruz (vā´rä kroos') and Acapulco to engage in trade. 

9. The Immediate Effects of American Colonization. 

As a result of the Spanish colonization, there arose beyond the Atlantic a new Spain founded on the ideals and culture of the mother country. The Spaniards had come as conquerors, and, confident of their racial and cultural superiority, they intended to hold that position in their relations with the rest of the population. In the cities of the New World they built great churches, many of them still standing as memorials to their builders. Even in the little villages they established missions for the uplifting of the natives both spiritually and socially. At 

Mexico City and Lima (le'mä), the two capitals of their great Spanish-American empire, they founded universities which are the oldest in America, and they set up in the former place the first printing-press on this side of the Atlantic. 

Great as was the Spanish influence on America, it was as nothing compared with that of America on Spain. No sooner had the Spaniards begun to plant their colonies than Spain began to look to the West Indies for her sugar, and to Central America for her dye stuffs. It was not long before these imports were completely overshadowed by the quantities of gold and silver from Mexico and Peru. When we learn that the amount of gold and silver in Europe was increased fifteenfold, it is not surprising to find that during this period Spain became the richest and most powerful country of Christendom. 

But, inasmuch as this wealth was largely secured through exploitation, when the gold and silver began to diminish, Spain's prosperity waned with it, and the nation sank to the position of a second-rate power.

It was not Spain alone that felt the effect of this tremendous amount of gold, for throughout all Europe prices rose and there was an enormous development of capital. So great be-

came the wealth of the Fuggers (fōo'gers) and Welsers (věl'zers) and other German capitalists that they embarked on the capitalistic exploitation of undeveloped countries.

CHAPTER XLI THE RENAISSANCE SPREADS TO NORTHERN EUROPE 

We have seen how a European civilization emerged from the Middle Ages that was a fusion of Roman and Teutonic elements converted to Christianity. Certain translations from 

Aristotle were all that came down from the old Greek and Roman learning. We shall see how during the early years of this period the Renaissance revived all the learning in literature and art of the old Greek and Roman worlds that could be found. In this chapter we shall find how the spirit of the 

Renaissance, expressed in the countries of northern Europe not only by an interest in the old learning but also by free inquiry and discussion, led to conflict with the Church. We shall see how an outburst of human achievement took place in literature, art, architecture, and in science and how the invention of the printing-press made learning and literature, formerly the privilege of the few, available for the many. 

1. The Renaissance Crosses the Alps. During the fifteenth century Italy became a centre for many scholars from northern Europe. The most famous of these northern pilgrims was Děs-i-de'ri-us Erasmus (é-răz'mus) of Rotterdam. Erasmus became an orphan at an early age and was placed by his guardians in one of the schools of the Brethren of the Common life. After his little fortune had been stolen by these guardians, he entered the service of the Church as a means of earning a living. He studied for a time in Paris and then visited England where he met some of the northerners who already had become interested in the new studies. Later he visited Italy and took up his residence at Basel, to be near his 387

printer. He undertook to reorganize German education. For this he found the soil prepared, thanks to the work of the sect known as the Brethren of the Common Life.

ERASMUS 

This picture now in the Louvre was painted by Hans 

Holbein, the great German artist of the day. 

Erasmus first gained fame by the publication of a collection of sayings from classical authors that ran through many editions and was constantly improved on and enlarged. His distinctive work, however, was an edition of the Greek 

New Testament in which he applied the same principles of criticism that had been used in editing the 

Latin and Greek classics. He accompanied it with a Latin translation, and because this differed in places quite materially from the Vulgate, Erasmus incurred the ill-will of the Church. 

2. John Reuchlin and the Hebrew Books. Another northern humanist was John Reuchlin (roik'lin). He prepared the first modern Hebrew grammar and devoted himself to a critical study of the Old Testament in much the same way that Erasmus had studied the New. Reuchlin entered into a controversy with a converted Jew over the wisdom of destroying the Jewish books and was accused of heresy. The discussion dragged on until most scholars had taken sides. Those

THE RENAISSANCE SPREADS 

389 with the newer ideas sided with Reuchlin and wrote him letters which he published under the title of Letters of Illustrious Men. 

This caused some clever writer to prepare a counter collection entitled The Letters of Obscure Men. These letters, which purported to be written by students of the inquisitors, were composed in barbarous Latin intermixed with German. They set forth so clearly the ideas of the humanists and ridiculed so effectively the pretensions of the older scholars, that when they were read, the scholastics were laughed out of court, and a victory was won in Germany for the new ideas. 

3. The French Invasion of Italy Brings Elements of the 

Renaissance into France. In 1494 Charles VIII of France undertook an invasion of Italy to assert his claims to the Duchy of Milan and the Kingdom of Naples. Lō-ren'zo de' Medici, the only Italian by whom he might have been opposed successfully, was already dead, and Florence was in control of the re- 'forming monk Săv-ó-na-ro'là, who looked upon the invasion as God's method of avenging the vices of the Italians. Although 

Charles occupied Milan and Florence, and even got as far as Rome before he was compelled to withdraw, he acquired little except a desire for further Italian conquests. 

Out of this invasion there developed one important consequence. Charles and his followers became much impressed with the art and refinements of the Italians. In the years which followed many architects and artists were brought from Italy to France to build and adorn the beautiful palaces and castles of the Loire (lwär) valley which even to-day make that region of great attraction to the tourist. Thus the material side of the 

Renaissance was brought across the Alps. 

4. The Renaissance Expresses Itself in the New Na tional Literatures. While scholars studied the classics, and kings and nobles built stately homes, the new spirit was inducing another group of persons to begin to produce a literature in their native tongue. In France Margaret of Navarre and

her courtiers wrote the Hěp-tăm'é-ron in imitation of Boccaccio, and Rabelais (rȧ-b'lē) so cleverly satirized the older ideas and education in his Gär-găn'tú-à and Pantagruel (păntǎg roo-ěl) that it is said more copies of this latter book were sold in two years than of the Bible in nine years. In Spain 

Cervantes (ser-văn'téz) wrote the story Don Quixote (kehō'tā), in which he ridiculed the worn-out romances of chivalry, A FIFTEENTH-CENTURY MEDICINE SELLER 

This picture shows that the modern medicine man has long been in existence. 

After a contemporary manuscript in the Library at Cambrai. and Lope de Vega Carpio (ló'pā dā vā'gä kär'pyó) flooded the Spanish theatre with his eighteen hundred plays. In Portugal the exploits of Vasco da Gama inspired de Căm'ó-ens to write his Lu'si-ăd, while in Germany a translation of the Bible by Martin Luther served to popularize the German language. In 

England there was a crowd of writers expressing the ideas and inspiration of the Italians. Foremost were Edmund Spenser, with his Faër-ie Queene, Christopher Marlowe, William

Shakespeare, Ben Jonson, and John Milton. All this literature differed from that in the south of the Alps in combining nationalistic feelings with the ideals of the Renaissance.

6. Copernicus Makes a Revolutionary Scientific Dis covery. The most revolutionary scientific discovery of the 

Renaissance was made by a northerner-Nicholas Co-perni-

cus, a Pole, who had spent ten years studying in Italy. After returning to Poland, Copernicus devoted the remaining forty years of his life to study and reflection. Only on his death-

Presses exactly like this have not been long out of use in some parts of the United States. bed did he see the proof-sheets of his great work on the revolution of the celestial bodies. In this book he maintained that the earth 

Iwas not the centre of the universe, but only one of several planets which revolved around the sun. Although the idea had been held centuries. before by the Greek philosophers, it was frowned upon by churchmen, because it seemed to throw discredit on the religious teachings of the day, that the earth, and with it man, was the centre of things. 

7. What Printing with Movable Type Meant to the 

World. One of the chief reasons for the rapid expansion of the ideas of the Renaissance was the discovery-new to Europe at least-of printing with movable type. As we have seen, the 

Chinese had long before this invented printing by wooden blocks and even by movable type. When the Mongol invasions reached Europe in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, they seem to have brought with them from China knowledge of

THE RENAISSANCE SPREADS 

393 games played with cards, and apparently the technic of printing these cards from wooden blocks. 

At any rate card playing spread rapidly in Europe during the later fourteenth century, and soon afterward the making of cards became an industry in Venice and elsewhere. About the same time sacred pictures began to be printed in the same way, and books were produced from wooden blocks on which whole pages had been cut in relief. 

About 1450, John Gutenberg (goo'těn-běrk) made a metal cast of each letter and thus invented movable type. Fifty years before, movable bronze type for the Chinese characters had been cast in Korea, but the alphabetic type of Gutenberg was far more convenient to use. With this invention it was possible to make books cheaply and in large quantities provided there was something to print them on. 

Gutenberg printed his Bible on parchment but this was far AL

too costly a material. Already the Arabs had brought to the 

West the knowledge of paper made from rags. As early as the end of the twelfth century it had been produced in France, and in the thirteenth and fourteenth its manufacture had been developed in Italy and Germany. Thus the age of cheap books was at hand. As a final step, the new knowledge of painting

helped in the preparation of an oily ink which would work well on metal.

Since the invention of writing no discovery has been more important than printing with movable type. The learning and the literature which before had been the privilege of the few now became available for the many, and the ideas which formerly had lain forgotten or had travelled painfully along a few well-trodden paths now spread in every direction.

CHAPTER XLII MARTIN LUTHER LEADS THE GERMAN REVOLT FROM THE CHURCH 

We have seen that the Roman Catholic Church during the Middle Ages was the one supreme Christian Church for all the people of western Europe and that all religious matters were under the control of the Pope. The Church was a sort of international state which collected taxes, enacted laws and enforced them in its own courts-powers which came into conflict with the national aims and feelings of independence of the rising nations. Here was a setting for revolt from the Church. 

All that was needed for such a revolt was a leader who could take advantage of the discontent over corruption in the Church, the sale of indulgences, the worldiness of the papal court, and the untaxed wealth of the Church. How this leadership came first in Germany in the person of Martin Luther, a professor in the University of Wittenberg, with the result that his followers became known as Protestants; how the Protestant revolt developed in other countries in northern Europe under various other leaders such as John Calvin; and how the movement was accompanied by a reformation within the Catholic Church, will be explained in the next four chapters. 

1. For Years Germany Had Been in a State of Unrest.

The great councils of the Church in the early part of the thirteenth century had led to much thinking throughout western Europe, especially in Germany. This was later increased by the 

Hussite revolt in Bohemia and by the work of the Brethren of the Common Life. With the invention of printing from movable type books became so cheap that even the common people 395

could begin to enjoy them. As was to be expected, the first book to appear was the Bible. Before the end of the fifteenth century, parts of it had been translated into all the German dialects. 

The fact that Germany lacked the political unity of France, England and Spain made it difficult for her people to adjust themselves to the new social and economic conditions. In the 

German cities there was now a wealthy burgher class with such high standards of living that the old feudal nobility found it difficult to keep up with them. Not only were these burghers developing radical ideas about the privileges of wealth, but the knights were becoming continually less important as the medieval system of warfare disappeared. And finally, even the princes of many of the states were being outclassed by the great ecclesiastical nobles, whose territories now included nearly half of the country, while the peasants at the other end of the social scale were being crushed by increasing burdens. 

2. How the Sale of Indulgences Started and What the 

Practice Led to. Early in the sixteenth century Pope Julius 

II commissioned the great Italian architect Bramante (brämän'tā) to design a new church to replace the old dilapidated St. Peter's at Rome. The plans for the new building were so elaborate that all sorts of means had to be resorted to in order to pay the expense. One was the sale of indulgences. 

According to the medieval theory people were helped through Purgatory by good works. These good works, consisting of religious exercises such as prayer and fasting, were supposed to be deposited in a great treasury to which the Church alone had the key. It was impossible for ordinary persons to indulge in sufficient good works themselves. In order to cut down the time which they would have to spend in Purgatory, they were allowed to draw upon the excess time which had been laid up in this treasury by saints, martyrs, and other holy persons. 

According to the papal theory, an indulgence was simply a draft for that particular purpose. 2

There was nothing wrong about the general theory of indulgences, but like all selling propositions they were open to abuse. 

It is not strange, therefore, that men like Těť zěl, who was sent to Germany to sell indulgences to raise money for the new church, should exaggerate the advantages to be derived from them. These claims led a university professor at Wittenberg (vit'en-berk) to question the sale of indulgences and to discuss it in his class in theology. According to custom he posted on the church door, which served as the university bulletin board, ninety-five propositions or the'sēs, which he proposed to discuss. An enterprising publisher issued a German translation of them. 

3. Why Martin Luther Tired of Monastic Life. This university professor was named Martin Luther. His father was a slate-cutter, who had sent his son to the university to study law. At the close of his university career young Martin became convinced that he was not going to Heaven without special efforts. He entered an Augustinian monastery and tried to find peace of mind by doubling the number of prayers and fastings. When this failed, he found what he desired through studying, at the suggestion of his prior, the ideas of faith held by St. Paul and St. Augustine.

Luther soon tired of monastic life and obtained a position as professor of philosophy in the newly established University of Wittenberg. Here he continued his studies and developed the idea that salvation depended not upon good works, but upon faith. It must not be thought, however, that the Church had ever rejected the necessity of faith, although it had placed more emphasis upon good works. 

4. Luther Breaks with the Church. When Luther suddenly found himself famous as a result of the publication of his theses, he was drawn into other discussions. At first his idea was to reform the Church, not to oppose it, but two years later, after a debate at Leipsig (lip'tsik) with a Catholic clergyman

MARTIN LUTHER LEADS REVOLT 

399 named Eck, he became aware that he was a heretic like John Huss. The Pope, who at first had held that this was only a monkish squabble, decided that stern measures must be taken, and sent Luther a bull of excommunication. 

Luther publicly burned the bull to show his defiance, and when he was put out of the Church, proceeded to attack its whole organization. He condemned the clergy for many of the abuses and attacked the Pope's position in a pamphlet called The Babylonish Captivity of the

Church. In another, An Address to the German Nobility, he summoned the rulers of his country to make the needed reforms.

6. The Revolt Leads to Much Violence and Destruction of Life and Property. His stay at the Wartburg was cut short by the rash doings of some of his followers. In their desire to take the 

Bible literally, they began to insist that the monks and nuns should abandon monastic life, and they turned to merchants and children to settle theological questions, on the ground that it was said that God would withhold the truth from the wise and reveal the same unto babes. To put a stop to such extravagance Luther hurried back to Wittenberg, where he brought his 83 ය 

A CARTOON AGAINST MARTIN LUTHER 

He is here pictured with seven heads labelled, "Doctor, Martin, Luther, clergyman, fomenter of trouble, rounder, traitor." followers back to reason by a series of powerful sermons. By this time, however, he had alienated certain of his humanist adherents, including the great Erasmus. 

When Luther escaped from Worms, the knights felt that the time had come to attack the princes of the Church, and some of them started a campaign against the Archbishop of Trier. This turned out disastrously and in a short time the castles of many

other knights were taken and destroyed by the supporters of the Archbishop.

Two years later a more serious revolt broke out in southern Germany, where the peasants, influenced in part by Luther's charges against some of the landowners, rose to better their conditions. Most of their demands were perfectly reasonable and would have freed serfdom in Germany of many of its worst features. But no sooner had this revolt started than some of the more violent leaders urged the killing of priests and nobles indiscriminately. All southern Germany was aflame and Luther was aghast at the destruction that he had precipitated. In desperation, he turned to the nobles and urged them to put down the peasants, a thing that they were only too glad to do. This so angered the latter that when the revolt was over they gave to Luther the name Herr Doktor Lügner or "Mr. 

Doctor Liar." The result of all these disturbances was that the 

German conservatives formed the so-called League of Dessau (děs'ou) to stamp out further revolts. 

7. The Lutherans Become Protestants. The situation in 

Germany had become serious. The emperor was away and could not return for the present, and the Diet did not feel competent to deal with religious questions. It decided that until a council of the Church could be held, each prince or knight or town whose authority had come from the emperor could decide whether to adhere to the Roman Catholic Church or to follow the teachings of Luther. Although this was only a temporary solution, eventually it became permanent. 

In 1529 another Diet ordered the enforcement of the Edict of Worms and those princes who had accepted the teachings of Luther drew up a Protest. From this act came the term Protestants, later applied to all who revolted from the Church of Rome. As a result of this Protest Charles commanded both parties to prepare a formal statement of their beliefs to be laid before a Diet at Augsburg (ouks'boorkh) in 1530.

MARTIN LUTHER LEADS REVOLT 

403 The Lutheran statement was drawn up by Melancthon (mélănk'thun), a close friend of Luther's, noted for his scholarship and moderation. In this so-called Augsburg Confession, which became the creed of the Lutheran Church, Melancthon made the differences between the old and new churches as small as

Even so, when the Diet met, Charles ordered that it be refuted by the Catholic theologians, and commanded the Protestants to give up their heresy, although he did agree to urge the Pope to call a council to bring about reform within the Church. Nothing came of these decrees, for Charles was soon called away again and was unable to enforce them. 

8. The Peace of Augsburg Brings About the Recogni tion of Lutheranism.

This time it was the Turks who kept

Charles busy, first in Hungary and then in the Mediterranean area where they were allied with the French king. In the midst of this fighting Luther died (1546). In the same year the first religious war broke out in Germany. The Protestant princes were easily overcome because of a lack of unity, and their leader, the Elector of Saxony, was captured. Even the Pope was now troubled by the growing power of Charles. As a result, after Maurice (mô'ris), the new elector, had won a decisive victory over the imperial forces, the Pope agreed in 1555 to the Religious Peace of Augsburg. Under its provisions each prince, knight, or town could choose between the two faiths. 

Whenever a prince embraced Lutheranism, he must surrender his possession to the Church, except that land belonging to princes who had become Protestants before 1552 need not be returned. 

9. How Lutheranism Expanded into the Scandinavian 

Countries. The followers of Luther were mainly in central and northern Germany, so it was natural for the movement to spread northward into the Scandinavian countries-Denmark, Norway, and Sweden. In 1397 by the Union of Kälʼmär, Norway and Sweden came under the rule of the Danish king, but by the sixteenth century the latter's grip became so weak that, in 1523, a Swedish noble, Gus-tā vŭs Väså, with the aid of the peasants and mountaineers, obtained the crown of Sweden for himself. During this time students returning from Germany brought to both countries the teachings of Luther. In both these countries the desires of the rulers led to attacks upon the bishops. In Denmark the king was assisted by the lay nobles who received a share of the episcopal property. In 1527 the Swedish Diet expelled the leader of the papal party and arranged for the teaching of Lutheranism. In 1530 Lutheranism became the official church of Denmark and extended to all its possessions. Priests were banished under penalty of death while the Dominicans were expelled from Sweden. In both

countries the state church became a strong weapon in the hands of the king.

CHAPTER XLIII THE REVOLT DEVELOPS IN SWITZERLAND UNDER THE NAME OF CALVINISM 1. The Beginnings of Swiss Independence. In 1291 the men of Schwyz (shvēts), Uri (oo'ré), and Unterwalden (oon'ter-väl-den), the three "forest cantons" or districts surrounding the Lake of Lucerne (lú-sûrn'), formed an alliance against their ruler, the Count of Habsburg. Although they were successful in the struggle that followed, the Habsburgs did not give up their claims to the region for over two hundred years and frequently renewed hostilities. One by one the "forest cantons" were joined by others until their confederation, known as the "Everlasting League," included thirteen German-speaking cantons besides two which spoke French. Their federal government was necessarily weak. To this day two of them retain their democracy, and make and execute their laws through an assembly of all the citizens.

During the long period in which the Swiss were struggling to keep their independence against the Habsburgs, they gained the reputation of being such hard fighters that they were frequently used as mercenaries by other countries. To-day they serve as the papal guard at the Vat'i-can at Rome, where their sixteenth-century uniforms always attract attention. 

2. Zwingli Leads the Reformation Movement in Switzerland. About the time of Luther's attack on the sale of indulgences, a similar attack was made in Switzerland by a parish priest, Ulrich (ool'rik) Zwingli by name. Zwingli had been educated at Vienna and Basel and was a genuine humanist. 

He was also an ardent nationalist, and resented the fact that the Swiss were fighting other people's battles. In 1519 he was 406

THE REVOLT DEVELOPS 

407 called to Zurich (zoo'rik) where he set up a church of his own. 

His ideas were much like those held by Luther, though he insisted that the bread and wine used in the Lord's Supper were only symbolical, while Luther believed in the "Real Presence." 

Although one would have expected the two men to join forces, and friends did make an effort to accomplish this, Luther refused to have anything to do with Zwingli because of this difference of belief.

From Zurich the Zwinglian movement spread rapidly to the other Swiss towns. In the "forest cantons" where mercenary service was an important employment for the surplus population, the older religion held its ground, and the inhabitants undertook to stamp out by force all the heretical teachings. 

This led to much fighting. At first Zwingli and his followers were successful, but in 1531 they were defeated in the decisive battle of Käp'pěl, and Zwingli himself was killed. Shortly afterward peace was made on the basis that each canton might adhere to whichever religion it pleased, and so, like Germany, Switzerland is still partly Catholic and partly Protestant. 

3. John Calvin Builds a New Church Doctrine Upon the Bible. The third great leader of the Protestant revolt was 

John Calvin who was born in 1509 at Noyon (nwȧ-yôn') in France. He settled at Basel where he published in 1536 his 

Institutes of the Christian Religion. This book, which went through many editions and deeply influenced the religious thought of many nations-France, the Netherlands, England, Scotland, Poland, Hungary, and even western Germany-was the ablest attempt of the Protestants to found a new church doctrine entirely upon the Bible. It did for Protestantism what 

St. Thomas Aquinas had done for the older church. Shortly afterward, Calvin chanced to visit Geneva and was induced to remain and assist in stamping out Catholicism. 

Geneva was a French city situated at the western end of Lake Geneva. It was an important trading centre, for it con-

trolled the pass through the Swiss Alps into the valley of the Rhone.

CHAPTER XLIV HOW ENGLAND BECAME A PROTESTANT COUNTRY 1. The Renaissance Gets Under Way in England.. Eng land was in the grip of the Renaissance movement in the early years of the sixteenth century. John Co'lět became famous at 

Oxford as a teacher of the new ideas and as a lecturer on the New Testament, and Sir Thomas More published his famous book, U-to'pi-a, in which he criticised the social, economic, and political ideas of the day, and pictured an ideal state where men lived together as equals and enjoyed full religious freedom. 

Colet and More were only two of a large circle of thinkers with whom Erasmus came into contact in his frequent visits to England. Although they sympathized at first with the 

Lutheran movement, later, like many of the German humanists, they turned against it because of the violence which accompanied it. 

2. How Henry VIII Develops the Balance-of-Power Theory, and Why He Receives the Title "Defender of the 

Faith." When Henry VIII came to the throne of England in 

1509, he inherited almost absolute power. He was proud and somewhat arrogant, and was determined to make himself felt in Europe.

In continental politics Henry was disposed to support Charles V of Spain so as to embarrass his traditional enemy, Francis I, yet he was clear-headed enough to agree with his minister, Cardinal Wolsey (wool'zi), that England's interests lay in maintaining a balance of power between the countries on the continent.

When Henry first heard of Luther and of Luther's attack on the Church, he was greatly incensed and published a pamphlet defending the sacraments and papal supremacy. As a reward 4II

for this, the Pope conferred on him the title of "Defender of the Faith," which is still used by English kings. A few years later Henry changed his ideas of the Pope, but he never revised his opinion of Luther. 

3. Henry's Wish for a Divorce Leads to a Break with 

Rome. Henry had married Catherine, the daughter of Ferdinand and Isabella, after she had become a widow by the death of Henry's elder brother Arthur. This marriage, which was contrary to church law, had been made possible by a papal dispensation. All the children of the marriage except a sickly daughter Mary died in infancy, and Henry became worried about the succession, since it was considered improper for a woman to succeed to the rule. To make matters worse, he fell in love with Anne Boleyn (bool'in), maid of honor to Catherine, and at once he began to have doubts about the validity of his marriage with Catherine.

When Cardinal Wolsey asked the Pope to annul the dispensation by which Henry had been allowed to marry Catherine, the Pope sent a legate to England to deal with the matter. The case was removed to Rome, and Henry felt humiliated. He became so angry that he removed Cardinal Wolsey from the lord chancellorship, and determined to separate the church in England from all papal control. To this end, in 1531, he called together the leading church dignitaries and declared himself head of the Church of England. By forcing them to surrender their right to legislate without his consent, he placed control of religion in the hands of Parliament. The latter hastened to complete the break with Rome by forbidding the English clergy to send any further tithes to the Pope or to appeal to him any of their legal questions. The way was now open for Crăn'mer, whom he made Archbishop of Canterbury, the ranking prelate of the Church, to issue the desired divorce. 

4. Henry VIII Is Made Head of the Church in England as Drastic Changes Are Made. The Pope now pro-

413 nounced a bull of excommunication against Henry. Parliament retaliated by passing the Act of Supremacy, which made the king the head of the Church in England. Because Sir Thomas 

More, the new lord chancellor, had conscientious scruples against supporting these high-handed measures, he was put to death. 

Although Henry treated the reformers in the same brutal way

The Bible was translated into English, and laws were passed against indulgences and pilgrimages. The vast wealth of the monasteries had excited Henry's cupidity, and consequently a special investigation was made, resulting in a report which greatly exaggerated the evils of monastic life. On the strength of this report, the smaller houses were suppressed, and within a few more years even the larger ones. Most of their property

passed into the hands of the king and of his courtiers, but a small part was set aside for schools. 

5. The Revolution Follows Under Edward VI and the 

Act of Uniformity Is Passed. Before Henry died, he arranged for the crown to pass to his children in the following order: first to Edward, then to Mary, and finally to Elizabeth. 

As Edward was only nine years of age, Henry appointed a council of regency to rule the kingdom until he was old enough to assume the crown. However, this council soon turned over its powers to the Earl of Somerset, who was a believer in Protestantism. Under Somerset's influence English took the place of Latin in the church services, the images were removed from the churches, and the clergy were allowed to marry. At this time the first Book of Common Prayer was issued. 

Somerset's regency came to an end in 1549 with a revolution. 

This was caused by the economic distress which had been brought on the land as a result of some of the innovations. 

Somerset's successor, Warwick (wor'ik), Duke of Northumberland, permitted the Protestant fanatics to carry on a campaign of destroying material evidences of the old faith, such as the altars, statues, and stained-glass windows. Members of the Roman Church were vigorously persecuted. A new Book of Common Prayer, more Protestant in character than the earlier one, was issued, and the doctrines of the church were formulated in forty-two articles. Parliament passed an Act of 

Uniformity which compelled all Englishmen to accept the new faith. 

6. During the Catholic Restoration Under Mary the 

Protestants Are Severely Persecuted. After the death of 

Edward, an attempt to set aside the will of Henry VIII failed and the Catholic Mary came to the throne. She restored the 

Church to the position which it had held before 1529, but she could not return its confiscated property. In 1554 Mary married Philip II of Spain, who spent barely a year in England.

ENGLAND A PROTESTANT COUNTRY 

415 After reviving the laws against heresy and forcing Parliament to confess to the papal legates, she started a persecution which led to her being called "Bloody Mary." Less than three hundred persons, mainly of the lower classes, were put to death, but among them were Archbishop Latimer and Bishop Ridley. 

As the fire was being lighted, Archbishop Latimer turned to Bishop Ridley and with prophetic vision said, “Master Ridley, play the man. We shall this day light such a candle in England that it shall never be put out." And so it happened. 

Before Mary's death, England lost Calais, its last foothold on the continent. This, and the poor harvests and a terrible plague at home so completely turned popular opinion against Mary that Elizabeth succeeded to the crown without opposition. 

7. Under Elizabeth the Church of England Becomes a 

National Institution. The accession of Elizabeth made England a Protestant country once more, for in the eyes of the old Church the daughter of Anne Boleyn was illegitimate. The new queen was not deeply religious, but she was a stanch follower of the learning of the Renaissance. She had studied Latin and 

Greek, and she knew something of the literature of the continent. She was a woman of strong intellect, broad vision, impetuous will, and intense patriotism. 

When she called together her first Parliament, she steered a middle course. At her command, it passed a new Act of 

Supremacy making England independent of Rome, and it passed a new Act of Uniformity, which once more required the second Book of Common Prayer. But she was so clever in the pursuit of her middle-of-the-road policy that the Pope did not excommunicate her until 1570. Throughout her reign, her interest in the Church was political rather than religious. Her one ambition was to see England mighty and prosperous and she knew a closely united people was essential in order to bring this about. Thus under her guidance the Anglican Church became a national institution and assumed a position between the

CHAPTER XLV HOW REFORMATION TOOK PLACE WITHIN THE CHURCH 1. The Beginning of the Catholic Reformation under 

Clement VII. During the sixteenth century there had been much talk of a reformation of the Church, but the movement was begun by Ferdinand and Isabella. Under their leadership some of the more important abuses were done away with, and the Inquisition was revived to settle questions of doctrine and church discipline. While the movement proceeded slowly at first because the popes were still renaissance princes rather than spiritual leaders, eventually fear lest other lands would be lost to the Church led to the elevation of men of fervent piety to the papacy. Foremost among these was Clement VII who in 

1524 organized a new order-the The'a-tines to improve the character of the priesthood. Another order-the Căp'ûchins-was organized to work among the common people. Due largely to the influence of these two orders Italy remained faithful to the papacy, but in the end they were completely eclipsed by another order which had its origin in Spain. 

2. Ignatius Loyola Founds the Society of Jesus. In 

1521, Ignatius (ig-na'shus) Lo-yoʻlä, a Spanish cavalier, was wounded at the battle of Päm-pē-lū'nä. While he was in the hospital, he read lives of Christ and of some of the saints, and vowed that if he got well he would devote the remainder of his days to Christian work. At first Loyola started to convert the infidels and travelled as far as Jerusalem. After several years of fruitless effort he decided that he must obtain a theological education if he was to accomplish anything. He went to Paris to study and was joined there by a group of young men with a similar desire. In 1540 Loyola got permission from the Pope to found the Society of Jesus. This little group became the nucleus of the new order. 419

Loyola organized his order on a military basis. The territories of the Church were divided into "provinces." Over each there was a "provincial" or governor, while over all there was a "general" with absolute authority. On entering the order, each novice was compelled to submit to strict military discipline, Alippo & Sons Intrega 

A JESUIT MISSION 

From an early drawing, in Concepcion Beaumont. and by the study of Loyola's book, Spiritual Exercise, to make a surrender of his individual will. After a novitiate of two years, one became a "scholastic" and was sent to college to prepare for teaching. Specially qualified scholastics were trained for the priesthood and became "spiritual coadjutors" (kō-a-jooters), less able scholastics not fitted for teaching became "temporal coadjutors." The Jesuits (jěz'ú-ĭts), as the members of the order were called, took the triple monastic vow, and also a fourth vow of obedience to the Pope. 

3. The Jesuits Do a Wonderful Work as Educators, 

Missionaries, and Explorers.

Loyola's interest in education

REFORMATION WITHIN THE CHURCH 

421 gave him one of the most effective means of service, and consequently education became one of the chief aims of the Jesuits, whose schools were for a long time the most perfect institutions of learning in the world. They were frequently attended by Protestants, and thus did much to weaken the hold of 

THE COUNCIL OF TRENT 

This interesting drawing, now in the Louvre, of the council in session, was made by the 

Venetian artist, Titian, who happened to be present.

Protestantism in some parts of Europe. The Jesuits paid strict attention to morals and manners, and sought to lead rather than to drive. This latter aim they accomplished by cultivating a spirit of comradeship and by the liberal use of prizes and honors.

Missionary work had been the first aim of Loyola, naturally it became the first activity of his order. Jesuit missionaries were among the first to carry the teachings of Christ into the newly discovered lands beyond the sea, and they sought boldly to win back to the faith the seceding Protestants. Francis

Xavier (zăv'i-er), one of Loyola's original companions, set out

for the Portuguese colonies in India to Christianize the oriental peoples. Other Jesuits gave their lives to converting the 

Indians of both Americas and to teaching them the ways of civilized life. In South America, they intervened between the natives and their Spanish conquerors, and in Paraguay they even organized a native state. To the official reports of these missionaries we owe our first accurate knowledge of the Great Lakes and of the upper Mississippi Valley. 

4. The Council of Trent Introduces Reforms but Reaf firms the Dogmas of the Thirteenth Century. From the posting of Luther's theses many Catholics, and Christians outside the faith, kept demanding that a church council be called to settle the questions raised by the revolt. After much delay, such a council met at Trent in 1542. It had been expected that some of the Protestants would attend. This proved to be a vain hope, for not only did they stay away, but at times not even all the Catholic countries were represented. The problems before this council were so many and so perplexing that it continued in session for twenty-one years. 

The council was faced with two major tasks, the introduction of reforms and the formulation of a church doctrine. In both tasks the influence of Protestantism caused the reforms to be more far-reaching and the doctrines to be more uncompromising. All priests were required to spend years in preparation for their holy offices. They were forbidden to hold more than one office at a time or to be absent from their assigned fields and their sermons must be in the language of the common people. Indulgences were not to be sold nor money charged for the sacraments. The dogmas of the thirteenth century were reaffirmed and the supremacy of the pope was established beyond question.

The Council of Trent revived the Inquisition to deal with heretics, and drew up a list of books which a good Catholic was not permitted to read. This list, known as the Index of

REFORMATION WITHIN THE CHURCH 

423 Prohibited Books, still exists and is added to from time to time as occasion demands. For some reasons it was unfortunate that the decrees and canons of the Council should have been drafted at that time, for they did much to widen the breach between Catholics and Protestants, and to crystallize the doctrines of the older church at one of its most uncompromising stages. 

5. How the Revolt and Reformation Affected Society. As a result of these fifty years of religious upheaval, western Europe was split among four bitterly hostile Christian faiths-the Roman Catholics, the 

Lutherans, the Calvinists, and the 

Anglicans. Each was supplied with a set of beliefs and with machinery ready to punish any deviation from those beliefs. 

In the Protestant lands the wealth of the older church had passed 

TORTURE HELMET AND DOG COLLAR 

These articles of Spanish workmanship now in the Metropolitan Museum, New York, belong to this period. The helmet was painted to represent the devil who possessed the heretic. into the hands of the kings and princes, and had increased their power. The medieval connections between church and state had been revived. Now the civil authority was in control, and used the power of religion to keep its hold on a subject people who were already showing signs of discontent. 

There had been a great improvement in morality of the people although the theological disputes had caused much bit-

terness and extreme intolerance. The renaissance movement had been quite definitely checked. This was shown by the revival of the medieval belief in witchcraft. 

The king and the influence of Calvinism had done much to improve the conditions of the middle class, but the peasantry and serfs had gained little except a change of masters. In 

England, poverty assumed a new role when those who had formerly received charity from the Church were compelled to wear a badge on their hats and cloaks to show that they received doles of nineteen pence a week from the royal purse.

Indeed, it may be said that the Protestant revolt and the Catholic reformation bequeathed to the next century almost as much trouble as social betterment.

CHAPTER XLVI WITHIN A CENTURY SPAIN RISES TO WORLD POWER AND THEN RAPIDLY DECLINES 

We read in Chapter XLI how the accidental discovery of the New World by Columbus sailing under the banner of Spain caused all Europe to face westward. This directing of European civilization across the Atlantic to America was destined to be Spain's great contribution to the modern world. In this chapter we shall see how Spain became exhausted in her efforts. to rule Europe and why the defeat of the Spanish Armada in 1588 caused her star of Empire rapidly to set, and she dwindled into a second-rate power. 1. Charles V Abdicates His Several Crowns and the 

Empire Is Divided. In 1555 Charles had been compelled to give sanction to the Religious Peace of Augsburg. The following year, broken in spirit by the disastrous ending of his war with the Protestant princes of Germany, and by his failure to recapture Metz from the French, Charles abdicated his several crowns and retired to a monastery. To his son Philip II he gave Spain with her wide-flung dependencies, the Netherlands, and the Franche Comte (fränsh kôn-tä'). His brother Ferdinand, to whom he had already turned over his Austrian possessions, now became Emperor.

3. Spain at the Zenith of Her Power. In the sixteenth and early part of the seventeenth centuries Spain was the greatest and most powerful state in Europe. On account of the great wealth which Charles V had wrested from America, he had been saved for a time from bankruptcy, and his successors were able to organize an efficient government and to develop superb armies. Great fleets had been built to carry the rapidly

expanding Spanish commerce and to protect it from the pirates.

The universities increased in size and importance, and many writers dealt with the new geographical and scientific knowledge which the discoveries were revealing. Philip himself gave much attention to internal improvements. 

4. The Problems That Confronted Philip II. Under

Philip's two immediate predecessors the government of Spain had become centralized in the king and nobles. The local authorities had lost most of their authority. Philip built for him-

SPAIN RISES TO WORLD POWER 

429 self a new palace, El Es-co'ri-ăl, in the suburbs of Madrid, and from that as a centre undertook to oversee every side of the administration of his vast empire. The details were so many that he was soon obliged to call on others for aid, and even then he was hardly able to keep up with the work. 

As the champion of Catholicism, he had troubles with England and France, and also undertook to crush the heresy of his own subjects in the Netherlands. Moreover, he was frequently at war with the Muslims. In addition to all this, he found it increasingly difficult to protect his treasure fleets from the Dutch and English freebooters, while at home he faced an uprising of the Mō-ris'cōs-Moors who had been forcibly converted to Christianity. 

5. Philip's War with England Ends in Disaster. After the death of his English wife, Queen Mary, and the Protestant restoration under Elizabeth, Philip still hoped to bring England back into the Catholic Church. With this in mind he encouraged Mary, Queen of Scots, to aspire to become Queen of England. Even after she was imprisoned by Elizabeth, he participated in a number of plots to set her free. Elizabeth retaliated by giving support to his rebellious Dutch subjects, and by allowing such freebooters as Sir Francis Drake and Sir John Norreys to ravage the Spanish colonies and to attack his treasure ships. Finally, when she allowed Mary to be put to death, Philip decided to undertake the conquest of England.

First he got together a fleet of about one hundred thirty war-ships, the best in all Spain. So sure were the Spaniards of victory that they boastingly named the fleet the Invincible Är-ma'da. The plan was to sail up the English Channel and ferry the Spanish commander in the Netherlands across with his veteran troops, so that after the English navy had been annihilated, these soldiers would follow up the victory on land. 

But things went awry. When the Armada sailed into the Chan-

nel, it was not able to cope with the smaller and more easily managed English ships, manned chiefly by buccaneers and fishermen. Consequently, it was badly handled even before reaching the Netherlands. Then, when it sailed again with the army on board, it was struck by a terrific storm and many of the ships were wrecked north of Scotland and on the west coast of Ireland. 

6. Reasons for Spain's Decline. Spanish prestige was shattered by the defeat of the Armada, and still further by the successful revolt of the northern Netherlands, of which we shall hear more in the next chapter. Although it enjoyed a temporary revival from a favorable treaty with France in 1598, by which both countries agreed to a common suppression of Protestantism, certain internal factors slowly brought about the decay of Spain's power. The attempt to control the world had cost the Spanish rulers most of the wealth they had gained from their colonies, and the wars had taken a tremendous toll of the nation's man-power.

But the real trouble with Spain was her internal economic condition. Spaniards have often been more interested in fighting than in trading. The expulsion of the Jews and Moors at the beginning of the fifteenth century had deprived the country of the one important commercial part of its population. Meanwhile the Turkish côr'sairs in the Mediterranean were bringing ruin to the merchants of Catalonia, the one section of Christian Spain interested in commerce. And to complete the story, the destruction of the Moriscos by Philip II, and his limiting the trade with the Indies threw further obstacles in the way of commercial development. 

Spanish agriculture suffered likewise through the Města. 

This was a great organization of sheep-owners who pastured their flocks in one part of Spain during the summer, and in another part during the winter. In driving the flocks back and forth they damaged the crops along the road, but the Mesta

SPAIN RISES TO WORLD POWER 

431 was so powerful that the farmers were unable to secure any redress.

CHAPTER XLVII THE NETHERLANDS REVOLT AND THE DUTCH REPUBLIC ARISES 

The Netherlands or the "Low Countries" just grew. They consisted of seventeen provinces which from time to time the dukes of Burgundy and their successors had joined together. 

The people of the Netherlands spoke two different languagesin the northern provinces, a German dialect; and in the southern, a tongue closely related to French. In the south there had developed during the Middle Ages many manufacturing towns, foremost among them being Antwerp, which had been one of the great trading centres of northern Europe. In the north towns were fewer, and agriculture and fishing were the principal industries; in fact, even then the inhabitants of that region, to secure more land for farming, had begun to reclaim great tracts from the North Sea by means of dikes, just as is being done to-day.

We have already mentioned the spread of the new learning to the Netherlands in connection with their renowned scholar, Erasmus. When Luther and Calvin started their revolt from 

Rome, the Netherlands showed interest in the movement. Inasmuch as their sovereign lord, the Emperor Charles V, had been born and brought up among them, he understood his Dutch subjects so well that he did not resort to measures to stamp out their heretical notions. Consequently there was never any serious trouble in the Netherlands. Philip II, however, was a Spaniard, and neither understood the people of the Netherlands, nor did they understand him, and as soon as he came into power he set the land aflame by undertaking to enforce Catholicism. 

1. When Philip Attempts to Stamp Out Protestantism the Netherlands Revolt. Philip visited the Netherlands in 

1559 and on his departure from the country left secret in- 433

structions that every vestige of Protestantism should be wiped out. Many of the more moderate Catholics did not sympathize with the harsh measures, and there arose in every direction a bitter opposition to Spanish rule. When a delegation of Netherlanders presented to Margaret of Pär mä, the regent, a plea for moderation, one of her courtiers derisively called them "Beggars." This term was immediately adopted by the Dutch, who began wearing little wallets and other insignia of beggars. 

Margaret resigned and Philip sent the Duke of Äl'vä with an army of Spanish soldiers to carry out his decrees. 

Alva's one purpose was to break the will of the Netherlanders. The ruthless way in which he proposed to do this may be seen from the message that he sent Philip during one of his sieges: "If I take Alkmaar (älk'mär), I am resolved not to leave a single creature alive; the knife shall be put to every throat." Such a reign of terror did he begin―he boasted of having put to death over eighteen thousand persons-that he drove the Netherlanders into open revolt. 

2. William of Orange Becomes the Great Leader Against

Spain. At first the Netherlanders lacked organization. But when Alva began such extreme cruelty, a number of the towns in the northern provinces formed a league. They voted a sum of money to William, Prince of Orange, commonly known as "William the Silent," to induce him to take command of their little army. William was able to make small headway against the well-trained Spanish soldiers, but he played havoc with Spain's commerce by issuing "letters of marque" to Dutch seamen.

The war was carried on with barbarous cruelty on both sides. Many towns were captured and sacked. Leyden (li'den) was saved only when the patriotic Dutchmen cut the dikes and flooded the fields where the enemy was camped. The capture of 

Brielle (brē-ěl'), in 1572, by Dutch privateers marked a turning point in the revolution, and a large part of the northern

THE NETHERLANDS REVOLT 

435 provinces soon passed into the hands of the rebels. At this time Prince William was elected Stad'holder of Holland, Zedland, Friesland (frēz'lănd), and Utrecht (u'trěkt), and Protector of the Netherlands during the king's absence. Even yet the Netherlanders looked upon themselves as loyal subjects. 

THE SURRENDER OF BREDA

3. The Dutch Win Their Independence. The next year 

Alva was recalled. Thanks to the more moderate policy of his successors, the southern provinces in which Protestantism had never taken much root were won back to the crown, but reconciliation with the North became increasingly difficult. At last, the Dutch-speaking Netherlanders declared themselves independent under the name of the United Provinces, but the struggle was by no means won. By this time, however, William had learned the need of trained armies, and the Dutch fleets were systematically hindering communication between Spain and the

Netherlands. At this critical moment William was assassinated by a religious fanatic.

With the loss of prestige which Spain suffered from the destruction of her Invincible Armada came a corresponding rise in the fortunes of the Dutch. Although by 1593 the seven

4. The Rise of the Dutch Colonial Empire. Ever since the Portuguese had established their colonial empire in the East, the Dutch had served as the exclusive distributors of their spices and other rich products in northern Europe. One of the immediate results of Philip's conquest of Portugal was to deprive them of this monopoly by excluding their shipping from the port of Lisbon. The doughty Dutchmen had no alternative except to enter the Eastern trade. By 1602 sixty ships were plying regularly between the Dutch ports and the East Indies, combining trading with preying on the Spanish and Portuguese shipping. In fact, the foundation of their great colonial empire dates from the chartering of the Dutch East India Company that same year.

The Dutch planted substantial colonies along the southern

coast of Africa and on the island of Mauritius (mo-rish ĭ-us), and by the end of the seventeenth century they seized from the Portuguese nearly all their posts in India except Goa, and intrenched themselves in Ceylon, Java, Sumatra, Celebes (sěl'ébēz), and the Mó-luk'kȧs or "Spice Islands," and Borneo. In 

1609 one of their explorers searching for a new route to the Indies sailed up the Hudson River, with the result that they founded twelve years later the colony of New Netherlands. 

During this time one of the Dutch admirals sailed up the English Channel with a broom at his masthead to indicate that he had made a clean sweep of the English fleet.
