CHAPTER XLVIII THE OTTOMAN AND MOGUL EMPIRES FLOURISH IN THE EAST 

We read about the great empires of Chingiz Khan and Tamerlane and about the Ottoman Turks and how they took Constantinople from the Christians. In this chapter we shall read about the Ottoman Empire at its height. How the Turks acquired the Caliphate under Selim the Grim and extended their power along the north African coast as far as Morocco and to the walls of Vienna. We shall also read about the rise of another great Mogul Empire which was consolidated in India under Akbar the Great who set up an organization. This organization lasted until England took part in affairs in India about the middle of the eighteenth century. 

1. How the Ottoman Empire Was Organized. When 

Muhammad II occupied Constantinople, he reorganized the whole Turkish governmental machine, although he was careful to retain the fief system which had been the basis of the Ottoman state from its earliest days. The empire was divided into districts over which were placed governors called på-shäs', distinguished in rank by the use of one, two, or three horse-tails.

A fleet was built and placed under the command of the governor of the Ægean Islands. All the administrative machinery of the empire was in the hands of slaves. Because these men were carefully trained, Turkey was during the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries the most efficiently governed state in Europe. When engaged in war, the sultan frequently used feudal levies, yet he relied for his military strength on a standing army of welltrained "slaves of the palace" together with the Janissaries, who also were really slaves.

4. The Conquests of Suleiman the Magnificent. After the fall of the states founded by the Crusaders, the Hospitalers, or the Knights of St. John, as they were more often called, withdrew to Cyprus, and settled on the island of Rhodes. From this island stronghold they waged constant war against the rising power of the Ottomans and seriously interfered with its advance upon the sea. Although the Turks made various expeditions against them, it remained for Suleiman (sōō-lá-män') the Magnificent to bring about the capture of Rhodes after one

OTTOMAN AND MOGUL EMPIRES 

443 of the great sieges of history. The Knights were allowed to retire to Malta (môl'tȧ) and Suleiman became master of the eastern Mediterranean.

With the fall of Rhodes, the corsairs, as the Turkish privateers were called, spread over the Mediterranean, and although nominally under the control of the government, often they were little better than pirates. Not only did they prey upon commerce, but they descended upon the hamlets along the shore, and plundered and carried away the inhabitants into slavery. 

Even to-day the southern coast of Europe is dotted with little towers which were erected to give warning of their approach.

Eventually they conquered all of northern Africa except Móroc'co, and made Trip'ó-li, Tu'nis, and Algiers (ǎl-jērz') the centres from which they carried on their raiding. This region, which became practically independent of the Ottoman government, was known as the Bär bär-y Coast, until well into the nineteenth century. In 1526 Suleiman started up the valley of the Danube with a great expedition, and on the battlefield of Mohács (mo'häch) so completely destroyed the Hungarian army that its king was never seen again. Practically all of 

Hungary passed under Turkish control, and three years later the Ottomans encamped before the walls of Vienna. Such was the consternation of Christendom that there was added to the 

Litany the phrase, "From the Turk, the comet, and the devil, good Lord deliver us," the comet being the one known as

Halley's, which is visible every seventy-five years. After a long siege Suleiman was compelled to withdraw, and never again did they make such a great advance. 

5. Why the Ottoman Empire Declined. After the death of Suleiman in 1566, the power of the Ottomans declined. We have already seen how their prestige on the sea was broken in 1571 by the disastrous battle of Lepanto. Although the Ottomans rebuilt their fleet, they were no longer looked upon as invincible; even so, the real cause of their decline was some-

thing far more fundamental. Not only did the later sultans not lead their armies in person, but they often did not even take any active part in the administration of the empire. 

With the halting of the conquests of the Ottomans, came a falling off in the income of the state and a lowering of the efficiency of the government. Moreover, their lack of interest in trade and commerce kept from them much of the world's store of knowledge and prevented them from developing along the same lines as the peoples of western Europe. But no matter how low they sank they still retained their arrogance and looked with haughty contempt upon the Christian world. 

6. The Capitulations Are Granted to All Christian 

Powers. When western Europeans in the sixteenth century began to take up their residence in Constantinople, the Ottomans often made life miserable for them. Finally, in 1535, the 

French made a treaty with Suleiman the Magnificent, granting to the traders who resided within the Turkish domains certain extra-territorial privileges, somewhat like those which the Iian merchants had enjoyed in the days of the Byzantine Empire. 

They were freed from subjection to Turkish law, and were allowed to set up courts for the settlement of their difficulties. 

They could not even be arrested by a Turkish policeman except in the presence of their own consul or his representative. These privileges were known as the Ca-pit-u-la'tions. Eventually they were extended to other Christian powers, and remained in force until 1914. 

7. A New Mogul Empire Extends into India. During the Middle Ages India had come under the rule of Muslim dynasties, some of which had been able to control the greater part of the peninsula. In the main, however, they were limited to small areas and fought constantly among themselves; in fact, they offered little resistance to the raid of Tamerlane in 1398, when he plundered Delhi (děl'é) with many other cities.

CHAPTER XLIX HOW THE BACKGROUNDS OF MODERN ECONOMIC LIFE WERE 

LAID

At the basis of medieval business stood the idea of a just price, derived mainly from the cost of production, instead of the modern idea which rests on profit. Next in importance was the lack of money, caused by the draining of gold to the East, the hoarding of it by rulers, and its use in church utensils. 

Credit, without which modern business could not last a day, was practically unknown. Capital for use in carrying on trade was also almost entirely unknown except in the case of a few great families. Even these had no conception of its possibilities, for the great loans of the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries were made to kings and princes for unproductive enterprises. The reason for these conditions lay in the fact that trade and industry were largely of local character. Not only was the area in which trade could be carried on greatly limited, but was controlled by the town and all outsiders were looked upon as interlopers to be excluded. This chapter will indicate how modern business methods came into practice. 

1. The Influences Which Changed the Economic Life. 

The change in the economic life of Europe began with the medieval fairs. There merchants stood on the same footing regardless of whence they had come, and the restrictions hindering the free exchange of goods in the towns were wholly absent. In the second place, the rise of royal power and the development of national states brought the regulation of trade into the hands of the kings, thus permitting easier movement from place to place. So rapid were the developments in navigation that long sea voyages with all the risks were less expensive and vexatious than much shorter voyages by land. And finally, in the fifteenth century the development of mining in Europe began to add to the supply of gold and silver. This was tremendously increased by the output of the Mexican and Peruvian mines. All these factors broke down the older traditions of industry and trade, and furnished the means for the establishment of a new economic life. 

2. What It meant to Antwerp to Do Away with Medieval Restrictions. Flanders had been during the Middle Ages a great manufacturing centre and the city of Bruges had become an important. meeting point for the merchants of the 

Italian cities and the merchants of the Hanseatic League. Early in the fifteenth century Bruges' harbor silted up and Antwerp took its place. To secure an advantage over the other Flemish towns, the merchants of Antwerp removed the restrictions on foreigners doing business there and bought off the people who charged tolls on the river Scheldt (skĕlt), making Antwerp a free port. By the opening of the sixteenth century it had become the most important commercial city in Europe. Consequently when the Portuguese began bringing Indian goods to Lisbon, Antwerp became the centre for their distribution throughout northern Europe. In this way the centre of trade passed from the Mediterranean to the Atlantic seaboard. 

3. The Use of Capital in Large-Scale Trading Opera tions Begins. The fourteenth and fifteenth centuries saw the growth of a number of large fortunes, of which the most famous was that of the Fuggers. This family began at Augsburg as weavers and later entered the cloth trade, but their real success came with the exploitation of silver and copper mines.

BACKGROUNDS OF MODERN LIFE 

451 Being real financiers, they used their fortunes in trading operations. They also loaned money to rulers, especially to the Habsburgs, and took in payment mines and other kinds of concessions. Their profits sometimes amounted to fifty per cent a year and at one time they possessed as much as forty million.

4. Why the Domestic System of Industry Developed. 

When trade went beyond the borders of the town and capital began to develop, the medieval guild system began to change. 

The master guildsmen hired more journeymen and enlarged their workshops while they themselves ceased to work at the trade and spent their time in supervision, or went into buying and selling exclusively. At the same time guilds were strong enough to limit the number of their members, so there arose a large group of journeymen forced to set up independent shops. This meant that they had to leave the towns and establish themselves in the country, where they began to manufacture goods to sell to merchants. 

In the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, in order to protect

their rights, these independent manufacturers formed organizations of their own. Although these organizations were shortlived, the movement led to the creation of a new form of industry, known as the domestic system. Under this system much of the manufacturing was hired out by the independent manu- TTTT

As a result of the increasing demands of the merchants and traders, these independent manufacturers became important. 

5. Far-Sighted Kings Encouraged Business and Indus try. As the power of the kings increased, they turned to the merchants for financial aid. In France the resources which the taille furnished to the kings were in part devoted to the building of roads and canals, and to stimulating agriculture. In Spain the Habsburgs, although they received vast quantities of gold

Although the crown in England was not wealthy, it saw the advantages from attracting foreign artisans and capital to develop the nation's resources. Consequently during the period of the religious wars much capital and many workmen from the

6. Why the Mercantile System Was Developed and

How It Worked. Out of this royal interest in the development of trade and industry arose the theory that the prosperity of the state depended upon the amount of gold and silver the nation possessed. This was known as the Mercantile System. 

According to this system, trade was to be regulated so that raw

materials alone should be imported and only manufactured articles exported. In this way the "balance of trade" would always be in favor of the country. To carry this out, royal regu- 

GROCERS' HALL, BREMEN 

An example of the ornate, or baroque, architecture of the Renaissance. lations of all kinds were adopted and monopolies in trade and manufactures were established. In the sixteenth century when England's overseas trade developed, the trading companies were granted charters giving them a monopoly of the trade with certain countries.

The Lé-vant or Turkey Company traded with the eastern Mediterranean, the

Müsci-vy Company with Russia, the East India Company with southern Asia, the Guinea Company with Africa, and a number of companies with different parts of 

North America. The Dutch and French also formed East

India and other companies. 

All of these were known as regulated companies, because they operated under royal charters which specified their rights. 

7. With the Joint Stock Companies and Exchanges Modern Business Methods Were Well Under Way. Me dieval systems of family control, or partnerships, were hardly adequate for the great risks and problems of the new trade beyond the seas. To meet the new conditions, there was formed a new kind of organization, the joint stock company, in which

a considerable number of persons contributed the capital and shared the profits and losses in proportion to their contributions. From this has come our modern idea of corporations. 

To take care of the greater mass of wares and the increased volume of trade, exchanges were established where goods could be bought and sold in great quantities. At first the goods were actually there, but gradually only samples were brought, and this led to a system of grading and the establishment of general standards, both of quality and weight. With these developments modern business can be said to have begun.

CHAPTER L 

THE SIGNIFICANCE OF THE READJUSTMENT PERIOD 1. Evidences of the Passing of the Medieval World. 

During the period which we have been studying, the medieval world lost many of its distinguishing characteristics. The growing power of the kings ruined the medieval empire, and broke the control of the universal church. The invention of gunpowder undermined feudalism, already greatly weakened as a result of its struggle with the rising tide of monarchy. The invention of printing with movable type gave wings to ideas and opened to the common people the knowledge that had been restricted to a few. The development of the ǎs'tró-labe and compass led men across the seas to a new hemisphere and around the southern extremity of the old. The increase of capital revived the economic theories of the ancient world and opened a new phase in the human effort to amass wealth. The rediscovery of the Græco-Roman world focussed man's attention on this life instead of on the world to come. Each of these forces helped to lay the foundations of a new type of society which was eventually to make Europe the dominant power in the world. 

2. Some Medieval Ideas Which Survived. In spite of these new inventions and ideas the medieval structure of society held on tenaciously. Even though the great Protestant leaders broke away from the ritualism and formalism of the Church, their eyes were as firmly fixed on heaven as were those of the medieval saints. Far from freeing men to worship God as they pleased they called in the state to assist the Church, and in the end the Church became the handmaid of the state. The divine right of kings was reinforced, but without the check which the medieval Church had offered. 456

THE READJUSTMENT PERIOD 

457 Although feudalism fell, its titles, its privileges, and its code of chivalry remained, even though its ideals were ridiculed in the deeds of the immortal "Don Quixote." The labor service of the manorial system retreated with the rise of trade and the expansion of markets, and the serf became economically free although still bound by the restrictions upon the free use

Although the spirit was fired by the Renaissance, the Protestant revolt buried it again under a load of dogma and superstition, which found an expression in the spread of the witchcraft delusion. 

3. The Passing of the East in Power and Influence. In each of the periods which we have already studied there has been present more than one great centre from which power and influence radiated. That distinction began to disappear and western Europe became more and more the single centre; in fact, from the close of the sixteenth century until the beginning of the twentieth it dominated and moulded the course of history. Only in the Ottoman and Mogul empires were to be found the last flickers of the Oriental world. When they de-

clined before the advancing power of Europe, the modern period of history may be said to have begun, for China and India had alike failed to be caught in the stream which arose from the Renaissance and were destined to become the prey of the more aggressive West. 

4. Forces Which Led to the Disruption of Christendom and Medieval Unity. During this period two powerful forces operated to break up the Christian world-the ambition of the kings, who constantly strove to add to their powers, and the rise of new religious sects, which created a chasm between the followers of the prophet of Nazareth. Both forces contributed to a third-the rise of national feeling which was destined to become such a powerful influence in society. Not less significant in breaking up the unity of the medieval world was the overthrow of Latin by the vernacular languages. Both church and state aided in the development of the separate tongues, and the new national literatures combined with translations of the Bible gave the necessary force and stability to the innovations. 

5. The Development of Individuality and the Foundations of Democracy. To the Italian Renaissance we owe the rediscovery of individualism. This new-born confidence in one's self was responsible for the splendid achievements in art and the new theory of politics, and for the braving of the horrors of land and sea to discover new lands and new stores of wealth. 

Medieval traditions and mysterious terrors fell before the courage of men who believed in themselves and who believed that they could do things. Although the increased weight of dogma and creed brought about by the Protestant Revolt stilled and hampered individuality, the seed was planted which was to bear fruit of inestimable value to civilization. 

6. New Arts of Living Are Practised. The natural out come of the new interest in this world and the rediscovery of the individual was a new zest in life itself. While the Italian burghers and princes surrounded themselves with all sorts of

THE READJUSTMENT PERIOD 

459 luxuries in the form of magnificent palaces and beautiful gardens, the Italian courts evolved a new code of gentlemanly conduct, artificial it is true, but tending to do away with the rudeness and boorishness of the Middle Ages. The decline of feudalism also saw tournaments with their dangerous consequences give way to less bloody diversions. And finally, when one

THE PERIOD OF EARLY MODERN CIVILIZATION Chapters LI-LIX The Foreword 

When Europe began to settle down after the Protestant revolt, it was ready to undertake the building of a civilization in which religion could share but not dominate. The reaction against theological control opened the doors to scientific investigation and by so doing prepared the way for the "Age of Reason." The invention of instruments of precision placed in the hands of those who were devoting their lives to the investigation of the secrets of nature tools for laying the foundation of modern science. The effects of this new science were not restricted to the study of nature, for soon they were felt also in the relationships of human society. Europe, with her religious differences quiet for a time, turned with renewed interest to the lands beyond the seas, whose products were becoming important. With a swiftness which tried to make up for the inertia of the past, she forged ahead into the position of world leadership. Then the march of modern civilization can be said to have begun. 462

CHAPTER LI THE THIRTY YEARS' WAR DISCREDITS RELIGIOUS DIFFERENCES AS A CAUSE FOR STRIFE 

The Peace of Augsburg brought about a stopping of the war in Germany between the Protestant and Catholics. It did not really solve the religious question. The surrender of church property was required whenever a Catholic bishop went over to Lutheranism, but since no machinery was set up to enforce this provision, it soon became a dead letter. Besides, Lutheranism was the only form of Protestantism recognized by the treaty, when as a matter of fact there were many Calvinists in 

Germany. Fortunately for the cause of peace, Charles V was followed by two rather moderate emperors, who refused to become excited by the rapid expansion of Protestantism in central and northern Germany.

The situation changed, however, with the accession of Rudolph II to the imperial throne in 1575. Rudolph was an ardent Catholic and desired as far as possible to restore the power of the Church. By this time, too, the Jesuits had become such a powerful and effective machine for stamping out heresy that the Protestant advance was definitely checked and the Catholics began to take heart once more. Just what a change of temper had taken place in Germany was revealed by the Affair of Donauworth (dō-nou-vûrt'). Donauworth was a 

Protestant town, which prohibited any Catholic demonstrations, but the Catholics there in defiance of this injunction held a religious procession which ended in a riot. The Catholics appealed to the Emperor to take action against the town and the Catholic princes of southern Germany formed a league for mutual protection. This was quickly offset by a union of the 463

Protestant princes. Naturally, for the next few years relations became strained, each side being desperately afraid of the other and ready to interpret any move as a hostile act. 

1. How the Thirty Years' War Started. Matters were finally brought to a head in Bohemia.

Ever since the days of 

THE DEFENESTRATION 

An early picture of this dramatic incident.

From Gottfried's Historische Chronica. 

John Huss, the Bohemians had been more or less opposed to the Church. Although they were subjects of the Habsburgs, they had insisted on their religious freedom. Finally, in 1618, they decided to depose their Catholic king, and began by hurling three of his representatives out of the castle window at Prague (prāg). This act introduced the Thirty Years' War. 

Commencing as a war between the Catholics and Protestants

THE THIRTY YEARS' WAR 

465 of Germany, it soon developed into a war between Catholicism and Protestantism in general, and ended as a struggle between the Bourbons and Habsburgs, involving almost all the powers of Europe. 

2. The Protestants Were Badly Defeated in the First

Stage of the War. The Bohemians selected for a new king 

Frederick, the Count of the Pā-lǎt'ĭ-náte, and a son-in-law of James I of England. Urged on by his ambitious wife, Frederick accepted the crown and hastened to Bohemia to take command of the royal forces. He met defeat in the battle of White Hill and was dubbed the "winter king" from a suggestion of the Jesuits that he could hardly last through the winter. The following spring the imperial forces invaded the Palatinate and occupied it almost without resistance. 

The occupation of the Palatinate caused the whole Protestant world-England, the Dutch Republic as the United Provinces were known, Denmark, and Sweden-to see the danger to Protestantism. However, King Christian of Denmark alone rose to the occasion. James I could not get Parliament to make the necessary money grants, and the Dutch were busy with the Spaniards who had been trying to win back the Netherlands; and the Swedes were involved in difficulties with the 

Russians and Poles.

The Emperor, realizing the danger of the situation, grasped at anything which promised assistance to the Catholic cause. 

Consequently when Count von Wallenstein (fŏn välĕn-shtin) offered to raise an army provided he be paid with plunder, the offer was accepted. This army made such short work of King 

Christian and his Danes that the Catholic forces would have overrun Denmark had it not been for the Dutch fleet which controlled the sea. The Emperor now issued the Edict of Restitution, which ordered the return to the Catholics of all their property which had been seized by the Protestants since 1552. 

Shortly after this, the excesses committed by von Wallenstein's

soldiers led even the Catholics to join in a demand for his dismissal and a cessation of the reign of terror. 

3. Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden Brings Victory to the Protestants. Since her separation from Denmark and 

Norway early in the sixteenth century, Sweden had been growing in power. Her king, Gustavus Ä-dolphus, had the idea of making the Baltic a Swedish lake, and already had annexed all the territory along its eastern shore. As a champion of Protestantism he was interested in seeing the Catholics beaten, yet a motive for entering the war was the opportunity for gaining control of the southern shore of the Baltic. Not long after the dismissal of von Wallenstein, Gustavus landed in Germany, and the Protestant princes, who were thoroughly frightened by their loss of Magdeburg (mägʻde-boork), hastened to enter into an alliance with him. 

Not only did Gustavus Adolphus, to the surprise of Europe, rout the imperial army, but he defeated it a second time, although at the cost of his own life. 

4. Cardinal Richelieu Ends the War by Entering the 

French Forces against the Catholics of Germany. The murder of von Wallenstein a year or so later left all Germany ready for peace. Meanwhile the great French chancellor, Cardinal de Richelieu (de re-she-lyu'), because of his hatred of the Habsburgs, had brought his country into the war on the side of the Protestants. Richelieu was not yet ready for peace. 

He desired to humiliate further the Habsburgs, and sent an army to co-operate with the Swedes. The victories of this army eventually compelled the Emperor to sue for peace. 

5. The Peace of Westphalia Marks the Beginning of 

Modern Diplomacy. The Thirty Years' War was brought to a formal end in 1648 by the Peace of West-pha'li-ȧ. This marked the beginning of modern European diplomacy, with the sinister meaning which the term implies. By the terms of this treaty, absolute religious equality was guaranteed in Ger-

Out of the horrors of the war came one important contribution to human progress. In 1625 Hugo Grotius (grō'shius), a Dutch jurist, published in Paris a book entitled On the Laws of War and Peace. This was the first great treatise on international law. It had the more force because it suggested many of the 128 articles of the Treaty of Westphalia, which became the basis of the public law of Europe; in fact, dealings between European states on a basis of equality may be said to date from this work of Grotius.

CHAPTER LII 

 BECOMES COMPLETE UNDER LOUIS XIV 

The period of early modern civilization after the years of religious strife became a great age for monarchies in Europe. 

We shall see how certain kings not only came to exercise absolute powers, but also claimed to rule by divine right. They were able to accomplish this by doing away with various restraints upon the royal power. This chapter will show how 

Cardinal Richelieu broke the power of the nobles; how Mazarin carried on the work by ignoring the parliaments of the provinces; and how Louis XIV revoked the Edict of Nantes so that little self-government remained in the cities. These accomplishments, along with the wars of aggression, the establishment of a magnificent court at Versailles, the centring of culture in the throne, made Louis XIV "Le Grand Monarque" (grän mó-närk'). 

1. Religious Warfare Leads to Edict of Nantes, Guaranteeing Protestants the Right to Hold Services. By the middle of the sixteenth century there were a considerable number of Calvinists in France. They were called Huguenots (hu'ge-nots) and were scattered through the country, being especially numerous in the cities. The death of Henry II in 1559 brought on a contest between various groups of nobles. The 

Huguenots became entangled in this trouble and there followed nearly forty years of warfare between the Catholics and Protestants. During this period the Huguenots insisted on controlling the government of certain towns as a guarantee that their religious rights would be respected. This, along with the quarrels of the nobles, led to a number of serious incidents, of which the worst was the nation-wide massacre that occurred 470

47I on St. Bartholomew's Day in 1572, and cost the lives of several thousand Protestants.

The crown finally passed to Henry IV of the House of 

Bourbon. Henry had been a Huguenot, but when he became king he went over to Catholicism, because he realized that only by so doing could peace be brought to France. However, he 

THE MASSACRE OF ST. BARTHOLOMEW'S DAY AT PARIS 

A modern attempt to depict this tragedy.

From a lithograph after the painting by François Dubois. did not wholly desert his former co-religionists, and he issued the famous Edict of Nantes in 1598. This granted to the 

Huguenots the right to hold religious services in certain towns in France except in Paris, and handed over to them a number of fortified places as a guarantee of the rights named in the Edict. 

2. Henry Begins the Rebuilding of France. Although

France did not suffer from her religious warfare as Germany did in the Thirty Years' War, still she was in serious difficulties. To the Duke of Sully (sü-le') Henry intrusted the straightening out of the finances of the realm. He encouraged

agriculture and the production of silk in every way, and he built roads and canals. Henry was the first king of France to see the advantage of extending French power beyond the seas, and encouraged the planting of colonies in North America. 

3. Cardinal Richelieu Comes into Power. Henry was succeeded by his son, then only nine years of age. For a time it looked as if the good work already accomplished would be undone. While the matter hung in the balance, there appeared a man destined to do as much for France as any one man ever did. This was the young nobleman, Richelieu, whose life had been spent in the service of the Church. Because of his noble birth, Richelieu had been made a bishop when very young, and the Pope had conferred on him a cardinal's hat. 

Cardinal Richelieu entered the royal council in 1624, and for eighteen years directed the destiny of the French ship of state. 

During this time he had two very definite aims to make the power of the king absolute in France, and to establish the supremacy of the Bourbons over the Habsburgs. To carry out these aims the Cardinal was willing to sacrifice the interests of the Church, just as we have seen him do when he brought France into the Thirty Years' War on the side of the Prot- estants. 

4. How de Richelieu Proceeds to Establish the Royal

Power. In matters of religion Cardinal Richelieu was disposed to be tolerant, but he was strongly opposed to the political privileges which the Huguenots enjoyed under the Edict of Nantes and he was determined to do away with them. He captured La Rochelle (rō-shel'), one of their strongholds, in spite of English assistance which it received, and he gained control of their other fortified towns, but he did not interfere with the civil and religious rights granted to them by the Edict. 

To break the power of the nobles, Richelieu ordered the destruction of their fortified castles except those which were necessary for the defense of the frontier. He then despatched

officials called in-ten'dants to the provinces to take charge of the finances, the police, and the administration of justice. By these means he broke the political power of the nobility. This power was further lessened by the refusal of the kings, to call together the Estates General from 1614 to 1789. 

5. Mazarin Makes the Power of the King Absolute. 

Although Richelieu died before the Thirty Years' 

War ended, his work was ably carried on by Cardinal Mazarin (mȧza-rǎN'), his successor.

His policies were much the same as Richelieu's, but unlike his illustrious predecessor, he was avaricious and given to political trickery. As a result, he was hated by the nobles, who tried in every way to get rid of him. 

Since the days of

Henry IV, parlements had been established in

FRENCH DEATH CRIER 

In that day there were few papers to publish obituary notices.

From Parton's Caricatures. 

every province to register royal decrees and to make representations to the king. They even enjoyed the right to initiate certain laws and to veto royal decrees, unless the king was present in person to overrule this action. Mazarin practically ignored the Parlement of Paris, and by so doing caused the nobles to revolt. This revolt, which spread quickly to many other provinces, is known as the Fronde, from the name given the slings used by French boys in their fights. Although the nobles were assisted to some extent by the bourgeoisie (boor-

zhwa-ze') of Paris, they were so completely defeated that henceforth the power of the king of France was absolute. 

The bourgeoisie constituted the upper group of the Third Estate. It included the professional classes, the shopkeepers, and manufacturers, the bankers and all other townsmen who did not work with their hands. Often wealthier than the nobility, yet it could never aspire to more important position in the king's service. It could buy the hereditary right to a judgeship or a seat in a parlement, and hence became known as the "nobility of the robe." Below the bourgeoisie came the artisans and peasantry, both of whom were for the most part freemen, except that the latter were bound to forced labor, the corvée (kôr-vā′), on public works, and to pay tolls to the nobility for the use of mills and wine presses, bridges and turnpikes. Besides they were required to pay tithes to the clergy, amounting sometimes to a thirteenth of the produce of their little farms. 

6. Louis XIV, "Le Grand Monarque." When Mazarin died, the young king took the reins, and during his long reign of seventy-two years ruled France without a chancellor. 

Louis XIV was every inch a king-a man of magnificent physique who blended beauty with dignity. Although uneducated and superstitious, he had much native ability. Blessed with a retentive memory and a disposition for hard work, he was a capable ruler, although excessively vain and delighting in such flatteries as the title "Le Grand Monarque." By his tutor, Bishop Bossuet (bó-sü-e'), he had been carefully trained to use the absolute power which Richelieu and Mazarin had built up for him. In order that Louis should be thoroughly steeped in the theory of the divine right of kings, the good bishop wrote a book entitled Politics Drawn from the Scripture's Own Words. In this he tried to prove that kings ruled with absolute power and were responsible to God alone, that they were the image of God on earth, and that their person was sacred, and he also insisted that they must provide for the

welfare of their people and look after them as would a father. 

With such teaching it would not be surprising for Louis to utter the expression so often attributed to him, "I am the state." 

7. Why the Age of Louis XIV Became the "Golden 

Age" of France.

Such an extraordinary person naturally had

Here he transformed a sandy waste into a beautiful park, and within it he built an enormous palace, with gorgeous så-lôns', imposing terraces, and superb gardens, at a cost of $100,000,000, to say nothing of the forced labor of thousands of peasants and soldiers. Buying ornaments for Versailles gave great impetus to the fine arts and made France for years the centre for superb sculpture and paintings, delicate wood carving and metal filigree, beautiful furniture and tapestries, and magnificent printing and

binding. From this period, too, began the reputation of France for cooking and wines of unequalled excellence.

The reign of Louis XIV 

may truly be called the "golden age" of France, for the court was the patron of both art and literature. Among the writers of the period are some of the great names of classical French literature Corneille (kôr-ná'y'), the father of the French stage; the dramatists Molière (mó-lyâr') and Racine (ra-sen'); and La fables. 

Louis surrounded himself with the most elaborate ceremonials. The manners of Versailles became the standard of every court in Europe, and they even reached the untitled classes. 

For the next century and a half no gentleman's education was complete without a knowledge of the language and literature of the French, and a familiarity with their etiquette. In spite of his insistence on these ceremonials, Louis took the business of governing seriously. By toiling long hours each day he proved himself an earnest and faithful ruler, though not a bril-

liant one. He fully realized his responsibilities and in his old age he wrote to his grandson, "One reigns by work and for work." 

8. How the Genius of Colbert and Others Helped Louis 

XIV.

A great part of the brilliancy of the reign of Louis XIV

depended upon the ability of the men trained by the two great cardinals. It was the military genius of Vauban (vō-bän'), the builder of fortresses, Louvois (loo-vwä'), the drill-master, and Condé (kôn-dā') and Tü-renne', the generals, that enabled France to control the affairs of Europe for a century. Foremost of all these protégés was Jean Colbert (zhän kól-bâr'), Louis's first minister of finance.

Colbert straightened out the tangled financial system and did away with the farming of taxes, which had impoverished the people and almost ruined the treasury. He gave attention to

the economic conditions of the country and undertook to build roads and canals which connected the Mediterranean Sea with the Atlantic Ocean by way of the Loire valley. To strengthen the position of French industry Colbert levied a heavy protective tariff on goods imported from abroad, and revived the medieval guilds. He gave bounties to French shipping and imposed restrictions on foreign ships entering French harbors. He bought from the Spanish the West Indian islands of Martinique (mär-ti-nek') and Guadeloupe (gô-de-loop') and helped to organize two great trading companies with a monopoly of the trade with the East and West Indies. 

9. Louis's Attack on the Huguenots Resulted in a Great 

Loss to France. Louis XIV was an ardent Catholic and felt that the Huguenots were a blot upon his fair land. He did not take drastic action against them until about 1681 when he fell under the influence of Ma-dame' de Maintenon (măn-t'nôn') whom he later made his second wife. Starting with certain minor annoyances, such as interfering with printing-presses and education, he forced the Huguenots to send their children to Catholic schools and quartered in their homes his troops, who were guilty of all sorts of excesses. 

Satisfied that the Huguenots had been checked by these measures, Louis revoked the Edict of Nantes on the ground that it was no longer necessary. Those who still persisted in the heresy became common outlaws. Their ministers were either banished or put to death. Many of the laymen-perhaps 50,000 -moved to various Protestant countries, especially to England, Holland, and Brandenburg, or crossed the Atlantic and settled in America. Because these Huguenots were mainly connected with business and industry, their leaving meant an economic loss to France, as they took with them many of the secrets of the French arts. 

10. By Costly Wars of Aggression Louis XIV Extends the Frontiers.

Since the beginning of the century, the states-

men of France had been talking about the natural frontiers of their country. They meant the Atlantic Ocean, the Pyrenees 

Mountains, the Mediterranean Sea, the Alps, and the Jura (joo'ra) Mountains, and the Rhine River. Louis wished to see France extended to these frontiers. To realize this he waged four great wars, and left France financially exhausted.

The first of these wars began after the death of Philip IV of Spain. Citing an old Flemish law by which inheritances put daughters by a first wife ahead of sons by a second wife, Louis demanded in the name of his wife the whole of the Spanish Netherlands-what is to-day Belgium. The fortresses of the southern Netherlands soon fell into his hands, and not long afterward the land of the Franche Comté. Holland was convinced that a barrier between herself and France was essential to her security, so she hastened to make an alliance of Sweden, England, and herself, in order to force France and Spain to settle their difficulties. Louis was compelled to be satisfied with only a few of the border fortresses, and was so enraged at the Dutch that he resolved to wipe out their little republic. He first bribed Charles II and the Swedish king into a coalition, then he overran the southern counties at will. Amsterdam and the northern counties were saved only by the heroism of the Dutch who cut the dikes and flooded the country, under the leadership of William of Orange. In spite of his successes, Louis got no nearer to the Rhine in the north than he had been at the beginning, but he did acquire the Franche Comté.

Louis now set up Chambers of Reunion to determine what dependencies had belonged to the territories which had been ceded to France, for under the treaties title to these would also pass to him. By this means he laid claim to Strassburg, Luxemburg (luk'sěm-bûrg), and other towns between his eastern frontier and the Rhine. This "sharp practice," and an invasion of the Palatinate while the Emperor was busy fighting the Turks, led to a great coalition against him, in which

Emperor Leopold was joined by William of Orange, now king of England. The war lasted until 1697, by which time Louis succeeded in breaking up the Grand Alliance by using bribery. 

By the Peace of Rys'wick Louis secured definite title to Strassburg and to the whole of Alsace. He gave up Lorraine and the 

Palatinate and allowed the Dutch a favorable commercial treaty. 

He had involved his country in a new struggle with England which was to last for a century. We shall leave the last years of his long reign to be studied in connection with the new general European war which followed.

CHAPTER LIII ABSOLUTISM IN ENGLAND FAILS UNDER THE STUART KINGS 

The Tudors had ruled as absolute kings. Henry VII had brought the nobles under the control of the crown and Henry VIII had done the same for the church. Under Elizabeth the building up of the merchant and land-holding classes begun by her father bound those groups to the throne. Through the court of the Star Chamber and the dismissal of parliaments all these rulers had overridden the constitutional forms of the English government, but their personal popularity led the mass of the people to overlook these usurpations. The royal resistance to Catholic and Spaniard awoke a hearty response in the minds of Englishmen. They accepted the absolute rule because they felt that their sovereigns expressed their own desires. 

1. James I, the First of the Stuart Kings, and His Pretensions. When Elizabeth died, she bequeathed her crown to 

James VI of Scotland, son of the unfortunate Mary Stuart, and he became king of England without opposition, at last uniting the two kingdoms under a single ruler. James was an extremely well-educated man, but he was so lacking in common sense that he was called "the wisest fool in Christendom." So strongly did he believe in the divine right of kings that he declared, "It is presumption and high contempt in a subject to dispute what a king can do, or to say that a king cannot do this or that." Although he had been brought up in Scotland where the church was free, when he arrived in England and found himself at the head of the Anglican Church, he insisted on be- 481

ing the spiritual leader of his English subjects; indeed, “No bishop, no king" was a favorite expression of his. 

2. James's Autocracy Leads to Trouble with Parlia ment. By the time of James there had grown up in England many sects of non-conforming Protestants, known to this day as Dissenters Presbyterians, Puritans, and Separatists or Independents-who had little in common save resistance to the state church. Foremost among them were the Puritans, who, although anxious to remain a part of the Church of England, demanded that it should be "purified" of some of its customs and rites which it had inherited from the Catholics. 

The accession of James was received with delight by Catholics and Dissenters, for each expected greater toleration of their views at his hands. In this all were disappointed, for at the king's command Parliament enacted laws requiring all Englishmen to attend the state church and to partake of the sacrament administered by the priests. Those who refused to do this were liable to fine and imprisonment. It is hard to say on whom- 

Catholics or Dissenters-the stern measures bore more heavily. 

At any rate they failed, for the Puritans had by 1621 become so strong politically that they controlled the House of Commons. 

James's reign was a continuous struggle with Parliament. over taxation, and the duties on imports and exports which under the Tudors had been imposed by the king. The situation was further embarrassed by his attempt to arrange a marriage between his son Charles and a Spanish princess. Parliament refused him money to assist his son-in-law in the Thirty Years' War, and they sought to check his authority by reviving the right of parliamentary impeachment, a prerogative which had lapsed under the earlier Tudors. The first to feel this was 

James's own chancellor, the scholarly Francis Bacon, Lord

Věr ú-lăm, who was found guilty of accepting bribes. Death came to James while he was in the midst of this quarrel, and the crown passed to his son, Charles I.

Charles had to accept this against his will. When Parliament met the next year, trouble broke out again, and for a third time he dissolved it. 

4. Charles Institutes "Personal" Rule and Gets into

More Difficulties. For eleven years Charles ruled England without a Parliament, assisted in ecclesiastical matters by William Laud (lôd), the Archbishop of Canterbury and ex officio head of the Church of England, and in civil matters by Thomas Wentworth. The first years of this "personal rule" were on the whole years of peace and quiet. The country was prosperous and with the aid of the Star Chamber the poor were protected from the oppression of the rich.

ABSOLUTISM IN ENGLAND 

485 5 For years it had been the custom of English kings to levy ships or money from the seacoast towns for the support of the royal navy. In 1635 Charles extended these levies to the inland counties. John Hampden (hăm'den), a rich squire of 

Buckinghamshire, resolved to test the right of the king to levy this "ship money" without an act of Parliament, and refused to pay the twenty shillings levied on his estate. 

When the case was tried in the courts, Charles won by a majority of one vote, but "ship money" became the war cry of disaffected English- men generally, and

Hampden became a 

MORRIS DANCE 

hero. To make matters worse Archbishop Laud stirred up the non-conforming Protestants by attacking Calvinism among the clergy and silencing the Puritan ministers, and especially by the Declaration of Sports which made Sunday the holiday it had been during the Middle Ages. 

The end came when Charles tried to force on Scotland the Book of Canons, a service book of the Church of England. 

The Scotch Calvinists resented this and signed an oath, the so-called Covenant, to defend true religion but at the same time affirming their loyalty to the crown. Charles despatched troops. 

When they were unsuccessful, he was compelled to call together Parliament. 

5. The Long Parliament Starts Reform Which Charles 

Tries to Ignore. This Parliament, called the Long Parliament because it remained in session twelve years (1640-1652), met and began its attack on the king. It put to death some of

the royal ministers and imprisoned Archbishop Laud. It forbade the levying of ship money and other unauthorized taxes. 

It abolished the Star Chamber and the High Commission as well as other evidences of absolutism. It published an indictment of the king's acts, the Grand Remonstrance. It ordained that Parliament should meet every three years regardless of the royal will, and it even demanded that the ministers should become responsible to it.

Charles waited until the members of the House of Commons were in conflict over religious differences and then he took advantage of the situation and invaded its precincts to arrest the hated Puritan leaders. Warned in advance, Hampden and the others made a hasty exit. A few days later the latter came back in triumph and both sides prepared for civil war. 

In the long struggle the royal supporters consisted mostly of the nobility, the Anglican clergy, and the Roman Catholics. 

They were known as Cavaliers, because of their jolly, rollicking ways, while the parliamentarians were dubbed Roundheads from the Puritan custom of cutting their hair closely instead of wearing it in flowing locks like the Cavaliers. The Roundheads included principally the tradesmen of the towns and the small landowners. The masses were only interested onlookers since they had no part in the government. 

6. The Royal Forces Are Defeated by Cromwell's 

Roundhead Army. After his trouble with Parliament, Charles withdrew from London to the north of England, and began to assemble his forces. At first the Cavaliers had the best of the struggle, for the parliamentary army was inefficient and uniformly unsuccessful. Although the Roundheads made a secret alliance with the Scotch agreeing that the church government of Scotland was to be applied to England, affairs went from bad to worse until Oliver Cromwell, a cousin of Hampden's, organized a new body of cavalry called the "Ironsides." 

After they defeated Charles at Marston Moor, the whole

ABSOLUTISM IN ENGLAND 

487 Roundhead army was reorganized. Within two years the royal cause was lost. 

7. Charles I Is Tried for Treason and Loses His Head. 

Charles fled to Scotland where he surrendered to the Scots in the hope that he might be able to stir up dissension between them and the 

Cromwellian forces. 

The Scots, however, promptly surrendered him. Parliament and the army were now in open opposition. Charles would probably have remained king in name at least, had he kept aloof from trickery, but when it became known that he was conspiring with the Scots to restore him to the throne, the army began to demand his head. 

The army found

The mutilated Commons, afterward known as the Rump Parliament, then passed a resolution setting forth that supreme authority resided in the House of Commons because that body

was chosen by the people, and that laws passed by it were binding without the consent of either King or House of Lords. 

Next it appointed a "high court of justice" of 135 commissioners. Charles was arraigned before this court on the charge of treason. He was doomed from the start, for when the competency of this court was attacked, Cromwell replied fiercely, "I tell you, we will cut off his head with the crown upon it." 

By vote of a bare majority, for many of the commissioners absented themselves when the balloting took place, Charles was found guilty, and on January 30, 1649, all England was aghast at the spectacle of her king being beheaded under the windows of his own palace. So great was the shock to the monarchs of Europe that the Czar of Russia dismissed the English envoy to his court because he would not have dealings with such uncivilized nations as the English had shown themselves to be by this act of lese majesté (lěz mā-zhěs-tá').

CHAPTER LIV HOW PARLIAMENTARY GOVERNMENT CAME ABOUT IN ENGLAND 

We now come to some of the most important years in English history. We shall see how a government known as the 

Commonwealth representing a minority of the people was set up by Cromwell and his army; and how as Lord Protector of 

England Cromwell ruled in as autocratic fashion as had James I, with this difference, that Cromwell claimed that his mission was from God and the people, how after the Glorious Revolution of 1688, Parliament dealt the principle of the divine right of kings a fatal blow by declaring the throne vacant; and how with the passage of the Bill of Rights Parliament came into effective control of the government. These considerations will be the high points in this chapter. 

1. The Commonwealth Is Established under Cromwell.

After the execution of Charles I, England was without a king and Parliament was composed of only a fraction of its legal membership. Responsibility for restoring the government rested with the army which was made up of Puritans. Cromwell and his followers in theory believed in a government by the people, and that it should be responsible to the people like the church. In practice we shall find that he instituted a government by Puritans for all the people. Although the Rump Parliament was continued under the Commonwealth, as the new government was called, the real power rested in a council of state, consisting of persons under the control of Cromwell and the army. This government then proceeded to exclude Catholics and Royalists from any part in the government, and Presbyterians as well, for Cromwell believed that only the Puritans would safeguard the principles for which they had fought. 489

In Ireland and Scotland, the people refused to accept any such tyranny and proclaimed the Prince of Wales as king, under the name of Charles II. In Scotland he pledged himself never to tolerate Catholicism in any part of his kingdom, and TORED

4. Under the Protectorate Cromwell Ruled as a Military Dictator. The army proceeded to draw up a document called the "Instrument of Government," which was England's first and only written constitution, as well as one of the earliest written constitutions of modern times. Cromwell was made. 

Lord Protector for life. Puritanism was to be the state religion, and there was to be a merciless persecution of the Catholics, and even the Anglicans were not to be allowed to worship privately. It was not long, however, before Cromwell and Parliament were in dispute, and he dismissed it altogether. For the last three years of his life, Cromwell ruled England without Parliament, maintaining an autocratic position not unlike that which had been claimed by James I. 

5. Why the Stuarts Were Asked to Return to the 

Throne. Richard Cromwell succeeded his father as Lord Protector but held the office only for a few months because of his weakness. Although the Rump Parliament insisted that it was the legal government, General Monk (munk), who commanded the army, summoned the deposed Long Parliament and issued writs for a new election. Monk knew that the greater part of the English people still favored a monarchy and that many

others had become irritated by the harshness and austerity of Puritan rule, so he began negotiations with Charles II for his restoration. Charles issued a general pardon to all except some regicides designated by Parliament, and promised liberty to "tender consciences." When the new Parliament met, it passed a resolution that "according to the ancient and fundamental law of this kingdom the government is, and ought to be, by 

King, Lords, and Commons."

In May, 1660, Charles ascended the throne, personally resolved "never to set out on his travels again." He took an oath to observe the Magna Charta and the Petition of Rights, and his whole reign was characterized by a display of tact and a willingness to yield whenever he saw that Parliament or his ministers were insistent. At heart a Catholic, although not baptized until on his deathbed, Charles undertook to make it easy for the Romanists by advocating religious toleration for all non-conformists. In this he was blocked by Parliament. 

6. The Government of the Returned Stuarts Tries to Make All Accept the Anglican Creed. The Parliament which recalled the king consisted chiefly of Cavaliers determined to do away with all evidences of the revolution. The

religious questions were still paramount with them and they set out to make it as hard as possible for the Puritans and other Dissenters. By the Corporation Act, they required the officers of all towns to be members of the Church of England, and they compelled all ministers to accept the Anglican creed. In the 

Conventicle Act they fined all who attended meetings of other sects, and provided that those who persisted should be transported to the colonies. Finally by the Five-Mile Act they made it a crime for any dissenting minister to come within five miles of an incorporated town. 

7. How the Tory and Whig Parties Arose Out of the 

Wrangle Over a Successor to Charles II. The latter years of Charles's reign were much occupied with a parliamentary wrangle over the question of his successor. Since he was childless, the crown regularly would pass to his brother, James, Duke of York, for whom New York is named. The country was thrown into consternation when James embraced Catholicism in 1672. Parliament tried to enact a law making James ineligible to be king, but this was defeated in the House of Lords.

Out of the agitation over the Exclusion Bill came a division of Parliament into two parties. The members who supported the rights of James were called Tories from an Irish word meaning "robber"; those who opposed him, Whigs, a nickname often applied to the Presbyterians. This division of Parliament into two parties continued and out of it grew the political notion still held in England and America that two parties are essential for the maintenance of a proper government. 

8. The "Glorious Revolution" of 1688 Deals Divine

Right Idea a Fatal Blow. When James II came to the throne in 1685, he released several thousand Catholics and

Quakers who had been imprisoned. Two years later he issued the Declaration of Indulgence granting liberty of conscience and private worship to all dissenting sects. The Anglicans were

PARLIAMENTARY GOVERNMENT 

497 furious and refused to read the king's orders in their pulpits. 

While James was busy prosecuting the recalcitrant Anglicans, his second wife, an Italian Catholic, bore him a son. Up to this time he had been accepted in hope that the crown would pass at his death to the Protestant Princess Mary, wife of William of Orange, stadholder of the Netherlands, and a daughter of James by his earlier marriage. It now seemed certain that it would pass to another Catholic. A group of Whigs and Tories met and wrote to Mary and her husband, imploring them to come to England and save the country from a "Catholic tyranny. 1. 

The affair was managed so quietly that there was no chance for another civil war. As soon as William and Mary landed in 

England, most of the officers of the army deserted James, and he fled to France. The "Glorious Revolution" was an accomplished fact. The principle of the divine right of kings had been dealt a fatal blow, and Parliament, by declaring the throne vacant, showed that it could at will make and unmake a sovereign. 

9. The Bill of Rights, a Great Document of English Constitutional History, and the Toleration Act Are Passed. 

The crown was offered to William and Mary conjointly, but not until Parliament made a definite Declaration of Right, which became one of the great documents of English constitutional history. Among other things, this forbade the sovereign to make or suspend any law, to levy money, or to maintain a standing army without consent of Parliament. It guaranteed to Englishmen the right of petition and the right to carry arms. 

It demanded frequent sessions of Parliament and the election of members to the House of Commons without any interference of the crown. It also insisted that they should be free from arrest for whatever they might say or do within Parliament. 

And lastly, it settled the religious question by requiring that thereafter the sovereign of England should be a member of the 

Anglican Church.

In the same year, Parliament passed a Toleration Act which granted to Dissenters the right to worship publicly and freed them from necessity of attending services in the Anglican Church. Although Catholics, Jews, and Unitarians were expressly excluded, they were permitted to worship unmolested. 

For years, however, all non-conformists were denied the privilege of holding any civil or military office under the old Test 

Acts of 1673 and 1678. 

10. How the Privy Council Developed in the Cabinet. 

Under the Act of Settlement passed by Parliament in 1701, William and Mary were succeeded by Mary's sister Anne. 

During her reign the Scotch agreed to do away with their separate parliament and to accept forty-five seats in the English House of Commons and sixteen in the House of Lords. With this union, the ancient feuds between the two kingdoms came to an end. Since 1707 Great Britain has been one nation. 

Queen Anne died seven years later, and the crown passed, as had been provided, to George I, elector of the German principality of Hanover, a descendant of Elizabeth, daughter of 

James I.

For a long time the English kings had been assisted in governing their realm by a body of men chosen by themselves and known as the Privy Council. Since the Glorious Revolution, they discovered that when a majority of the members of Parliament were Whigs, it was better to have Whig councillors; and when Tories, Tory councillors. They had discovered also that the Privy Council was too large to transact business easily, so they began to choose a select few to meet with themselves regularly. Because this smaller group often met in a small room or "cabinet," it gradually came to bear that name. 

Since George I was a German and knew no English, sitting with the Cabinet became such a bore to him that he eventually left the members to themselves. By this time, too, control of 

Parliament had passed into the hands of the Whig landowners,

who were supported by the towns because of the interest they took in keeping down taxes and encouraging commerce. This 

Whig control lasted for nearly fifty years and during that time the power of the Cabinet continued to increase.

CHAPTER LV HOW REIGNING FAMILIES STRUGGLE FOR POWER IN EUROPE DURING THE EIGHTEENTH CENTURY 

By the middle of the seventeenth century, the religious troubles of Europe were over, but the quarrels of its great ruling families were increasing. These centred in the Habsburgs and the Bourbons, who held the thrones in Austria, Spain, and France. There were other families, like the Hohenzollerns (hōĕn-tsól'ĕrns) of Brandenburg, the Wittelsbachs (vit'ĕls-bǎks) of Bavaria, and the Romanovs (ró-män'ófs) of Russia, each with great aspirations.

Of the continental powers France easily stood foremost, Spain was on the decline, and Sweden, which had been powerful since the days of Gustavus Adolphus, lost its position under the erratic Charles XII early in the eighteenth century. Russia was just beginning to enter into European politics under the leadership of Peter the Great. The monarchs of England, safe within their island kingdom, watched the struggles of these families and threw the weight of their strength first to one side and then to the other, in order to maintain a "balance of power" in Europe, and at the same time carried on a continuous struggle with the French beyond the seas. 

Out of all these wars few changes in territory were made in Europe. Prussia did become one of the foremost states that was to figure in modern history, and England in acquiring vast new colonial possessions came into a commanding position in world affairs which she has held to this day.

3. The Question of Who Should Succeed to the Span ish Throne and Its Consequences. The Turkish war was no sooner ended than Europe faced a much more serious problem. 

Charles II, the Habsburg ruler of Spain, had no children. His elder sister was the wife of Louis XIV, and his younger, the wife of Leopold II of Austria. This problem of Spanish succession reopened the old rivalry between the Bourbons and the Habsburgs. The balance of power was held by William III of 

England. Louis felt that his claims were the better and tried to influence William to agree to some scheme for the partition

of the Spanish territories, but William leaned toward the Habsburgs. Meanwhile French diplomats at Madrid persuaded 

Charles II to make a will bequeathing the realm to Louis's grandson, Philip of Anjou. Louis had already agreed with 

William that the Spanish domain should be divided among four different princes, and when Charles died he insisted on this being carried out, knowing that it would mean war. 

Early in 1701, with the aid of the Spanish Netherlands Louis seized the Dutch fortresses separating Holland from France. 

William III at once sent the Duke of Marlborough (märľ'bóru) with an English army to assist the Dutch, and the War of the Spanish Succession was on. Louis now made the blunder of proclaiming the son of the exiled James II as the rightful English king, and thus drove England to the support of King William. William organized the Grand Alliance-England, Austria, and Holland, the Duke of Så-voy' and several of the German electors-to support the claims of the Archduke Charles, the second son of the Emperor Leopold. In 1703 England drew Portugal into the alliance by means of the Měth'u-ěn Treaty, which gave the English special commercial privileges within the Portuguese domain and established the close connection between the two countries that has lasted ever since. 

Sweden and Russia did not come in, for they were engaged in a war of their own. 

4. The War of the Spanish Succession. William died just as the war broke out, but his successor, Queen Anne, carried out his part and gave her name to a secondary struggle which was waged with the French in America. The great generals who had won Louis's previous victories were now dead and their successors were no match for the Duke of Marlborough and Prince Eugene of Savoy. At Blěn'heim in 1704, the

French were defeated so badly that they were forced to retire from the Empire. During the next few years, while Prince 

Eugene was chasing them out of Italy, the Duke of Marlbor-

6. Emperor Charles VI of Austria Rounds Out His 

Realm. The new emperor, Charles VI, was now the ruler of a wide-flung group of territories. They were inhabited by many different nationalities, and they were without any geographical unity. Of all of them, only Austria, Bohemia, and Hungary could be looked upon as forming a unified state, and even there three different peoples-Germans, Slavs, and Magyars-had to be reckoned with.

Although he was emperor, Charles had little power in Germany; in fact, he was such a source of envy to Bavaria and 

Prussia that the Bavarians even sided with France during the War of the Spanish Succession. Moreover, before his death he was faced with the same problem of succession as had been Charles II. Being without a male heir, he entered into an elaborate series of treaties-the so-called Prăg-măt'ic Sanctionwith the German princes and the monarchs of Europe to bind them to recognize the title of his daughter, Ma-rì'à Theresa (tě-re'sȧ), to the Habsburg dominions. 

7. The Rise of the Hohenzollerns from Petty Lords to 

Kings of Prussia. The original Hohenzollerns were petty lords in southern Germany who became imperial officials in Nu'rěm-bûrg. In 1415, one of them bought from the Emperor Sigismund the mark of Brandenburg, a strip of territory extending perhaps a hundred miles east and west from Berlin, then a town of only a few thousand inhabitants. The history of Brandenburg during the next two centuries was much like that of the other German states. Early in the seventeenth century its margrave, who was also an Elector, that is, one of the seven German princes whose votes elected the Emperor, fell heir to two widely separated duchies-Cleve (klā've) in the valley of the Rhine and East Prussia on the shores of the Baltic. At this time East Prussia was inhabited mainly by Slavs and was under the suzerainty of the king of Poland.

Brandenburg escaped much of the devastation of the Thirty

REIGNING FAMILIES STRUGGLE FOR POWER 507 

Years' War and its ruler, Frederick William, obtained the whole of eastern Pomerania and incidentally became the most powerful prince in Germany. The remainder of his long reign was devoted to the material improvement of the realm. While other German princes were busy with their personal ambitions and pleasures, the "Great Elector" was building roads, digging canals, draining swamps, improving agriculture, and seeking in 

THE PALACE AT POTSDAM NEAR BERLIN 

This palace was built by the kings of Prussia in a large garden in imitation of Versailles. many other ways to advance the prosperity of his people. At the same time he took away their ancient assemblies and other local privileges and centralized the government at Berlin. 

We have already seen how his son Frederick III became the first king of Prussia. His successor was Frederick William I, a drill master with a passion for tall soldiers and for saving money. He was a crabbed old gentleman, who used to cane any loafers he met on the street and then put them in the army, and who required rich men to build fine houses to improve the appearance of Berlin. To his son, Frederick II, who was later known as "the Great," he bequeathed an army almost equal in size to that of France or of Austria, and vastly superior in organization, together with a well-filled war chest.

8. Frederick the Great a New Type of Ruler. Fred erick, when he came to the throne in 1740, had the best political training of any European king, because he had learned the whole system of administration from the bottom up. In addition, Frederick was exceedingly clever and was acquainted with the best intellectual development of the age. At the royal palace of Pots'dam literary men from everywhere were made welcome. 

For a time the Frenchman Voltaire (vól-târ') was one of 

Frederick's closest friends. 

Frederick II may be looked upon as the best expression of the "benevolent despot," because of his grasp of the ideas of his day, and particularly because of his devotion to rationalism. 

He was selfish, crafty, and cynical, and yet Frederick was a man of large parts, and was well entitled to be called "the Great" in consideration of his ability as a ruler and of the services he rendered to Prussia. 

9. Maria Theresa Becomes Queen and the War of the 

Austrian Succession Is On. When Maria Theresa ascended the throne of Austria, Frederick seized the Austrian province of Silesia (si-le'shi-a) in the upper valley of the Oder, which the Hohenzollerns had long coveted. This action stirred the enemies of Austria to violate the Pragmatic Sanction by seizing whatever they wanted of the Austrian domain. France, Spain, Bavaria, and Saxony allied themselves with Prussia and brought about the election of Charles of Bavaria as Emperor. 

For fear that France might annex the Austrian Netherlands, and disturb the balance of power, both England and Holland went to the assistance of the young queen.

For eight years the War of the Austrian Succession continued. Finally in 1748, after the death of the Emperor, all the belligerents were glad to lay down arms. The Peace of Aixla-Chapelle (ěks-la-shȧ-pěl') returned to their original owners all the conquests except Silesia, and including Louisburg, Nova Scotia, which the English colonists in America had wrested from

REIGNING FAMILIES STRUGGLE FOR POWER 509 

the French. At the best it was only a truce, for it settled nothing except that Prussia had become a power to be considered. 

10. By a Diplomatic Revolution Maria Theresa Brings about a New Alignment of Powers.

Aix-la-Chapelle caused hostilities to break out in America in 1754 between England and France, although war was not declared until 1756. In this same year Frederick learned of the secret negotiations between Austria, Russia, Sweden, and Saxony to divide up his possessions. He at once invaded Saxony. 

11. The Seven Years' War Follows. For the next seven years, Europe at home and beyond the seas was engaged in war. The armies of Frederick and of Hanover were less than half the size of those of their enemies. At first England was so much engrossed in America and India that she furnished. little aid, but when she saw that France might seize Hanover to make up her losses beyond the seas, she began to contribute heavy subsidies to Frederick.

Frederick gradually lost ground, and finally, in 1759, was driven out of Berlin by the Russians. Still he managed to hold on, and in the following year England broke the French power beyond the seas by some decisive victories in both America and India. Frederick was saved from defeat only when the death of the Tsarina, in 1761, brought to the Russian throne a friend in the person of Peter III. Russia now withdrew her armies, and Sweden soon followed. After that Frederick easily drove the Austrian and French forces out of his territories, and peace negotiations were commenced in 1762.

CHAPTER LV1  OF RUSSIA MAKE A PLACE FOR THE SLAVS IN EUROPEAN AFFAIRS 

Stretching away to the east of the Carpathian Mountains is a great plain, broken only by the Ū'răls which separate Europe from Asia. Consequently, eastern Europe is distinct geographically from western Europe and is more oriental than European in its outlook. To the north of the Carpathians this plain extends into Germany, as far as the North Sea. There is nothing to form a natural boundary between the lands of the Germans and those of the Slavs. For the most part the rivers which drain the Slavic portion of the plain flow southward into the Black and Caspian Seas. There is one notable exception-the 

Vis'tú-lȧ, which flows northward and empties into the Baltic Sea, partly explaining why Poland has always had more cɔntacts with western Europe than has Russia. 

The population of the greater part of this enormous area is made up of Slavs who constitute one of the important branches of the Indo-European-speaking peoples. They were never very successful at political organization, consequently throughout the greater part of their history they have had as rulers persons of foreign blood. The Slavic birth-rate has always been high and as a result they have been almost continuously pressing westward and southward into other parts of Europe. 

In the tenth century we saw the Huns penetrate into the valley of the Danube and cut off the southern Slavs from the main body of their kinsmen farther north, and at about the same time we saw the beginning of the struggle between the Slavs and the Germans. Christianity was brought to the Slavic world in the early part of the Middle Ages. The western Slavs became converts to the Roman Church; the eastern and south- 513

ern, to the Greek. This difference of church divided these two divisions of the Slavic people and it was still further increased by the differences in political development. 

1. Poland Covers a Large Area in the Early Modern 

Period. Poland first appears in history as a duchy under the control of the German king, Otto I. While Otto's successors were busy with their imperial problems in Italy, Poland took advantage of the situation to gain its independence. Although it received the shock of the Mongol conquest, by the fourteenth century it had become a considerable state with its capital at Cracow (krā kō). Later in the same century the heiress to the 

Polish throne married a grand duke of Lith-ú-a'ni-à, a large country on the north which extended far into what is now Russia. The union thus brought about continued for over two hundred years. During this period the Poles began the conquest of West Prussia and extended their control in a southeasterly direction almost to the Black Sea. With the collapse of Hungary before the Turks, Poland became one of the chief defenses of northern Europe against those dreaded infidels. 

2. Due to the Weakness of Poland She Was a Prey to 

All Her Neighbors. While other states were growing strong, Poland, the second largest in Europe, remained weak because of its political organization. Its king was elected for life by the greater nobles, but he had practically no power. There was a Diet which met occasionally and for any binding action required a unanimous vote of the members. One of the members might stop the passage of an act, and force the immediate dissolution of the Diet itself.

Lack of a strong central authority was by no means the only difficulty that Poland had to face. She was a poor country without large towns, and with no manufacturing and little foreign trade. Included in her population were various peoples

who chafed under Polish rule. Among them were the Lithuanians, and the Cos'sǎcks, semi-nomads dwelling in the southeast and much given to robbery and pillage. There were ten or twelve million peasants in abject serfdom and a million or so EK JERSE 

A MEETING OF THE POLISH DIET 

One of the most ineffective legislative bodies ever devised. nobles, mostly ignorant and with such small estates that it was said a dog sitting in the middle of one estate would touch another with every wag of his tail. Poland had no natural boundaries except on the southwest. It is not surprising then that 

Poland was continually the prey of her neighbors. 

3. The Beginnings of Modern Russia. The Norse king doms of Novgorod and Kiev all but disappeared in the thirteenth century before the Mongol conquest. For the next three hundred years, the Russians were more closely associated with Asia than with Europe. They very largely adopted oriental customs, and when they did escape from the Mongol yoke, the Christian centre from which they could have received inspiration most easily had come under the control of the Turks. To

this oriental influence, too, we may trace the moving of the political centre of Russia to Mos'cow, for when the national spirit of the Russians began to revive in the middle of the fifteenth century, the leadership was taken by Ivan (e-van') the Terrible, who was prince of Muscovy or Moscow. 

MODERN COSSACKS 

Under the later Tsars they were no longer the undisciplined horde of the sixteenth century.

As soon as Ivan freed himself from Mongol control, he assumed the title of Tsar, and by this title the monarchs of Russia were ever afterward known. To his successors Ivan bequeathed a country reaching from the shores of the Caspian Sea to the Arctic Ocean, and eastward from the valley of the upper Dnieper to the Urals and beyond. Although Russian emigrants had spread southwestward into the fertile plains of the lower Dnieper, known as the Ukraine (u'krān) from the Slavic word krä'i meaning "frontier," Russia was cut off from the Black Sea by the Ottoman Turks.
