581 Meanwhile a bitter struggle was going on between the Girondists and the radicals. What to do with Louis the important. question became, for he had been caught in more treasonable conduct. As a result of Robespierre's insistence that "Louis must die that the country may live," he was compelled to plead 

MARIE ANTOINETTE BEFORE THE REVOLUTIONARY TRIBUNAL 

She never forgot her royal birth. to the charge of treason before the Convention sitting as a high court of justice, and by an overwhelming vote, he was found guilty. Although the Girondists opposed the death penalty, Louis was guillotined on January 21, 1793. His execution drove all the wavering powers into a union against France, and added fuel to the flames of internal revolt. 

6. The Committee of Public Safety Institutes a Reign of Terror against the Enemies of the Republic. The situation now became more perilous than ever. The French troops who had invaded Germany and the Austrian Netherlands were

in retreat. At home the Girondists proposed that the Commune should be dissolved because it was making the Convention a mere tool of the Paris mob. Finally, on June 2, 1793, twenty thousand of the city rabble forced the Convention to expel the Girondist members. In retaliation the citizens of Marseilles, Caen (käN), Bordeaux, and Lyons took up arms. Toulon (too-lon') was surrendered to an English fleet and a great Věn-de'an army crossed the Loire and laid siege to Nantes. 

Vigorous measures were needed to meet this situation. The 

Convention suspended the recently adopted constitution and created a Committee of Public Safety, of stanch "Mountain” men. Almost absolute power was given to this Committee. As one leader expressed it, "We must found a despotism of liberty in order to crush the despotism of kings." After the murder of Marat in July by a young Girondist maiden from Caen, the Convention decreed that "Terror shall be the order of the day." 

Special courts were set up to condemn the "suspects" promptly-in groups of twenty, fifty, or more, as the Reign of Terror advanced. Among the first to meet death as a result of this new policy were Marie Antoinette, the king's sister, and the Duke of Orleans, a member of the Assembly who had voted for the execution of Louis. Equally horrible scenes were enacted in the departments during the fourteen months while this terrible delusion reigned. Carrier (kȧr-ya'), the Committee's deputy at Nantes, put to death not less than fifteen thousand persons. The excesses of the Terror brought about a reaction; so that in the end the radical element was overthrown and a moderate party was again in control. 

7. The Constitution of the Year III Provides for a Leg islative Council and a Directory of Five Members. Once more the Convention settled down to draft the new constitution-the work for which it had been elected. Heeding the injunction of Danton, who had said that "Next to bread, educa-

SECOND PHASE OF REVOLUTION 

583 tion is the need of the people," it planned a comprehensive system of national education, including the first normal school in history. It prepared a new Civil Code, which provided that direct heirs should share equally in an estate, thus doing away with the special privileges of the firstborn. It abolished imprisonment for debt and gave property rights to women. 

13TH VENDEMAIRE IN THE COURT OF THE TUILERIES 

From the original of Lebarbier in the Musée Carnavalet, Paris. 

In October, 1795, the Convention completed the new constitution, the Constitution of the Year III. It provided for two legislative bodies instead of one-a Council of Five Hundred to propose laws, and a Council of the Ancients, composed of two hundred fifty elderly statesmen, to approve or reject them. 

The executive power was given to a Directory of five members, who were elected by the Ancients from a list prepared by the Five Hundred. This avoided the danger of concentrating power in the hands of one person, yet it proved ineffective and aided the very thing which it tried to prevent. As in the old constitution, suffrage was still based on a property qualifica-

tion, and yet a large part of the people had no part in the government. 

8. A "Whiff of Grapeshot" Puts an End to Mob Control. After the Constitution of the Year III had been ratified by the nation, the Convention, alarmed by the reactionary movements of the royalists, decreed that two-thirds of the two councils had to be chosen from its own membership to insure a revolutionary majority in both houses. This caused so much bitterness that a mob of forty thousand undertook to frighten the Convention. The latter placed its defense in the hands of a young artillery officer, Napoleon Bonaparte, who had distinguished himself at Toulon. Bonaparte mounted cannon which could command the approaches to the Tuileries, and when the mob crossed the "dead line," it received a "whiff of grapeshot." Paris realized that an era of law and order had been ushered in. Three weeks later the Convention dissolved quietly, the executive power passed to the Directory, and France started on a course of constitutional government. 

9. The Achievements of the Revolution. In order to understand what the Revolution accomplished, as well as what it tried to accomplish, we must bear in mind the ideals of its leaders. First of all, the Revolution was primarily the work of the bourgeoisie. Although for a time it was under the control of the lower classes, yet this middle class really triumphed. In the second place, the demand for liberty stood uppermost in men's minds. They expected to achieve it by applying the principles of reason to human affairs, as their laws so amply show. 

The Revolution destroyed the privileges of the nobility and of the church, and established the principle of equality of men. 

To bring about reason in material things, it established a new system of weights and measures, and even reformed the calendar. To establish reason, it abolished the worship of God, closed the churches, and melted down their sacred vessels into coin and their bells into cannon. One of the most deplorable

results of the attack on the churches was the destruction of many of the medieval stained-glass windows and carvings.

CHAPTER LXIII NAPOLEON BONAPARTE ENFORCES THE REVOLUTIONARY IDEAS AND BECOMES MASTER OF WESTERN EUROPE 

The island of Corsica passed from the control of the Genoese to the French in 1768. In the following year was born Napoleon Bonaparte, the son of a native Corsican family of Italian descent, which had played a considerable rôle in the island. 

He was sent at an early age to a military school in France where he learned the French language, although he never could speak it well. He distinguished himself in school especially in mathematics and in history, and at the age of sixteen received a commission as second lieutenant of the artillery. 

Napoleon's comrades, who were mostly from the French nobility, had snubbed him a great deal, and this, together with his reading of Rousseau, made him despise aristocrats and wish to free his native island from French control. After several unsuccessful attempts to do this, he fled to France in 1793 and joined the Jacobins, whose belief in the power of reason he had already accepted. He began his real military career by planning the scheme which forced the English out of Toulon. We have already seen how he won recognition from the government by repelling the attack of the mob upon the Convention. In 1796 

Napoleon married Josephine Beauharnais (bō-år-ně′), a widow with friends among the Directors. We shall now see how he made himself Emperor of France, and dictator of European affairs, and became liberal leader in reforms that last to this day. 

1. In a Brilliant Italian Campaign Napoleon Defeats the Austrians and Greatly Extends French Control. The war against Austria was still going on although the French 586

NAPOLEON BONAPARTE 

587 were having no success along the Rhine. Through his wife's influence, Napoleon obtained command of the poorly equipped army which had been organized to invade northern Italy. 

In the words of Count Von Metternich (mět'ĕr-nik), the great Austrian chancellor, Italy at this time was "only a geographical expression." The Austrians held Milan, while the 

Duchy of Tuscany was ruled by an Austrian prince, as were the smaller Duchies of Parma and Modena (mó-dā'nä). The rich kingdom of Naples, the States of the Church, Piedmont (pēd'mont), and the Republics of Genoa and Venice, which still possessed Venetia (vé-nē´shì-à) and Dalmatia (dăl-ma'shi-ȧ) and a part of Lom'bar-dy, made up the rest of the peninsula.

Napoleon defeated the Austrians before they realized that he had arrived. He then struck at the Piedmont and forced its king to make peace, and to admit French garrisons to certain towns. After that, many of the other Italian princes, including even the Pope, hastened to buy a truce with the sacrifice of many of their finest pictures and sculptures, and some of their rarest old books and manuscripts. All of these were sent to 

Paris to the recently created museums and libraries, and to endear Napoleon to the French people whose vanity he understood so well.

By April, 1797, Napoleon had defeated the Austrians in eighteen pitched battles. His outposts advanced to within fifty miles of Vienna. The Emperor sued for peace, and while the negotiations were proceeding, Napoleon captured Venice. 

Using that city and Dalmatia as a bribe, he induced the Emperor to agree to the famous Treaty of Cam'pó Fôr'mi-o, by which France acquired the Austrian Netherlands, the Emperor pledging himself to use his influence in the forthcoming Diet of the Empire to aid her in advancing to the Rhine. Napoleon made 

Lombardy into the Cis-ălpine Republic, and Genoa and the adjacent seacoast into a Li-gū'rì-ăn Republic, both of which were under the control of France.

2. 

Napoleon Strikes at England through the Egyptian Expedition. Napoleon returned to France as a national hero. 

England was now the only power left to be dealt with. He reasoned that the best way to bring her to terms was to strike at her rich Indian trade. Then as now the key to India was 

Egypt, nominally a dependency of the Turks but in reality dominated by the Măm'e-lukes, a military aristocracy. So great was 

Napoleon's popularity that the Directory had to agree to his plan. He reached Egypt in the spring of 1798 with a small army, after occupying Malta and barely escaping the English fleet under Lord Nelson. However, the French fleet was destroyed shortly afterward by Nelson in Ä-bü'kir Bay and Napoleon was cut off from France. 

On July 21, he fought near Cairo the famous Battle of the Pyramids and became master of lower Egypt. After invading 

Syria and failing to capture Acre, he abandoned the undertaking, owing to the activities of the English fleet. When he learned that the power of the Directory was on the decline and that a new coalition had been formed against the country, Napoleon set sail secretly for home. 

Out of the Egyptian Expedition came some very important results. Napoleon had carried with him a large body of scientists and to these the modern world owes its first knowledge of the remains of ancient Egypt. It was one of his officers who found the Rosetta stone. 

3. Napoleon Becomes First Consul. As soon as Napoleon reached France, he laid plans to gain control of the government. With the collusion of one of the directors, the same 

Abbé Sièyes (a-bā' sya-yes'), who ten years before had fathered the resolution that the deputies of the Third Estate were the National Assembly, he caused three of the Directory to resign and the other two to be arrested. Then with the assistance of his own brother, who happened to be a member of the Council of Five Hundred, he ousted all the members of

NAPOLEON BONAPARTE 

589 that body opposed to his scheme. Thereupon, the Five Hundred proceeded to elect as consul Napoleon, together with Sièyes and another willing tool. To Sièyes was intrusted the task of drafting one more constitution for France. Napoleon's popularity was so great that, when this constitution was submitted for ratification, barely 1,500 votes were registered against it. "Now," said Jacques (the nickname of the French peasantry), "we shall have peace, thanks to God and Napoleon. 

By this constitution, Napoleon became "First Consul" with two associate consuls who had no executive power. As First 

Consul, he was commander of the army and navy and in control of all the important officials of the government. Legislation was to be accomplished by four bodies, each with a separate task. Needless to say, under any such system legislation was quite impossible, so the power of the First Consul was almost absolute. 

4. Napoleon Makes Peace. Napoleon's first effort as 

First Consul was to conciliate just as many disaffected Frenchmen as possible; then he turned his attention to foreign affairs. 

Realizing that France needed peace in order to effect reforms essential to a return of prosperity, he made overtures to George III and the Austrian Emperor. When they refused his proposals, he made another surprise march over the Alps and forced the Emperor to agree to peace on the basis of the Treaty of Campo Formio. By this time the English people were beginning to become tired of war, and the two countries arranged the Treaty of Amiens (à-myǎn') in 1802. The English agreed to restore to France and her allies the colonies which they had seized during the war, except Ceylon and the Spanish island of Trin'i-dăd. 

5. How the Reforms of Napoleon Complete the Work of the Revolution. With the conclusion of peace, Napoleon undertook a series of reforms which might be considered as completing the work of the Revolution. He started building roads and canals, which were destined to be of great aid to the

commercial development of Europe. He wiped out the assignats, which had become worthless, and established a sound currency, permitting a revival of industry and commerce. He organized the National Bank of France, which is still in operation, and he reopened the universities under the control of the state. By far the most outstanding of his reforms was the codification of the law. This had been started during the Revolution, but little progress had been made. Napoleon appointed a commission which carried it through, and to this day it is known as the Code Napoleon. It was based upon the Roman law and was such an able piece of work that it formed the basis of the codes of continental Europe and Latin America. 

Napoleon's most difficult problem was the question of religion. Although he was not a churchman, he realized that civil order could not be secure in France without religion. He also knew the love of the French people for the Catholic Church, and so he ordered the churches to be reopened and sought an understanding with the Pope. He entered into a formal agreement with the Pope, the so-called Con-côr'dăt, by which the Catholic faith was acknowledged as the religion of the majority of the French people, but freedom of worship was guaranteed to all religious bodies. All bishops were to be nominated by the 

First Consul but invested by the Pope; priests were to be appointed by the bishops subject to approval by the government. 

The church lands were not to be returned but the clergy were to be supported by the state. This arrangement worked so well that it continued in force until 1905. 

6. Napoleon Becomes Emperor. Napoleon had no intention of remaining a consul. He had been elected in 1799, for ten years, and three years later was made consul for life and given the right to name his successor. But he now determined upon the restoration of monarchy. As an aid to this, he instituted a new decoration, called the Legion of Honor, which he bestowed with a lavish hand. He also got rid of as many of

NAPOLEON BONAPARTE 

591 the remainders of the Revolution as he could. The republican title "citoyen" (se-twȧ-yǎn')-citizen-was supplanted by the older "monsieur" (me-syû')-mister; the new calendar was abandoned and the old calendar with its Sundays was restored; the former titles of nobility were again brought into use. An attempt of the Bourbons to restore the old dynasty gave Napoleon a pretext for claiming that the only way to eliminate royalist uprisings was to give France a hereditary ruler. The 

Senate accepted the suggestion and invited Napoleon to become the "Emperor of the French." Its action received the approval of the nation by an overwhelming vote. And so, on December 2, 1804, in the Cathedral of Notre Dame (nōtr' dam') he crowned himself and Josephine, while the Pope was present as an onlooker. The next year at Milan he also crowned himself king of Italy with the Iron Cross of Lombardy.

7. Napoleon Seeks for More Power. The peace with 

England was of short duration. England had failed to give up some of her conquests, and France had compelled Holland and Spain and the other European countries under French control to impose prohibitive duties on English manufactures. Finally, William Pitt formed a coalition of England, Russia, Austria, and Sweden, for the purpose of restoring the balance of power.

The result of all this was ruin for the trade of Europe, and for America, too. The commercial and industrial prosperity which had developed in France was crippled, and many of the bourgeoisie blamed him for the business stagnation. The trade of the neutrals, especially that of the United States, began to suffer from the privateers of both countries. President Jefferson had Congress pass the Embargo Act, to the great disgust of the American ship-owners. It was to the shortage of sugar caused by these blockades that the beet sugar industry of Europe may trace its beginning. Opposition to Napoleon arose in every quarter. 

9. The Beginning of the End of Napoleon. When Por tugal refused to submit to Napoleon's Continental System, a French army was dispatched thither by way of Spain. The defeat of Portugal, whose royal family fled to Brazil, was of little importance, but it led to one of the chief causes for Napoleon's downfall. With his army in the Peninsula, Napoleon obtained the Spanish crown by a trick and bestowed it on his brother Joseph. The incensed Spaniards of all classes rose to drive out the French, and established jun'tăs or local assemblies. 

They carried on guerilla warfare until England sent an army under the command of Sir Arthur Wellesley (wělz'li), afterward known as the Duke of Wellington.

Once more Austria joined the struggle, but she suffered new defeat at Wagram (vä’gräm) and had to sue for peace. In the 

Treaty of Vienna which followed, Napoleon took more territory from the Emperor. Shortly afterward the Emperor was forced to allow Napoleon to marry his daughter, the Archduchess Marie Louise, as Josephine had been divorced because she had given Napoleon no children. 

10. Napoleon Unwisely Invades Russia and Loses His 

Army. Napoleon's marriage to the Archduchess Marie Louise was regarded by the Tsar as a menace to his own sovereignty.

He prepared to invade Russia, against the advice of his more farsighted counsellors. Late in the summer of 1812, he started with six hundred thousand men.

Napoleon waited This policy was issued by the famous English firm of for a month, trying to bring the Russians to battle, and then, with winter staring him in the face, and without proper supplies for such a climate, he was compelled to retreat. Beset by great hardships-hunger, cold, and incessant harassing by countless swarms of Cossacks -barely twenty thousand of the huge army that had crossed the Neiman (ne'măn), only six months before, finally reached Poland. It was only the iron will of Marshal Ney (nā), who protected the rear with a body of picked troops, that saved the army from complete destruction. 

11. The War of Liberation from Napoleon Is Started. 

The conquest of Prussia in 1806 had furnished her great statesman, Baron von Stein (shtin), an opportunity to carry out

some reforms. Industry had been freed from all restrictions, serfdom had been abolished, and the public finances had been improved. At the same time, General Schärnhôrst had introduced universal military service and begun the training of a new army according to the best practices of the day. More than that, the presence of French garrisons had stimulated tremendous national feeling, much as it did in other parts of Germany.

Immediately after the Russian disaster, the German and Austrian princes began negotiations with the Tsar. Von Stein urged him to assume the rôle of "Liberator of Europe from the Napoleonic menace." England was prevailed upon to finance the undertaking, and in return for her subsidies even Napoleon's former marshal, Bernadotte (bûr-na-doť′), who had been elected king by the Swedes, took the field against his former chief. Finally, on March 16, 1813, the weak-kneed 

Frederick William declared war against France.

Before Napoleon could assemble a new army, the French garrisons were driven out of Prussia and other parts of Germany. Napoleon won a doubtful victory, but he was forced to retire to Leipsig to escape being cut off from the Rhine. 

Here, on October 16, began the so-called Battle of the Nations. 

Napoleon was completely defeated, barely escaping capture, and his control in Europe completely collapsed. 

12. Napoleon Abdicates and a Bourbon Prince Is Once

More Made King of France. The allies now offered Napoleon the Rhine and the Maritime Alps as the "natural frontiers" of France, but these favorable terms, just as after the revolutionary wars, were rejected. At that very moment three large allied armies were approaching the Rhine, and the Duke of Wellington was threatening to cross the Pyrenees. Napoleon attempted some resistance, but the allies marched directly on 

Paris and on March 31, 1814, the city surrendered. Napoleon soon abdicated and he and his empress were separated, but they

NAPOLEON BONAPARTE 

599 were allowed to keep their imperial titles. He received the little island of Ĕl'bȧ in the Mediterranean as a principality, and an annual pension of two million francs. Louis XVIII, the brother of Louis XVI, who had been living in England, was recalled and placed on the throne with the support of the allied armies. Louis then concluded with his benefactors a treaty in which the boundaries of France were fixed as at the beginning of 1792. After that, he proclaimed a Charter which made 

France a constitutional monarchy. 

13. The "Hundred Days," Napoleon's Return and His 

Decisive Defeat at Waterloo. But Napoleon was not finished. While the allies were gathered at Vienna rearranging the affairs of Europe, Napoleon escaped from Elba and landed in France. His journey to Paris was a triumphal march. One general after another returned to his banner, including even Marshal Ney, who had promised Louis to bring Napoleon back in an iron cage. Napoleon re-entered the Tuileries without shedding a drop of French blood. The king and his supporters fled across the frontiers. The powers at Vienna at once proclaimed Napoleon the public enemy of Europe and to meet the menace, laid aside their map-making. 

As usual, Napoleon struck first by advancing against an English army near Brussels, commanded by the Duke of Wellington. At Waterloo the failure of a lieutenant to stop a Prussian army led to his defeat. 

He hurried to Paris and, after abdicating a second time, set out for the coast, in hope of embarking for America. When he found that this was impossible, he surrendered to an English admiral. Thus ended the "Hundred Days" that cost Europe the useless loss of forty thousand lives. To prevent any possible recurrence of such a disturbance of the peace, the allies decided that Napoleon should spend the remainder of his days on the rocky islet of St. Hě-le'nà in the South Atlantic. There he lived a prisoner of the British government, devoting his time

to writing his Memoirs, until his death on May 5, 1821. 

14. The Significance of Napoleon. In the short space of less than twenty years Napoleon had created more changes in the map of Europe than any other man up to that time, or since. 

He had plunged Europe into a series of wars, yet not all his efforts must be measured in terms of bloodshed. As an administrator, he gave France strong government and laid the foundation of much of her later greatness. By his canals and roads and other public improvements, he fostered industry and commerce. In warfare, his use of artillery marked a new development in tactics which accounts in part for his victories and changed the course of military science. 

Absolute though his power was, he enforced the revolutionary idea of equality by furnishing opportunity to the people of the lowest ranks to rise high in government service. Wherever his soldiers went, they carried with them many of the concepts of the Revolution. He created the first Kingdom of Italy and compelled the first steps toward the unification of Germany. It was his control, too, that inspired in Italians and Germans their first feelings of nationalism. Nor were his reforms confined to the territories under his control, for in order to compete with him his enemies had to inject many modern ideas into their obsolete political machines. No doubt, his political influence would have been greater if he had not been considered the natural outcome of the French Revolution, the ideas of which the monarchs of Europe had agreed must be rooted out for the sake of the welfare of society.

CHAPTER LXIV  RESTORES THE OLD RÉGIME IN EUROPE AND REVOLUTIONARY IDEAS ARE REPRESSED 

When the allies met at Vienna in September, 1814, to remake the map of Europe, they were faced with a number of serious problems. The Congress was presided over by Count 

Metternich, who was the leading statesman of Europe and who hated everything connected with the Revolution. The cleverest person in attendance, however, was Talleyrand (tǎl'î-rănd), the French minister of Foreign Affairs, whose skill won for him a place in all the discussions against the intention to allow France no voice in the arrangements. 

Each power desired to gain as much as possible from the struggle, regardless of racial or religious responsibilities, or national aspirations. The outstanding problems were the restoring of the rulers, the status of Italy and Germany, and the control of the new possessions. It was decided that the frontiers which existed before the Revolution should be restored, and that the several crowns should be returned to the legitimate rulers. 

1. The Congress of Vienna Remakes the Map of Eu rope. Holland was made into the Kingdom of the Netherlands, and to it were added the Austrian Netherlands, much against the wishes of the inhabitants, in return for the Dutch colonies given to England. Switzerland was organized as a loose confederation of cantons and pledged to observe neutrality in European affairs in return for a guarantee of protection. In Italy, the old princes were given back their little principalities, Genoa was given to the king of Sardinia, and 602

Venice and her possessions to the emperor of Austria. Norway was taken from Denmark and given to the king of Sweden. in place of Pomerania, which went to Prussia, and of Finland, which was handed over to Russia. England received Malta, the Ionian Islands, Ceylon, and Cape Colony. 

THE CONGRESS OF VIENNA 

One of the more formal sessions of this gathering where the great questions of European diplomacy were said to have been settled at balls and banquets. 

In central Europe the problem was more difficult. The Congress almost broke up over what to do with Saxony and Poland. 

The king of Saxony had been allied with Napoleon, and Prussia insisted that his kingdom should be taken away and handed over to her. She was also strongly opposed to Russia's getting 

Poland. Although to comply with Prussia's wishes in the matter of Saxony would violate the rights of a legitimate ruler, the Tsar was willing that an exception should be made in this case, provided Frederick William would consent to his acquiring Poland. Finally, through the skill of Talleyrand, a com-

promise was effected. Prussia was given her old Westphalian lands together with territory on both sides of the Rhine. Part of Poland was made into a new kingdom with the Tsar as its king, but with an administration entirely separate from that of Russia. 

2. A Loose German Confederation under Austrian

Domination Replaces the Independent States. It was impossible to restore the old Germany. Napoleon, in reducing the more than three hundred states to thirty-eight, had ended the Holy Roman Empire. No one, not even Metternich, cared to restore either the lost states or the Empire, so the question was what sort of organization Germany should have. 

Many of the states, including Prussia, were desirous of a close organization, but Metternich would not agree to this because he feared the power of Prussia. Instead, he insisted upon a loose 

Confederation, with a permanent council, called the Diet of Frankfort, under the presidency of Austria. In this Diet two foreign monarchs-the kings of the Netherlands and of Denmark-were represented. 

Each member of the Confederation retained full sovereignty but agreed not to enter into foreign relations which would be harmful to Germany. War among the states was also proscribed. The constitution of the confederation provided that each prince should grant a constitution to his subjects, but this provision was delayed in some instances for nearly thirty years.

This proved a great disappointment to the German patriots, who had fought so bravely to overthrow Napoleon, in the hope of winning constitutional government. 

3. The Aims of the Quadruple Alliance and the "Holy 

Alliance." At the close of the Congress, England, Austria, Russia, and Prussia continued their Quadruple Alliance to enforce the settlement. Three years later they admitted France to membership. During the next few years this organization under the resounding title of the "Concert of Europe" held

4. Metternich Overawes the Germans. Under the influence of the French Revolution and the national feeling caused by French occupation, there had developed in Germany a widespread liberal feeling. In southern Germany it was strong enough to cause a number of the princes to grant constitutions similar to the Charter proclaimed by Louis XVIII. These lib-

eral ideas appealed especially to literary men and students; in fact, the development of a national feeling in Germany was due largely to the liberal writings of Schil'ler and other men of letters.

The students formed societies known as the Tugendbund (tü'gent-bünt). As the three hundredth anniversary of the publishing of Luther's theses approached, they planned a great celebration at the Wartburg. When the day came, in imitation of Luther's burning the papal bull, they proceeded to burn various things connected with the old régime. This event alarmed Metternich greatly and he began to consider a way to suppress the society. The opportunity came two years later when a fanatical student assassinated a Russian spy. Metternich then got the Diet to promulgate the Karlsbad (kärls'bät) Decrees, placing restrictions on professors and students, and the press, and declaring that constitutions were not consistent with monarchy. 

5. Liberal Movements Are Put Down in Spain and

Portugal. The struggle against the French occupation of Spain had resulted, in 1812, in the proclaiming of a liberal constitution by the Spanish people themselves. When Ferdinand VII was reseated on the throne in 1814, he proceeded to abolish this, and to re-establish the Inquisition and to restore the privileges of the clergy. Yet, the liberal movement was kept alive, largely through the influence of secret societies, like the Freemasons. Finally, in 1820, several regiments, which were about to sail for America to put down revolutions in the colonies there, revolted. Before long all Spain was ablaze. Ferdinand appealed to the other European powers for assistance, and Tsar Alexander, whom Metternich had converted to the reactionary point of view, was anxious to send an army to help put down this insurrection. However, there was some opposition, so the powers held a Congress at Verona in 1822. 

In this Congress George Canning, the new English minister

of Foreign Affairs, opposed the employment of the Quadruple Alliance to stamp out every movement to extend constitutional government. When this Congress adopted a regulation against revolution and agreed that Louis XVIII might intervene in behalf of his unfortunate Bourbon relative, England withdrew from the Alliance. With the assistance of the French, Ferdinand succeeded in putting down the revolt, and Spain remained on the reactionary side.

King John of Portugal returned in 1815 from his flight to Brazil and consented to the constitution which had been proclaimed in his absence. Soon afterward, however, the reactionaries, led by his son, Dom Miguel (mé-gěl'), started trouble. When the French arrived in Spain in 1823, the latter obtained control of the government and hastened to revoke this constitution. Since that time Portugal has been a constant prey to revolution. 

6. The Reaction Takes Place in Italy in Spite of the 

Liberals. All the restored states of Italy were of the reactionary type, although there were many liberals among the people. 

As in Spain, secret societies, including the Freemasons and the Carbonari (kär-bó-nä're) or "charcoal burners," carried on revolutionary ideas. They were especially strong in the Kingdom of Naples and the Two Sicilies, whose king had privately promised Metternich not to recognize the new ideas in his government. When news of the first successes of the revolt in 

Spain reached Naples, a revolution broke out. The king was forced to grant a constitution, but afterward appealed to the powers for help. Metternich immediately sent an army which crushed the liberals with extreme cruelty. For the next few years, Naples and the Two Sicilies enjoyed the reputation of having the worst governed state in Europe. A similar revolt broke out in Piedmont and this also was put down with the aid of Austrian troops. By 1821 the control of Italy by the 

Emperor, and therefore by Metternich, was complete.

7. The Greeks Win Independence from Turkey. South eastern Europe had largely escaped being drawn into the French Revolution, chiefly because of its remoteness. It continued to suffer, however, from the old government of the Turks, who had not yet been able to adapt themselves to modern political 

THE ARREST OF THE CARBONARI 

The authorities used every means possible to suppress these revolutionary organizations to which men of even the highest classes belonged. 

After a drawing in Bertolini's Storia del Risorgimento Italiano. conditions. Of all the people under their control, the Greeks were the most progressive and the most prosperous. During the Napoleonic wars they had profited greatly, for, protected by the neutrality of the Turkish flag. they had extended their trading throughout the Mediterranean. At last, aroused by the

stirring folk songs of their struggles with the Turks and by the work of their poet Korais (kō-rās'), they had begun to aspire for independence. In 1815, they organized a patriotic society known as the Hetaria (hé-të'ri-ȧ) Phil-i-kē', whose object was to restore the Greek Empire. 

The war for Greek Independence began in 1821 in an outbreak of the Hetaria of Moldavia, but it spread to Greece and the islands where it became a pitiless contest between the Christians and Muslims. America and western Europe made generous contributions to the war chest of the patriots and so many young European and American adventurers like Lord Byron took up their cause that the Turks complained that they were having to fight all Europe. The war dragged for years, partly because of the weakness of the Turks and partly because of quarrels among the Greeks themselves. Metternich from the beginning was opposed to the Greeks and their aspirations, while England and France, and eventually Russia, were in favor of them.

By an accident the combined English and French fleets which had been sent to watch developments destroyed the entire Turkish navy in the harbor of Navarino (nä-vä-rēnō). The Russians declared war on Turkey and forced the Turks in a humiliating treaty to recognize the independence of Greece. Two years later, the new Greek state was definitely established but with restricted boundaries and with a foreign king. Thus began the modern dismemberment of Turkey and the Eastern Question appeared in the front rank of European problems. 

8. The July Revolution of 1830 in France Brings the 

Bourgeoisie into Control Again. Louis XVIII died in 1824, and his brother, Charles X, a Catholic and a strong absolutist, became king of France. During the Revolution he had made himself especially objectionable to Frenchmen by plotting against the republic. France was now regarded the soundest country in Europe in spite of bad harvests and the recent oc-

cupation of her border fortresses by the allied armies. Her national debt was only one-sixth of that of England and her taxes were correspondingly low. Thanks to her new tariff on corn, silk, iron, and steel, agriculture and industry were thriving. The quick recovery of France from twenty years of social and military disturbances was the marvel of the day. 

At Charles's instigation, laws were enacted to restrict the liberties of the press, and to increase the privileges of the clergy and of the nobility. In 1825, a bill was passed to pay the émigrés for their losses during the Revolution by reducing the interest rate on the public debt. This aroused the anger of the bourgeoisie, for they were the principal bondholders. Matters became worse especially when Charles, in 1830, appointed a reacitonary minister and promulgated his "Five Ordinances" disfranchising three-fourths of the electorate and depriving the press of its liberty. An insurrection broke out. In three days the "divine right" monarchy was overthrown and Louis Philippe (fe-lēp'), the Duke of Orleans, a Bourbon who had taken sides with the Revolution, was placed on the throne. By this action France returned to the theory of the earlier revolution and the bourgeoisie came again into power. 

9. The July Revolution Spreads and Belgium Gains 

Her Independence. The July Revolution was the first real break in Metternich's system. Its significance was immediately felt all over Europe, and popular outbursts occurred in many countries. As a rule, they were easily put down. In the Papal states, Parma, and Modena Austrian troops restored the old conditions. In Poland the Russians had little difficulty in crushing the Polish rebellion and in making the country a part of the Russian Empire. Henceforth, Poland became one of the "sore spots" of Europe.

In the old Austrian Netherlands, the revolution accomplished its purpose. The inhabitants were Catholics and French sympathizers, and resented being placed under Dutch control by

10. The End of the Metternich Régime. The revolu tions in Greece, France, and Belgium can be said to mark the end of the genuine reactionary period, even though Metternich did remain in power in Austria until 1848, and continued to dominate the affairs of Germany and Italy. Outside of those areas, however, the newer ideas had freedom to grow, and new

means of communication and changes in economic conditions made it difficult to keep the ideas from spreading. Moreover, the fact that Metternich still forced his reactionary policies on Germany and Italy did much to stimulate among the peoples of both countries a growth of democratic ideas and a rise of nationalistic feelings. But before we consider the changes, we must look at the revolution which had been going on in the economic world and which was now beginning to have an influence upon the affairs of the continent of Europe.

CHAPTER LXV HOW  COMPLETELY CHANGED THE SOCIAL AND ECONOMIC ORDER OF THE PAST 

It is hard to realize how little progress Europe had made in industrial methods prior to the middle of the eighteenth century. Thread was still spun with the distaff; cloth was woven on crude hand looms; iron was smelted in small brick forges with the aid of hand bellows; fields were barely scraped with cumbersome wooden plows; grain was cut with sickles and threshed with flails; and lumber was sawed and planed by hand. 

But during the last quarter of the eighteenth and the first half of the nineteenth centuries, the process of production and distribution of goods was greatly changed. Through the development of the steam engine and its application to newly invented machinery, and because of improved methods of transportation, industry was taken out of the homes and concentrated into workshops and factories. 

Accompanying these developments was a long series of social and economic changes, which more completely altered the world in a short time than any other single series of events. In order to understand the meaning of this Industrial Revolution, it is necessary to study some of the important improvements and to note their effect. 

1. The Industrial Revolution Begins in England with 

Improvements in the Textile Industry. In the eighteenth century, cloth was the most important manufactured product. 

When England gained control of the markets of the world in 1763, the English cloth-makers began to prosper greatly, their only complaint being that the spinners could not produce yarn fast enough to meet the needs of the weavers. This was partly 613

overcome in 1770, when James Hargreaves (här'grēvz) invented a machine by which eight threads could be spun at once. However, this "jenny," as it was called, did not make

Thread was now produced so fast that the weavers could not keep up with the spinners.

The cotton growers in the southern part of the United States could not supply the raw material fast enough to keep pace with

the demand, until Eli Whitney, in 1792, invented his cotton gin, which would clean as much lint in an hour as a negro in a week. 

2. The Steam Engine Is the Next Big Step in the In dustrial Revolution. Although the steam engine invented by 

Thomas Newcomen was used for pumping water out of English coal mines, it was not very satisfactory because the steam pushed the piston in only one direction. In 1764, James Watt, a Scotch instrument-maker at the University of Glasgow, became interested in Newcomen's engine and invented the present steam engine. After many disappointments, with the assistance. of Matthew Bolton, he built an engine which could be connected with machinery by means of shafts and cranks. The first of these engines was set up in 1776 in an iron foundry and nine years later another one was put into operation in a cotton mill. 

A MODEL OF WHITNEY'S 

COTTON GIN 

In the National Museum, Washington. 

How much cost did this save?

From this beginning we may reckon the Age of Steam. 

Henceforth man was independent of the changes of nature for his power. By the end of the century, many of the textile mills had set up engines to re-enforce their water power during the dry season. 

3. The Development of Iron and Steel Aids the Various 

Inventions. The development of machinery and of the steam engine demanded large supplies of cheap iron and steel. England had great beds of iron ore, but she had not mined much of it before the eighteenth century. Charcoal was used for smelting and the supply of English timber was greatly limited,

consequently the larger part of the iron of Europe came from Norway, Sweden, and Russia, where there were great beds of ore and also enormous forests. In 1713 Abram Darby discovered that coal could be used in the smelting process in place of charcoal, and some years later his son began the use of coke. 

About the same time, John Huntsman discovered a new method of producing steel and this substance proved far more durable in machinery than the softer iron. In his process, however, he used the purer Swedish iron ore, until, in 1775; Henry

Quart found out how to refine the English ore. A few years before this, other iron workers had developed the blast furnace which cheapened the process of smelting. And not long after the perfection of the steam engine, a great steam-driven hammer was invented. As a result of all these discoveries and improvements, England could make use of her other inventions in a large way. 

4. The Improvement in Transportation Makes the Industrial Revolution Possible. The Industrial Revolution would not have been possible if there had been no revolution in transportation, because successful manufacturing depends on an easy and cheap movement of raw materials and finished products. Before the application of steam power to transportation, the only known motive forces were wind, water, and the muscle of man and beast. For this reason all the earlier manufacturing centres were located close to navigable bodies of water, or on highways. Europe at the beginning of the Industrial Revolution was without any adequate system of roads. 

Even as late as the Napoleonic Era, people travelled on horseback or in litters, or at the best in cumbersome stage coaches, and were fortunate if they could make fifty miles a day. Goods moved on pack animals even more slowly. 

One of the first effects of the Industrial Revolution was to stimulate the construction of roads. During the eighteenth century, England and Scotland built a system of hard-surfaced

highways-the first since the Roman era over which wheeled traffic could move-and during this same period a number of canals were completed. Long before this, however, it had been discovered that, by the use of wooden rails, the movement of wagons could be made more quickly, but they had been employed mainly in connection with the mining of coal. When iron became cheap in the latter part of the eighteenth century, these wooden rails were covered with strips of iron. 

5. The Railway and the Steamship 

Supply the Need for Quick Transportation. As soon as the steam engine was perfected, engineers began to study how to apply it to transportation. The

STEPHENSON'S ENGINE, THE "ROCKET" 

Compare it with "Puffing Billy" and with a modern locomotive. question was solved by George Stephenson, an engineer at one of the collieries. It was not until 1784, when he discovered how to use exhaust steam to improve the draft of the fire, that his "Puffing Billy" proved that cars could be pulled by travelling steam engines. Then eleven years followed before the idea was applied to the transportation of passengers and goods on the little twelve-mile tramway known as the Stockton and Darlington Railway. Shortly after that, a railway was built connecting Manchester with Liverpool. Within the next thirty years, the device spread over the world.

While these changes were taking place in transportation on land, the use of the steam engine was also being applied to the

driving of vessels on water. As early as 1802, a boat driven by steam-driven paddles appeared on the Firth of Clyde Canal in northern England. Five years later Robert Fulton with his

Clermont on the Hudson river showed that steamboats could be successful. In 1819, a sailing vessel equipped with steam engines crossed the Atlantic in twenty-five days, and in 1833, the Royal William steamed from Quebec to London. Regular

THE BRITANNIA-1840 

This first steamer of the Cunard Line began regular trips between England and America in 1840 with sixty-three passengers. sailings across the Atlantic were established in 1838 by the Great Western, which made the passage in fifteen days. Two years later the Cu-närd' Steamship Company was founded. 

Until 1845, all steamships were built of wood and equipped with paddle wheels. In that year the iron steamer Great Britain driven by a screw propeller began a new era in steamship construction. Iron ships can be built much longer and larger, and carry twice as much cargo as wooden ships. 

6. The Telegraph and Cable Provide Rapid Communication. The experiments with electricity in the early part

of the nineteenth century led the American, Samuel F. B. 

Morse, to invent the electric telegraph in 1837. In the following year it was adopted by one of the English railway lines, but it did not come into general use until 1843. The following year, a telegraph line connected Baltimore and Washington. 

THE COMPLETION OF THE CABLE 

The arrival of the Great Eastern in Newfoundland, July 27, 1866, marked the successful completion of the first Atlantic cable. How many cables now cross the Atlantic?

From a contemporary print. 

No sooner was the land telegraph established than an attempt was made to lay telegraph lines enclosed in a cable under the sea. This was easy under small bodies of water like the 

English Channel, but very difficult in the Atlantic Ocean. Cable communication between England and America was not completed until 1865. In this year, the Great Eastern, a steamship of twenty-four thousand tons, which had been, because of her size, a loss to her owners, proved to be the very thing needed to carry the enormous length of cable required to reach across the Atlantic.

7. How the Industrial Revolution Spreads to Other 

Parts of the World. The greater part of the earlier inventions had their origin in England and the English manufacturers tried to guard them as trade secrets. However, after the 

Revolutionary War, workmen began to cross to America to introduce them, and the first cotton mill was established in New England in 1789. At first the American cotton mills were run by water power, but by 1800, steam engines had come into use. 

A great stimulus was given to manufacturing in the United States by the changes in international trade due to the Napoleonic Wars, and especially to the War of 1812 with England. 

By the time this war was ended, cotton milling gave employment to over one hundred thousand persons, and woollen mills took care of fifty thousand more, while the smelting of iron in New Jersey and Pennsylvania had increased very rapidly. 

It was the haste of the English manufacturers to attempt to win back their American markets by flooding them with the accumulated stocks of their mills and factories that embarked the United States on its policy of high protection. 

The spread of the Industrial Revolution was much slower on the Continent. In France it did not really get started until 

1825, because the guilds controlled industry, and because of the demoralization occasioned by the French Revolution and the Napoleonic Wars. Within twenty years, as many as thirty thousand power looms had been set up, and Bordeaux, Lyons, Toulouse, and Paris had become great manufacturing centres. 

Indeed, we shall find that it was the factory workers of Paris that started the revolutionary movement ending in the overthrow of Louis Philippe in 1848. The industrialization of other parts of Europe did not begin until much later. For example, the Germans were a poor agricultural people until 1870, and manufacturing had been free from control by the guilds for only a few years. Their great industrial growth may be said to date from the acquisition in their war with France of the rich

iron deposits of Alsace and the coal beds of the Saar (zär).

8. The Revolution in Agriculture Also Begins Late in the Eighteenth Century. During the later eighteenth century the older systems of cultivation and farm management also felt the influence of the scientific discoveries, and England had what has been called the "Agricultural Revolution." The old strips and common fields disappeared and farms of considerable size, operated for profit, took their place. New vegetables, such as turnips and the common meadow grasses like timothy, were introduced. By scientific selection of seed and the use of fertilizers, the yield was doubled. The farm animals were also improved by scientific breeding, and their weights were increased by a half, certain strains from particular sections like Southdown sheep, Berkshire hogs, and Clydesdale horses becoming famous. And last but not least, agriculture became so popular that George Washington and George III were notable as scientific farmers. 

With the Industrial Revolution came improved farming tools, and, more slowly, the use of machinery in farming operations. We have already noticed the invention of the cotton gin near the close of the eighteenth century, but even earlier had come the seed drill. In the next century, the mower and the reaper lightened the labor of harvesting, although the use of improved machinery for plowing and harrowing was delayed until a light engine had been made available. With this development came the rise of farming on a large scale, made possible by the use of heavy, labor-saving machinery. The absence of such farming in England and on the Continent explains why Europe fell behind in the adoption of the new methods, although she retained her superiority in yield ner acre and excellence of quality. 

9. The Separation of Capital and Labor Takes Place under the Factory System. The building and equipping of factories involved the expenditure of large sums of money.

The capitalists who supplied the money naturally were anxious to obtain as great profits as possible from their investments. 

The laborers were paid by time rather than by output, and the superintendent tried to get the greatest amount of work of which they were capable. Human life counted very little. 

The rapid increase in the use of machinery threw many of the old hand-workers out of work. In England the workers resisted the factory system as long as they could, and from time to time attempted to destroy the machines to which they attributed all their troubles. In many cases, especially in spinning, women and children could do the work as well as men, and could be had for much lower wages. As the number of employees increased the contact between them and the owners became correspondingly less. Very often the owners never visited the factories but controlled them through hired superintendents, whose jobs depended on keeping down the cost of production. There soon developed a wide chasm between capital and labor. 

10. Disastrous Social Conditions Accompany the Industrial Revolution. The concentration of the workers in factory towns so different from the little villages in which they had formerly lived, together with the employment of women and children, and the long hours of labor, had disastrous social effects. One can scarcely believe the horrible accounts of the poverty, vice and crime, in the early English factory towns. 

Men, women, and children were thrown together under the most disagreeable conditions, and the monotony of their tasks led them to drink and gambling.

The streets of these first "mill-towns" were nothing more than filthy alleys filled with the most offensive refuse. The only water supply came from foul cisterns and shallow wells in yards little better than quagmires. The overflowing of cesspools, and the presence of open toilets, caused sickness to be rampant, and the death rate, especially of children, was very

רית gh. Tuberculosis, or as it was called "quick consumption," took a heavy toll, and many became old prematurely. 

These conditions led to a demand for legislation. In spite of the insistence that employers ought to be allowed to do as they pleased since they were bringing such great wealth to the nation, Parliament passed a series of laws which kept the children from night work and long hours, and protected the adults against too great use of them. The more spectacular 

WOMAN'S SHARE IN COAL MINING 

evils slowly disappeared, but many still remained. Work in the factory took the woman away from home and frequently allowed her no opportunity to do those things which are usually thought of as woman's work, such as the preparation of food and clothing for the family and the care of the children, therefore she gradually lost her interest in home life. We are only now beginning to realize what effect this is going to have on society. 

12. Every Nation Feels the Political Effects of the In dustrial Revolution. The industrialization of a country depends upon machinery and power, hence an adequate supply of iron and coal becomes of importance. A study of the map of 

Europe will show that those countries which became industrial-

ized first were liberally supplied with both of these essentials. 

But since the output of manufactured goods could be increased with the aid of power-driven machinery, supplies of all sorts of raw materials became more and more necessary. At the same time expanding markets were equally essential, for it was soon discovered that goods could be made more cheaply in large quantities.

Another question was presented whether factories should be given protection from foreign competition. Influenced by the old idea of mercantilism, some believed that industries should be protected by tariffs; others, who accepted Adam Smith's theories, insisted that the best results would be obtained by free competition since competition would allow each nation to develop those industries for which it was best fitted. Behind these two views lay widely different theories of international relationships; the protectionists wanted a strong self-contained nation, the free traders would sacrifice nationalism for a united world. At the same time, England developed free trade because her factories had already won their markets before those of other countries had risen. 

13. The Industrial Revolution, the "Laissez Faire"

Theory and the Working Man. It should not be forgotten that the Industrial Revolution came in England just when Adam Smith's book on The Wealth of Nations expressed the laissez faire theory of economics. According to this theory, the government must not interfere in business, and individuals must not be restricted in their right of making contracts. This meant that the government must not concern itself with such things as wages and conditions of labor, but that they should be left for private agreement between the worker and his employer. After the rise of the factory system, the laborer was more at the mercy of the employer. What seemed to be freedom was often no freedom at all, because the workman lived in the employer's house, bought what he needed at the employer's

store, and had to accept the wages and hours of labor which the employer proposed.

While Parliament argued about this policy, the factory workers began to organize unions in order that they might better their conditions. The employers declared this a conspiracy in restraint of trade, which was a crime under English law. Parliament enacted laws subjecting offenders to imprisonment at hard labor, and finally to deportation to the new penal settlement in Australia. The unions were then organized as social clubs or funeral societies. Like the Carbonari and other secret organizations existing contrary to law, they were soon characterized by extreme violence, directed especially against the "black-legs" and "rats," as those workers who refused to join were called. 

14. Socialism Arises Out of the Industrial Conditions. 

There were, however, a few men who had not lost sight of the individual. They insisted that the betterment of society as a whole was more important than that of a few individuals. 

These reformers came to be called socialists and their theories socialism. One of them, Robert Owen, a wealthy Scotch mill owner, tried to ameliorate the conditions of his workmen and to make New Lăn'ark a model mill village. He cut down the hours of labor, educated the children, and improved the condition of the older people. Although in twenty-nine years he had paid interest on the capital invested and had made a profit of three million dollars, the experiment failed, just as a similar one at New Harmony, Indiana, failed. However, there did survive one feature that has borne rich fruit-the scheme of co-operative shops, now popular in England and on the Continent, in which the profits are divided among the members of the society.

CHAPTER LXVI ENGLAND GRADUALLY BECOMES LIBERAL 

The liberal and democratic movement was slow in getting under way in England. But she had developed parliamentary government as her gift to the world. We have also seen how the 

Industrial Revolution developed in England long before other countries. We shall now see how parliamentary government became more and more popular government. 

1. England Returns to Cabinet Government with the

Retirement of George III. The failing mind of George III 

necessitated the appointment of a regency. Once more the government in theory passed into the hands of the king and Parliament, or, as it was generally stated, of "king, lords, and commons." In reality the country was governed by the cabinet headed by the Prime Minister. So powerful did the cabinet become that it determined not only every policy of the government, but even the words addressed to Parliament by the king, whose chief function came to be that of neutral adviser. 

Regardless of his personal feeling for the individual, the King of England must appoint as the Prime Minister the leader of the leading party in the House of Commons. Then this man selects the other ministers from his party. A ministry may remain in office only so long as it receives the support of the House of Commons. Defeat of one of its measures requires the Prime Minister to resign or call on the king to dissolve Parliament, which means a new election of members of the House of Commons. If the country shows by its votes that it 627

approves of the policy of the ministry, that body will continue in office, otherwise it must retire and the king will then summon the leader of the new party to form another ministry. 

2. The House of Commons Had Not Fairly Repre sented the English People. At the beginning of the nineteenth century, the House of Commons was composed of 625 members. There had been no redistribution of seats since the reign of Charles II, so many of the boroughs had either ceased to exist or could boast few inhabitants, on account of the shifting of population occasioned by the Industrial Revolution. Because their seats were bought and sold, these boroughs had come to be known as "rotten boroughs." There were also many "pocket boroughs," so called because they had become the private property of wealthy men, whose tenants and dependents elected whomsoever the master desired. On the other hand, new industrial cities, such as Birmingham, Manchester, Leeds, and 

Sheffield, were entirely without representation. 

3. With New Issues Old Parties Take New Names. 

The Tory party formed the stronghold of the old régime. The 

Whig party was usually the party of reform, but neither of these party names retained its original significance. The 

Whigs, especially, under the influence of the manufacturers, changed their ideas and stood more and more for the ideals of the middle class. It was because of their attitudes on these questions that the Whigs came to be known as the Liberal party and the Tories as the Conservative party. The wageearners supported the demands of the Liberals because they expected the Liberals to support universal manhood suffrage, which the Liberals had no intention of doing. 

4. Recognition of Trade-Unions Marks the Beginning of Parliamentary Reform. After the Napoleonic Wars Eng land, too, passed through a reaction accompanied with terrible financial depression and acute labor troubles. All sorts of repressive legislation were enacted-the unemployed were even

denied the right of holding public meetings and the writ of ha'bé-ăs côr'pus was suspended. The result was discontent with the existing political conditions. Finally in 1825, the Tories Elecoma

Whigs, it was the first constructive labor legislation in modern times. Three years later it was followed by the repeal of the 

Test and Corporation Acts. None of these acts proved satisfactory, and the demand for reform became more and more insistent.

The property qualification was lowered enough to increase the number of voters fifty per cent, and the time of voting was restricted in each constituency to two days. However, in spite of all these reforms, neither the workmen in the cities nor the laborers in the country had the privilege of suffrage. 

6. The Wage-Earners Draw Up Six Demands in Their

So-Called "Charter of Liberties." The demand for reform did not stop with the passing of the Act of 1832. The wageearners were particularly bitter because they had been ignored after all they had done to aid the demand for reform. Finally, when a shortage of bread developed in 1837, the workmen demanded seats in Parliament, in the hope that they might gain some relief.

In 1839, they formulated their demands in the so-called Charter of Liberties and thereafter were known as the Chartists. 

This charter contained six demands-manhood suffrage, a se-

cret ballot, annual parliamentary elections, equal electoral districts, abolishment of property qualifications for membership in the House of Commons, and payment for service in Parliament. Nine years later the Chartists became militant and threatened a nation-wide strike of all labor until these demands were granted, at the same time announcing that a half-million armed men would bring to Parliament a new petition with six million signatures. 

7. The Chartist Demands Were Refused but Other Important Reforms Were Made. Although the Liberals were now in power, they refused to sponsor any such radical programme. They did, however, effect a number of very important reforms. By the Factory Act of 1833 children were restricted to nine hours work a day, and youths to twelve; and by the Act of 1842 the employment of children under ten years and of women in underground work was forbidden. In 1834, the Poor Law was changed so as to restrict public support to the sick and aged, and to compel able-bodied paupers to go to work. This saved the state a great deal of money, and brought order out of the chaos which had existed ever since the government took over from the church the care of the poor. 

One of the problems confronting the Liberals was the Corn Laws. These laws had been enacted to encourage English agriculture by high protective duties but they had raised the cost of food until it was causing much discontent among the wageearners. The manufacturers favored cheaper food so as to pay lower wages. In 1842, the Liberals put through Parliament a bill which arranged a sliding scale of duties. Meanwhile Richard Cobden and John Bright with their "Anti-Corn Law

League" were leading the country to believe that actual famine would result unless the Corn Laws were repealed entirely. 

Ireland's potato crop failed and thousands of Irishmen perished from starvation. This terrible object lesson proved too much for the Conservative Prime Minister, Robert Peel. Even

though his government favored no change in the Corn Laws, and in the face of a charge of treason to the party, he led Parliament to repeal the obnoxious laws. This brought about a return to power of the Liberals and such a sweeping destruction of the old tariff wall that England has remained to the present day a country with free trade. 

8. Parliament Looks into the Operations of the East India Company in India. The overthrow of the French in India changed the East India Company from a great trading corporation enjoying a monopoly of the trade with India and China into a semi-independent state, whose governors played one native prince against another for the purpose of advancing the company's interests. To meet

WARREN HASTINGS' ELEPHANT From Knight's Picturesque History of England. 

the cost of the wars which followed such a policy, the government had to depend on irregularly assessed fees and on levies, for the directors in England were more interested in dividends than in an empire in the East. Such conduct eventually brought the actions of one of the governors, Robert Clive, before the House of Commons for review, and led to the famous impeachment of Warren Hastings in the House of Lords. 

Out of the investigation came the East India Company Regulating Act of 1784, limiting the powers of the proprietors and

compelling them to submit to the ministry copies of all the "regulations" which they proposed to send to India for their agents. When the East India Company's charter came up for renewal, in 1813, the India trade was thrown open to every one. Twenty years later, the East India Company ceased to be a trading corporation and was reimbursed by Parliament for the value of its commercial assets. 

From a western view-point the years 1833 to 1865 were a period of tremendous progress for India, especially under the governor-generalship of Lord Dalhousie (dăl-hoo'zi). The 

Ganges Canal was completed, greatly increasing the agricultural acreage of Bengal; many miles of roads, telegraph lines, and railways were built; an up-to-date postal system was installed; laws were enacted prohibiting the practice of widows burning themselves on the funeral pyres of their husbands, and other cruel customs; and an educational system was projected reaching from the primary school to the university. 

10. Following the Indian Mutiny India Becomes a 

Crown Colony. The larger part of the troops maintained by the East India Company was made up of natives. Just when the country was full of suspicion because of the work of the missionaries, some cartridges wrapped in greased rags were issued to the troops. As soon as it became rumored that this grease was made of cow's fat and hog's lard, the whole country was aflame, for the cow was sacred to the Hindus and the hog an unclean animal to the Muslims. Both peoples saw in the affair a scheme to spread Christianity at the expense of their ancestral religions. In May, 1857, a mutiny broke out among the Sepoys in northern India and spread with great rapidity, accompanied with more or less massacring of the English. The 

Sikhs and other Punjab troops, however, remained loyal, and the insurrection did not spread to southern India. On September 14, the Sepoys were decisively defeated at Delhi and by the following spring the British once more were masters of India.

11. The Suffrage Reform Bill of 1867 Is Followed by the Secret Ballot in 1872. After the failure of the Chartist movement, the wage-earners kept their demands alive through their trade-unions. The Liberals, still under the control of the middle class, continued to oppose further concessions to democracy, although such leaders as William E. Gladstone (glăd'stun) realized the working classes would soon have to be recognized. When it looked as if the American negroes were going to be freed after the Civil War, John Bright of Corn Law fame started a nation-wide campaign in behalf of England's white working men.

Gladstone introduced into the House of Commons a new re-

form bill which failed to pass and the Conservatives came into power under the leadership of Disraeli. Disraeli insisted that his party should give the country the reform it wanted, so, in 1867, the Conservatives passed a Reform Bill which extended suffrage. This law increased the number of voters to approximately three million, out of thirty-two million. In 1872, Gladstone, who was now Prime Minister, carried an act establishing the secret ballot, which had been used so successfully in the colony of Victoria and hence was and still is known as the Australian Ballot. 

12. The "Eternal" Irish Question Remained Unsettled.

In 1798, the Irish, expecting assistance from the French Directory, rebelled and suffered defeat. The immediate result of this was that the British Parliament passed the Act of Union, which did away with Ireland's ancient parliament and gave the island instead the one hundred seats that it had in the House of Commons, and admitted twenty-eight Irish peers to the House of Lords. Catholics were then without political rights within

the realm, so Ireland's representation, although nearly seveneighths of the Irish were Catholics, consisted largely of descendants of those English and Scotch Protestants who had been settled years before on the estates of the dispossessed 

Irish nobles.

No sooner had Parliament passed the Act of Union than the 

Irish revolted once more, this time under the leadership of Robert Emmet, who paid for his futile effort by dying on the scaffold. After that, Ireland settled down to another long period of 

English severity, broken only by the unsuccessful uprising in 1848. The failure of the potato crop in 1845 and this insurrection were the causes of the great emigration of Irish to the United States, which began about 1850 and reduced the population of the island fully fifty per cent and left it a land of old people.

The Fe'ni-an Conspiracy of 1866, organized by returned Irishmen who had fought in the Civil War in the United States, turned the attention of Englishmen toward Ireland. Many Liberals insisted that Parliament should wipe out the causes of 

Irish unrest. One of the acts of Gladstone's first ministry was to put through Parliament a bill disestablishing the Anglican Church in Ireland, so as to free Irish Catholics from paying tithes for its support. This was followed by a reform of some of the land laws. Hereafter when tenants were thrown out, the landlords were required to pay for any improvements which the tenants had made. Provision was also made for the government to lend money to tenants with which to buy farms. 

These concessions, instead of satisfying the Irish leaders, only increased the demand for "Home Rule."

CHAPTER LXVII THE REVOLUTIONS OF 1848 LOOSEN THE GRIP OF THE CON- SERVATIVES ON THE CONTINENT 

The attempt of the reactionary governments, under the leadership of Metternich, to suppress ideas which had found expression in the French Revolution, resulted in a strict censorship of speech and press. Things connected with contemporary politics and conditions were not to be discussed. Consequently people generally preferred to talk of doings of the past. Thus the second quarter of the nineteenth century saw a great enthusiasm for the study of history and a rapid development of romanticism in literature. This led to many curious results of which the most significant was the encouragement given to the growth of nationalism. As people came to know more about their past history, the more they wished to glorify their ancestors and to think of those ancestors in terms of their own ideals. This chapter will show how the liberals in France, in the German and Italian states, and the peoples in the Austrian Empire tried to realize their ideals. 

1. Forces That Tended to Undermine the Reactionary 

Governments. While the study of history and the development of nationalistic ideals were making it more difficult for a reactionary movement, the Industrial Revolution was spreading over much of the Continent, with the same results as in England. The oppressed working classes began to feel their wrongs more keenly and to demand participation in the government. This time, however, the movement was more nearly universal, for the railway and telegraph were bringing people of different countries so closely together that the ideas and accomplishments of one group were quickly made known to all. 639

2. Louis Philippe Opposes Reforms and the Revolution of 1848 Takes Place in France. After Louis Philippe came into power in France, control of the government passed to the bourgeoisie to whom he owed his election to the throne. As with the Liberal party in England, the dominant faction of the bourgeoisie wished to keep things as they were, but an increasing minority insisted on reform. The number of working men increased and Socialism spread. The Socialists realized that little could be hoped from any of the older parties, and therefore began to assume political independence. Out of this, developed the Socialist party with many of the same aims as the 

Chartists in England.

Louis Philippe sided with the conservative wing of the bourgeoisie but his position continually grew weaker, as the Liberals aided by the Socialists gathered strength. By 1847, they were attacking the restrictions on suffrage and the corruption of the government by great demonstrations of reform banquets and processions. An outbreak of the mob occurred in Paris in 

February, 1848. Louis abdicated and fled to England. While the provinces were once more receiving a "revolution by post," the liberal faction of the bourgeoisie proclaimed a republic on the west side of Paris while the Socialists proclaimed another on the east side. 

3. The Second French Republic Is Established. The two parties soon came to an agreement, permitting a provisional government to be established. As a concession to the Socialists, "national workshops," or industrial associaitons, were opened and every enrolled workman received two francs a day whether he worked or not. Within a month the enrolment reached one hundred thousand and the government's deficit was daily increasing in spite of the doubled taxes. Finally, the scandal became so great that the "workshops" with the assistance of the country districts were closed but not until after four days of rioting. The victorious Assembly then declared Paris in a

THE REVOLUTIONS OF 1848 

641 state of siege, ordered the working men disarmed, closed the revolutionary clubs, and passed a law of deportation. In the elections which followed, Louis Napoleon, a nephew of the great Napoleon, who had already tried twice to seize the throne, was elected president. Louis owed his election to the magic of a great name, the fame of which had been growing espe- IIE
