4. Louis Napoleon Plays a Skilful Hand and Is Elected 

Emperor Napoleon III. The new president believed that the 

French people really preferred a monarchy to a republic, although he had accepted many of the reform ideas and had corresponded with the Socialists and even with anarchists. While lending his support to the aims of the bourgeoisie, he quieted the working men by an old age insurance bill. To secure favor from the peasantry, he established a close friendship with the church, and confiscated the property which Louis Philippe had given to his children and used it to pay for all sorts of public improvements. Finally, he proposed the re-establishment of

universal manhood suffrage. When the Assembly refused to agree to this, he seized the government and proposed the restoration of the empire with himself as emperor. 

So skilfully had Louis Napoleon played his hand that, when the proposition was submitted to the nation, it was carried by a vote of seven and a half million to about two hundred and fifty thousand. On the forty-eighth anniversary of the coronation of the first Napoleon, his nephew became the Emperor of the French, with the title of Napoleon III, declaring that his reign would be devoted to keeping peace at home and abroad. 

5. All Europe Responds to the French Revolution of 

1848. The effects of the French Revolution of 1848 were felt all over Europe. The same forces which were working in 

France were also working in Italy and central Europe. On the one hand they were checked, on the other hand they were intensified by the reactionary control of Austria in both these regions. The Zollverein (tsōl'ferin), or customs union, established by the German states after the Congress of Vienna, had done much to make communication easier and to develop an economic basis for the growing national consciousness of the German people. In Italy, secret societies constantly stirred the embers of the national movement. In the Austrian Empire, the Magyars and Slavs were also developing national aspirations through a study of their past and were holding congresses to discuss their economic problems. 

When news of the successful overthrow of the "July monarchy" came, these movements began to work. The effect was felt first at Vienna. On March 12, an angry populace presented to the Emperor a petition for the reform of the government, and on the following day rioting broke out in the capital. The aged Metternich was only too glad to resign and to escape in disguise to England, which had become the refuge of political exiles from every quarter.

6. Revolution in the Italian States Is Put Down by 

Austria. In Italy, the king of Sardinia had already granted a constitution to his people, but when news of the doings at

Vienna and of the flight of Metternich reached the peasants, the Venetians declared their independence and the other Italian states revolted and wrung constitutions from their rulers. 

So sure were the patriots that the risorgimento (ré-zôr-jé-

měn'tō) or "day of resurrection" was at hand that an attempt was made under the leadership of King Charles Albert of Sardinia to free all Italy from Austrian control. Dissension, however, soon broke out among the leaders and by the end of July Austrian control was re-established. The constitutions which had been wrung from the princes were withdrawn and all Italy except Sardinia was in a state of reaction. 

7. In Germany the Liberals Fail in Efforts for Unification. At Berlin, the popular leaders demanded that Frederick 

William should not only grant a constitution insuring freedom of speech and of the press, and full equality in civil and political affairs, but demanded also that he should champion the cause of a national parliament for all Germany. He yielded in the face of open insurrection and an assembly convened at Frankfort to draft a constitution for the German people. While this assembly wrangled over whether the government should be a republican confederation or an empire, trouble arose with Denmark over the duchies of Schleswig (shlās'vik) and Holstein (hōl'shtin) which ended in war.

When the position of head of the new state was offered to 

Frederick William, he announced that he would accept it only with the free consent of all the German states. There followed two years of wrangling, occasioned by Prussia's efforts to form a union of German states with Austria excluded. In the end she yielded, for the Emperor was backed by the kings of Bavaria and Württemberg (vür'tem-běrk) as well as by the Tsar. 

The old German confederation was restored and all that Germany could show in return for her struggle was the limited constitution which Frederick William grudgingly granted Prussia in 1850. 

8. The Revolution in the Austrian Empire Is Stamped 

Out with the Aid of Russia. Austria was a conglomerate. state made up of Germans in the west, of Slavs in the north and south, and of Magyars in the centre, with smaller groups

THE REVOLUTIONS OF 1848 

645 of Italians and Roumanians scattered along the southern and southeastern borders. The Slavs, in spite of the fact that they were the most numerous, were almost without political power, due to their lack of common language and interests; in fact, they were so split up that, at the congress in 1847, they had to

Notice the tricolor flags on the belfry. resort to German in order to understand one another. The 

Magyars were the most compact group, and they had the most vivid traditions and the strongest nationalistic feelings. As a result, they were the first to catch the spark that had been lighted at Paris. It was their demand for a Diet and a ministry of their own at Pěst (pěsht) that was largely responsible for the overthrow of Metternich. 

They were not content with wringing from the Emperor these contentions; they demanded that their ancient laws and

language should be supreme not only in Hungary but in Transylvania, Dalmatia, and other southern provinces. This demand was so much resented by the Slavs and Roumanians of those regions that by June, 1848, they had staged a revolt against the new Pest government. While this was going on in the south, the Czechs of Bohemia rebelled. In despair, the Emperor abdicated in favor of his young nephew Francis Joseph. 

The Magyars proclaimed Hungary a republic with the patriot, Louis Kossuth (kosh'oot), as president. This act stirred up Tsar Nicholas I, who dared not have a republic so close to his unruly Polish provinces. A concerted attack was made against the Magyars by the two emperors, and by July of 1849, Kossuth had fled to Turkey. Many of the Hungarian patriots were put to death and all of them lost their estates. The constitution granted the year before was annulled, and Hungary was merged with Austria. This practically ended the revolution. in the Emperor's domains. It had failed because of the enmity that existed among the different peoples composing the population, and to a less extent because of the friction between the middle and lower classes. 

9. The Significance of the Revolutions of 1848. The real gains from the Revolutions of 1848 were relatively small. 

Serfdom was abolished in the Austrian Empire, and constitutions were won by Prussia and by some of the other German states. Conservatism was once more in control, but the masses had shown that they would have to be reckoned with in the future development of Europe. While democracy was retarded for a time, nationalism had shown such life that the next two decades bore the fruit of this nationalistic feeling in the formation of two great states.

CHAPTER LXVIII THE  MARKS THE FRUITION OF THEIR NATIONAL AIMS 

We have seen that the Revolutionary movements of 1848 met with little success. It was evident, however, that the feeling for liberty, democracy, and nationality was running high; and that important changes in Europe were inevitable. We shall learn now how unification and nationality were attained under the leadership of ambitious rulers in Italy and in Germany, but how with the national aims the people had to be content with limited achievements in parliamentary government. France, we shall see, paid dearly for having made Louis Napoleon Emperor. Due to his folly the German Empire under Prussian leadership was formed, and France lost Alsace and Lorraine. 

1. The Nationalistic Movement Keeps Alive in Italy. 

Metternich spoke the truth when he said that Italy was only a geographical expression. Not until Napoleon created his shortlived Kingdom of Italy was there an Italian nation. In spite of this, the people south of the Alps spoke a common language, which had been made famous by Dante and many later writers. 

The spark of nationalism was kept alive during the reaction by the secret workings of the Carbonari and of the Young Italy Movement, organized by the Italian patriot Mazzini (mätsē-nē). After the failure of 1848, Charles Albert abdicated the throne of Sardinia in favor of his vigorous son, Victor Ěmmăn'ú-ěl II. The new King became at once the hope of the 

Italian patriots for he was devoted to the cause of a united Italy. 648

2. Sardinia Takes the Lead under Cavour's Direction. 

Victor Emmanuel was fortunate to have as his prime minister Count di Cavour (dē kȧ-vōōr′), one of the ablest statesmen of the day. Like his king, Cavour had liberal ideas, and was an admirer of the government of England. Under his leadership there was such improvement in the agriculture, industry, and commerce of the kingdom that the Italians longed to be under the rule of Sardinia. Cavour realized that, if the Austrians were to be driven out of Italy, the Italians needed outside assistance, and that to obtain this some way must be found to win the sympathy of the powers. An opportunity came when the Cri-me'ăn War broke out in 1855 between England and France on the one side, and Russia on the other. While Austria hung back for selfish reasons, Sardinia, at the instigation of Cavour, took an active part, and won for herself a seat in the Congress of Paris, and the strong sympathy of both England and France. 

3. In Helping Victor Emmanuel Defeat Austria Napoleon III Helps Himself. Cavour soon found Napoleon III the friend he had been looking for. Although Napoleon had once been a member of the Carbonari and still retained some of the liberal ideas he had then entertained, he was more interested in gaining fame for himself by striking a blow at the power of Austria. Therefore, he formed an alliance with Victor Emmanuel for the purpose of driving the Austrians out of Italy. 

The war broke out in April, 1859. From the first the advantage lay with the allies. When Napoleon found that his scheme of making a kingdom for his cousin Jerome out of the central duchies would fail because their inhabitants wished to join Sardinia, he arranged an armistice with Emperor Francis 

Joseph without consulting his ally. Victor Emmanuel handed over to Napoleon Savoy and Nice, but Sardinia was partly paid by being allowed to annex Parma, Modena, and Tuscany.

4. Garibaldi and His Thousand "Red Coats" Win

Southern Italy Over to the Cause of Nationalism. Hardly had the war with Austria ended before Mazzini and another patriot, Giuseppe Garibaldi (joo-sep'pé gä-ré-bäl'dē), with the secret assistance of Cavour, organized an expedition at Genoa to attack Sicily. There he stirred up an insurrection which resulted in the Sicilians chasing out the rulers and handing over the government to him. He then crossed over the mainland and advanced toward Naples.

His success caused Victor Emmanuel to march with his army, violating the sovereignty of the Pope and even capturing several papal towns along the way. As a protest against this, all the continental powers withdrew their ambassadors from Tu'rin. When the king reached Naples, Garibaldi generously surrendered to him his dictatorship of southern Italy.

5. Victor Emmanuel Becomes King of Italy. With the greater part of the peninsula now in his hands, Victor Emmanuel summoned a national parliament to meet at Turin. With its consent on March 17, 1861, he assumed the title of King of

Italy. The new kingdom included all the territory south of the 

Alps, except Venetia and the city of Rome, and boasted some 22,- 

000,000 inhabitants.

The same liberal government which Sardinia enjoyed was extended to it. Cavour died not long after this, happy in the realization that the work he had set out to do was almost completed. 

The new kingdom was still not complete so long as Austria held Venetia, and the Pope held Rome and its environs. When war broke out between Prussia and Austria in 1866, Victor Emmanuel saw an opportunity to obtain Venice by allying himself with Frederick William. They did prevent the Emperor from giving undivided attention to the Prussians, although his troops were no match for the Austrians. In order to win the support of Napoleon III, who was pretending to play the part of mediator, Francis Joseph offered to give him Venetia, but in the final settlement it passed to the Italians.

6.

Victor Emmanuel Occupies the Papal Territories in 1870, and Makes Rome the Capital of United Italy. An opportunity to acquire the remainder of the papal territories came four years later as a sequel to the war between the French and the Prussians. Victor Emmanuel had promised Napoleon not to attack Rome after the French garrison was removed, yet he was compelled to move against the city in order to prevent the followers of Mazzini from seizing it and proclaiming a republic. Over the protests of the Pope, his soldiers entered 

Rome on September 20, 1870, and the National Assembly declared it to be the capital of the kingdom. The Holy Father had ten years before excommunicated Victor Emmanuel and everybody else connected with the seizure of the papal territories at that time. Now the Pope could only retire to the 

Vatican, for this and a villa outside the city were all the papal possessions remaining. He remained within the Vatican a selfimposed prisoner, refusing to set foot on Italian soil or to accept the subsidy granted by the Italian government. His hostility to the Italian government has formed one of its most vexatious problems, until the treaty made through the efforts of Mussolini in 1929 recognized territorial rights of the Pope and restored to the Catholic church its position in the Italian state. 

7. The Slow Rise of Nationalism in Germany. Through its long history the forces of disunion in Germany had been stronger than those of union. While the kings of France and 

England were helping to build their countries into strong national states, the Emperor of Germany was trying to keep alive the fiction of the Holy Roman Empire. Even when Martin 

Luther became for the moment a national hero, the struggle between the Catholics and Protestants gave rise to disunion which had a climax in the Peace of Westphalia. For nearly two centuries Germany remained a land of hundreds of little independent states.

During the latter part of the eighteenth century, there had been springing up in different parts of the country writers and thinkers who took real pride in things German. With this development of a national consciousness came the problem of who should lead in bringing about the unification of the German people. No longer could Austria with her many subject peoples of non-German stock claim to be the undisputed leader, for Prussia had already become one of the most powerful states in Germany and was eager to represent the German people in all things. 

8. William I with Otto von Bismarck as Chancellor 

Sets Out to Dominate Affairs in Germany and in Europe.

We have seen that the timid, vacillating Frederick William was offered the opportunity to become the leader of the German people, and that he declined the honor because he feared Austria. Thirteen years later, he was succeeded by William I, a different type of man. The new king was a firm believer in the old idea of the divine right of kings. One of his first acts was to double the strength of the army and to equip it with a new type of gun superior to anything in Europe. When the lower house of the Prussian Parliament refused to vote the necessary funds for keeping up the army, he summoned from Paris the Prussian ambassador, Otto von Bismarck, to undertake the task of training the opposing legislators. 

Bismarck was well known for his extreme views. As a member of the first Prussian Parliament, he had shocked his colleagues by roaring, "Let all questions to the king's ministers be answered by a roll of drums." He had such contempt for the ballot-box, that he usually referred to it as a dice-box. He struck terror into the hearts of the liberals by declaring that it was not by speeches and majorities that the great questions of time would have to be decided, but by blood and iron. As ambassador at the courts of Russia and France, he had gained a valuable knowledge of the workings of diplomacy and of the

weaknesses of diplomats. The ruling passion of his life had come to be the complete elimination of Austria from German affairs. This was the man in whom William I placed unqualified confidence, and who was destined to control the affairs of Europe for almost a generation. 

9. Austria Is Eliminated from German Affairs. In 1863,

Frederick VII of Denmark died without direct heir. Fifteen years before, his duchies of Schleswig and Holstein had, with the aid of Prussia, made an unsuccessful effort to free themselves from his control. England and Russia had guaranteed them to the King of Denmark with the proviso that they should never be incorporated into the Danish kingdom. Shortly before his death, Frederick had allowed the Danes to draft a new constitution which did that very thing, and when the new king, Christian IX, came to the throne, his assent to it was a direct insult to the German Confederation. Bismarck then persuaded

William I and Francis Joseph to occupy jointly the two duchies. The Danes resisted, but they were hopelessly beaten and the duchies were surrendered to the allies. 

Trouble soon broke out between Austria and Prussia over the disposition of the two duchies. Austria wanted them given to a minor German prince, while Bismarck demanded their annexation to Prussia. The matter was settled temporarily while Bismarck negotiated secretly with France and Russia for their support and made a treaty with Italy. Then he invaded Holstein which was being governed by Austria and, when the Dutch objected, Prussia withdrew from the Confederation. In the short war which followed, Austria was beaten at Sadowa (sä'dó-vä) and excluded from German affairs.

This defeat gave the Magyars an opportunity to win important favors from Austria. As a reward for the efforts of Deák (dā´äk) in keeping the Magyars loyal, the Emperor granted the Ausgleich (ous'glik), or compromise, by which the local government of the Kingdom of Hungary was separated from

that of Austria and their common affairs were to be managed by a joint parliament and joint ministers of foreign affairs, army, and finance. Henceforth this combination was known as the Austro-Hungarian Empire or "Dual Monarchy." 

10. The North German Confederation Controlled by

Prussia Displaces the Old Confederation. By the Treaty of 

Prague, the two duchies, Hanover, and some of the opposing German states were annexed by Prussia. The old Confederation was dissolved and its place was taken by a North German Confederation, composed of all the states north of the Main. 

Bismarck did not attempt to force the southern states into this organization, but contented himself with a treaty by which they agreed to place their troops at the disposal of Prussia whenever she was engaged in a war. Well could the Prussian Parliament forgive the conduct of Bismarck when they saw the results of this war-the area of the kingdom had been increased nearly one-third and the population by over five million. 

Under the constitution of the new Confederation there was a federal council or Bundesrath (boon'des-rät), composed of representatives of the several states in proportion to their importance; and a lower house, the Reichstag (riks'täk), whose members were elected by universal manhood suffrage. The king of Prussia was made hereditary president of the Confederation and to him was intrusted the conduct of foreign affairs and the control of the army. He had the right to declare war and to conclude peace, but in a war in which Germany was the aggressor he must have the consent of the Bundesrath. 

11. Napoleon III Takes a Hand in European Politics. 

To no one was the work of Bismarck a greater source of irritation than to Napoleon III. Ever since he had become emperor, he had desired to imitate his illustrious uncle in controlling Europe. He had managed to satisfy the French people by various measures which improved the economic conditions and which were intended to beautify Paris. He had entered the Crimean

War and caused the conference which ended it to be held in Paris.

We have already noted the Italian intervention in that year. 

Three years later, Napoleon tried to help the Poles but only gained the ill will of the Tsar. In the following year, he undertook an unfortunate expedition to Mexico which we shall discuss later. Nevertheless his desire for territory and power kept him constantly intriguing, while the rise of Prussia both irritated him and threatened his position. 

In 1860, a revolution ended the rule of the Bourbons in Spain and the Spaniards invited Prince Leopold of Hohenzollern, a distant relative of King William, to become their king. After 

Napoleon had made a diplomatic issue out of this, Prince Leopold finally refused the offer. Not satisfied, the French ambassador at Berlin insisted that King William should give a definite assurance never to give consent to Leopold's accepting the crown. When he persisted in this demand, William refused to discuss the matter further with him. Bismarck seized the opportunity to embroil the two countries in war by publishing a telegram from the King so that public opinion in France forced Napoleon to declare war. 

12. Napoleon III Is Decisively Defeated in the Franco- 

Prussian War. Both monarchs took the field in person. The 

German army was splendidly organized and fully equipped; the 

French were almost wholly unprepared. Napoleon withdrew the French forces from the papal territories, hoping to gain thereby the support of both Austria and Italy, but the terrible defeats sustained by his armies on August 6, 1870, ended hope of assistance from either quarter. The battle of Gravelotte (grav-lót'), a few days later, was decisive, for the strategy of Prussia's great general von Mölt'ke cut the French forces in two. As soon as the Germans had shut up the army of Marshal 

Bazaine (ba'zēn) in Metz, they set out for Paris. On August 

30, they surprised the French in a small valley near Sé-dän'

and for three days subjected them to such shell fire that Napoleon ordered Marshal de MacMahon (måk-mȧ-ôN') to surrender. 

13. Bismarck Imposes Severe Terms upon the Third

French Republic. Two days later the Empire collapsed and for a third time France was proclaimed a republic. A pro-

visional government was set up and met the German demand for a surrender of

Meanwhile Găm-bět'tà, the Minister of Interior, had escaped in a balloon and, as a dictator, was undertaking to enroll southern France for the relief of the capital. He was not even daunted by the fall of Metz with the loss of 150,000 prisoners.

On January 10, 1871, while the siege of Paris was still going on, King William was proclaimed German Emperor in the Hall of Mirrors of the great palace at Versailles, where the Germans had established their headquarters. Bismarck had realized his ambition-all Germany had been united under the leadership of Prussia. We

shall soon see what an important part the new state with the "Iron Chancellor" was to play in the march of civilization.

CHAPTER LXIX RUSSIA AND THE EASTERN QUESTION BECOME A NIGHTMARE TO EUROPEAN DIPLOMATS 

At the beginning of the nineteenth century, not only was Russia the largest state in Europe but the word of the Tsar was supreme throughout much of northern Asia as well. As early as 1727, his title to Siberia as far as the Okhotsk had been recognized by the Chinese in the Treaty of Kiakhta (kyȧk'tȧ), and now the lands of the Kirghiz, to the northeast of the Caspian Sea, were incorporated into his empire through an invasion of Cossacks from the region of the Urals. 

European Russia had a population of about forty-five millions, nine-tenths of whom were in abject serfdom, and the densest ignorance and superstition. All the land belonged to the Tsar and the nobility, which consisted of approximately one hundred twenty thousand families. The "Little Father," as the Tsar was popularly called, controlled the intellectual thought of his people, and their religious ideas through the Orthodox Church, which had its own head or Metropolitan. The tsars had inherited from Peter the Great and his successors, as their most cherished ambition, an outlet to the Mediterranean through 

Constantinople and the Straits.

How the Tsar took advantage of the weakness of the Turkish Empire, until England and France came to the rescue of the Sultan; and how Serbia and Roumania were freed from the 

Turks; and finally how the building of the Suez Canal further complicated the Eastern question, will be discussed in this chapter. 

1. The Eastern Question Centres about the Ottoman 

Empire.

The Ottoman Empire lay across the Russian road to 661

the Mediterranean. As we have seen, it had completely lost its sixteenth-century glory and had fallen behind in the march of civilization. The Sultan was at its head, a ruler with absolute power, whose authority was held through his widely flung empire by the well-earned reputation for ruthlessness of his soldiers. Turkey was a land of many widely different peoples, but its greatest difficulties were due to religion. Numerous Christian sects dwelt in Europe, along the coast of Asia Minor and of Syria, and in the mountains of Armenia, while south of the Taurus Mountains and in northern Africa the country was almost wholly Muslim. Most of the business was in the hands of the Christians, thus adding jealousy of their wealth to the Turks' inherent disdain of their religion. 

As early as 1699, the European frontiers of the Turkish Empire had begun to recede. There had developed, helped by intrigues of European powers, a strong desire on the part of the Christians north of the Bosphorus to win back the political rights which they had lost in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. The wave of national feeling which swept over Europe after the French Revolution had little influence on Turkish lands because of their backwardness. Out of this discontent. of the Christians arose, as we have seen, the Kingdom of Greece. The Serbians and the inhabitants of Wallachia and 

Moldavia gained some political privileges. 

2. Russia Takes Every Possible Occasion to Increase 

Her Power in Turkey. Desiring to reach the Mediterranean,

Russia continually sought occasions for differences with the Ottoman Empire. She had extended her power to the Black 

Sea in the days of Catherine the Great, then she claimed the right to act as protector of the Greek Christians living within the Turkish domain. It was her defeat of Turkey, in 1829, that made possible Greek independence and a separate administration for the provinces of Moldavia and Wallachia.

Mehemet claimed that he had been cheated and proceeded to occupy Palestine and Syria. 

This proved so easy that he ordered his son, Ibrahim (ib-rȧhem') Pasha, to advance on Constantinople to force the Sultan to recognize him as heir to the rule of both Egypt and Syria. 

The Sultan accepted the offer of the Tsar to furnish him troops with which to put down this new insurrection. At the same time, Ibrahim made a secret agreement with the Tsar by which the Straits were to be open to Russian warships but closed to any

Turkey practically a protectorate of Russia and both England and France became alarmed. 

3. The Powers Block Russia's Plans in Turkey. The opportunity to interfere came in 1840 after an uprising of the Maronite Christians of Syria against Mehemet Ali. England and Austria entered into agreement with Russia to go to the assistance of the Sultan, but France refused to join and came near declaring war. In the end, a settlement was reached by which Russia had to surrender the advantages she had secured by her recent agreement with Turkey, and the integrity of that country was guaranteed by the powers and the Straits were closed to the warships of all. In the meantime, the Sultan issued a firman (fer-män′) or decree, pledging to his Christian subjects the rights enjoyed by the Muslims. 

4. Russia Attempts to Dismember Turkey but Is Defeated in the Crimean War. Nicholas I visited England in 

1844, and discussed the question of dividing up Turkey. He got the impression that the British government would join in the undertaking. In 1853, Nicholas once more interested himself in the dismemberment of Turkey, suggesting to the British ambassador at St. Petersburg that "We have a very sick man on our hands, whom no doctor can cure, and we ought to take measures to deal with the situation." Inasmuch as Lord Aberdeen, the English statesman with whom he had talked in 1844, was now Prime Minister, Nicholas expected no difficulty in getting England to take a hand. On the strength of that, he had his ambassador at Constantinople make some outrageous demands of the Sultan. When these were refused, Russia declared war on the Ottoman Empire. 

The excitement aroused by the Russian destruction of the Turkish fleet led the English to go to the assistance of the Turks while the desire of Napoleon to win glory for himself caused the French to do likewise. Because this war was waged

mainly in the peninsula of Crimea, it is known as the Crimean War. The principal event was the Siege of Sé-vas'tó-pól, in which occurred the charge of Irish cavalry at Ba-la-cla'va which Tennyson has immortalized in The Charge of the Light Brigade. 

5. The Treaty of Paris Makes Some Important Settle ments. Russia was ready by the fall of 1855, to acknowledge defeat. The allies were also eager for peace, for the cholera and the bad weather were taking a tremendous toll. By the 

Treaty of Paris which followed, the Straits were again closed to all foreign warships. Both Russia and Turkey were forbidden to keep any armed vessels on the Black Sea, a prohibition repudiated by Russia in 1870. Serbia was freed of Turkish garrisons and the principalities of Moldavia and Wallachia were made independent. The last two were forbidden to unite but they did so a few years later, giving rise to the Kingdom of Roumania. Once more the integrity of Turkey was guaranteed by the powers, and again the Sultan renewed his pledges to his Christian subjects.

The Crimean War made two important contributions to the cause of humanitarianism. From the labors of Florence Nightingale, an English nurse, in behalf of the sick and wounded of both sides, sprang relief work of an international character. 

Out of this developed, in 1863, the Red Cross Society, which to-day reaches into almost every part of the world. The Congress of Paris added to international law a number of principles which were agreed to by all the leading powers except the United States, Mexico, and Spain. Privateering was abolished; blockades to be binding had to be effective, that is, had to be maintained by sufficient vessels to prevent ships from violating the blockade; all goods on neutral ships, except contraband of war destined for the enemy, were free from capture; neutral goods, except contraband of war, even on an enemy's ship, were not subject to capture.

RUSSIA AND THE EASTERN QUESTION 667 6. Alexander II Initiates Much Needed Reforms in 

Russia. The effect of the Crimean War on Russia was very great. To it is traceable the beginning of the Russian Industrial Revolution and the growth of many important manufacturing cities such as Moscow, Kief, Vilna (vēl'nȧ), and Warsaw. The dream of the tsars for a road to the open sea

British light cavalry making an attack upon Russian guns at Balaclava, October 25, 1854. 

It is important only because of the poem. received a check. For once the whole country was full of discontent-many of the nobility had been ruined or impoverished; the liberal-minded townspeople had become angered by the corruption of the bureaucracy; and the serfs were groaning under the terrible epidemics that had been spread by the returned soldiers.

Unlike his father, the new Tsar, Alexander II, was well disposed toward liberal ideas and set out to play the part of a benevolent despot. During the first ten years of his reign, he freed the press, introduced trial by jury, modified the criminal

law, established primary schools, and on March 3, 1861, in utter disregard of the views of the Russian aristocracy, freed all the serfs within the empire. This last reform did not turn out to be an unmixed blessing, for although the serfs gained their individual freedom, they did not acquire land on which to make a living. To remedy this, the government bought from the nobles a part of their land and turned it over to the mirs, or villages, to be cut up and sold to the peasants on the installment plan. Frequently the price was so high that it took so much of their labor to make the "redemption payments" and to pay the taxes that it was said they had become serfs of the state.

Alexander, however, persisted in his programme, opened the universities to the poorest peasant in the empire, and called together zemstvos (zěmsť fōs) or district assemblies, composed of representatives elected by both the aristocracy and peasantry. 

To these zemstvos were handed over such local problems as control of the recently established primary schools and of public health. Thus the Russians had an opportunity to obtain some experience in government. 

7. Reaction Sets in Against Liberal Ideas. A revolt broke out in Poland in 1863. It was put down without difficulty but it gave an opportunity to Alexander's reactionary advisers to argue that it was the result of too humane rule. 

They were successful and, for the rest of his reign, he was as reactionary as he had previously been liberal. Decrees were issued forbidding political discussion. In order to discover anything suggestive of reform agitation, the Third Section, or secret police, was reorganized and strengthened. But the seeds of liberalism had been sown and the country was honey-combed with socialistic ideas. 

8. The Socialists Counter the Reaction with Nihilism.

CHAPTER LXX HOW  IN THE AMERICAS 

It will be of interest to see what was going on in the Americas during this period of revolution, reaction, and nationalistic struggle in Europe. We shall find that the development of nationalism and democracy did not take place at once in America. 

At the close of the War for Independence, the Colonies had become thirteen independent states, and even the adoption of the Constitution did not carry with it nationality. Conservative democracy was established with the Constitution, but the aristocratic idea in government continued in the East and South of America to the extent that full manhood suffrage was not generally allowed until Jackson became president. How democracy continued to grow in the United States; how the spirit of nationalism became stronger as our boundaries extended to the Pacific, and the questions of slavery and secession were settled; and how the Latin American countries achieved nationality without democracy, will be the important subjects of this chapter. 

1. The United States of America Becomes an Established Fact by the Adoption of the Constitution. The independence of the thirteen colonies was recognized by England in 1783. Then the Americans found their task just begun and discovered that independence brought more problems than it solved. Their government under the Articles of Confederation was cumbersome and futile, and when the pressure of war was over, it was powerless to compel the several states to carry out pledges to which they had agreed in the Treaty of Paris. Fortunately, they were able to devise a new scheme of government before the great wars which followed the French Revolution broke out in Europe. 672

The United States of America became an established fact by the Constitution, which was drafted after much compromise in 1787, and ratified by a majority of the states two years later. 

In this Constitution, the legislative, executive, and judicial departments of the new government were carefully separated. 

The old colonial pride and independence were kept alive by reserving to the states the sovereign powers not specifically surrendered to the Federal government. As a result, each state had its own qualifications for the right to vote, but in all the states the possession. of property or the payment of taxes was an essential requirement. 

THE CONSTITUTIONAL CONVENTION OF 1787 

George Washington is presiding. Can you identify any of the others? 

From a painting by Sidney M. Chase. 

The Constitution itself was little more than a framework of government, which had to be filled in by the First Congress in 1789. For example, it was to their action that may be traced the establishment of the President's cabinet. It reaffirmed the fundamental rights of man, in the form of ten amendments to the Constitution, to meet the objections of those who feared that otherwise these rights might be violated in the future. The differences of opinion in this 

Congress on the question of what to do with the debts incurred by the Revolution brought about the first political parties—the

Federalists, who desired the Federal Government to assume the debts, and the Republicans, who were opposed to this policy. 

2. The United States Proclaims Neutrality in the Wars Growing Out of the French Revolution. America and 

Americans had played a large part in the development of republican ideas in France so the French expected the sympathy of the United States after France became involved in war with England. She felt that the old treaty of 1778 with the United 

Colonies was still binding and sent a representative to organize privateering against English commerce from American ports. 

General Washington was the President, and looked upon the alliance only as a defensive one and proclaimed neutrality. 

American opinion itself was divided, some favoring the revolution, but the majority opposing it, especially after 1791. 

In the ensuing troubles, influence of French agents in America during the presidency of John Adams brought about the passage of the Alien and Sedition Laws, which caused the Republicans, now led by Thomas Jefferson, to insist on state rights and to accuse the government of militarism. While the war caused so many political difficulties, it was proving very profitable to American pocketbooks. A commercial treaty with 

England permitted American ships to carry on trade with both belligerents, and American merchants were reaping a rich harvest. Incidentally the irruption of the Barbary pirates into the

Atlantic, in 1793, caused the United States to build its first warships, and before the end of the Napoleonic period this new navy had fought several engagements with the pirates in the Mediterranean and brought an end to the ridiculous system of tribute which had previously prevailed.*

IMPRESSING AMERICAN SAILORS 

The trouble which developed out of the continued war between England and Napoleon was of quite another character. On the one hand the English claimed the right to board American ships and to impress their sailors into the royal navy; on the other hand the trade regulations of both England and France were so destructive to American shipping that American trade had decreased two-thirds. As we have seen, Congress in desperation passed the Embargo Act in 1808, but this served only to ruin further American business. 

The situation was little improved by the repeal of this act, for England did not rescind her Order in Council, forbidding trade with those parts of Europe controlled by Napoleon. She was ready to do this by 1812, but that was too late. A group of patriotic Americans, who had become incensed by her arbitrary conduct and by difficulties along the Canadian border, forced 

British officers seized seamen on American ships and forced them to serve in British ships on the ground that they were British subjects. 

From a painting by Stanley M. Arthurs.

President Madison to agree to a declaration of war against her. 

The ensuing struggle showed that the United States had not yet become a united nation, for the war was so unpopular that talk of secession was rife. After heavy losses on both sides, peace was made at Ghent without any acquisition of territory or any mention of impressment, but England had learned the spirit of the American people and the end of the Napoleonic wars lessened her need for aggressive measures. 

4. The Spanish Colonies in America Revolt. The Span ish colonies in America at the close of the eighteenth century were divided into the vice-royalties of New Spain, New 

Granada, Peru, and Rï'o de la Plä'tä, the captain-generalcies of

Cuba and Guatemala, Venezuela (věn-é-zwe'là), and Chile (chēlā), and the presidency of Chär'cäs. Trade was permitted with Spain alone and only recently had there been direct contact between her and Buenos Ayres (bwa'nōs i'rās). Serious friction had already developed between the Creoles and the European-born Spaniards, by whom most of the offices were held, while the heavy taxes and forced labor bore heavily upon the native population.

In 1789, a descendant of the Incas, Tupac Amaru (too'päc ä-mär'oo), started a revolt in Peru which cost the lives of thousands of natives. Other revolts took place in Chile and Venezuela. All owed their inception to local difficulties, for the contacts with North America and France were so slight that the revolutions in these two countries had no noticeable effects at this time. So completely was Spanish America cut off from the rest of the world that it was only toward the end of the century that the ideas of Montesquieu, Rousseau, and the other political reformers reached there. For some time, however, there had existed at Bō-gó-tä' and Lima societies devoted to the study of literature and science.

Joseph Bonaparte was as little acceptable as in Spain herself. 

Juntas, or local councils, were set up at Quito (ke'tō), Bogota, Cä-rä'cäs, Buenos Ayres, and Sän-ti-ä'go de Chile, and revolts took place in many other places. 

In Mexico, an insurrection was started, in 1810, by a native priest named Miguel Hidalgo (é-däl'gō). Although this man was soon defeated and executed, his place was taken by José (hō-sa') Maria Morelos (mó-ra'lōs), who held out until 1815. 

At Caracas, in 1812, Francisco Mi-rän'da, who had visited the 

United States, made a vain attempt at revolution. Miranda's lieutenant, a rich planter named Simon Boli-var, fled to New Granada where he was given command of the troops of the recently established state. After an unsuccessful attempt to invade Venezuela, he returned to New Granada to assist in organizing the new government, but the revolt collapsed on the arrival of fresh troops from Spain and Bolivar fled to the West Indies. At Quito the insurrection was put down and in 

Chile also through the efforts of the viceroy of Peru. In fact, only in the viceroyalty of Rio de la Plata were the revolutionary movements following the accession of Bonaparte to the Spanish throne successful. 

6. The Southern States of South America Revolt. The people of Buenos Ayres were brought into the struggle when they drove out the English. They organized the provisional junta in May, 1810, which declared its independence and called on the patriots of Uruguay (u'roo-gwa) and Paraguay to do likewise. In Uruguay, the Brazilians seized Mon-té-vid'é-ō and

held it until 1825, when it became independent, while in Paraguay the people set up an independent government led by José de Francia (frän-së´ä) who as dictator soon gained the title of El Supremo (ěl soo-prā mō). 

Plans were made in Buenos Ayres for an attack on Peru by way of Charcas, but this soon proved to be impossible and on the advice of José de Sän Mär-tin', who had served in the Spanish army in Spain, it was given up. Not only did San 

Martin bring military science to the rebels but he conceived the idea of attacking Peru through Chile. He also prevailed upon the members of a congress which met at Tucuman (tōō-kōōmän') to declare the independence of the "United Provinces of 

South America." Meanwhile, with the assistance of refugees from Chile, he had begun to organize an army which crossed the Andes and in two battles completely broke the Spanish power. Then on February 12, 1818, the Chileans under the leadership of Ber-när'dō O'Higgins (ó-ē'gēns) declared the independence of their country. 

7. Bolivar Frees the North. In the meantime, Bolivar had landed in Venezuela with a small force. By the end of 1818, he liberated the lower valley of the O-ri-no'cō. He then organized a government of which he became the president and established a capital at Angostura (àn-gos-too'rä). With the aid of six thousand British and Irish mercenaries, he undertook the conquest of New Granada. After a terrible march over the Andes, he defeated the Spaniards at Bō-yä-cä' and consolidated his two conquests into the Republic of Colombia with its capital at Bogota. However, northern South America was not wholly freed from Spanish control until the royalists were finally beaten at Cä-rä-bō'bō in 1821. 

Following the Spanish revolution of 1820, another wave of revolts swept over the Americas. As soon as the patriots at 

Quito had organized a new junta, Bolivar sent General de Sucre (soo'krā) by sea with a strong force to their assistance

and then he followed by land. As a result of the victory at 

Pi-chin'chä on May 24, 1822, the presidency of Quito was made a part of the Republic of Colombia. In the meantime, San Martin, with a force of rebels from the South, invaded Peru, drove the viceroy out of Lima, and proclaimed the independence of the viceroyalty on July 28, 1821.

The royalists still held the interior of the country. During the following summer San Martin met Bolivar at Guayaquil (gwi-ä-kel') to unite forces with him. No one knows what happened there, but he withdrew his army and sailed for Europe. Bolivar then sent Sucre to Peru. The royalists were finally defeated at Ayacucho (ä-yä-kōo'chō) on December 9, 1824, and at last all South America had been freed from Spanish domination. Early the next year Sucre decreed the independence of the presidency of Charcas, which took the name of Bó-liv'i-a in honor of the patriot and named its capital Sucre. 

8. Mexico Becomes Independent. The Spanish revolution had also rekindled the desire for independence in Mexico, where guerilla warfare was still being carried on by Vicente Guerrero (vě-sen'tě gĕr-ra'rō). The viceroy appointed the ruthless Creole Agustin de Iturbide (ä-goos-ten' dā e-toor-be'thä) to command the army with which he hoped to crush the rebels, but not long afterward the two leaders reached an agreement and Iturbide published the Plan of Iguala (e-gwä'lä) by which Mexico was to become an independent nation with a Bourbon emperor. The clergy were to be protected and citizenship was to be granted equally to Europeans, Creoles, and Indians. The new viceroy, who was sent over to take charge of affairs, agreed to this plan with the proviso that the emperor should be elected by the Spanish Cortes. However, the Cortes repudiated the arrangement and proceeded to elect Iturbide emperor on May 18, 1822. In the meantime, Guatemala had proclaimed her independence, and Iturbide sent an expedition which annexed all of Central America as far south as Panama.

9. Brazil Becomes an Independent Empire. The Portu guese revolution of 1820 led to immediate results in Brazil. 

In 1816, Queen Maria I had died and her son Dom John, who was serving as regent in Brazil, had become king of Portugal, although he still continued to reside in America. When the revolutionists deposed his regent in Europe and promulgated a constitution to which John had to assent, the Brazilians also demanded political concessions. It was finally agreed that the new constitution should apply to them too. Shortly after this 

John made his son, Dom Pe'drō, the regent in Brazil and sailed for Portugal.

The Portuguese Cortes enacted some laws that tended to reduce Brazil to the status of a colony, and the leading Brazilian patriots demanded an assembly of their own. Dom Pedro agreed and on September 7, 1822, actually proclaimed the independence of the country, whereupon he was elected emperor and crowned on December 1 of the same year. In the constitution drafted soon after, the emperor was given extensive powers, although legislation was placed in the hands of a congress consisting of two houses. 

10. How the Monroe Doctrine Grew Out of the Latin 

American Revolutions. The relations between the United 

States and Spain had become strained over the boundary of Florida and the depredations of the Indians. The differences were finally settled, in 1819, by a treaty which transferred to the United States not only Florida, but all the territory between the Rocky Mountains and the Pacific Ocean north of the forty-second parallel.

The people of the United States had watched the revolts in Latin America with interest and sympathy although the government had remained neutral. As soon, however, as the various leaders seemed to be successful, recognition was accorded the new governments. As a result, by the time the Congress of 

Verona convened in 1822, the United States had established

diplomatic relations with several of them and trade was developing rapidly with all. Naturally the United States regarded with displeasure the suggestion of France that the Quadruple Alliance should intervene and help Spain reconquer her revolting colonies. As we have seen, England also had established profitable trading relations with them and these would be lost were the colonies to lose their independence. To prevent this, England suggested that the United States should join her in opposition to any European intervention in American affairs. 

President Monroe was willing to do this, but on the advice of John Quincy Adams, his secretary of state, he included in his message to Congress in December, 1823, the solemn warning to the world since known as the Monroe Doctrine, which among other things declared:

With the existing colonies or dependencies of any European power we have not interfered and shall not interfere. But with the governments who have declared their independence and maintained it, and whose independence we have acknowledged, we could not view any interposition for the purpose of oppressing them, or of controlling, in any other manner, their destiny by any European power, in any other light than as a manifestation of an unfriendly disposition towards the United States.

It is doubtful whether the United States at that time could have enforced this "hands off" policy without the aid of the British navy, if Europe had decided to intervene. Still the 

Monroe Doctrine immediately became one of the fundamental bases of its foreign policy, and has so continued to the present day. 

11. The United States Develops Rapidly Following the

War of 1812. After the War of 1812, the United States entered upon a period of steady development along its own lines, little influenced by the affairs of Europe. The great prairies of the 

Mississippi valley furnished an almost unlimited supply of cheap land to which the only obstacles were a few tribes of

Indians and lack of transportation. The Indians were gradually pushed westward and the problem of transportation was solved, first by canals and highways, and later by railroads. 

Primitive ideas about money led to occasional panics, but the great problem confronting the nation was the question of slav-

Slavery served to substitute for the old colonial jealousies a feeling of sectionalism which made impossible any genuine national sentiment. It came up most unexpectedly in connection with all kinds of questions pertaining to the territories and it led to war with Mexico, and finally to the sad struggle between the North and the South known as the War of Secession. Not until it was finally settled could a national spirit really develop. 

12. The United States Expands to the Pacific. Ex tensive as was the territory controlled by the United States, it

was not big enough to satisfy the Americans. The northern frontier had not been exactly determined and it was only after a bitter political campaign in which one of the slogans was "54-40 or fight" that reason prevailed. An agreement was then entered into with England by which the imaginary line of the 49th parallel became the longest unfortified frontier between

The northern part of Mexico, known as Texas, after having been invaded by American settlers in search of lands had proclaimed its independence in 1836. Nine years later it was annexed by the United States and a dispute as to its southern boundary led to war with Mexico. The Mexicans were easily defeated, and, in 1848, by the Treaty of Guadeloupe Hidalgo they gave everything north of the Rio Grande (Grän'dā) and Gila (he'lä) rivers to the United States. As a result, the first transcontinental railroad was completed in 1869. 

13. Democratic Ideas Replace Aristocratic Ideas in the 

North and West. Slowly but surely the aristocratic ideas of the founders of the Republic began to give way to more democratic ideas. The influence of the pioneer spirit brought new ideals into politics. The holding of public office came to be looked upon as the reward of victory at the polls, and the electoral college cease 1 to function except as the expression of party will. At the same time, the restrictions on voting slowly disappeared until practically all white males over twenty-one years of age, and, in some states, negroes, were given the ballot. Women also began to demand the privilege of voting along with other "equal rights."

With this expansion of suffrage came a lowering of the standards of political life, the rise of popular demands of a primitive type, and certain intolerance which expressed itself in movements against the Masons, Catholics, and foreigners. 

There arose a demand for public education to take the place of the earlier private and parochial schools. This became so insistent that, by the opening of the War of Secession, systems of free public schools had been established in all the northern states. While this expansion of democracy had been quite general throughout the North and West, the South, due to the influence of slavery, remained aristocratic and retained many of the ideals of the eighteenth century. 

14. England and France and Their Interests in the War.

The sympathy of England was largely with the South in the

War of Secession. Only with the greatest difficulty was she kept from intervening on more than one occasion. The rela-

cotton. England's interests might have profited by two American nations instead of one, yet she was kept from intervention by the enthusiasm of her common people for the northern cause, especially after President Lincoln issued his Emancipation Proclamation on January 1, 1863. She did, however, recognize the belligerency of the Confederate States of America, as the southerners called their government. 

Napoleon III seized the opportunity to send an expedition to Mexico to put down a revolution there and to make the Archduke Maximilian of Austria Emperor. All that President Lincoln could do at the time was to protest this invasion of the Monroe Doctrine, but, as soon as the War of Secession was ended, an army was ordered to the Rio Grande. This forced 

Napoleon to withdraw his support, and the Emperor was soon overthrown and put to death by the Mexicans. 

15. Nationalities Emerge in Latin America. In Latin 

America, unification was less successful. The control of Mexico over Central America disappeared almost immediately, and in 1825 Guatemala, Hon-dü'ràs, Nicaragua (nik-a-rä'gwa), Sälvà-dōr', and Cos'tà Ri'ca formed a union. This in turn broke up, but in 1842 the first four countries attempted it again, and five years later a third unsuccessful attempt was made by 

Honduras, Nicaragua, and Salvador. In South America the "Greater Colombia" of Bolivar was also short-lived. The union had been largely the work of the great leader and when he retired from the presidency, both Venezuela and Ecuador (ěk'wȧ-dôr) declared their independence, while New Granada drafted a new constitution and in 1860 changed her name to Colombia.

The connections between Uruguay and Paraguay, and the rest of the Rio de la Plata states were severed, and, in 1835, the latter took the name of the Är gen-tine Confederation. 

In 1864, Paraguay was almost destroyed when her dictator made war on both Brazil and Argentina, for she lost more

than half her territory and a large part of her male population. 

In fact, throughout the nineteenth century, almost constant friction existed among the various South American states, owing to conflicting border claims. 

16. Outside of Argentine, Brazil, and Chili, Dictatorships Prevailed in Latin America. The growth of democracy in Latin America was therefore less successful than in the Anglo-Saxon countries to the north. The chief difficulty lay in the character of the population, which consisted of a few Europeans of Spanish or Portuguese descent, a larger number of Creoles, and a great mass of natives of varying degrees of civilization. For the most part the Europeans and Creoles were educated, but the natives, although in theory Roman Catholics, were almost wholly without any education and were little removed from savagery. Everywhere exploitation of the natives was the rule, just as in some parts of Latin America to-day.

Despite the paper constitutions, many of them based on that of the United States, there could be little real democracy or even orderly government, except where control was in the hands. of some powerful man. In general these countries throughout the nineteenth century were ruled by dictators, who usually obtained their power and held it by military force with little reference to the law. Whether the government was good or bad depended upon their personal ambitions. There were three notable exceptions to this-the Argentine Confederation, Brazil, and Chile-but in two of these countries the percentage of European blood was much greater than in the rest of Latin America, and in all three, railroads and telegraph lines did much to develop unity and to encourage a stable régime. 

17. The Dominion of Canada Is Established. When the 

Thirteen Colonies revolted, the colonies of Canada, Nova Scotia, and Prince Edward's Island remained faithful to the Empire and became the refuge for the "Loyalists." As a result,

two new colonies-Upper Canada and New Brunswick-were established and the English population of the others increased greatly. Friction soon developed between the newcomers and the French and the later immigrants. To make matters worse, the royal governors defied the rights of the provincial assemblies and insisted on allotting the church grants to the Anglicans exclusively. Eventually this led to an ill-planned and unsuccessful rebellion in Upper Canada and to a French nationalist uprising in Lower Canada. Matters became so serious that Lord Durham (dûr'ăm) was sent over in 1838 to investigate conditions. As a result of his report, the two Canadas were united and given a responsible government, and the other colonies were granted similar concessions. 

The common interests of the colonies, especially after the coming of the railroad, stimulated a desire for closer association. Finally, delegates from all of them met at Quebec in 1864, and drafted seventy-two resolutions, which were adopted with modifications by Upper and Lower Canada, New Brunswick, and Nova Scotia. When these were submitted to England, Parliament passed the British North American Act, establishing the Dominion of Canada with a responsible government and a governor general to be appointed by the Crown. This act went into effect on July 1, 1867, and so the first day of 

July is known as "Dominion Day" and is celebrated as a national holiday throughout Canada. Six years later Prince Edward's Island joined the Dominion, but Newfoundland has always remained apart.

CHAPTER LXXI SOCIAL AND INTELLECTUAL REVOLUTIONS OF THIS PERIOD ARE NO LESS STARTLING 

The political and industrial revolutions grew out of forces which had their origin in the preceding period, but these same forces produced no less great results in the social and intellectual world. Science continued to interest scholars who carried forward the work of the early eighteenth century to wonderful conclusions. At the same time, the increasing wealth afforded more leisure and a larger support for these scientists. The political and economic changes brought new problems to be solved, while each advance in knowledge opened new fields to be explored and to be conquered. 

Like the Athens of Pericles and the Italian Renaissance, the period of revolution was a time of intellectual activity and discovery. The rule of reason gave men new confidence to challenge old theories and to propose new theories. The attack upon the divine right of kings and upon the old social order led thinkers to assail the authority of tradition and to set up new standards more in keeping with the new human knowledge. 

1. Many Minds Bring About the Revolution in Chem istry. The "phlogiston" theory had been developed before the nature of gas was known. The discovery of oxygen by the 

Frenchman Lavoisier (lå-vwȧ-zya'), in 1774, marked a new attitude toward the whole field of chemistry. However, modern chemistry did not really begin until early in the nineteenth century, with the work of the two English scientists, Sir Humphrey Dav'y and John Dalton. Davy was the first to dis- 692

SOCIAL REVOLUTIONS 

693 cover the compound nature of alkalis and to use electric currents in chemical operations. He was the inventor of the safety lamp which is still employed in coal mines. Dalton discovered the principle of atomic weights, although it was a later Russian chemist who arranged them in a regular series. 

These discoveries led to others. What was more important, chemistry became of increasing value to the industrial world. 

2. The Revolution in Physics Is 

Equally Significant.

The advance in physics was not less startling than that in chemistry. To Benjamin Thompson, an 

American Loyalist who fled to England to escape the Revolution and became 

Count Rumford, we owe the discovery of the mechanical theory of heat, though many years had to pass before it was accepted. 

OF. E. Compton Company.

THE DAVY SAFETY LAMP 

The use of this lamp has made mining much safer and made possible the opening of mines that were formerly unworkable.

From this there was only a step to the most important contribution to physics since Sir Isaac Newton had announced the theory of gravitation, namely, the idea of the conservation of energy. This was established in 1847 by the Englishman James 

Joule and the German Herman von Helmholtz and placed

physics in a new position. The discovery of "spectrum analysis" opened the way to a new knowledge of the heavenly bodies and furnished the physicist the spectroscope, probably his most important tool.

Electricity, next to the steam engine in importance to modern life, also owes its development to this period. Just at the close of the eighteenth century two Italians, Gäl-vä'nï and Vôľtä, made an electric battery and shortly afterward Sir Humphrey Davy invented the electric arc light. This battery was so costly and cumbersome that little practical use could be made of it until the Dane Oersted (ûr'stěth) found the connection between electricity and magnetism. This discovery made possible the invention of the electric telegraph by Morse. 

Then came an improved battery, and, what was more important, the discovery by Michael Făr'a-day, a Scotchman, that electricity could be developed by induction. To this we owe the invention of the first electric dynamo by Henry Wilde in 1865. 

It remained, however, for the Frenchman Grämme to perfect this invention and give to it a practical value. Although now the groundwork was all prepared, the "Age of Electricity" was still to come. 

3. The Revolution in Natural Science Clashes with 

Generally Accepted Belief. Great as were the changes in physics and chemistry, much more far-reaching were those in the other natural sciences. Until the beginning of the nineteenth century, the generally accepted belief of the origin of the world was in the book of Genesis. According to this, the universe was a special creation and had been subjected to various catastrophes like Noah's flood. James Hutton had insisted, as early as 1785, that geology must not bother about origins but deal with the materials of the earth. This new idea found its expression in 1830 in the Principles of Geology of Sir Charles Lyell. Seven years later Louis Agassiz (ăgʻi̟se), a Swiss scientist who had removed to the United States,

SOCIAL REVOLUTIONS 

695 presented his theory of glaciers to account for the wide distribution of scattered boulders in certain regions. 

No less epoch-making was the progress in the study of living things. During the first half of the nineteenth century a series of scientific expeditions to various parts of the world made available to scientists a vast collection of specimens of plants and animals. To account for this great variety of living things became a scientific problem of the first importance. 

The Frenchman de Lä-märck' suggested that different organs were developed to meet the demands of new environments, instead of being originally created. 

In 1842 Charles Darwin, an English naturalist, worked at a new theory called "organic evolution" upon which he wrote an essay, which, however, he did not publish. Eight years later, Alfred Wallace sent to Darwin a paper with almost the same ideas, and in the following year Darwin published his famous Origin of Species. He attempted to account for the differentiation of animals and plants, and included man among the animals. Seven years later the German Men'děl published the results of some experiments which considerably modified, but did not destroy, the theories of Darwin. This theory of evolution has been responsible for much of the progress in natural science since that time, even though the "missing link" is still to be found. 

4. The Revolution in Practice of Medicine and Surgery 

Is a Boon to All Mankind. Nowhere were the scientific discoveries of this period of greater benefit to the human race than in medicine and surgery; in fact, it was not until then that medicine really became a science. The first of these discoveries was made in 1796 when Edward Jenner, a country physician in England, observing that milkmaids were seldom attacked by the terrible scourge of smallpox, vaccinated a patient with virus taken from a cow suffering with cow-pox and rendered the patient immune to the other disease. As a re-

sult, smallpox has all but been eliminated from civilized countries, and the principle of inoculation has been applied to many other diseases.

Operations, which before had been few, now became common but not without great risk until Lord Lister discovered the necessity of cleanliness and antisepsis. 

The greatest discovery was yet to come. In 1861 Louis Pas-

5. The Revolution in Mode of Life Was Due to Many 

Factors. Side by side with this mastery of the enemies of mankind went an increasing betterment of the daily life of humanity. Machinery tended to lessen the amount of work necessary to earn a living.

The extension of the factory system gradually took out of the home many of the industries like spinning and weaving, and freed the women of the household from some of their more monotonous tasks.

The improvement of transportation made available even to the lower classes new foods and new materials of all sorts. 

The invention of a new kind of lamp in 1782 and of matches in 1827 revolutionized lighting, even though the electric light was still unperfected. With the development of cities housing conditions, especially for the middle classes, began to improve. 

Elaborate water systems became necessary and these led to the

In fact, in 1840 a theological student was denied ordination because he had taken a bath, and in Boston as late as the middle of the century a person had to get a physician's permission to bathe. The phenomenal growth of cities also was marked by attempts to control and beautify the cities as in the planning of Washington and the laying out of the great boulevards and parks of Paris by Baron Haussman under the direction of Napoleon III. 

6. The Revolution in Warfare Was Accompanied by 

Devices More and More Destructive. Unfortunately the contributions of science were not all for the betterment of society, for under the influence of Napoleon warfare became more deadly as a result of more effective artillery. Until his day cannon had played a minor rôle in battle, but from then on

699 they became increasingly important. Chemistry also came forward in 1847 with nitric compounds to enlarge their range and destructive power, and the next decade saw the development of breechloading guns and the use of cartridges which increased the rapidity of fire. During our Civil War the use of steel armor had been devised for protecting naval vessels, and steam had been used for their propulsion. That warfare was becoming more hazardous was evident from the terrible death toll it exacted. 

7. Education Becomes a Public Concern. With the rise of the concepts of democracy and nationality came a new reason for education. Democracy demanded a certain amount of intelligence and knowledge on the part of the voters, and na-

tionality inspired citizens to seek an acquaintance with their country's history. Even the rise of large conscripted armies. meant a certain amount of intermingling of ideas and the imparting of some knowledge. That education was beginning to be looked upon as a public concern is shown by the presence of a Minister of Education in the cabinets of nearly every one of the newly established constitutional monarchies. 8. The Revolution in Printing Makes Knowledge Avail able for the Masses. The application of steam power to the printing-press made possible the extension of education and the spread of knowledge to the masses. It greatly cheapened the production of books but its most far-reaching effects were upon the newspaper. The London Times began to operate its presses by steam power in 1814, and from that time newspapers could be produced cheaply enough for everybody. In 

1847 the Hoe "Lightning" press increased the speed so that as many sheets could be printed in an hour as by the old hand presses in a week. The middle classes tried to keep papers for themselves with the aid of taxes and stamp duties, but eventually they had to fall back on the "reviews" or magazines, which

SOCIAL REVOLUTIONS 

701 began to appear in the early part of the nineteenth century. 

Through these reviews information about the new books and the new discoveries in science were spread to the ends of the earth. 

9. A New Literature Distinguishes This Period. We have seen how the rise of the national movement in Germany was accompanied by a great development of literature. Goethe (gû'te), Schiller, and Heine (hi'ne) are only the more outstanding of a large group of writers who created a literature in the German language. In England, too, Byron, Wordsworth, and Coleridge revived the literary glories of the Elizabethan days. The French Revolution interposed such obstacles in the way of literature in France that not until far into the nineteenth century did Victor Hugo and Flaubert (flō-bâr') restore to it a certain amount of prestige. During this period, too, the literary movement struck Italy and Russia. 

Of special importance was the rise of the novel, a new type of literature which was destined to become the most popular of all forms of literary expression. Like other literature it expressed the aspirations of the age. Consequently when the rapidly expanding national feeling turned men's attention to the past, the historical novel became one of the fruitful devices for aiding the new nationalistic movement. 

10. Writing History to Reveal the Truth Becomes the

Aim. The application of scientific methods to the study of literature and history caused some important developments. At the close of the eighteenth century a new type of criticism led Wolff (vólf) and Niebuhr (në'boor) to attack the traditional conception of Homer's poems and to question the traditions associated with Ancient Rome. The work of these men brought in a new method of studying history from the sources. 

This method was carried further by Leopold von Rän'ke, who declared that the aim of historical study was to "find out what really happened." Since that time, historical scholars have de-

voted their attention to shifting the documents of the past in an attempt to choose the true from the false, and to write history solely with the idea of revealing the truth. 

11. A Humanitarian Attitude Toward Criminals and 

Unfortunates Develops. The publication, in 1764, of the treatise On Crimes and Punishments by the Italian jurist di Běc-cä-rï'ä marked the beginning of a new era in penology. Heretofore punishment had had as its object the torture of the guilty person, on the theory that such cruelties as branding and burning, emasculating and flaying, pillorying and breaking on the wheel, would deter others from becoming lawbreakers. For this reason, too, executions took place in the open and were one of the excitements of the day. 

Just how little value society placed on human life is indicated by the fact that as late as the end of the eighteenth century English law recognized over two hundred offenses punishable by death, including such petty misdemeanors as stealing from a shopkeeper goods to the value of five shillings, or "picking" as little as a shilling from a person's pocket. Inability to pay one's debts was also looked upon as a crime and led to imprisonment often for years. However, with the acquisition of colonies it became the custom to sentence to transportation thither, debtors as well as persons who otherwise would be liable to the death penalty or to long terms at hard labor. Even in England this did not wholly cease until 1857. 

An era of prison reform came with the humanizing of punishment that began in France during the Revolution, and across the Channel twenty years later. The leader of this movenent was an English Quakeress, Elizabeth Frye, who devoted her life to working for better prison conditions. The jails and workhouses were made more sanitary, and shackles and underground cells were done away with. Men were separated from women, and children and first offenders from hardened criminals. So great was the change in the attitude of the public

SOCIAL REVOLUTIONS 

703 that by the end of the nineteenth century the list of capital crimes had been reduced in most civilized countries to only two or three, and there was a distinct movement to do away with the death sentence altogether.

With the change in the treatment of criminals came also new attention to the care of defectives. It was the Frenchman, Philippe Pi-něl, who first preached the idea that the insane and feeble-minded members of society should be treated like other diseased persons and should be placed in hospitals under the care of competent physicians, instead of being left to wander at large, or worse still of being chained in dark dungeons and flogged for their irresponsible outbreaks. As a result of a parliamentary inquiry in 1815, asylums for the insane were opened in England, and before long in every civilized country these unfortunates were being gathered up and cared for by the state. Well-kept almshouses and poor-farms were also established in which the aged indigent could end their days in a limited degree of comfort. 

12. Slavery Gradually Disappears. A direct result of eighteenth-century ideals was a war on slavery. The question vexed the founders of the American government but they thought they had settled, or deferred, it by the constitutional provision that the importation of slaves should not be interfered with by Congress before 1808. With the abolishment of the slave trade by England in 1807, and the condemning of it by the Congress of Vienna in 1815, such an impetus was given the anti-slavery movement that, after 1819, the United States remained the only great Western nation in the world in which slavery was tolerated. In that year, however, she did join England in an effort to stop the kidnapping of negroes in Africa for export to other parts of the world by declaring the foreign slave trade to constitute piracy. However, the institution continued in the United States until the adoption of the Thirteenth 

Amendment to the Constitution in 1865.

In South America slavery had largely disappeared by 1850, although it was not abolished in Brazil until that country became a republic in 1888. By the close of the period of revolution it had also been largely stamped out in Asia and Africa, although it was not until the end of 1927 that it finally disappeared from the Gold Coast. 

13. Foreign Missions Carry Christianity and Civiliza tion to Backward People. Another phase of the humanitarian movement was the development of foreign missions within the Protestant churches. This had its beginning in England where the Society for the Propagation of the Gospel in New England was founded in the seventeenth century, followed by the Society for the Propagation of the Gospel in Foreign Parts in 1701. Within the next half-century the Moravian. 

Brethren had set forth from their homes in Bohemia for the spread of the Gospel into remote lands. The founding of the 

Century Baptist Missionary Society was the first of a long series of similar societies in England, Protestant Europe, and America, representing all the Protestant denominations, that undertook to carry the blessings of Christianity not only to non- Christian lands but even to Roman Catholic countries. 

Beginning as bearers of the Gospel, the missionaries soon discovered that educational and medical work was fully as important as religious, and much easier to accomplish. In connection with this they found it necessary to prepare grammars and dictionaries of unwritten languages and to translate the Bible and other books into many tongues. They became also the advance guard of science in the most remote corners of the world. Among the older civilizations of Asia they had little to offer except the humanitarian conceptions and the scientific knowledge of the West, but to Africa and the Islands of the Sea they brought civilization. Wherever they went, they became the source from which sprang interest in the intellectual and material accomplishments of Europe and America.
