CHAPTER LXXII THE SIGNIFICANCE OF THE PERIOD OF REVOLUTION 1. A Changing World in Ways of Doing Marks This 

Period. Remarkable as has been the progress of our own day with its automobiles, radios, and airplanes, the great change in the world was wrought during the period of revolution. Never before in the history of mankind had so complete a change been made in man's habits and outlook upon life. An Egyptian pharaoh would have found little difficulty in adjusting himself to the life of Europe before 1789, but George Washington would have been completely mystified if he had come back to earth in 1870. New ways of doing things, new means of communication and travel, and new ideas and theories made an almost complete break with the past, although it must not be forgotten that to the mass of mankind, and even to most of its leaders, the older ideals were still valid, and that little progress had been made in the readjustments necessary to adapt society to the new conditions of life. 

2. The Economic Changes. Of prime importance were the changes that took place in the methods of production. 

Never before had such progress been made in the conquest of nature and in the processes of changing raw materials into products for man's use. With the steam engine and machinery, man was now master of his environment in a way that before he had never dreamed of being. Failure of his crops did not any longer necessarily mean starvation, although on the other hand he was becoming increasingly dependent upon the crops of others. In his puny struggle to win a livelihood from a hard soil he now had at his command far better tools than ever before, and far greater knowledge and skill as to what to grow 706

SIGNIFICANCE OF THE PERIOD OF REVOLUTION 

707 and how to grow it. In mine or quarry, and on land or sea, he could use the stored power of past ages and multiply his own strength many hundred fold.

At the same time he was losing his own economic independence, and becoming more and more dependent upon machinery and its owners. With the development of great factories men were crowded into cities and were set to work on tasks of increasingly specialized character. This limited their freedom of movement and placed them almost wholly at the mercy of the factory and mine owners. To meet this situation, they organized into unions to bargain their services with the capitalists. 

3. The Social Changes. With these economic changes came correspondingly important social changes. New classes were formed and the chasm between them became wider even than that between the older groups. Slavery disappeared from the civilized world, but in its place there came the serfdom of labor, for the factory and mine workers in the early days of the industrial revolution found themselves little better off than slaves. They lived in company houses, bought supplies at the company store, and depended upon the company for a job, so life held little to suggest freedom.

For woman, the new situation proved both a blessing and a curse. It opened to her new avenues and gave her a position of economic importance such as she had never before had. 

But at the same time she often found the work of the factory far harder than that of the home, and the conditions of her new life much more severe than had been those of former days. Thanks to many new inventions, her labors within the home were lightened and she had opportunity for greater leisure. But even so, it was the home itself which was destined to suffer most from this revolution. Not only did it lose its economic status when so many of its tasks were taken over by the factory, but it lost its director when the mother became a factory worker. Nevertheless, the standards of living slowly rose

under the vast increase in wealth and the necessity for improvement and sanitation enforced by the rapid growth of cities and towns. 

4. The Political Changes. To the casual observer it was the political system which showed the greatest changes. The rise of democracy brought a new concept of government but one which after all was not really democratic. In spite of the fine-sounding phrases about equality common in the eighteenth century, political rights were still largely the exclusive privilege of the upper and middle classes, who alone had been able to make profit out of the Industrial Revolution. Civil rights were given to the masses, but political control remained in the hands of the more fortunate classes and was exercised almost completely in their interests. Only in more backward countries like Russia and Turkey did the autocratic ideas of the past still hold sway, although everywhere a reactionary party contested stubbornly each new advance proposed by the liberals. 

Under the influence of democratic ideas nationality took on a new meaning. For the first time every one had a share in the state. This was true especially with the middle classes, for the state through its power of legislation could greatly influence trade and commerce, and thereby have a direct influence on their pocketbooks. Needless to say the feeling of nationality, once started, grew with leaps and bounds, and by means of language and literature began to influence many peoples whose destinies were controlled by others. 

5. The Intellectual Changes. Many of the startling discoveries in science were revolutionary in character and compelled a readjustment of the whole intellectual world. Indeed, the study of science took on a new meaning when its discoveries were connected with the field of invention. It then began slowly to take the place of the classics which had dominated education since the days of the Renaissance. On the other hand, the critical use of the documents forced a revision and ex-

pansion of the social studies. At the basis of this was the new conception of the evolutionary development of human society, which had grown out of the study of the natural sciences. This new concept caused a new attitude toward the universe as a whole and led to new attempt to demonstrate its unity. At the same time the industrial revolution added a whole series of problems whose solution was attempted on a new basis by the socialists. 

6. The Religious Changes. It was the work of Darwin which precipitated the real struggle between religion and science, and yet much of the study of the revolutionary period led to friction with the church. Under the influence of the eighteenth-century thought there had been an attempt to separate religion and politics, as was shown in the Constitution of the United States where all reference to religion was limited to the recognition of Sunday. During the French Revolution the state even went so far as to establish a worship of reason and to expel the church from France.

THE PERIOD OF CONTEMPORARY CIVILIZATION Chapters LXXIII-LXXIX The Foreword 

The Industrial Revolution brought in a new period of world history. With its inventions in the field of communication and transportation, distance was all but annihilated and the nations were brought together into one economic whole. At last, the isolation of Europe was brought to an end and the United States and Japan were admitted as partners into the galaxy of great powers. In the scramble to acquire the unoccupied parts of the world which marked the later years of the nineteenth century, great waterways took on an added importance. 

Stirred by economic competition, nationalism became imperialistic. States tried to increase their strength by forming powerful alliances, and watched one another with jealous eyes while they piled up armaments as a guarantee of peace. In the end this bore fruit in a tremendous catastrophe involving almost the whole world and revealing the complete interdependence of the nations. From this calamity emerged the idea of a political union embracing all peoples, an ideal which may contain the germs of a solution for the major difficulties of society. 711

CHAPTER LXXIII  IS ONE OF ARMED PEACE AND CLEVER DIPLOMACY 

The success of Germany in the Franco-Prussian War demonstrated the importance of military preparedness. For more than forty years the general peace of Europe had not been broken, but each of the leading nations was perfecting its armament and establishing closer friendships. Conscription and prolonged military training became almost universal. Vast plants for the manufacture of munitions were built. There were rumors that the owners kept national fears alive for the purpose of creating a demand for their products. Bismarck's part in all this easily made him the leader in European diplomacy, while his clear thinking and far-sighted vision combined with his intimate knowledge of statesmen and of continental politics made it possible for him to retain that position for nearly twenty years. 

1. France Smarts under Defeat and Longs for Her

Lost Provinces. France raised the money for the German indemnity by heroic efforts and got rid of the German armies within the incredibly short space of eighteen months. But she could not get rid of her desire for the return of Alsace and Lorraine, and the idea of revenge controlled her politics and thought for many years. No less troublesome was her problem of government. In spite of the establishment of the Third Republic, at heart she favored a monarchy, but owing to the number of candidates for the throne she soon discovered that after all a republic was the only form of government that promised domestic peace. This, however, did not prevent the possibility of the seizure of the control by some strong military man; in 713

fact, in 1885 it was prevented only by a threat of intervention from Bismarck. 

2. The Eastern Question Revives in the Balkans. In spite of all the decrees issued by the Sultan, the condition of the Christian population of the Ottoman Empire failed to improve, due in part to the weakness of the government. There were a few liberalminded Turks who saw that the only salvation for their country lay in modernizing its government and in adopting western ideas generally. However, no matter how much the sultans might wish 40 CHAM

This was especially true in the European part of the Empire where the Russians more than once had gone to the assistance of their 

Slavic cousins-the Bulgarians, Serbs, Croats, and Montenegrins. To complicate matters still farther, ever since Prussia had forced them out of the German Confederation, the Austrians had been casting longing eyes upon Bosnia (boz'nĭ-ȧ) and Herzegovina (her-tsé-gó-věna), and other Turkish regions in the 

Balkan peninsula.

Suddenly the Herzegovinians rebelled against the oppressive taxation and the arbitrary demands of their Turkish landlords. 

Turkish fanaticism retaliated by murdering the French and German consuls at Sä-ló-nï'ki. Then the Bulgars rose and the 

Serbs and Montenegrins took up arms in self-protection. When the local authorities found that they could not put down this disturbance, the imperial government brought in half-wild Circassian (ser-kǎsh'ăn) troops from Asia. In the "Bulgarian atrocities" which followed, over twenty thousand Christians were massacred and whole villages were wiped out. 

Meanwhile, the powers had been sending notes to the Sublime Porte, as the Turkish Government was called. This government, relying on the backing of England, remained defiant. 

In the midst of a conference of the powers, which was trying to work out some reforms for the unfortunate land, the Sultan suddenly proclaimed a liberal constitution. 

3. In the Russo-Turkish War Russia Defeats Turkey and Frees the Balkans. In spite of the sultan's eleventh-hour conversion, the Tsar declared war against Turkey in the spring of 1876. The Roumanians cast their lot with Russia and the 

Serbs renewed their uprising. For months the contest fluctuated with varying success until the fall of Plěv'nȧ and the advance on Erzerum (ĕrz-room'), in eastern Armenia, opened the road to Constantinople, and gave all the advantage to the Russians. England then decided to go to the assistance of the 

Turks once more. Before she acted the Russians had advanced to San Stefano (stā'fä-nō), only seven miles from Constantinople, and the panic-stricken Turks had agreed to preliminary terms of peace. According to this convention, Roumania, Serbia, and Bulgaria were to become independent states, and Bosnia and Herzegovina were to enjoy local autonomy under the rule of the Sultan.

Great was Austria's consternation when she realized that her disgruntled Slavic provinces would be bordered by inde-

pendent Slavic states under the influence of her mighty Slavic neighbor. In her protests to this arrangement, she had the support of England, which saw in the treaty the extinction of Turkey as a European nation and a disturbance of the balance of power in the Near East. For a time it looked as if the much-dreaded European war was inevitable, but finally the

5. England Intervenes in Egyptian Affairs. The acquisi tion of Cyprus was part of a far more extensive programme which Disraeli had in mind. By 1875 the Khedive (kě-dev') of Egypt had got into such financial difficulties that he had to offer for sale his shares in the Suez Canal. They were bought by Disraeli for the English government, much to the chagrin of France. Because the Khedive's financial trouble still remained acute, his European bondholders-mainly English and 

French bankers-demanded a governmental inquiry. In spite of a report that showed Egypt to be solvent, they insisted upon European control of the Khedive's finances. This was undertaken jointly by the two governments and the indebtedness was funded, i. e., made into a single loan.

Meanwhile so much friction developed between the Khedive and his foreign assistants that the former was compelled to abdicate. The new Khedive was more amenable but the Egyptians resented foreign control and a nationalist uprising oc-

Colonel Gordon, better known as "Chinese Gordon" because of his service in China, lost his life trying to hold Khartoum (kär-toom') against the Mahdi. The fall of the city ended for a time England's efforts in the Sudan. 

6. The Triple Alliance Is Formed. France occupied 

Tunis in 1882. Although it bordered upon Algeria, the greater part of the foreigners who had established themselves there were Italians, and Italy had long dreamed of occupying it herself. So great was her anger over this occupation that she sought means of obtaining revenge for what she felt was a direct blow at her national aspirations. Quite naturally she turned to Bismarck who reluctantly agreed to admit her to the alliance which he had already formed with Austria. Although the Triple Alliance was primarily defensive and secret, Italy hoped to obtain through it recognition of her interests in the 

Balkan peninsula and in northern Africa. At first it was made for only five years, but through renewals it lasted until 1914, insuring both Italy and Germany against any attack on the part of the French. 

10. Germany Becomes Powerful and Prosperous under 

Bismarck's Leadership. Under Bismarck's leadership, Germany became one of the most powerful nations of Europe. 

Although the payment of the French indemnity caused a great inflation of credit and much speculation, ending in a panic, the country soon recovered and embarked on a period of great prosperity. Manufacturing increased so rapidly that the Germans came to be thought of no longer as an agricultural peo-

ple but as one of the great industrial nations of the world. 

This progress was hastened after means were found to eliminate the sulphur from the iron ore of Lorraine, insuring an abundant supply of cheap pig iron for the production of steel. 

In order to improve communication, the railroads were nationalized and numerous canals were built to supplement them. 

An index of the greatness of Germany's industrial progress during this period was the tenfold increase in her foreign trade. 

8. Bismarck Defeats the Social Democratic Party by

Putting Their Programme into Effect. Along with this industrial development came serious social and political questions which greatly strengthened the Social Democratic Party. Because it consistently refused to support Bismarck's militaristic programme and policy of high protection, he tried to crush it by measures aimed at socialists. Socialistic meetings were forbidden; the publication of books and articles on socialism was banned; and socialists themselves were liable to imprisonment and to expulsion from the country without a court trial. When these measures failed, Bismarck suddenly changed his policy and adopted the scheme of giving the empire the very things which the socialists claimed the ideal industrial state should supply. His theory was that if you "give the workingman the right to work while he is well, assure him care when he is sick, and keep him when he is old, the Social Democrats will get no hold upon him." Thus Germany owed to Bismarck her laws providing workingmen's insurance against old age and incapacity, and this in time became one of the most important factors in German industry. 

9. Nationalistic Aspirations Were Always a Problem for Austria. The situation of the other great central European state was quite different from that of Germany. Although the Ausgleich of 1867 had settled the most insistent of her problems, numerous other problems presented themselves. At the bottom lay the question of nationality. The Czechs in Bo-

hemia, the Poles and Little Russians in Galicia, the Croats and Slovenes in the south, and the Roumanians and Serbs in the southeast, were all clamoring for political rights. Some statesmen believed that yielding to these demands would satisfy most of the nationalistic aspirations, but they were in the minority. In Hungary, the Magyars overrode ruthlessly at the

The situation was further complicated when the Congress of Berlin intrusted to Austria the administration of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which were inhabited by Slavs, and worse still by Slavs who were close relatives of the independent Serbians.

10. William II Drops Bismarck and Heads Germany toward Disaster. With the death of William I in 1888 and the accession of his grandson, William II, in the same year, Bismarck's influence began to decline. 

The new Kaiser, although barely twenty-nine years of age, possessed unusual self-confidence and signalized his coming to the throne by such statements as "We consider ourselves as designed by God to govern" and "The soldier and the army, not parliamentary majorities, have welded together the German Empire. I put my trust in the army." He was an ardent nationalist and believed thoroughly in

CHAPTER LXXIV INDUSTRIAL DEVELOPMENT ENCOURAGES A TRADE AND CO- LONIAL EXPANSION KNOWN AS NATIONAL IMPERIALISM 

By the last quarter of the nineteenth century the changes which had been wrought by the Industrial Revolution began to have their effect. By that time the factories were doing most of the manufacturing of western Europe, and as a consequence there had come a great shifting of population from country to town. It became clear that there would be a great difference between the interests of the city and the rural dwellers. The national movement which up to this time had been devoted largely to the state and to obtaining privileges for its citizens now developed a new set of ideals. How these ideals were expressed in a national imperialism with the leading nations contending with each other in policies of world-wide trade control, colonial expansion, and spheres of influence will be considered in this chapter. 

1. Coal, Iron, and Cheap Labor Are Essential Elements in the New Industrial Development. This industrialization did not take place with the same degree of completeness in all countries. A great factory system required three essentials-coal, iron, and cheap labor. Only those countries which had all these could hope to become fully industrialized. England had a special advantage, not merely because she had almost inexhaustible supplies of coal and iron, and an abundance of cheap labor, but because her manufactures had become standard in the markets of the world, since she had been first in industrial development. 

Germany's acquisition of Lorraine had given her the necessary supply of iron to supplement her coal fields in the Ruhr (roor) Basin. Moreover, her constantly increasing population 723

and labor legislation furnished plenty of cheap and reasonably contented workers. Although France had developed a factory system earlier in the century, she still remained largely an agricultural country. Among the less industrialized countries of 

Europe were Italy, thanks to a lack of coal; and Russia, which suffered from too much land. Like Spain, Russia also lacked one other important factor-a middle class. 

The United States had both coal and iron in abundance, but, as in Russia, vast unoccupied lands proved a magnet which still drew the population into the country. It was not until the great immigration after 1870 that she was really able to develop fully her industrial opportunities. But the scarcity of cheap labor had one compensation-it led to such a wide use of machinery that by the close of the nineteenth century the output in her factories was far greater than in any European country. Japan, also, at the end of the nineteenth century had become industrialized although she lacked large supplies of coal and iron. 

3. England Leads in Providing Capital for World-Wide 

Industrial Development. Under this new system of industry, capital became of prime importance. During the nineteenth century great banking-houses developed in most of the countries of Europe, particularly in England. They sought far and wide for opportunities to invest the large amounts of money they controlled. When these opportunities were lacking at home, they went abroad; in fact, the greater part of the early railway building in America was financed in England and on the Continent. These European bankers also loaned money to foreign states and rulers. We have already seen the consequence of this in Egypt. Turkey likewise fell a victim to the ill-advised borrowings of her sultan. Early in the eighties, she found it necessary to hand over to an international commission the administration of the customs and the supervision of the internal improvements.

INDUSTRIAL DEVELOPMENT 

725 Naturally England took a leading part in the exportation of capital, for London was the financial centre of the world. But the French and Dutch were not far behind. Germany was necessarily slower in getting into international banking, owing to her late industrial development. The United States was so large and her needs for capital were so insistent that throughout the nineteenth century she had to be a borrower instead of a lender. 

4. Markets for Surplus Production and Colonies to Produce Raw Materials Assume First Importance. The advantages of large-scale production under the new industrial system placed a premium upon markets and upon raw materials. 

With the exception of England, all the industrialized nations erected tariff barriers in order to preserve their own markets for home manufacturers, and then they looked abroad for every possibility to dispose of their surplus production. As soon as this possibility became clear to the governments, control of the less civilized parts of the world assumed a new importance. 

For over a hundred years the colonization movement had been retarded, but now at the close of the nineteenth century it took a new lease on life. Within a relatively short time all of the unclaimed lands had passed into the hands of one or another of the great powers. These primitive countries offered good markets and assured supplies of raw materials which the new inventions were making increasingly desirable. This new expansion afforded the bankers an opportunity to finance such modern improvements as railways, telegraphs, and harbor works, while the newly acquired territory gratified the national pride.

Here again England occupied the best position, for she boasted that the sun never set on the "British Empire." Close behind her came France and the Netherlands because of their earlier interest in colonization, while Germany and Italy were having to start from the bottom. Russia's position was pe-

On the sea, regular steamship communication had been established in every direction. In this the English had taken the lead with the organization of the Cunard Steamship Company, but the French and Dutch were offering stiff competition, and by the nineties the Germans also had entered the field. The larger open seas were naturally free to all, but the smaller en-

closed ones were subject to more or less national control. Here, too, England had the advantage because her far-flung possessions and her growing dependence upon food from abroad made this increasingly important. Gibraltar, Malta, Egypt, and 

Aden controlled the great sea lanes from Europe to the Far East; and Singapore and Hongkong served as keys to southeastern Asia. The very position of her island carried control of the North Sea, by which alone could the commerce of Belgium, Holland, and Germany reach the ocean. In truth could she be called "Mistress of the Seas." 

6. In the Partition of Africa England and France Get the Most Desirable Locations. The first of the continents to fall a victim in this new race for territory was Africa. We have already seen how England obtained the Cape Colony in 1806 and established a protectorate over Egypt in the eighties. In addition she held various strategic positions along the Guinea coast. France had occupied Algeria in 1830 and also held some minor places in the Senegal area, as well as the great island of Măd-a-găs'car off the southeastern coast. Portugal had a reminder of her former colonial greatness in the colony of Ango'la near the mouth of the Con'go and that of Mō-zăm-bique' opposite Madagascar, and even Spain had a few trading factories in the northwest. But the interior of the continent remained an unknown land except for the explorations of such men as Mun'gó Park in the Niger (ni'jěr) country and David Livingstone, the Scotch missionary who worked his way across the continent by way of the valleys of the Zăm-bēʼzi and Congo. 

However, it was to the work of Henry M. Stanley, a newspaper man sent out to find Livingstone, that the world owed its first real knowledge of the vast resources of the interior of the "Dark Continent." In 1874-1878, Stanley crossed from the mouth of the Congo to a point on the mainland opposite to Zǎn'zi-bär, discovering en route the great lake of Albert Nyän'zä and the source of the Congo in Lake Tăn-găn-yï'kä. 7. The Boer War and What It Led to. The rapid mi gration of Englishmen to the Cape Colony after the Napoleonic Wars resulted in the introduction of the English language, and finally, in 1833, in the abolishment of slavery. Disgruntled by these changes, the native Dutchmen, or Boers (bōors), made a grand trek in their ox-carts to the inhospitable veldt beyond the Orange, later called Nå-täľ, where they established new homes. However, this region was soon annexed and they settled in what was subsequently known as the Orange Free State and the Transvaal (trăns-väl'). 

There they were left alone until their harsh treatment of the Zulus (zoo'lōos) brought on a native uprising. Fearful, as it claimed, that this would spread to the Cape Colony, the imperialistic government of Disraeli intervened and, after the uprising had been put down, declared a protectorate over the two half-organized states. The Boers rebelled and administered a disastrous defeat to the Cape troops at Majuba (må-jōō'bä) Hill. Disraeli's government acknowledged the independence of the Boers under British "protection," completely ignoring the Majuba affair. After this came the discovery of gold in the 

Transvaal and a rush thither of hordes of adventurers from every quarter. These Uitlanders (oit'lån-dērs), naturally largely 

British, got along badly with the Boers who refused them any share in the government of the country. With the connivance of Cecil Rhodes, Cape Colony's richest man and at the moment her premier, Dr. Jameson made an unsuccessful raid into the 

Transvaal to force a change in the constitution. War began

under the leadership of President Paul Krüger. In the end the Boers were beaten by sheer weight of numbers. The war was not popular in England and when another party came into power they sought to undo the injustice of the past by giving the conquered states freedom in local affairs. So successful did this prove that in 1910 Parliament set up another self-

8. China Is Forced to Open Certain Ports. Shortly after the establishment, in the seventeenth century, of the Manchu (măn'choo) dynasty in China, these rulers became suspicious both of foreigners and of Christianity. Not only did they put an end to all missionary work but they restricted the foreigners to Canton and Ma-cä'ó, a bit of territory rented for years to the Portuguese as a place to cure their fish. After that, numerous attempts were made by the English to establish trade relations

INDUSTRIAL DEVELOPMENT 

733 through other ports but with no avail. As we have already seen, English trade with China at this time was a monopoly of the East India Company, and one of the most profitable items was opium, which had been introduced among the Chinese in the fifteenth century.

During the Napoleonic wars, the English seized Macao and, in the War of 1812, their warships played havoc with American shipping in Chinese waters in total disregard of the sovereignty of China. Protests failing, the Chinese resorted to a boycott of the tea trade, and this led to much bitterness. When 

England threw trade with China open to all Englishmen, the opium question became a most vexatious problem. Early in the nineteenth century, the Manchus banned its use, but this was difficult to enforce.

Finally, in 1836, the Chinese demanded the surrender of all the opium in the hands of the foreign traders at Canton. In the war which followed, the Chinese were defeated and by the Treaty of Năn-king were compelled to pay a large indemnity, to give to England the island of Hong-kong, and to throw open to foreign trade four more ports, including Shăng-hä-Ĭ at the mouth of the Yangtze. By a subsequent treaty they were allowed to levy a five per cent duty on both imports and exports, and England was granted extraterritorial rights. An 

American naval officer in China at the time of the "Opium War" procured a treaty with similar privileges for the United States and shortly after the French also obtained one. 

9. Foreign Influence Expands throughout China. Five ports could not long satisfy the trade requirements of the western powers. Within a few years, the murder of a French missionary and the seizure of an English ship led to more wars in which China was again hopelessly beaten. Six additional ports were opened to foreign trade, and it was also agreed that foreign ministers could reside at Peking. Besides, foreigners were to be allowed to travel into the interior of the country and pro-

tection was to be given to missionaries. It was during one of these struggles that the French seized Saigon (si-gōn') and laid the basis of their rich colony of Indo-China. 

After this, western influence in China began to spread rapidly. Trade grew by leaps and bounds and foreign missions were

Although it was difficult for the missionaries to meet on equal terms with the higherclass Chinese because the latter were often intellectually superior, they did bring to the lower classes education and the benefits of medical science.

10. Japan Becomes a "Hermit" Empire. As in China, in the early sixteenth century, during the reign of the great Hï-děyō-shï, Spanish friars from Manila invaded Japan. At that time Japan was a feudal state, governed by an emperor who was a direct descendant of her earliest rulers, but whose power was wholly theoretical, since the actual control of affairs was in the hands of the Shogun. All the wealth belonged to the daimyos, who lived in luxury, surrounded by hordes of retainers, while the great mass of the people was composed of serfs. 

Their lot was especially hard because the population was large and the amount of land suitable for cultivation was greatly limited. It was the determination of the friars to convert the 

Japanese, that was partly responsible for the decision of the Shogun Lyemitsu (lē-yě-mē-tsoo) in 1638 to close the country against all foreigners, Oriental as well as European. 

The Dutch purchased immunity by agreeing to retire to the tiny island of Deshima (dā-she-mȧ) in the harbor of Nä-gåsä-kï, and to accept what was equivalent to imprisonment, for they were allowed to leave it only once a year. At first they were permitted to receive seven ships annually but eventually these were reduced to one; and then for two hundred years this was the only contact between Japan and the outside world. 

11. Commodore Perry Opens Japan to Foreign Trade. 

Throughout the early part of the nineteenth century, various western powers attempted to establish direct communication with the Japanese government. Invariably their missions were refused permission to land and even their letters had to be dispatched through the Dutch intermediaries at Deshima. The 

United States felt the lack of direct communication most keen-

ly, because Japan lay on the trade route between China and America, and, in case of shipwreck, survivors had no way of returning home. Finally, in 1853, Commodore Perry with two

American warships sailed into the Bay of Tokyo and insisted on landing and leaving with the Shogun a letter addressed to 

COMMODORE PERRY ARRIVES IN JAPAN 

From this historic event the modernization of Japan can be dated. the Emperor. When he received no answer to this letter, he announced that he would return the following spring.

On March 31, 1854, the Shogun signed with Perry the Treaty of Kä-na-gä-wa, his country's first convention with a foreign power. In this treaty Japan pledged herself to afford humane treatment to shipwrecked Americans and to open two ports to American trade. Shortly afterward, other treaties were made with the United States and the European powers, and Japan was invaded by numbers of foreign traders. Such radical action led to dissatisfaction with the Shogun and to eco-

INDUSTRIAL DEVELOPMENT 

737 nomic distress. Government officials were slain; attacks were made upon foreigners; and foreign shipping was burned. 

Finally, when a feudal noble caused trouble in the Straits of Shimonoseki (shē-mó-nō-sā-kē), an allied fleet of foreign warships bombarded his forts and forced the Emperor to pay the damages which he had caused. 

12. Reform Comes to Japan. Soon after this last affair, a new emperor ascended the throne, and the Shogun surrendered to him. Then began the "Period of Enlightened Rule.' 

The keynote of Mutsuhito's (moot-soo-hē-tōs) long reign is found in the words from his Charter Oath: "Wisdom and ability should be sought after in all quarters of the world, for the purpose of firmly establishing the foundation of empire." 

Reforms were inaugurated in every direction. A cabinet was created after western models and the capital was moved to Tokyo. With the consent of the daimyos themselves, the feudal system was abolished and a new army was organized on the basis of national conscription. A public school system was established and state railways and telegraph lines were built. 

Finally, in 1899, the Mikado gave his people a constitution which provided for a parliament with two houses. While at first suffrage was limited to the large tax-payers, by 1925 it had been extended to all adult males. The ministers, however, were responsible to the throne, and the Parliament might be dissolved at the will of the emperor. 

13. Japan Becomes Westernized. The establishment of these reforms was not a mere gesture, for thousands of young Japanese journeyed to Europe and America to learn in schools and shops the technic of western civilization, and then returned home to apply their knowledge. With the railroad and telegraph came factories and industries. Many of the old cities were remodelled. Water-works and electricity were introduced, and modern office buildings and stores began to appear. With such an amazing facility did the Japanese adapt themselves to west-

ern ideas, that soon their factories were turning out imitations of western goods in ever-increasing quantities. But Japan lacked the large supplies of coal and iron essential for the development of a great industrial nation. This and their dense population made it necessary for the Japanese to look abroad for room to expand and for controlled supplies of raw materials.

14. The Dismemberment of China Is Begun. Just before the end of the nineteenth century, Japan tried to imitate in China the imperialistic methods of the western powers. 

Starting a war with that country over Korea, she soon forced the cession of Formosa and the Pès-ca-do'rěs, and would have taken the Liaotung (lé-ou-toong) peninsula had not Germany, France, and Russia objected. Not long afterward the Tsar found a way of wringing from China a lease of Port Arthur in that very territory, so as to give his Trans-Siberian Rail-

INDUSTRIAL DEVELOPMENT 

739 way a winter port free from ice. Not to be outdone, Germany seized the Tsing-tao (tsing-tou) in the Shantung (shän-toong) peninsula as indemnity for the murder of two German missionaries; France and England also took sections for themselves. 

15. The Chinese Resent These Seizures and the Boxer

Uprising Results. Such a violation of China's sovereignty naturally stirred up bitter resentment on the part of the Chinese. 

EASTERN WEAKNESS BOWS TO WESTERN FORCE 

American soldiers entering Tang-Chow, China, during the Boxer uprising.

With the probable connivance of the Empress Dowager, an old secret society, the Righteous Harmony Fists' Association, but more commonly known as Boxers, was encouraged to attack the foreigners. The secret was kept so well that the outbreak came unexpectedly. Foreigners were attacked, and the legations in Peking were besieged. The latter held out until the arrival of an international relief expedition in which the United States took part. This expedition captured Peking. 

China was forced to pay a large indemnity and to grant privileges to foreigners. Much of this indemnity was used to pay for foreign property which had been destroyed, but the United

States magnanimously returned a part of her share to the Chinese with the understanding that it should be set aside as a fund to provide for the education of young Chinese students both at home and in America. 

16. Japan Becomes a Dominant Power in the East. The results of the Chino-Japanese War of 1894 were fully as important for Japan as for China, although in an entirely different way. Her success demonstrated how completely she had profited from her study of western military and naval science, and led the powers to terminate the extraterritorial rights which they had had in Japan under their original treaties. Henceforth Japan had full control in tariff matters, and foreigners living there became amenable to Japanese laws and had to depend for justice and protection on Japanese courts.

When Russia occupied Port Arthur, the Japanese statesmen realized that she was destined to be the great obstacle to the western expansion at the expense of China which they had in mind. Fortunately for Japan, in 1899, when she turned to the 

West for allies, the English were isolated from the European powers, and her overtures were welcomed by the British government, which entered into an alliance with her. This alliance was important, for it recognized the acceptance of Japan as a world power. 

17. As a Result of the Russo-Japanese War Japan Be comes the Dominant Power in the Far East. The advance of the Russians into Manchuria and their encroachments upon Korea, both of which had been encouraged by Emperor William II, soon involved them in war with the Japanese. The war was made difficult for the Russians because they had to depend for supplies and re-enforcements on a single-track railway six thousand miles long, while their fleet had to steam twothirds the distance around the world to reach the enemy. The 

Russians were beaten in every engagement, but Japan was almost bankrupt, and consequently welcomed the mediation of

Japan was now the dominant power in the Far East. She

at once began the reformation of Korea, and when the Koreans objected, annexed the country. Of far greater importance, however, was the influence of this war upon Asia. Asiatics had watched with deep interest the struggle between the Orient and the Occident, and when Japan won, they felt that once more 

Asia had begun to assert her rights. 

18. The United States Grows Imperialistic. South of the United States lay the islands of the West Indies, of which

The sinking of this ship here aided in causing the Spanish-American War. the two largest-Cuba and Porto Rico-were Spain's sole remains of her former empire in America. For years the people of the United States had looked with a friendly eye on the attempts of the Cubans to secure their independence. The 

Spanish government was antiquated and short-sighted, and met these attempts with methods suggestive of the Middle Ages. 

Finally, the cruel conduct of General Weyler (wa'lĕr) so outraged the humanitarian feelings of the American people that relations between Spain and the United States became tense. 

When the battleship Maine was blown up in the harbor of

Havana, the American people demanded war. Although Spain indicated a willingness to meet the demands of the United 

States, on April 18, 1898, Congress recognized the independence

of Cuba. Spain retaliated by declaring war. The United States occupied Cuba and Porto Rico and also dispatched her Asiatic fleet to the Philippines, and took all but four of the cities from the Spaniards. With the assistance of the Filipino patriots, Manila was captured and the war was then brought to an end by the Treaty of Paris. Spain recognized the independence of 

Cuba and, in return from a payment of $20,000,000, ceded to the United States Porto Rico, the Philippines, and her other island possessions in the Pacific. 

19. The United States Builds the Panama Canal. The war with Spain gave the United States new interests in the Car-ib-be'an Sea and brought home the necessity of a shorter water route between her two coasts. The idea of a canal between the Atlantic and Pacific by way of Nicaragua had been discussed as early as 1846 in a treaty with England, but nothing came of it. Meanwhile the gold rush to California had resulted in the building of a railroad across the Isthmus of Panama. In 1878, de Lesseps organized a French company to

build a canal in this same region, but after a part of it had been dug, the undertaking was abandoned because of yellow fever and other tropical diseases.

Twenty-five years later, the United States determined to complete this canal and bought from the old French company all its rights. When the government of Colombia placed obstacles in her way, President Roosevelt took advantage of a revolution in

Panama to obtain from the newly recognized republic the strip of territory necessary for the project. The work was finally completed after American medical men had discovered how to combat yellow fever and malaria, and after engineers had found ways to protect the great cut from landslides. 

The Panama Canal gave the world another great highway of commerce which was under the control of the United States; and at the same time greatly increased American financial interests in Central America. Thus, the United States became an imperialistic power in spite of herself.

CHAPTER LXXV  OPPOSE ONE ANOTHER IN THE TRIPLE ALLIANCE AND THE TRIPLE ENTENTE 

The removal of Bismarck had many important results, of which the most far-reaching was the weakening of the close relations that had existed between Germany and Russia. For a long time France had been looking for friends. This offered her an opportunity to take the place formerly held by Germany. 

Although it seems a little unusual for an autocrat like the Tsar to establish a close friendship with a republic, by this time the French government had become stabilized and Russian interests in the Balkan peninsula were being menaced by the Triple Alliance, while the new policy in Germany no longer sought to keep Russia friendly. Consequently, when Count Witte (vit'ē), the Russian Minister of Foreign Affairs, found that the French were willing to help finance the industrial development of his country, the two nations arrived at an understanding. This resulted in a second alignment of European powers, the Dual Entente (äN-tänt'), which was opposed to the Triple Alliance. 

Although the Dual Entente was not as formal as that alliance, the financial ties between the two countries made it quite as binding. We shall see how England found it to her interests to form an alliance with Japan, and a Triple Entente with France and Russia, to offset Germany's ambitions and the Triple Alliance. A setting was thus made for the World War in the race for armaments. 

1. Germany Decides to Build a Navy. The Dual Entente between France and Russia was a distinct blow at Germany, so William II immediately cast about for means to restore German prestige. As we have seen, he was interested in the 746

programme of the great industrial leaders and consequently looked with favor on the development of a colonial empire. To further this, it was announced in 1897 that Germany was going to build a fleet large enough to secure on the water a position as commanding as that which she held on land. Because England had been mistress of the seas for over a century, she looked upon this announcement as a measure aimed at herself. 

Two years later, by taking part in the relief of Peking, Emperor William found an opportunity to make a gesture with this new fleet, and at the same time gave utterance to an unfortunate speech in which he compared his soldiers to the Huns. 

These actions, together with Germany's seizure of Tsing-tao, were largely responsible for bringing about the alliance between England and Japan. 

During England's difficulties with the Boers, Germany's sympathies had been strongly with the latter. When Doctor 

Jameson's raiders were captured and imprisoned in 1890, Emperor William sent President Krüger a congratulatory telegram which created tremendous excitement in London. Later, during the Boer War the English had brought home to them just how isolated they were, for throughout Europe public opinion generally was on the side of the Boers. 

2. The Anglo-French Entente Is Formed. Before long the English statesmen began to feel that this Japanese Alliance was not sufficient, especially in view of the frank statements of Emperor William in some of his public speeches and the exaggerated claims of the more violent German nationalists. When 

Edward VII came to the throne in 1901, his friendship for France led him to encourage an understanding between the two powers whose hostility had become almost proverbial. Moreover, time and again questions like the French claim to the Upper Sudan brought them to the verge of war. Finally, those questions which had caused the greatest irritation were formally settled by treaty. In return for being allowed a free hand in

Egypt, England surrendered her rights in Morocco and agreed that France might establish a protectorate over that country. 

Other minor questions, such as the fishing rights on the banks of Newfoundland, were also adjusted. This agreement, the

3. Germany Stirs Up Feeling in the Morocco Affair.

As soon as news of the Anglo-French Entente reached Germany, plans were laid to break it. The next year, after the defeat of Russia by Japan, Emperor William visited Tangier

(tăn-jēr′) at the request of the Foreign Office and in an ostentatious manner addressed the Sultan of Morocco as an independent sovereign, emphasizing the need of an "open door" policy in his country. Soon Germany insisted that the Morocco 

Question, that is, the future status of Morocco, could be settled only by a conference of all the powers which had signed the old treaty of 1880, among which was the United States. 

To satisfy the Germans a conference was held at Algeciras (ǎl-gé-se'ràs) in 1905. Although this became a diplomatic duel between France and Germany, an agreement was reached, by which Morocco was to remain independent but to be policed under French control, and all nations were to have the right to engage in the Moroccan trade and to acquire Moroccan concessions. This arrangement settled little and left a legacy of trouble. 

4. The Russian Revolution of 1905 Brings Slight Re forms. When the weak but genial Nicholas II came to the throne of Russia in 1894, it was hoped that the despotic régime would be modified. Instead, however, he allowed himself to be swayed by reactionary officials. Finland was deprived of its former rights and war was declared against all intellectuals, since students and teachers in particular were showing too much interest in reform. By this time the industrialization of Russia was well under way, and along with it had come labor unions and other movements for social betterment, which began to add to the demand for reform. To meet the situation the secret police were increased and agents provocateur (ȧ-zhän' pró-vó-ká-tûr')—government agents who acted as leaders in unlawful acts-were employed to trap the revolutionary leaders. Because the Jews had insisted on keeping their religion and peculiar customs, they were denounced and a series of attacks, called pó-gròms', were made against them, ending in the massacre at Kishinev (ké-she-nyôf'). Because of this hundreds of thousands of Jews fled abroad and contributed so

greatly to the immigration to the United States. In retaliation for this reactionary policy, terrorism was revived and no official's life was safe.

Russia's troubles were greatly increased by the war with Japan which was very unpopular with the masses. Mutinies occurred in many quarters, especially as the terrible defeats of

While the more moderate members of society satisfied themselves by sending petitions to the "Little Father," many of the socialist workmen went on strikes. Finally, when the Cossacks fired on a large crowd of men and women who had assembled outside the Tsar's palace in St. Petersburg, the country became infuriated. In order to ease the situation, the 

Tsar promised to summon a Duma (doo'mä) or national assembly, but when it was found that the professional and working classes were not to help elect the members, a general strike took place and by the end of October, in 1905, Nicholas capitulated. 5. How the Anglo- French Entente Becomes the Triple Entente. One of the immediate results of the 

Morocco Affair was to show to the statesmen of France, England, and Russia that the Dual Entente must be extended and the breach between England and Russia healed. Ever since the English government had come to realize the importance of its Indian Empire and Russia had begun her advance into central Asia, their relations had been regarded with much suspicion. Whatever move Russia made was looked upon as a menace to British interests in India and we have seen how

England tried to block Russia's entrance to the Mediterranean. 

After Russia's defeat by Japan and her loss of Port Arthur, she was more eager than ever for an open window in the West area. For a long time, she had been slowly establishing her influence in Persia. Finally the situation became so acute that, in 1907, it forced the two powers to come to an agreement, the Anglo-Russian Entente. Persia was to be divided into two spheres of influence, the northern reserved for the Russians. and the southern for the English. Between the two there was to be a neutral zone including much of central Persia. The rights of the natives were quietly ignored in this understanding which changed the Dual Entente into a Triple Entente. 

6. Out of the Second Moroccan Affair Germany Gains 

Some African Territory. The Moroccans did not take kindly to the arrangements which had been made for them by the European powers and disturbances broke out in various parts of the country. Finally, the French dispatched an expedition to 

Fěz, which after having quieted things down showed no signs. of leaving. Germany, alarmed, had sent a gunboat to an obscure harbor on the coast of Morocco, ostensibly to protect German interests. This act created great excitement in France, and far more in England where it was feared that Germany was planning to establish a naval base near Gibraltar. However, before there was an open break, France and Germany began to bargain. In the end the French bought a free hand in 

Morocco in exchange for a large strip of territory in the French Congo. Its actual value was far greater than that of Morocco, but control of that country enabled France to round out her empire in northern Africa. 

7. Various Nations Wish to Establish Footholds in the 

Near East. By the close of the nineteenth century, the Near 

East had become a centre of international interests. Austria- 

Hungary wished to extend her territory southward to the Ægean Sea. Italy was anxious to obtain a foothold in the Bal-

kan peninsula; while Russia, especially after 1905, was eager to open the long-dreamed-road to the Mediterranean. England wished to keep her grip on Egypt to protect the way to India, and France was interested in re-establishing her former prestige in the Near East and in obtaining a share of the Sultan's domain in case it was divided. Meanwhile under the guidance of her reactionary sultan, Abdul Hamid II (äb-dool' hȧ-mēd'), Bernard Partridge.

A CARTOON BY PARTRIDGE IN PUNCH IN 1908 ILLUSTRATING GERMANY'S DESIRE TO CONCILIATE TURKEY 

the moribund Ottoman Empire was struggling along, trying on the one hand to postpone intervention of the great powers, and on the other to suppress every national movement among its unhappy peoples. 

8. William II of Germany Tries to Get the Exclusive

Concession to Build the Bagdad Railway. Germany had no direct interests in the Near East except as the ally of Austria- Hungary, but she saw in the economic possibilities of the Ottoman Empire an opportunity to obtain a valuable commercial foothold. As early as 1888, William II had visited the Near

East and in a speech at Damascus had announced himself to be a friend of the Muslims. He visited Constantinople again in 

1899, being the first European sovereign to offer his personal friendship to the Sultan, who had lost the respect of Christian 

Europe because of the massacres in Armenia.

As a result of this last visit, German capitalists were granted a concession to connect Constantinople with Bagdad by means of a railroad. Not only would this railroad link widely separated parts of the Sultan's Asiatic empire, but it would furnish a direct communication with India by way of the Persian Gulf. 

The Bagdad Railway stirred up a great deal of discussion, and England, which had long exercised control over the Persian Gulf, declared the Sheik of Al Kuwait (koo-wit'), the best available harbor at its head, to be under English protection. 

The Germans permitted the capitalists of other countries to participate in financing the venture, although few did. 

9. The "Young Turks" Start a Revolution and Depose the Sultan. After the conclusion of the Anglo-Russian Entente, the Turks realized that one of their most important safeguards was gone, for as long as England and Russia were opposed to each other, Constantinople and the Straits were safe. 

For a number of years, a movement to liberalize Turkey and to revive the old constitution of 1876 had been under way. 

It had been carried on by a secret organization composed largely of army officers, because they were the only Turks who had received a western education. These patriots were planning a revolution by which they hoped to overthrow the Sultan and to rid Turkey of foreign interference. 

Early in 1908, Abdul Hamid became aware of this plot and tried to seize the leading conspirators. This caused the revolution to break out immediately and by July the Sultan had been compelled to grant a constitution to the country. The "Young 

Turks," as the revolutionists were called, had had no experience in government, so most of the old officials had to be left

in power. In 1909, when Abdul Hamid with their help attempted to get back his lost authority by stirring up a reactionary movement, he was deposed.

In the fall of 1908, Austria-Hungary, over the protests of both England and France, proceeded to break the Treaty of Berlin by annexing Bosnia and Herzegovina, while Bulgaria declared its independence. From now on they ceased to take any interest in it, although technically they were still allied with Germany and Austria-Hungary. Italy herself decided to occupy Tripoli, robbing Turkey of her last territory in Africa excepting her rights over Egypt. 

These actions of Austria-Hungary and of the Bulgarians were a serious blow to the government of the Young Turks which was hampered by a lack of funds. With the customs and many other sources of revenue controlled by the Foreign Debt Commission, its only alternative was to negotiate a loan outside the country. Refused in England and France, the Young Turks turned to Berlin. Not only were the needed funds obtained, but the first steps were taken looking to the supplanting of Italy by Turkey in the Triple Alliance. 

11. The Balkan Wars Result in a New Division of 

Spoils. For years the province of Macedonia had furnished the 

Turkish government with one of its most harassing problems. 

Now the situation there became as dangerous as it had been before the Revolution. The three Balkan powers-Serbia, Greece, and Bulgaria-had long been anxious to get possession of this area, but their conflicting claims had prevented any concerted effort in that direction. Finally in 1911, through the endeavors of the Greek statesman, Venizelos (věn-i-za'los), they reached an agreement and formed an alliance. Then, to the consternation of Europe, they declared war on Turkey and occupied all of its European territory as far as Constantinople. 

The great powers worked to bring about a peace with Turkey which was barely signed when war broke out between the Allies. The division of the spoils had not been made in the treaty and when Bulgaria attempted to occupy more territory than had been allotted to her, Serbia and Greece, now assisted by Rumania, turned against her. The Bulgars were

easily defeated, after which the war was brought to a close by the Treaty of Bucharest. By this Bulgaria lost most of her foothold on the Ægean which she had hoped to gain and had to surrender some of her former territory to Rumania; Greece received Saloniki and the north coast of the Ægean together with more territory to the westward; and Serbia made expansion southward. Little Montenegro, which had played a prominent part in both wars, lost much of what she had conquered, for Austria-Hungary, with the Emperor's backing, forced the recognition of the new state of Ăl-ba'nì-à which had been set up to block Serbia's approach to the Adriatic. Turkey got back 

Adrianople and Thrace from Bulgaria. 

12. Fears Arising from the Balkan Settlements Lead to Huge Military Preparations. The outcome of the Balkan 

Wars was a diminished prestige for Germany through the defeat of the Turks, whose armies had used German guns; an increased worry for Austria-Hungary through the aggrandizement of Serbia, and a set-back for Russia, who saw in the defeat of the Bulgars another attempt to keep her away from the Straits. Of these, Russia's injury rankled most and her statesmen seized the first opportunity to reassert her interests in the Balkans. The results came quickly. 

In 1913, the German Reichstag passed a bill which increased the size of the German army nearly one-third. France at once retaliated by extending her term of military service from two to three years, and even Russia extended hers as much as ninety days. All the countries increased their appropriations for artillery and other means of making war, while Great Britain began to strengthen her navy. Along with this increased military expenditure, came a corresponding rise of hatred and fear among the peoples of Europe. Prominent position was given in the newspapers to articles on the military preparations of other countries, especially of those countries allied against their own, and insisting upon similar preparedness.

CHAPTER LXXVI  BETWEEN EUROPEAN POWERS LEADS TO THE WORLD WAR 

All Europe had been worried since the Franco-Prussian War by the spectre of a general European war. The improvements in guns and armaments and the higher power of explosives were making war so much more deadly that those who understood the possibilities were not anxious to assume responsibility for bringing on a war. Still, increasing national pride and fear of being caught napping if war should occur led each of the great European powers to pile up armaments and to enlarge its armies. Truly it was a curious situation with every nation fearing war and at the same time making preparations for it. Time after time the Foreign Offices brought about incidents which led the nations almost to war. Then at the last moment fear of the consequences prevented an actual declaration. Another powerful influence against war was its cost. 

Modern warfare had become so expensive that nobody knew exactly how a great war would affect the finances of the nations involved. Some economists even claimed that war was impossible because of the financial disorganization it would bring.

We shall see that this fear of war and understanding of its consequences did not avail against the enemies of peace. How exaggerated feelings of nationalism and eagerness to acquire possessions or concessions in the Balkans or Near East led to a condition of affairs wherein the Near East became the "tinder box" of Europe; how only a spark was needed to set the nations at war; and how the conflict developed into a World War with America finally entering in the hope that certain ideals could be realized at last, will be some of the important considerations of this chapter. 761

1. How Various Organizations Attempted to Bring About World Peace. In 1899, Tsar Nicholas II, following in the footsteps of his predecessor of a century before, tried to 

Bernard Partridge 

THE BLESSINGS OF PEACE 

An English cartoon of 1913 by Partridge in Punch pointing out the terrible burden of armament in France and Germany. lay the foundation of world peace by summoning to The Hague a gathering of international diplomats to study the problem of international law to discover ways to outlaw war. Although the first meeting was not very satisfactory, another was held eight years later and The Hague Tribunal was organized to settle minor disputes between nations. As a matter of fact,

however, the principal thing accomplished was that many persons thought that war was no longer possible. 

In addition to this semi-official organization, there was set up at Berne an International Peace Society, and, on this side of the Atlantic, the Pan-American Union which eventually embraced all the American republics. This latter organization through a series of congresses has established a certain good-will among the nations of the two Americas and managed to avoid a lot of needless fighting among the Latin peoples. 

2. How Extreme Nationalism and Special Interests of 

Different Nations in the Near East Were Enemies of Peace. Although at the beginning of the twentieth century many believed that there would never be another great war, this feeling was not shared by those who were responsible for the destinies of the nations, for in spite of all the influences designed to foster peace there were other influences working in the direction of war. First and foremost among them was an exaggerated feeling of nationalism. In Germany this expressed itself in the Pan-Germanic Scheme, which aimed at bringing all the lands between the Baltic Sea and the Persian Gulf under the economic control of Germany. In France it showed itself in an increasing desire to secure the return of Alsace and Lorraine, and everywhere in an exaggerated sense of honor which might be offended by the most trivial incident.

In the next place, there were certain interests which the people of the several countries felt were essential to their national existence. Of these, outstanding examples were Russia's insistence on free access to the Mediterranean, England's desire to maintain control of the sea route to India by way of the Suez Canal, and Austria's determination to develop her interests in the Balkan peninsula. It is important to note that all these problems centred in the Near East, which became the "tinder box" of Europe.

And, finally, the boundaries of so many of the European

states were in total disregard of national aspirations that no one knew just when some petty difficulty might set the 'whole continent ablaze. In this Austria-Hungary was probably the worst offender, but Russia was a close second. When Francis

3. The Assassina tion of the Austrian 

Archduke Leads to the Outbreak of the 

World War. After the annexation of their country by Austria-Hungary, the national idea became almost a religion with the Slavic students of Bosnia. In order to escape the espionage of the Austrian secret police, many of them fled to Serbia, where they became associated with societies engaged in propaganda for a "greater Serbia." Among these refugees was a certain Gä-v-rï'lo Princip (prin'sēp), a high-strung, nervous young man, whose reading of radical literature made him eager to do something extraordinary toward freeing his native land from Austrian control. When news came that the

Austrian Archduke was to visit Sarajevo (så-rä’yá-vó), Princip along with several other Serbians planned to assassinate him. 

With the aid of some Serbians the conspirators procured guns and bombs, and accomplished their purpose on June 28, 1914. 

The Austro-Hungarian government seized the opportunity to humiliate Serbia, and, on July 23, sent to Belgrade an ultimatum to be answered within forty-eight hours. Although this ultimatum involved a positive infringement on the sovereignty of Serbia, on the advice of England and France, the Serbians virtually accepted it. Russia, who regarded herself as the protector of all the smaller Slavic states, considered this a blow at herself. Sir Edward Grey, the British Secretary of Foreign 

Affairs, made an effort to adjust the difficulty by having it referred to a joint conference of all the great powers which were not directly interested. To this Germany objected, insisting that the affair was one which concerned only Austria-Hungary and Serbia.

Finally, on July 28, after Francis Joseph had rejected the Serbian concessions, Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia. 

Meanwhile the Tsar had begun to mobilize his armies along the Austro-Hungarian border. Thereupon Germany rushed to the assistance of her ally and demanded that this mobilization cease immediately. When the Russian government failed to answer within the allotted time, Kaiser Wilhelm proclaimed that a state of war already existed between Germany and Russia. 

Two days later he declared war against France, which also had begun to mobilize its armies. 

When the Germans showed that they were going through Belgium, Grey prevailed upon Parliament to join France and Russia. The Triple Entente was then changed into a new Triple 

Alliance, whose members pledged themselves to stand together until the end, and the long-dreaded World War was a reality. 

4. The German Strategy Gives Advantage to the Cen tral Powers.

Long before hostilities began, the German gen-

eral staff had worked out careful plans for such a contingency. 

Consequently during the early part of the war, the advantage lay with the Central Powers, as the Germans and their Austrian allies were known. These plans called for the crippling of 

France before Russia could get her armies into the field. With this in view many railway lines had been built to the Belgian frontier, beyond which there was an open road to Paris, for the French, relying on the neutrality of Belgium, had not fortified strongly their northern borders. Thus we see why the 

German forces began to advance through Belgium as early as August 4, destroying the fortification at Liege (lyāzh) and driving before them the army which King Albert had put into the field to defend the sovereignty of his little country. So rapid was the progress of the German forces that before the French could offer serious resistance, the Germans had swept down into northern France and had reached the Märne, barely twenty-five miles from the capital, where their drive was halted because their artillery could not keep up with the infantry. 

Meanwhile, in the East the Russians had upset the German plan by their unexpectedly swift mobilization, which had enabled them to invade East Prussia in spite of all that General von Hindenburg (hin'den-boork) could do. Although after the disastrous battle of Tannenburg (tăn'en-boork) they were forced to retire, farther south the Grand Duke Nicholas was holding Austria's great frontier fortress of Lim'běrg and had overrun most of Galicia. The Germans now launched two new offensives. Following up their defeat of the Russians, they invaded Poland, capturing Warsaw and making such a threat at Rï'gȧ that the Tsar moved his capital to Moscow. Almost at the same time, they undertook to take Calais to cut the supply lines leading to England. Here their plans were less successful, due to the resistance of the British troops, reinforced by strong contingents from the dominions beyond the seas. 

After that, there began a new kind of warfare. From the

North Sea to the Swiss border, and along the eastern frontier, the Germans "dug in" by making a line of trenches which were protected by barbed-wire entanglements. The Allies quickly did

5. The Strategy of the Allies Leads to Costly Defeats. 

While Germany was devoting the greater part of her effort to winning the war in Europe, the Allies allowed themselves to become involved in a number of "sideshows," all of which centred in the Near East. As early as July, 1914, Germany had made a secret treaty with Turkey and when the war broke out two German cruisers that happened to be in the Mediterranean took refuge at Constantinople. Unaware of this treaty and anxious to keep open communication with Russia by way of the Black Sea, the Allies tried to induce the Turks either to join

forces with them or at least to remain neutral. When this attempt failed and Turkey declared war against them, an expedition was dispatched from India to the head of the Persian Gulf, and at the same time the British took steps to defend the Suez Canal. Then during the following winter an attack was launched against the Dardanelles. When this failed, troops were landed on the Gallipoli peninsula and a tremendously costly, but fruitless, campaign was carried on for six months for the purpose of opening the Straits. Meanwhile the Mesopotamian expedition was surrounded and captured by the Turks. The immediate effect of these two reverses was Bulgaria's decision to cast her lot with the Central Powers. 

6. Secret Treaties Are Negotiated by the Allies as to the Division of the Spoils. Shortly after the war began, England, Russia, and France began to make plans for the partition of the Turkish Empire. When Turkey declared war, England had proclaimed a protectorate over Egypt and Cyprus.

In the spring of 1915, she and France came to an agreement in which sections of Asiatic Turkey were set aside for each of them to control, and later Russia accepted her share and gave her consent to the plan. At the same time they were negotiating with Italy to induce her to enter the war on the side of the Allies. In this they eventually succeeded by offering her those parts of the Austro-Hungarian Empire which were known as the I-täl'i-a Irredenta (ēr-rā-děn'tä) because Italians dwelt there in such large numbers. However, she insisted on a share of Asiatic Turkey when the dismemberment took place. 

While the European powers were staking out their claims in Turkey, the Arabs were scheming to obtain independence, and they had the encouragement of England, which promised the governor of Mecca that all the territory inhabited by them should become independent. England also promised that Palestine should become the homeland of the Jews without defining just what that meant. All these agreements, except the last,

7. New Methods of Warfare Bring Great Anxiety to the Allies. By the middle of 1915, the war had become a siege of the Central Powers by the Allies. Judged by the situation on the Continent, the advantage was largely with the Germans, for, owing to their previous preparations, they could move their forces from one place to another more quickly than the Allies. Besides, the entrance of Turkey into the war had placed 

Russia in an embarrassing position, for she was then cut off from the West. Although she had an almost unlimited supply of men, she was lacking in guns and shells, and her allies were now powerless to help her. 

But there was another side to the picture. Germany, too, had been cut off from the western world and most of her colonies had been captured. As a result, while the resources of the 

United States and other neutral countries were open to the Allies, they were almost wholly closed to Germany, and this gave the Allies their real advantage. This advantage was also strengthened by control of the cables by which they could send abroad whatever propaganda they wished, while Germany had to get her side before the world in a roundabout way. 

The Germans had a somewhat more realistic theory of warfare than the Allies. In the end this injured their standing in the eyes of the world. Not only were they the first to realize the possibilities of aircraft by employing great fleets of Zep'pé-lins to bomb the munitions plants in England and France, but they were also the first to use submarines for torpedoing merchantmen. 

8. The Germans Turn to Submarines to Offset Advantages Enjoyed by the Allies. The Germans realized that they were practically besieged and that their fleet had been driven off the seas, and were forced to turn to submarines to over-

come the advantage of the British and French because of the location of their countries. This was made even more necessary when England practically stopped all trade with Germany by refusing to allow Holland and the Scandinavian countries, although they were neutral, to import foodstuffs or munitions beyond what they needed for their own use. 

Consequently, the Germans announced in 1916 a policy of unrestricted submarine warfare. Up to that time they had been careful to warn and search merchantmen before they sank them, but from now on they began destroying vessels without warning. The United 

States, as well as other neutrals, protested against this new kind of warfare, but the Germans argued that it was a military necessity. Before 1917, they had sunk over 5,000,000 NOTICE!
