9. Germany's Submarine Policy Draws the United

States Into the War. This unrestricted submarine warfare eventually caused the United States to sever diplomatic relations with Germany and, finally, on April 6, 1917, Congress de-

clared that a state of war existed. The entrance of the United 

States into the war gave great impetus to certain ideals which as yet had only been talked about in a rather visionary manner. 

The American people were not very familiar with European politics, but they had an innate dislike for kings and emperors, and now that they were in the war, they began to look upon it as a struggle between autocracy and democracy. At first they quite naturally believed that their part would be to supply money and munitions, but soon every one realized that the United States would also have to furnish armies of soldiers to reinforce the Allies, who were almost exhausted. 

Consequently, in addition to making the most prodigious preparations for supplying food and munitions, plans were made for drafting and training the nation's entire man supply. 

And meanwhile the American navy took an active part in protecting shipping from the German submarines by convoying vessels through the danger zones, and the American shipyards turned out rapidly new tonnage to replace that which had been destroyed. Just how completely the whole country turned to winning the war may be realized when we read that within sixteen months an American army had been trained and placed in the field, although it had taken England two years to accomplish the same thing. By the end of the war over a million 

American soldiers were in France. 

10. The Americans Arrive Just at the Allies' Darkest 

Hour. The United States entered the war just when the cause of the Allies was passing through its darkest hour. From the start the Russians had fought under the most trying conditions, which had been made increasingly difficult by the discontent of the peasants and the treachery of the high command. As a result, their defense had completely collapsed in the spring of 1917 and a revolution had broken out. The rule of the Tsar was brought to an end and a constitutional government under

control of the socialists was set up. At this time, Russian socialists were divided into two groups-socialists and communists, or bōl-shě-vï'ki. Although the socialists had engineered this revolution, they were soon ousted from control by the communists, who were under the guidance of Len'în and Trotsky, two leaders who had been secretly transported from Switzerland to Russia by Germany. Through the efforts of these men a treaty was made in March, 1918, with the Germans at Brest- Litovsk (brěst lyé-tofsk') by which the Russians agreed to surrender Poland and their Baltic provinces. 

The Germans could now devote their full effort to winning the war on the western front. Convinced by this time that the 

United States could and would send formidable forces across the Atlantic, the German high command decided that one final attempt must be made to crush the Allies before that should happen. With this in view, on March 21, 1918, they launched a great offensive designed to separate the British and the French and to enable the Germans to get in behind both of them. 

Within ten days, they had pushed the former back twenty-five miles and had nearly captured the great railway centre of Amiens. Then, they literally hammered them back almost to the English Channel, and after that they turned against the French, who were holding the lines farther south. They drove the Allies back to the Marne, but although they were now within striking distance of Paris, they never got any closer, for the Americans had begun to appear in sufficient force to stop the drive. 

11. Following the Collapse of Turkey and Austria the 

Germans in Full Retreat Sue for an Armistice. The first result of this great offensive was to compel the Allies to place all their armies under a single command. Failure to do this before had been one of the principal reasons why the Allies had not been more successful. For the position of General-in-

chief they selected the great French strategist, Marshal Ferdinand Foch (fósh). The advantage of this new arrangement was felt almost immediately, for when the German offensive had spent its force, the Allies were able to launch, in July, a 

MARSHAL FOCH AND GENERAL PERSHING IN PARIS 

counter offensive. With the newly arrived American troops under General Pershing, for the first time they now had adequate reserves. When they began to push the Germans back, they never stopped until the latter asked for an armistice the following November. 

Even so, it is doubtful whether the end would have come as soon as it did, had not Germany's allies completely collapsed on

the other fronts. Early in September, the Bulgarians had been compelled to give up after the Allies had overrun their country, and, a month later, the Turks had been driven out of Palestine and Syria by General Allenby and had been forced to sue for peace. And finally, early in November, after the Italians had succeeded in crossing the Alps, Austria-Hungary quit. 

12. Why the Allies Were Finally Successful. The rapid success of the Allies during the last few months of the war was not due wholly to military skill. For nations to fight with a determination to win, they must have some great issue to fight for. Their belief in the right of this issue gives rise to an enthusiasm or morale which gives to the struggle the character of a crusade and makes men willing to endure any sacrifice needed to win. At first, the Germans believed it was a war of defense and this was largely responsible for the eagerness with which the whole nation fought. 

But later, much more depended upon the skilful propaganda carried on by each side. Soon it was discovered that propaganda in the country of the enemy was quite as effective as guns and bayonets along its borders. Agents of the Allies in 

Switzerland and in other neutral countries were spreading discontent among the enemy peoples, especially in Austria-Hungary, due largely to the ruthless way in which the government had ignored the nationalistic aspirations of its subjects. It remained for President Wilson to sound the death knell of the cause of the Central Powers, by declaring in his address to the Congress of the United States in January, 1918, that the Allies were fighting only to make the world safe for democracy by putting an end to secret diplomacy and the rule of might. 

The "fourteen points" which he enumerated in that address, brought hope to the common man everywhere. Just how much this broke the enemy's morale is shown by the fact that the Germans placed their case in President Wilson's hands because they had confidence in his sincerity. Why this should have

been may be appreciated by reading the following excerpt from his address:

No people must be forced to live under a sovereignty under which it does not wish to live. No territory must change hands except for the purpose of securing to those who inhabit it a fair chance of life and liberty. No indemnities must be insisted upon except those that constitute payment for manifest wrongs done. And then the free people of the world must draw together in some common covenant, some genuine and practical co-operation that will in effect combine their force to secure peace and justice in the dealing of nations with one another. 

13. The Militant Nationalists Are Faced by the Liberals Led by President Wilson in the Peace Conference. 

On January 18, 1919, the representatives of the victorious powers, led by Lloyd George, Prime Minister of England, Georges Clemenceau (zhôrzh klä-män-sō), Premier cf France, Vit-to'rï-ō Ór-län'do, Premier of Italy, and President Wilson, met at Paris to draft the terms of peace. Hither came delegations from all the oppressed peoples of both Europe and Asia. 

It became evident very soon that the conference was moved by two antagonistic views. On the one hand, the liberals, led by 

President Wilson, saw an opportunity to lay the foundation of lasting peace by putting into practice the ideals of democracy which had been the watchword of the Allies during the last years of the war. On the other hand, the militant nationalists. tried to gain every possible advantage by insisting that the several secret treaties be carried out to the letter. In this they had the support of their fellow countrymen, who, partly on account of propaganda, believed firmly in the sinister purposes of the Central Powers. They even went so far as to demand conditions which meant little less than perpetual enslavement for the Germans. 

14. What the Covenant of the League of Nations Pro posed to Do.

After the terrible ordeal through which Eu-

777. rope had gone, even the most militant statesmen realized that some way must be found to lessen the danger of such a catastrophe being repeated. Through the insistence of President 

Wilson, the conference reluctantly gave its consent, on April 19, THE BIG FOUR AT PARIS 

Lloyd George, Orlando, Clemenceau, and Wilson. to the Covenant of the League of Nations, which was designed to "promote international co-operation, peace, and security, through open, just, and honorable international relations." 

The Covenant provided that all treaties and engagements between members should be made public, that all disputes should be submitted to the council for inquiry or arbitration, and that, in no case was war to begin until three months after it had been decided upon. It also demanded that just treatment should be accorded to subject populations. Other articles dealt with

labor conditions, and with the traffic in women and children, opium and other drugs, and arms and ammunition. 

15. Germany Is Compelled to Submit to a Treaty

Severe Beyond Any in Modern Times. On the fifth anni versary of the assassination of the Archduke, the treaty was 

THE MEETING OF THE PEACE CONFERENCE IN THE HALL OF MIRRORS AT VERSAILLES 

signed in the Hall of Mirrors in the old palace at Versailles. 

In spite of all the protests against secret diplomacy, the treaty had been worked out behind closed doors by representatives of the five great powers-the United States, Great Britain, France, Italy, and Japan-and it had been presented to the German delegates with the understanding that it was not to be modified in any way. 

It began with a statement of Germany's responsibility for bringing on the war and then proceeded to punish her by taking away one-sixth of her territory and one-tenth of her population. Alsace and Lorraine were given to France, and a portion

of Silesia and West Prussia to the newly established Republic of Poland; while plebiscites were to be held in East Prussia, and 

Schleswig and Holstein, to determine whether their inhabitants wished to remain a part of Germany. Not only did the Germans lose all their colonies but they had to destroy fortifications on Hěl'î-gó-lănd, which controlled the North Sea approach to the Kiel (kel) Canal, to give up their navy, and to reduce their army to 100,000 men. They also had to submit to an occupation of their lands lying west of the Rhine, as well as of considerable areas east of it, and to a supervision of their disarmament by representatives of the Allies. Finally, in return for the devastation of their armies in France and Belgium and to reimburse the Allies in part for the cost of the war, Germany had to agree to pay an undetermined indemnity. 

When this treaty with the Covenant of the League of Nations attached to it was laid before the Senate of the United States by President Wilson, that body refused to ratify it. Its refusal was based on Article 10 of the Covenant which would violate a fundamental principle of American policy concerning "entangling alliances." After considerable delay, the war was brought to an official end so far as the American people were concerned by resolution of Congress. 

16. The Other Settlements Were Based on Nationalis tic Aspirations and the Secret Treaties. In due time treaties were worked out by the Allies for the other enemy nations. 

Austria-Hungary was recognized as two separate powers and their future status was determined by the Treaties of St. Germaine (săn zhěr măn’) and the Trianon (trẻ-i-nôn’) respectively. Efforts were made to satisfy so far as possible the nationalistic aspirations of her former subject peoples by setting up the Republic of Czechoslovakia (chěk-ó-slō-vä'ki-ȧ) in the north, and by bestowing large areas upon Poland, Rumania, Italy, and Serbia which then changed her name to the Kingdom of the Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes, or more briefly "Yü-gó-slä'-

via." As a result, Austria and Hungary became two rather insignificant and extremely poor states, and, to make matters worse, Hungary passed through the throes of a communist revolution. Although this was put down by a Rumanian army, the latter seized the opportunity to avenge some of the devastation of the Central Powers suffered by Rumania. 

By the Treaty of Neuilly (nû-ye') Bulgaria lost her approach to the Ægean Sea and part of the Dō'brü-jȧ was given to Rumania. Finally, in January, 1920, the Treaty of Sevres was concluded with Turkey and at last the war was officially ended. This treaty never went into force but all the southern part of the empire had already been taken over by Great Britain and France as mandates to be administered according to the terms of the Covenant of the League of Nations. Except for these mandates, however, most of the arrangements were soon upset by the revolution which broke out in Turkey. 

17. The Significance of the World War. It is not surprising that this war came to be universally known as the World War, for there was no part of the world which was not directly or indirectly involved in it. In addition to the belligerent powers, there were sixteen others which showed their sympathy for the cause of the Allies by breaking off diplomatic relations with Germany. Besides, the common people-men, women, and children of the warring nations and their neutral neighbors had suffered as never before in any other war. And finally, due to the close economic organization of modern society, it had been truly a war of nations against nations. 

The actual military operations were accompanied by many significant developments. Strategy was greatly modified by the use of motor transport and airplanes, while tactics were completely changed as a result of the use of new and more powerful explosives, and of such revolutionary innovations as tanks and chemicals. In consequence of all these things, there had never before been a war which was so destructive of life and

property. All told, it cost at least twelve million lives and property worth not less than two hundred billion dollars; and it left behind a burden of colossal debts which even the most hopeful economists see weighing down society for at least two generations. Brought on by the exaggerated nationalistic and imperialistic designs of the great powers, it resulted in the emergence of a score or more of minor states and saw rise in Russia an entirely new theory of government at the price of a complete upheaval of society and a wiping out of the middle as well as the upper classes.

CHAPTER LXXVII THE WORLD DISRUPTED BY WAR FACES SERIOUS PROBLEMS OF READJUSTMENT 

As in the case of all previous great wars, it was difficult for the world, after four years of such a struggle, to settle down again to the life of peace. Many of the new states, and some of the old states, were dissatisfied with the arrangements that had been made for them, and consequently hostilities were continued for several years. Moreover, the radical ideas of the communist government in Russia brought the wrath of the country's former allies, especially when the new régime refused to recognize its foreign debts and obligations of its tsarist predecessor.

In all the belligerent countries-victorious as well as defeated -the economic system, which had been strained to the breaking-point by the financial requirements of the war, was disorganized by issuing vast quantities of paper money. And finally, reactionary tendencies in many countries were stimulated by the attempts of the Russian revolutionists to bring about a world upheaval. Just what the result would have been had it not been for the financial exhaustion that prevailed and the steadying power of the League of Nations, it is hard to say. 

1. How Soviet Control of Russia Was Made Possible. 

The establishment of the Government of the Soviet (sō-vyět), as the communistic régime in Russia was called, had been possible only because of the disorganization brought on by the war. 

Communism was the outgrowth of industrialism and consequently was foreign to the traditions of more than ninety per cent of the Russian people, who were still primarily agriculturists. That the communists succeeded at all was due to the 783

desire of the peasants to obtain possession of the land. As soon as they had done this, their enthusiasm for the new régime rapidly cooled. At this critical moment the representatives of the older system prevailed upon the Allies to assist them in trying to wrest control from the Soviet and thus gave the latter an opportunity to appear to be the saviors of Russian liberty. 

In its eagerness to establish an entirely new world order, the Soviet gave up the concessions and extraterritorial rights which 

Courtesy of the Amtorg Trading Co.

MECHANIZING AGRICULTURE IN RUSSIA 

The Soviet government is applying the principles of factory production to agriculture on a large scale. 

Russia had long enjoyed in China, Persia, and Turkey, and established schools for training students from those countries in the principles of communism. Representatives of the Third International, as the organization of the communists was called, were sent into western Europe to plant the seeds of sovietism. 

In Hungary, as we have seen, they succeeded in causing a revolution, and for a time it looked as though they would do likewise in Germany, and especially in Italy, where they almost disorganized the government. They also crossed the Atlantic and established sufficient contacts with the working classes in the United States to cause considerable apprehension. Finally, they lent active assistance to the nationalist movement in China and brought down upon their heads the wrath of the western powers, whose imperialistic claims were seriously threatened by the violence that followed.

Meanwhile, the communist régime was compelled to modify greatly many of its original notions, laboring under the responsibility of re-establishing industry and transportation throughout the Soviet Union, and suffering from a lack of trained workers. In fact, it escaped overthrow only by permitting a steadily increasing amount of private business, which is more closely regulated than anywhere else in the world. Although the United States refuses to recognize the Soviet government, manufacturers and business firms are dealing with it. 

Many engineers and business men have been hired by the Soviets to reconstruct industry on a large scale. 

2. Turkey Revolts Against Western Domination and

Forms a Republic. When the armistice was signed in 1918, the Turks recognized their defeat and accepted the heavy conditions which were laid upon them. This was all changed, however, when the representatives of the Allies at Paris decided to allow the Greeks to occupy Smyrna. Realizing that this was only the beginning of the complete dismemberment of their country, a group of Turks led by Mustapha Kemal (moos'. tä-fä kā-mäl′) undertook the resurrection of Turkey. They began the task by a drive against the Greeks but soon came into conflict with the Turkish government itself. When that government signed the Treaty of Sevres, they repudiated it and for two years carried on a war with the Greeks of Asia Minor until they literally drove them into the sea. This they were able to do because they had the tacit assistance of the French, who were opposed to any increase of English influence in the 

Near East.

The Turks then established a new capital at Ăn-gō'rå, deposed the sultan, and proclaimed their country a republic. Not content with that, they even declared that the sultan was no longer the Caliph of Islam. The western powers were unable to resist this interference with all their plans for the Near East, so after a long delay and the display of much bitterness, a new

treaty was drafted at Lausanne (lo'zȧn') in 1923. Constantinople and the Straits were returned to Turkey and no mention was made of Armenia. This resurrection of Turkey may be looked upon as an example of oriental reaction against west- Courtesy of the "U.S.S.R. in Construction."

Modern Turkish women learning Turkish written with the Roman letters in the library at Baku, Adherbaijan. ern domination. Although it was marked by an outward adoption of the ideas of nationality and democracy held in the West, just what the final result will be no one can foretell, for Turkey is a republic in name only and its president has almost autocratic power. 

3. Asia Awakens and Struggles for Her Rights. The enthusiasm for nationalistic aspirations and democratic ideals of the public utterances of the spokesmen for the Allies during the World War struck a responsive chord among the Asiatic peoples, who had been stirred by the victory of Japan over

Russia in 1905. In Arabia, the rulers of Mecca and Näjd each claimed to be the leader of a national movement which had for its object independence for the Arabs. When the war was ended, the more vigorous Ibn Saud (sä-ood') of the Najd drove out his rival and brought the whole peninsula under his own sway. The attempt on the part of England to gain complete control of Persia after Russia withdrew from her sphere of influence there met with determined resistance. Under the leadership of an able soldier, the Persians asserted their independence. They deposed their old dynasty and established a new régime under Shah Rï'zà Khan and called in an American commission of economic experts to help them reform their finances.

In India, great hopes had been entertained by the Indians that in return for the loyal support which they had given England during the war, they would be granted self government, or at least a larger share in the administration of the country. When these hopes failed to materialize, a wide-spread nationalistic movement took place under the leadership of Gånd'hï. The result was that England made certain concessions, but nothing like what she would have made had it not been for the long-standing hostility between the Hindus and Muslims. The trouble is still going on.

Although China had declared war on Germany, during the progress of the Great War, an attempt was made by Japan to obtain a firm hold upon her. This was blocked by the United 

States, but it served to open the eyes of the Chinese, especially of the younger men who had been educated in the western way. 

Ever since the establishment of the republic in 1912, China had been in a state of chaos, due largely to its immense size and lack of adequate communications. Meanwhile, in the South, Sun (soon) Yat Sen had supported a national movement which sought to free the country from every form of outside control, but at no time could he persuade the warring factions in the

North to lay aside their differences and to join in the undertaking.

After Sun Yat Sen's death, the struggle was carried on. 

China was torn by civil war. The centre of government was moved from Peking to Nanking, but peace is not much nearer.

4. The Nations of Western Europe Struggle to Stabilize Their Currency. While the Asiatics were struggling for independence, the peoples of western Europe were fighting over the value of money. When they could no longer balance their budgets and yet needed supplies to keep their governments going, they turned to the printing-presses for relief. As always happens under such conditions, gold and silver coin disappeared before the flood of paper money and the value of the latter declined.

This went farthest in Germany, where the mark sank until it became practically valueless. As a result, the income of those who lived upon salaries or from the returns on investments was practically wiped out. Besides, far-seeing individuals took advantage of the situation to pile up debts through the purchase of real estate and other things of value, and then paid them with this cheap money. Finally, the situation became so serious that the Allies intervened to safeguard the payment of the reparations demanded by the Treaty of Versailles. Then all this valueless currency was repudiated and there was a new issue on a gold basis.

France and Italy, and the minor countries of Europe, too, passed through the same experience, although to a lesser degree. In France, thanks to the employment furnished by the reconstruction of the devastated area, the franc did not reach bottom in its decline until 1926, when by the most heroic efforts it was finally stabilized at about one-fifth of the pre-war value. 

In England alone was money brought back to its former value, but at the expense of disorganization of industry, for the change from cheap money to dear money caused such an increase in the cost of production that many factories could not continue and millions of workmen were thrown out of employment. 

5. The Problem of Debts and Reparations Seems to 

Defy Satisfactory Solution. Lack of a stable currency was only one of the obstacles to the economic recovery of Europe. 

The tremendous destruction of capital during the war and the establishment of new customs barriers brought ruin to many of the old avenues of trade. Most important of all, however, were the debts which had been entailed by the war, as well as the question of reparations. All the belligerents had borrowed vast sums of money, and much of it had been obtained from the United States. There was little possibility that any considerable part of these debts would ever be paid. To this there

were two notable exceptions. When the United States completed its period of readjustment, it entered upon unprecedented prosperity and immediately began the reduction of its obligations. England, too, although handicapped by the tre-

7. A Business Revolution of Great Importance Takes 

Place in Europe. The amazing prosperity which the United 

States has enjoyed since the readjustmert period has led Europeans to study closely her business methods with a view to imitating them. Moreover, both the Germans and the French have rebuilt their factories and have installed the most improved machinery. Besides they have formed great cärtels, or as-

sociations, in which the producers of a particular type of goods in different countries have combined to divide the markets so as to limit the competition in sales. Already the steel industry of France and Germany has formed such a cartel, while the chemical industry has almost done it. Besides, these countries have arranged a series of commercial treaties designed to enable the industrial life of one country to supplement that of the other. Meanwhile American manufacturers, like Henry 

Ford, are building factories in Europe and Europeans are copying American manufacturing and business methods. 

8. In the Reaction, Fascism, or Dictatorships, Prevail against Representative Governments in Several European States. One of the most striking consequences of the war, which was said to have been waged to make the world safe for democracy, has been the attack on democracy itself. Although governments which were democratic in form were set up in all the enemy countries as well as in the newly created nations, some of them have failed.

Italy suffered most economically during the war, for the reason that she was the poorest, and by 1920 and 1921 her conditions were so bad that she was near a bolshevik revolution. 

At this juncture a new movement called fascism (fȧs'izm) made its appearance and under the leadership of Benito Mussolini (bā-në'tō moos-ó-le'nē) got control of the government. By fostering national ideals and establishing peace and order, he has been able to put down opposition, although he has practically eliminated representative government in Italy. He has almost autocratic power. He is the bitter enemy of everything suggestive of bolshevism, for Fascism is a movement in the interest of property. Similar movements, but with less beneficial results, have taken place in Spain, Greece, Poland, Hungary, Turkey, and Albania.

of the post-war period revolved around the League of Nations. 

The failure of the United States to ratify the Treaty of Versailles and thus become a member weakened the League, and placed its control in the hands of England, France, and Italy. 

As a result, its decisions have often been influenced by the interests of these powers rather than by those of the world at large. In spite of this, however, the smaller nations have found a forum on the floor of its assembly which they have not been slow in using. Even if some of its business is still carried on in private discussions suggestive of secret diplomacy, the world is better informed than ever before as to the questions at issue. 

The League has also furnished an opportunity for statesmen of different countries to meet and discuss their problems, and already has proved its value as an aid in the prevention of war. 

Since the admittance of Germany in 1926, and the participation of the Soviet Union in the Disarmament Conference of 1927, the United States is the only important country which is not a member. 

10. The British Empire Becomes More and More a 

Partnership of Commonwealths. Although the British Empire still remains the most far-reaching single power in the world, it has undergone important changes. In spite of the loyal support given to the mother country during the war by the great self-governing dominions of Canada, South Africa, Australia, and New Zealand, there is an increasing demand for a larger voice in imperial affairs. In reality, the dominions tend more and more to become equal partners in a great commonwealth, as is shown by their participation in the League of Nations. In Egypt and India, the movement has taken the form of a demand for complete independence, while the Irish have actually obtained the rights of an independent state by separation from Protestant Ulster. This new Irish Free State hopes to establish an enduring government based on Irish traditions and the Gaelic language.

CHAPTER LXXVIII THE SIGNIFICANCE OF  1. The Extensive Use of Electricity Brings the Electric 

Age. Just as the steam-engine had brought the industrial development of the Period of Revolution, so has the use of electricity dominated the present period. Commencing with the telephone in 1876 and the electric light in 1879, it gradually invaded every phase of modern life. During the eighties electrically driven motors began to supplant horses in the operation of street cars, and by the end of the century electric locomotives had taken the place of steam locomotives in tunnels and for other uses where the latter were proving inconvenient. 

More important still was the employment of the electric motor for the driving of machinery of every type. So wide-spread has this become that the production of electric power is now one of the vital problems of the industrial world. 

Although steam is still used for generating electricity, water power is far more economical and consequently streams and water-falls have taken on a new importance. Especially did this become true after George Westinghouse invented the transformer which enabled electricity to be transmitted profitably over long distances. An important result has been that in countries like Italy where coal is lacking, this "white coal" has rapidly taken its place and removed much of the previous obstacle to industrial development. As we look into the future, the possibilities of electricity seem almost endless. 

2. The Internal Combustion Engine Eliminates Space in the Old Sense and Greatly Modifies Home Life. Next in importance in the industrial history of the present period is the internal combustion engine which dates from 1860 when the Frenchman J. J. E. Lenoir (lē-nwär') built an engine 797

which derived its power from the explosion of a mixture of gas and air. To this internal combustion engine we owe the automobile and the airplane, the two characteristic forms of modern transportation. Two more Frenchmen, Pannard (pȧn- Niagara Falls Buffalo

Orville Wright made the first successful flights in 1903. No other inventions have so completely annihilated space and permitted such rapid communication between far-distant places as these.

Although railroads and steamships still carry most of the

ri bulky goods and the "long haul" freight, automobiles and airplanes are caring for a constantly increasing part of the passenger traffic and of the package and "short-haul" freight. One result of this extensive use of motor vehicles has been a revival of interest in the building of substantial highways. Far more important, however, has been the revolution in the home life of the owners themselves.

Otto and Längen discovered that greater power could be secured from gasoline, which then was a waste product obtained in distilling kerosene from petroleum, than from a mixture of gas and air.

4. The Moving-Picture Is Perfected to Bring Universal 

Amusement and Education. Although the art of photography had been discovered in 1839 by the Frenchman Louis J. 

Daguerre (då-gâr'), it remained a clumsy and unsatisfactory process until the invention of the celluloid film toward the end of the century. This made possible the first moving-picture, entitled Annabelle the Dancer, which was shown in 1894 by its inventor, C. 

Francis Jenkins, to an Indiana audience. 

Since then the moving-picture has become the world's universal amusement and one of its largest industries. It has come to be also a great educational force, not only because of its use in formal teaching but also by its news reels which disseminate widely a knowledge of different peoples and cultures. During the year 

1929 talking, music, and moving-picture were synchronized in the movietone to such a degree of excellence that it seems now only a matter of time until the best in drama, art, and music will be within reach of every one.

5. The Radio Links the Whole World into One Community. In 1896, an Italian, Mär-co'ni, discovered a process of telegraphing without wires. From this has come the radio, probably the most remarkable of all modern inventions. By linking it with the telephone, people in every part of the world are now able to converse with one another and even to see each other at the same time. Although it is still too early to determine just what will be the effect of this wonderful inven-

tion, it seems likely to become a great aid in drawing mankind closer together in developing international understanding. 

6. New Inventions Cause Tremendous Social Changes and Give Rise to Serious Problems. These new inventions. 

have had far-reaching effects upon society.

Everywhere they From a photograph "Press Clich," Moscow. 

GOVERNMENT CONTROL OF NEWS AND EDUCATION 

Peasants listening to the government radio in Russia. In Russia and elsewhere the government controls the radio stations. have tended to raise the standards of living with the result that in many countries the poor now enjoy advantages which less than a century ago were the exclusive privilege of the rich. 

This has gone farther in America than anywhere else because of the extraordinary use made of machinery. Second only in importance is the gradual elimination of the harder kinds of labor and the lessening of working hours. In America, and to some extent in Europe, machinery has largely supplanted human labor, even in agriculture, while the radio and automobile are doing away with the isolation of rural life.

Wider educational opportunities, newspapers and magazines, moving-pictures and the radio, have increased tremendously the knowledge of the average individual, and discoveries in medicine have lengthened his life span. At the same time, he enjoys greater facilities for happiness than ever before. Even the struggle which the Industrial Revolution brought about between capital and labor is in process of solution—in capitalistic countries by an improvement in the conditions of labor, and in the Soviet Republic by an attempt to have labor control capital.

Along with all these improvements in society have come some serious problems. The drift of population to the cities has lessened the feeling of responsibility and tended to do away with need for the respect of one's neighbors, which is one of the most universal safeguards of morals. The new conveniences have supplied both a stimulus and an opportunity for lawbreaking on a larger scale than ever before, while the machinery of justice has failed to keep up with crime, at least in the United States. However, methods of dealing with criminals and defectives show a steady improvement along lines defined by scientific investigation. As a consequence, reform instead of punishment is becoming more and more the ideal. Through the League of Nations there is also developing the necessary knowledge and machinery to arouse the public opinion of the world to a demand for the suppression of the worst vices. It is significant of the present situation that a single nation cannot deal with these problems by herself, as is shown when the United States asks the aid of other powers in the suppression of the liquor traffic. 

7. Women Make Great Advances in Economic and Po litical Rights. During this period women have made greater advances than ever before. During the Industrial Revolution, women became part of the factory system and started on the road to economic independence, but it remained for the revolu-

tion in business in the late nineteenth century to place them in numbers in the schoolroom and office, and behind the counter. 

As a result of this there was a growing demand for women to 

CELEBRATING THE WOMEN'S VICTORY 

Raising the Flag at the Headquarters of the National Woman's party in Washington upon ratification of the 

Suffrage Amendment, March 24, 1920. share in the control of the state. In 

America and elsewhere, they have now obtained suffrage and the right to hold public office, although this has not yet caused any great change in the conduct of public affairs. Women have ceased, however, to be chattels and have become persons, not only in the eyes of the law but of society as well. At the same time, marriage is now often postponed till much later in life and divorce is much more frequent. 

8. The Political 

Problems of Far-Reaching Significance Mark This Period. 

Since 1870 the idea of nationalism has extended almost everywhere, even though in many localities it has not been entirely successful. The economic basis of nationalism has been so completely changed that nations are no longer able to stand alone. Some sort of international organization has become a necessity. Indeed, already many of the great services of life,

such as navigation, cables, and copyrights, are under the control of international commissions. 

Democracy has made progress, and yet has been challenged on the one hand by the bolshevism of Russia and on the other by the fascism of Italy. We often hear the statement that a business administration of government is needed. Other significant features are the vast increase in the cost of government and the variety of its present interests. So numerous and so complex has government become that the average person finds it difficult to understand just what is actually going on, and either fails to vote, or casts his ballot without conviction, thus helping to make democracy less effective. 

9. Above All Else Scientific Progress Characterizes 

This Age. This may truly be called the "Scientific Age." 

Never before has man gone so far in the same length of time in the bending of nature to do his will. Without the scientist and his laboratory, the achievements upon which so much of the material and social progress of the last sixty years has depended would have been impossible. Important as is the inventor who discovers some device to lighten the burdens of the multitude or to bring happiness into their lives, his work would often be impossible were it not for the patient investigation of the scientist.

It is impossible to enumerate even the outstanding discoveries which have been made during this period, but most of them have resulted from a labor of love on the part of the scientist rather than from the work done for mere gain. Frequently the investigator has won a martyr's crown, as did Major Walter Reed, a surgeon in the United States Army, who gave his life to find the source of yellow fever. So important are their labors now regarded that all the great manufacturing companies support research laboratories, and Nó-běľ, a Swedish manufacturer, has established a prize bearing his name to honor the most outstanding of the scientists.

Not so much progress has been made in the so-called social sciences. It is true that sociology has been developed to a considerable extent and that the study of psychology has been signally improved, while history, economics, and political science have been marked by the slow spread of clearer views. 

It becomes the privilege of those who study this book, and others like it, to do a good part in helping to lead humanity onward along these lines in the great march of civilization.

CHAPTER LXXIX OUR OWN TIME 

It is one of the unfortunate aspects of history that the closer we come to our own time the more difficult it is to see clearly what is really happening. The events of the last few years have shown that our civilization is undergoing a definite crisis which is not yet over and which can conceivably end either disastrously or favorably. Whichever way it does end will be determined by the amount of intelligence with which the problems which face the world to-day are understood and dealt with. Never before has it been so clearly demonstrated that the world has become closely bound together in a single economic development and that its political and social organizations are vitally affected by its economic conditions. 

1. The Evidences of a Changing World. As we look back over the seventeen years which have passed since the war "to end war" and "to make the world safe for democracy" stopped, we are struck with two facts: (1) that more money is now being spent for armaments than before the Great War, and (2) that to-day democracy is less extensive than it was in 1914. 

Beside these two facts belong two other developments of equal significance: (1) the astounding increase in the spirit of Nationalism, and (2) the world-wide economic crisis commonly known as the depression. The connection between these four factors will become fairly clear in the survey of the various countries during the period. 

The dominant states of the world may be divided roughly according to their system of control into three groups: (1) 

Democratic, (2) Fascist, (3) Communist. The democratic states consist of the kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, together with the self-governing dominions of the British Empire -Canada, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa; the United 807

In this group Japan might well be included since it is under the control of a relatively small group, with somewhat similar ideals to those of the dictators of Italy and Germany. The one 

Communist state is the Union of Socialist Soviet Republics which was formerly known as the Russian Empire. 

2. How the World Has Changed in Its Economic Con dition. It is a well-known fact that after each great war there occurs a serious economic disturbance which may last for years. It is also a well-known economic theory that depressions are of periodic occurrence. Either directly or indirectly the Great War took toll of 8,500,000 human lives, destroyed an untold amount of property, and saddled the chief partici pants with billions in debts. At the same time it greatly stimulated the productive capacity of the United States and Japan in both industry and agriculture and to a lesser extent that of other countries, especially the neutral countries of Europe. In the United States foodstuffs and manufactured goods for the allies kept our farms and factories at top speed. When the fighting was over the war-torn countries of Europe began to rebuild their factories and speeded up their agriculture. Germany with loans largely from America reconstructed her factories while northern France did the same with the aid of payments from Germany. To encourage both agriculture and industry nations began to set up tariff walls to keep foreign competitors out of their market. Even Great Britain, long the stronghold of free trade, began to levy duties on certain imports. 

3. The Burden of Debt. The tremendous cost of the war was largely paid by borrowing money. All the great powers found themselves at the end of the war with staggering burdens of national debt. Some idea of its size can be gained from the table on the following page.

During the following period down to 1929 came another great expansion of business and industry stimulated to a certain extent by an attempt to make up for the losses of the war. This brought about the issuing of many stocks and bonds on which interest and dividends had to be paid. 

4. The Great Depression. The course of this peculiar financial situation reached its peak in 1929, when the collapse of the Stock Market in New York furnished a spectacular climax. In the following years prices declined, world trade fell off, and unemployment in every country except Russia increased. The break in the stock market was not the cause but merely the evidence of the working of factors that had long been in existence. That its effects were felt not merely in the 

United States but everywhere throughout the world is the proof of the economic unity of the world to-day. It is also to be remembered that this depression is not something new, but merely the recurrence of what economists tell us is a periodic event in the economic life of a capitalist system. The reasons that are given for the excessive severity of this depression are not altogether clear nor are they all commonly accepted. 

5. Unemployment. One of the outstanding characteristics of industry during the period following the war was the

OUR OWN TIME 

811 great improvement in machinery. According to the generally accepted belief improvements in machinery, while they throw people out of work for the moment, eventually lead to further employment in other fields. The history of the nineteenth century goes a long way to prove this theory, but it must be remembered that mechanized industry in the nineteenth century was restricted to Western Europe and the United States, leaving the rest of the world for markets. In the twentieth century machine industry had spread to other parts of the world, particularly Japan, China, India and some of the South American countries. 

This increasingly forces industry to rely upon its home markets. 

Since the war also the establishment of high tariff walls has more and more restricted the freedom of world trade. These factors must be borne in mind when one comes to study the increase of nationalism on the one hand and the continuance of imperialism on the other.

CHAPTER LXXX  

To understand the period it will be necessary to review briefly the history of the leading countries of the world and then discuss the factors connected with international relations during the period. 

1. How Great Britain Felt the Effects of the War. 

England emerged from the war with very serious losses. She was no longer the money capital of the world and her industry was seriously dislocated. Only by the heaviest of taxation was she able to keep going and even then she was forced off the gold standard. The returning soldiers piled up a large body of unemployed which has continued ever since. Moreover her statesmen had made promises of furnishing better opportunities for life when the war was over and some of these promises had to be fulfilled. The coal industry felt the situation most seriously and had to be subsidized. When the subsidy was withdrawn and wages reduced the miners struck and brought on a General 

Strike in 1926. The Irish question too came to head and after several years of bitter guerrilla warfare most of Ireland was erected into the Irish Free State. 

2. The Attempts to Give England a New Deal. Eng land had already before the War done much for the poorer part of her population. Since the war she has expanded these efforts and started new ones. Unemployment Insurance has been extended, as has Compulsory Health Insurance and Old 

Age Pensions and Retirement Pensions for workers, widows and orphans have been added. A beginning has been made in improving the housing and the right of suffrage has been extended to women as well as men. The serious economic conditions however have forced some extensive changes in industry. 

The railroads have been combined into four great systems and 812

THE GENERAL STRIKE IN ENGLAND-1926 

During the General Strike armored cars were used to transport food through the streets of London.

Even a protective tariff has been imposed to help the declining industries. 

3. The Rise of the Labor Party. All these changes have not taken place without some considerable modification of the political complexion of England. When the Coalition Government which controlled England during the War began to break up the Labor Party withdrew first. The actions of Mr. Lloyd 

George led to serious defections from the Liberal Party and after the election of 1922 it became the "Opposition" party. 

In January, 1924, when the Conservative Prime Minister Mr. 

Stanley Baldwin received a vote of censure he resigned in

favor of Ramsay MacDonald, the leader of the Labor Party although there were 258 Conservative, 191 Labor, and 158

Liberal members. This first Labor Ministry, with such little support, lasted only ten months. The new election was a smashing Conservative victory but when this Parliament came to an end in 1929 the Labor Party won 289 members to 259

Conservatives and 58 Liberals. The depression was too much for the new Labor government and another election again gave the Conservatives the power, but Mr. MacDonald was retained as Prime Minister which cost him the leadership of the Labor Party. Since that time the bye elections have been often in favor of the Laborites and many of the city councils, even London, have become Labor wholly or in part. 

4. What Has Happened to the British Empire? The war led the self-governing dominions of the Empire to question whether they were willing to bear the effects of Imperial foreign policy. They insisted on their own representation in the 

League of Nations and they also stated that they would not be bound by some of the treaties which England made after the war. Some of them even announced that they had the right to withdraw from the Empire. English statesmen admitted that right, but suggested that the dominions stood to lose more than they would gain by withdrawal. To encourage trade "Imperial preference" treaties giving Dominion goods preference in English markets and "Buy British Empire" campaigns were launched. The decline in prosperity became so great that 

Newfoundland surrendered its dominion government. 

5. Why France Has Been Worried. The French people, who suffered more than any other allied power from the War, came out of it with one idea firmly fixed in their mindsthe need for security. They had in the Versailles treaty the means to keep Germany weak, and expected to receive from 

Germany vast payments in reparations to make up for the damage they had received during the War. This explains the

815. greater part of French actions since 1919; their insistence on the maintenance of the Versailles Treaty, their resistance to disarmament, and their system of alliances. 6. 

How France Has Tried to Solve Her Problems. The first few years after the War led to a tremendous increase in the

French debt since the Germans were slow about making payments and when they did they were much less than had been originally expected. This increase of debt and the difficulty of balancing the budget forced the value of the franc down. to one-tenth of its former value. By heroic efforts it was finally established at one-fourth of its former value. Since then the French have endeavored to maintain their money on the

gold standard. By raising tariffs and giving advantages to the farmers, France has attempted to protect her people from the worst of the depression. 

To ensure against a new German invasion a vast system of underground fortifications has been built along the frontier from Switzerland to Belgium. She has maintained a large army by conscription and now that the reduced classes born during the War are coming to the colors she has lengthened the period of service. Since Germany has over 50 per cent more population, France was not content with her own powers. 

She organized the Little Entente-Czecho-Slovakia, Rumania and Yugoslavia-and supplied them with loans to aid their military establishments. They, too, do not wish the war treaties, so far as they deal with boundaries, to be overthrown. She has also had a close friendship with Poland, but in recent years Poland has turned more and more toward Germany. In spite of all these efforts France is still worried for her safety, and has frequently attempted to get other countries, and particularly the 

United States, to pledge their assistance.

France has remained the only large democratically governed country on the continent of Europe in spite of some serious attempts to force her into a return to monarchy or into fascism, and she has a small communistic element. Her large percentage rural population is a stabilizing influence, but some constitutional reform may be forced upon her. 

7. The Troubles of Italy. Italy presents to the student of post-war history a type picture, for here we have the working out of a system of political control known as fascism (fǎshism). At the close of the War Italy was in serious condition. Her government was weak-it had never been a thoroughgoing parliamentary state. Her economic system was falling to pieces with strikes, lockouts, falling prices and wages, and unemployment. Communistic elements were gaining ground and the government seemed powerless to act.

8. How Benito Mussolini Started a New Idea. Into this situation a dynamic personality projected himself Benito 

Photograph by Underwood and Underwood.

BENITO MUSSOLINI, DICTATOR OF ITALY 

Mussolini saluting and addressing a Fascist Assembly in Rome. 

Mussolini. A former socialist editor, he changed his ideas and organized a group, called Fascisti, commonly known as the "Black Shirts," to uphold the national state against all antagonistic elements. It was organized first among the war veterans but soon spread rapidly to all classes of society. In

October, 1922, the organization marched on Rome and under Mussolini's leadership it began to take over the administration. Mussolini soon proclaimed himself head of the party and president of the ministry. By means of the organization the control of which he kept in his own hands, he was able to break down all local opposition to the movement while as the holder of several ministerial portfolios he was able to act. His power really lay in military-like discipline of the Fascisti. Whoever opposed them were beaten, dosed with castor oil, driven out of town, or even killed. After Mussolini was thoroughly in control his political opponents were exiled to a barren island in the Mediterranean. 

9. How Fascism Works. Although the movement started without much of a programme beyond a strong nationalistic idea, it gradually worked out its theory known as the "totalitarian state." The state is supreme over the economic and social groups within it. It supports private enterprise "as the most practical means for serving national interests" and capitalism as the "best method of production," but it insists that the state has a right to intervene in production if private interests are involved.

Both labor associations and employer associations are recognized by the state, but all strikes and lock-outs are forbidden. 

These associations are organized into confederations which choose candidates for the Chamber of Deputies. This council serves to maintain the contact between the government and the people. The real control of the State rests in the Great Fascist 

Council, the organ of the Fascist Party, whose head is Mussolini. This sovereign dictatorship controls all expression of public opinion. Critics of the government have no place in Italy. 

The government also controls the cultural life of the state and religious education is obligatory in Italian schools, and emphasis is placed on tradition as a cultural force. Hence Mussolini's constant reference to the glories of ancient Rome.

Like France, Italy had trouble with her currency but finally "pegged" the lira in 1927 at a little over one-fourth of its former value. To make Italy as independent of food imports as possible much reclamation work has been carried on and bounties placed on wheat raising. Primary education has been made compulsory, but only one newspaper is allowed in a province. The six-day week and vacations with pay, but no minimum wages, have been established in the Carta del Lavoro (Charter of Labor). In 1929 the relations with the Pope were adjusted and for the first time since 1870 the Pope has been able to leave the Vatican. His rights to the Vatican City as an independent state were recognized and Catholic participation in the schools arranged. 

10. Some Consequences of Italy's Problems. A dense population and few national resources have made the problem of developing a strong state a difficult one. The failure of 

Italy to obtain much of the spoils of war has made the demand for colonial possessions more urgent. The seizure of Fiume, and part of the Dalmatian coast, by the writer d'Annunzio at the close of the War, was extended by the practical control of Albania which is hardly more than an Italian protectorate. 

Various advances have been made in Northern Africa, but so far without furnishing much of an outlet for Italy's population. 

Italy's control of the Adriatic and her occupation of part of the Dalmatian coastline and Fiume have caused her relations with Yugoslavia to be hardly friendly which in turn has caused Italy to establish close connections with Hungary. 

While Mussolini seems to delight in rather belligerent talk at home his actual foreign policy has generally been peaceful, but there may come a time when popular enthusiasm will demand a war. 

11. How Germany Was Ruined. The history of Ger many since 1918 has been most exciting. With the establishment of the republic there seems to have been a widespread

feeling of relief. The saddling of all the guilt and the burden of reparations upon the weakened and bankrupt loser was a great blow to German pride. The necessity of signing so disastrous a treaty was a heavy burden to place on the new government. When the government found that it could not raise sufficient taxes it turned to the printing presses and issued paper money, which by 1923 amounted to 496,507,771,973,774,000 marks. The value of the mark fell until one gold mark was worth 1,000,000,000,000 paper marks. This inflation wiped out savings and rendered valueless the income of the middle class. Only those who were able to buy tangible things saved anything from the wreck. The great industrial magnates took advantage of the situation to modernize their plants. The wageearning classes suffered as wages went up slower than prices and large numbers became interested in communism. At last the paper money was abandoned and with the help of a loan arranged through the League of Nations a new currency was set up, with a gold Reichsmark worth 24 cents. 

12. How Germany Could Not Be Forced to Pay for the War. The burden of reparations was a constant irritant. 

A totally impossible amount was set in 1921 by the Reparations Commission at $32,000,000,000. When Germany was slow in paying French and Belgian troops occupied the Ruhr in 1923 and new negotiations opened. In 1924 the Dawes plan and in 

1929 the Young plan reduced the total amount to $28,800,000,- 000. Even this amount became unreasonable when the depression struck and in 1932 still another arrangement reduced the amount to $750,000,000. Up till then Germany had paid about $8,800,000,000 in money and goods. By 1929 these payments, large at the beginning, amounted to little more than 3 per cent of the national income. During the same time Germany borrowed a great deal more from other countries, over $2,000,- 000,000 from the United States alone, so that she never really paid any money of her own.

13. Why German Nationalism Burst Out Again. The loss of so much territory by the Treaty of Versailles and particularly the separation of Germany into two parts by the Polish corridor stirred the patriotic feelings of Germans deeply. The effects of the economic situation and the resentment to the War guilt charge, which had led to restrictions on German armament, weighed heavily on German minds and made them susceptible to any movement which promised to restore Germany to a place of equality among the nations. In 1920 Adolf Hitler, an Austrian born German who had fought in the German army, founded at Munich the National Socialist German Labor Party, later known as the Nazi Party. It was strongly anti-Semitic and opposed to the Social Democrats and the Republican Constitution. In November, 1923, an attempt to seize the government failed and Hitler was put in jail for a time. For the next few years the party amounted to little, but Hitler was a magnetic speaker and kept the movement alive by promises of economic reform and by the organization of groups of "Storm Troopers," wearing brown shirts and a swastika badge. The depression in 1929 furnished the necessary opportunity and in 1930 the party received over 6,000,000 votes which doubled in 1932. During this period Hitler attracted the attention of some of the great industrial leaders and they seemed to have furnished the funds for the organization of the Storm Troopers on a large scale. The difficulties of the government increased so much that no cabinet could be formed without Hitler and he refused to take part unless given full control. Finally on 

January 30, 1933, President Von Hindenburg summoned Hit ler, who had recently been naturalized, to be chancellor. He dissolved Parliament and in the election of March 5, 1933, the Nazis polled about one-half of the total vote. The Storm 

Troopers now numbered over 500,000.

man flag and beside it was placed the Swastika flag of the Nazis.

Germany's Place in the 

World. Ever since the signing of the Treaty of Versailles the Germans have been hoping for the return of some of their lost territory. The plebiscites in Silesia and Schleswig-Holstein placed large numbers of Germans under foreign control and the Polish corridor of the Baltic was a source of constant friction. 

One of the hopes was the unification of Austria and Germany. 

In 1931 a customs Union was quietly negotiated between the two countries. At once France became frightened, as she foresaw the eventual union, and brought pressure to bear on both countries and it was given up. When the Nazis came into power 

Hitler began to take immediate measures to restore Germany's equality among the nations. When the Disarmament Conference at Geneva refused to consider his demand that Germany be allowed to rearm, Germany withdrew from the conference and notified Geneva of its withdrawal from the League, effective in October, 1935. In February, 1935, the Saar region,

which had been under the control of the League of Nations since the War, held a plebiscite and voted overwhelmingly to return to Germany. In the spring of 1935, Hitler suddenly announced that Germany was going to increase her army to 645,000 men, and to establish an air force and build submarines in spite of the Treaty of Versailles. In the face of much protest from Italy, Great Britain, and especially France, Germany had her way.

CHAPTER LXXXI  1. How the Communists Took Control of Russia. In no part of the post-war world has more radical change taken place than in Russia, or as it is more correctly called, The Union of Socialist Soviet Republics. Already before the War was over the old Tsarist government had collapsed and a moderate Socialist group, led by Kerensky, took control early in 1917. Not much was accomplished by this group and when through the connivance of Germany the extreme Communist leaders, Nicolai Lenin and Leon Trotsky, were brought from Switzerland, the Socialist régime was overthrown. The new 

Bolshevik government made peace with Germany in 1918 at Brest-Litovsk and set out to establish the control by the working classes. The theory of procedure in the Communist revolution is that, although Communism is a goal to be striven for, while the process is going on the control of affairs must be in the hands of a dictator, supported by a small, well-disciplined party which can crush all opposition. Actual Communism cannot be applied until all opposition is wiped out and the population is well grounded in Communistic ideas. As the means of carrying out these ideas Lenin founded in 1919 the Third International or Communist Party. 

The new 

2. The Difficulties of the New Government. system faced a number of very serious difficulties. In the first place there were very few Communists. Next the ideas of 

Communism were easily understandable by industrial workers but nearly 90 per cent of the population were peasants. In the third place the economic organization of Russia was badly broken down by the War. Russia had few industries and poor transportation. Finally the establishment of a Communistic 825

State was felt to be a menace by the capitalistic countries of the world and they did not hesitate to aid with money and troops the remnants of the Tsarist régime who tried to drive the Bolsheviks out. Actually this attack served perhaps more than anything else during the first few years to keep the new government alive. The Communists agreed to the seizure of the land by the peasants and this secured their aid against invaders while the Communists acted as the defenders of Russia. 

The Bolsheviks established a "Red" army which could be depended upon and a secret police-the Cheka-to serve as spies and terrorize the opposition. In 1918 this organization executed the Tsar and his family while thousands of others were imprisoned, exiled or put to death. 

3. How the Communist Government Is Organized. In 

1918 a new constitution was adopted by the All Russian Congress of Soviets for the Russian Socialist Federalist Soviet Republic. Soviet is the Russian word for council. 

By this constitution all productive workers, male or female, eighteen years old or over could participate in political life. 

Persons who lived on income not from their own labor, or who hired for profit, private merchants and traders, members of the clergy, the Tsarist. family and the officials, police, spies, and criminals were excluded. Following the older administration system soviets were set up in the country villages which elected delegates to a district congress from which delegates were selected for the Provincial congress. In the cities soviets were organized according to occupation and delegates selected for the city soviet, which also sent delegates to the Provincial congress. At the top delegates from the Provincial congresses formed an All-Russian Congress in which the cities had a larger representation than the country, but recently it was arranged that country and city soviets elect delegates directly to the Congress. The All-Russian Congress selected an All-Russian Executive Committee to control the state

and it in turn selected a permanent executive group, or præsidium, called the Council of Commissars. In 1923 when similar Soviet organizations had been set up in three other Republics, the Ukrainian, White Russian, and Transcaucasian -the Union of Socialist Soviet Republics was formed with a Union Congress of Soviets elected by the Provincial Congresses and City Soviets of the Constituent Republics. To these the Uzbeg and Turkoman republics were added in 1924 and Tajikistan in 1929. Besides the seven Constituent Republics there are nearly twenty Autonomous Socialist Soviet Republics, mostly small although Kazak has a population of over 6,000,000 and about the same number of small Autonomous Areas, one with only 37,000 population. In this way 42 of the 182 nationalities in the U. S. S. R. are politically recognized. The real power rests in a Central Executive Committee of the Union composed of 450 members elected by the Union Congress and a Council of Nationalities of 139 members, 5 from each of the Constituent and Autonomous Republics, and one from each of the Autonomous Areas, elected at the Republican and Regional Congresses. Actually the control is exercised by the dictator Stalin, who is Secretary of the Third International. 4. The Problems of the New State. The new régime faced two connected but quite dissimilar tasks. The first was the establishement in Russia of a genuine Socialistic classless state. 

The second was the bringing about a world-wide revolution for Communism. Each was a tremendous job but for a number of years the leaders of the movement seemed to feel that both were possible of achievement. With the death of Lenin, however, in 1924, the two ideas became separated. Trotsky wished to continue the idea of world revolution, but Stalin who was less of a theorist felt that the best way to prepare for a world revolution was to build a genuine socialist state in Russia. In the conflict which followed Trotsky was driven out and the

whole attention of the party was concentrated in the development of a Communistic state at home.
