5. Planned Economic Development. 

Little progress was made in the modernization of Russia until the first "Five Year" plan was introduced in 1928. By it one-half of the national income was devoted to the building up of industry. Special emphasis was placed on heavy industry and large industrial and power plants were designed and partially executed by the end of the period in 1932. Two great tractor factories, a mass production automobile plant, two great steel plants, a 950-mile

railroad, dams, and power plants capable of producing 750,000 H.P. were completed. A similar revolution took place in agriculture. The cultivated land, 98 per cent of which was still tilled by peasants in 1928, was organized into state and collective farms and by 1933 80 per cent was so socialized. The peasants who objected were removed to other sections and placed on forced labor. 

In 1933 a second "Five Year" plan was launched. Special attention was to be given to transportation, the most neglected part of the industrial development. Over 7500 miles of railroad are to be built and 3200 electrified. In this period more attention was to be paid to consumption goods, and already shoes, clothing, and foodstuffs have become more plentiful and the system of rationing the necessities of life has been greatly modified. Four-fifths of the industry of the country is now under state control and much of the remainder in the hands. of co-operatives. Unemployment has completely disappeared and membership in the trade unions rose to over 17,000,000 in 1933. Distribution is assisted by Consumers Co-operatives which include 95 per cent of the adult population and handle four-fifths of the retail trade. 

6. How the Bolsheviks Attempt to Remodel Society.

In the program of education the Soviet government has done some of its effective work, as cultural development was considered a vital part of the whole programme. Both adult and child education have been carried on. In 1930 universal compulsory education for four years was decreed and in 1933 increased to seven years. In 1932-3 there were 167,000 schools with nearly 22,000,000 pupils. Literacy which in 1917 was estimated at 30 per cent was 90 per cent in 1932 and newspaper circulation increased from 2,500,000 in 1913 to 38,000,- 000 in 1932. The Communists believe that their main hope of success lies in the inculcation of their ideas into the boys and girls and have organized the Pioneers, children from 8 to 14,

and the "Young Communists," now numbering over 6,000,000.

In both of these organizations the ideals of the new order are studied and practised. In the army which is raised by compulsory military service more training in Communist ideals is given. All the museums and libraries of the old Russia have 

A GEOGRAPHY LESSON IN A PEASANT SCHOOL 

Education for all classes and all ages is compulsory in Russia. been thrown open for use and new books are being written and published in editions of millions. Organized religion has been one of the victims of Communist dislike on the grounds that it looks backward instead of forward and that it interferes with thinking. Many churches have been closed or made into community centres and Christian and Buddhist clergy and Muslim ulema have been deprived of their control over their followers.

7. Russia's Position in the World. Although the U. S. 

S. R. was not admitted to the League of Nations until 1934 it played a considerable part in world politics even before that. 

With one exception it has maintained peace with its neighbors and insists that its large army is only for defense. The new régime gave up the old Russian claims to special rights outside of Russia and recently sold its share of the Chinese Eastern Railway to Japan. Its influence in Asia is rather strong and in Europe it has non-aggression treaties with several states including France. To-day it is one of the most powerful influences in world affairs because of its size and compactness. Its effectiveness is increased by its centralized authority, its control of its foreign trade, and its lack of foreign debt. With continued peace it seems to have a fair chance of thoroughly carrying out its great experiment. 

8. How the War Affected Japan. The dislocation of 

European industry during the War led to a great expansion in 

Japan. Between 1913 and 1930 her foreign trade tripled.

Iron foundries increased from 20 to 250 and cotton spindles from 2,400,000 to 3,700,000 and her governmental expenses had doubled. During the period strikes had begun to occur in unprecedented numbers which continued to grow down till 1924 while Japan was suffering from the post-war decline in industry. During the later period of the war democratic ideas spread widely and the government was forced to extend the suffrage and between 1920 and 1922 there was a great expansion of trade unions. At the end of the War she had received the mandate for two groups of Pacific Islands and she sent an expedition into Siberia but withdrew it and signed a treaty with the U. S. S. R. in 1925. 

9. Japan Feels Her Inferior Position. The increased industrial equipment of Japan and her presence at the council table in Paris and later at Geneva gave her a feeling of her equality among the nations which soon met with rebuffs. At the

Washington Conference in 1922 she was forced to be content with an inferior ratio of ships. Two years later the United 

States government excluded Japanese along with other Asiatics from entering the United States. This was hard for a proud nation to bear and made difficult the task of the liberal states- 

BINDING NATIONS TOGETHER WITH FRIENDSHIP 

Distribution of American Red Cross supplies in Tokyo after the earthquake of 1923. men who controlled the government. In China too the aims of 

Japan found opposition in the American policy of the "open door," in addition to the opposition she had aroused by her demands on China during the War. To many Japanese the vast market of China meant the solution of her own population problem and they believed this market to be rightfully theirs. 

10. Japan Goes Imperialist. The depression hit Japan earlier than other countries and brought in a conservative gov-

ernment but its acts were not drastic enough to suit the militarist party. In 1931 several government ministers were assassinated. During the summer of that year several incidents happened in Manchuria which stirred up popular excitement in Japan. In September fighting began along the Japanese owned and guarded South Manchurian Railway. The Chinese troops were driven out and in February Henry Pu Yi, the former boy emperor of China, was made ruler of Manchukuo, with a full corps of Japanese officials. All this in spite of the protests of the League of Nations and the United States. When a Japanese boycott broke out in China and riots occurred in Shanghai, Japan landed troops and the fighting lasted for months before the Japanese withdrew. In January, 1932, the Japanese occupied the province of Jehol and even crossed the "Great Wall" but later withdrew. In the meantime a League of Nations committee had visited Manchukuo and when Japan heard the report she announced her withdrawal from the League to take effect 

March 27, 1935. Apparently these operations were instigated by the fanatically patriotic and nationalistic military and naval clique. With the purchase of the Russian share of the Chinese 

Eastern Railway in 1935 foreign influence was eliminated from Manchukuo and Japan could turn her full attention to China proper. 

11. The Troubles of China. The history of China since the overthrow of the Manchu dynasty in 1911 has been a chronicle of civil war and disaster. The vast population with poor means of communication, the difference between the north and the south, and the traditional independence of local governors have rendered almost impossible the establishment of a stable government. Already foreign governments had carved spheres of influence in most of China; and Japan, during and since the 

War, has been trying to enlarge hers. The pressure of Japan during the War and immediately after led to an anti-Japanese boycott and strong patriotic movement among the students.

Sun Yat Sen, the leader of the Republican movement, drew these students into his Kuomintang party. Some of them visited Russia and in 1924 a Russian Commission arrived in China to spread Communist ideas. A new government was set up in Canton and Communist propaganda spread widely through the south. With the death of Sun Yat Sen in 1925 and the rise of a strong anti-foreign and anti-Christian movement, the Kuomintang party split and under the leadership of Chang Kai Shek the Russians were forced out of China. It was not possible, however, to deport the ideas and since then the Communists have continued to hold certain provinces in spite of all the efforts to wipe them out. With the Communists on one side and the Japanese on the other the government of Chang Kai Shek has had a difficult task and yet it is said to be the strongest government China has had for some time. It has its capital at Nanking and exercises little control in the north. It is trying to modernize China with roads and railroads and modern buildings. Chinese as well as Japanese feel their inferiority with the foreign concessions, extra-territoriality, and foreign control of the tariff, all of which they hope to end. 

12. India Seeks National Expression. Although India properly belongs to the British Empire, its size and position permit a discussion here. Since the War India, under the influence of Mahatma Gandhi and nationalist feelings, has been seething with unrest. To England India means markets and imperial prestige while Indians demand at least a dominion status in the Empire with control of their own government. 

The chief difficulties in the way are the friction between the Hindu and the Muslim, the caste system, and the native states, all of which hinder Indian solidarity. During most of the period commissions have investigated and plans have been presented, none of which have been satisfactory to one side or the other. As long as the Indians continue to feel they are being

treated as inferiors there can be no lasting adjustment. The day of European control of Asia is on the wane.

THE WORLD COURT IN SESSION 

A modern attempt to apply the same principles to the relations between nations as have long held betwen individuals within civilized nations. 

CHAPTER LXXXII THE  

1. International Organization. International relations since the War have been centred about the League of Nations. 

This organization consists of an Assembly, meeting yearly in September, and is made up of a representative from each member of the League; a Council, the Executive organ of the 

League, made up of five permanent and, since 1926, nine nonpermanent members selected by the Assembly, meeting three times yearly; and the Secretariat, a permanent body with a trained staff to carry out the work of the League. Attached to the League are the Permanent Court of International Justice- 837

the World Court-and the International Labor Organization. 

The World Court was set up in 1922 and has been ratified by forty-eight nations. It is composed, since 1930, of fifteen justices nominated by the Permanent Court of International Arbitration at the Hague and elected by the League Assembly. 

Two attempts have been made to get the United States to enter the Court but both have failed. The International Labor Organization is a continuation of earlier international movements connected with labor. It was started at the Peace Conference and held its first conference in Washington in 1919. Since 1921 it has established its headquarters at Geneva. A governing body of twenty-four representatives meets four times a year and works in close co-operation with the International Labor Office of the League, which collects and publishes information on industry and labor. Its work has contributed much to the improvement of the conditions of labor in many countries. 

2. How the League Works. The purpose of the League of Nations is to organize a society of states, to create a system of law to control all the relations between states and to provide the institutions by which that law can be applied or in other words to keep peace and settle disputes between nations, to remove the causes of war and to develop international co-operation. Its policy of holding meetings of the assembly and council in public has added greatly to its success as it really applies the principle of democracy to international affairs. In settling disputes the Council handled over thirty cases and the Court about fifty, most of which have been successful. In spite of several serious situations the League efforts have failed completely in only a few cases, such as the trouble between Japan and China in Manchuria. There are now fifty-eight nations in the League, Costa Rica (1926), Brazil (1928), and Japan (1935) having withdrawn. Argentina withdrew but has been readmitted. Only the United States, Egypt, and Arabia have never joined. The actual control of the League has been dominated by the great

powers, England, France, and Italy, but in many instances the voices of the minor powers have compelled attention. 3. 

The Currents of International Affairs. The course of international affairs since the War has been determined mainly by the problems involved in the carrying out of the treaties, the economic disturbances and the rise of militant nationalism. In connection with the first, the refusal of the 

United States to enter the League of Nations has apparently interfered with the carrying out of some of the more important provisions, particularly the reduction of armaments, but the attempt to collect vast amounts of reparations from Germany has had even more serious consequences. In Europe the desire of France to obtain the position of leadership she once held is tempered only by Mussolini's aim to make Italy a great power and the policy of England to maintain the balance of power as she did before 1905. In many ways the conditions are not far different from what they were before the organization of the League of Nations, but the appearance of the airplane and the radio as the new weapons of warfare has gone far to wipe out the former defenses of a country. In Europe too, certain of the minor powers-Yugoslavia, Rumania, and Czechoslovakia -are anxious to keep boundaries as they were established in 1919 while Germany, Hungary, and Poland are equally desirous of changes. Japan's influence in Asia has already been discussed. In the American continent, aside from the conflict between Bolivia and Paraguay over the Chaco, there are no serious problems which might lead to genuine trouble. 

4. Debts and Reparations. We have already discussed reparations and their effect on Germany. The vast amount of debt piled up by the Allied Powers during the War and immediately after has also had a stormy history. Great Britain, France, and the United States were the countries which loaned most of the money. France had large loans in Russia, many made before the War, all of which were lost by the Russian

The hindrances to World Recovery as viewed by The News of the World (London). stantial reductions were made in the total amount of her claims on each country. With the economic collapse of 1929 and 1930 the situation became acute again and President Hoover in 1931 proposed a one-year moratorium on all inter-government debts. 

In December, 1932, after the German reparations were reduced, some nations defaulted in their payments and by 1934 only Finland continued to make full payments and Great Britain and

some others merely "token payments" or a small part of the payment. In all barely $200,000,000 per year has been collected by the United States on the debts since the War and there is little chance of their ever being paid. 

5. The Attempts to Disarm. One section of the Versailles treaty dealt with the question of disarmament and this was meant to bring about the accomplishment of the wartime slogan of the "War to end war." The armies of Germany, Austria, Bulgaria, and Hungary were fixed by the peace treaties but the victors were not ready. Actual attempts were made to limit armaments beginning with the Washington conference on Pacific affairs held 1921-1922. The United States, the British 

Empire, France, Italy, and Japan met and agreed to a treaty setting a ratio between the capital ships in their respective navies. 

6. Disarmament Proves Impossible. In September, 1925, the Council of the League of Nations finally set up a preparatory commission for a Disarmament Conference. For two years the commission argued over the English and American idea of separation of land and water limitation and the limitation of ships by classes, and the French belief in the inseparability of land and water limitation and limitation of ships by total tonnage. When they seemed to be getting nowhere 

President Coolidge called a conference on naval auxiliaries for 

June, 1927, at Geneva. Only Japan and Great Britain came and nothing was accomplished .because England wanted too many light cruisers and the United States wanted large cruisers with 8-inch guns, since we lacked the naval bases which Great Britain had. The only thing accomplished was increased bad feeling between the United States and England which was made worse the next year when England and France came to an agreement on naval construction. In January, 1930, the United States, Great Britain, France, Italy, and Japan met in London and after much negotiation signed a treaty which did not change

the situation at all. The divergent conditions and the difficulty of equating different kinds of ships made any real reduction of armament impossible. The launching of the powerful German cruiser Deutschland in May, 1931, made practically futile all From a photograph by International Newsreel Photos.

HOOVER, JULY, 1930 that had been accomplished. In the meantime the League Commission had been laboring faithfully with land disarmament and placed before the council in 1932 a draft treaty limiting the number of men in land, water and air forces, airplanes and total amount of expenditures. All of which were to be supervised by a Permanent Disarmament Commission. No limitation was placed on trained reserves or on war material outside of air-

planes and the prohibition of certain kinds of gases. The chances of the treaty being accepted or, if it is, of its accomplishing anything are slight. 

7. The Attempts to Get Rid of War. The specter of war has haunted all sensible people since the terrible slaughter of 1914 to 1918 and many have attempted to find some solution. 

In September, 1924, Ramsay MacDonald and Premier Herriot of France brought about the Geneva Protocol which labelled war as a crime and arranged to refer disputes to arbitration but it was never signed. However a really important step was taken in 1925 at the Locarno conference when treaties pledging arbitration were arranged between Germany, France, Great Britain, Italy, Poland, Belgium, and Czechoslovakia. In 1926 Premier

Briand suggested a treaty with the United States to "outlaw war." The idea was expanded by Secretary of State Kellogg to include all nations and was signed at Paris in 1928 by fifteen nations. This Pact of Paris, or Kellogg Pact, renounced war as a means of settling international disputes. It has already failed to keep Japan from fighting in Manchuria and at Shanghai and it is a serious question whether it will really work. Of more promise is the steady campaign of education for peace being carried on in many countries and the great peace poll held in England during the spring of 1935. 

8. The United States Incurs Dislike. Although she was largely responsible for it, the United States has never joined the League of Nations, and thereby has greatly weakened that body. 

At the same time she has always had an observer at important Geneva conferences and has sometimes assisted the League. 

In spite of the traditional American policy of non-interference with Europe, the interests of the United States demand that she deal with European powers especially with regard to the problems of the Pacific to say nothing of the war debts and the large American investments in Europe since the War. Our manufacturers are interested in the markets of China and long ago

John Hay established the "open door policy" which the recent actions of Japan have seriously infringed. Japanese exclusion and other actions have led to a feeling of bitterness in Japan while the raising of the price of silver under the New Deal has created a serious economic crisis in China. In those European countries which owe war debts to us considerable dislike has arisen because we would not cancel them. Now that it seems as if they would not be paid, we have lost the good will which we might have had, as well as the money. Some of the Nazi actions have caused unfriendly reactions toward Germany in the United States. 

9. The Favorable Results of Our Policies. In our relations with our Latin-American neighbors there has been decided improvement. They naturally fear so powerful a neighbor and the American occupation of Nicaragua and of Haiti furnished the anti-Yankee element with convincing arguments. The final withdrawal of the marines from Nicaragua in 1933 and from Haiti in 1934 and the abandonment of the Platt Amendment in Cuba in 1934 have done much to improve relations, even though our efforts have not been successful in ending the useless Chaco War. The decision to grant Philippine independence after a stated period will remove the United States farther from the highly dangerous area of the Far East and render trouble with Japan less likely. If we could accept the Japanese as our equals and accept her policy of her own Monroe doctrine for Eastern Asia there need be no trouble. After many years of delay the 

United States recognized the U.S.S.R. although it did not finally grant the expected credits for the purchase of American goods. The recognition did have a calming effect on the attitude of Japan in Manchuria and China.
